units.la: IBRORUM annalium, qui, definiente Gellio, res quoquo anno gestas nudè sine ornamentis, sine fuco, sine affectibus narrant, magnus semper usus fuit in Republ. in Ecclesia. Apud Romanos res omnes singulorum annorum mandabat literis Pontifex maximus, efferebatque in album & proponebat tabulam domi, potestas ut esset populo cognoscendi, ijque annales maximi nominabantur. In Republ. Hebræorum diaria & annales habebant, in quibus res gestas, ut quæque notatu dignissimæ, & ad doctrinæ sacræ propagationem utilissimę videbantur, continuatâ serie inscribebant ij, quos Deus fidei & vitæ Magistros populo suo præfecerat. Etenim ex diversis annalibus apud Ecclesiam Dei conservatis Ezdram sive solum sive cum æqualibus, insigni pietate & eruditione viris, cælesti spiritu afflatum, libros Josuæ, Judicum, Samuelis, Regum, alios compilasse, in eumque ordinem, qui jam olim habetur, redegisse atque disposuisse, gravissimi (quod optimè nostis, viri venerandi,) autores sunt qui credunt. Neque enim vero est simile, Samuelem cum Saulis se quærentis verba esseт recitaturus, sic esse præfatum: Eum, qui hodiè Propheta dicitur, vocabant olim Videntem. Sed verba potius hæc sunt Scriptoris res priscas & á suo seculo longè remotas narrantis.
units.tr: Annals, which according to Gellius's definition narrate the events of each year plainly, without ornament, without rhetorical colour and without emotion, have always been of great use in the commonwealth and in the Church. Among the Romans the chief priest committed to writing all the events of each year, and he brought them out onto a white tablet and displayed the tablet at home so that the people might have access to it; these were called the greatest annals. In the commonwealth of the Hebrews, diaries and annals were kept, in which those whom God had set over his people as teachers of faith and life recorded in continuous order the events that seemed most worthy of notice and most useful for spreading sacred teaching. Indeed, that Ezra, either alone or with colleagues, men of remarkable piety and learning, inspired by a heavenly spirit, compiled the books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings and others from the various annals preserved in the Church of God, and arranged them into the order they have held since long ago, is maintained by the most weighty authors, as you, venerable gentlemen, know very well. For it is not likely that Samuel, when reporting the words of Saul seeking him, would have said in passing: "He who is today called a prophet was formerly called a seer." Rather these are the words of a writer narrating ancient events far removed from his own age.

units.la: Quin ipsum Mosis opus, quod <bl>πεντάτευχον</bl> vocant, longo post Mosen tempore, interjectis duntaxat hîc, illic, verborum & sententiarum clausulis velut sarcitum atque omnino explicatius redditum esse, conjecturis minimè contemnendis probaverim. Certè, ut alia mittam, Cariath-arbe sæpe illic Hebron nominatur, & tamen hoc illi urbi nomen à Calebi filio Hebrone impositum esse, maximi
units.tr: Indeed, I would be inclined to hold, with conjectures that are not to be despised, that Moses' own work, which they call the Pentateuch [πεντάτευχον], was patched up and rendered altogether more explicit a long time after Moses, with only occasional sentence endings and phrases inserted here and there. Certainly, to pass over other examples, Kiriath-arba is often called Hebron there, and yet the great men have handed down that this name was given to that city by Hebron, the son of Caleb.

units.la: ):( 3 viri tradiderunt. Quapropter & Hieronymus in actione contra Helvidium, sive, inquit, Moses dicere voluerit autorem Pentateuchi, sive Ezdram eiusdem instauratorem operis, non recuso. Ac inter veteres Hebraeorum annales fuisse unos, qui Liber recti ideo vocabantur, quod optimâ fide atque serie res apud Dei caetum gestas perstringerent, aut quia Israelitici populi facta continerent, quem populum rectum tum Moses Deut. 32. 15. tum Isaias 24. 2. vocarunt: sive idem ille liber fuerit, qui in Numeris Liber bellorum Domini appellatus est, sive eius pars quaedam, aut etiam diversum opus; vel Josephus nobis persuaserit, qui in suis Antiquitatibus pro Libro recti, cuius in sacris literis est mentio, scripta in templo asservata dicit, libro quinto, capite sete secundo. Ut non immerito pro fabulis habeamus, quæ Rabbini Judæorum & cum his Lyranus de Libro recti, nugantur. In novo sedere quin ipsi Servatoris nostri discipuli quotidianos eius sermones in diaria & annales suos retulerint, ex quibus postea historia Evangelica est contexta, nemo sanus est qui dubitet. Temporibus Patrum laborarunt in eo Eusebius, Theodoretus, Socrates, Sozomenus; Orosius, Severus; ut quæcunque in Ecclesia Dei agebantur digna bonorum memoriā, ea monumentis Annalium consecrata ad posteritatem transmitterent. Horum ego sequutus exemplum pariter ac autoritatem, condere cœpi Annales Evangelij decimo quinto à nato Christo Iesu seculo passim per Europam renovati. Magnum & arduum opus, fateor: sed à quo nulla me potuit difficultas deterrere: non quod ignarus sim imbecillitatis meæ: sed quod laboris hujus jucunda utilitas & utilis jucunditas ita me occupaverunt: ut credam, me animum hunc Ecclesiæ Christi abundè satis probaturum: si vel de voluntate hac indicium ipsi fecero: vel hac qualicunque, rudi certè & impolitâ opellâ doctioribus ad accuratius aliquid in re tam sancta meditandum, ansam præbuero. Et sanè si res votis ageretur meis, in hoc viri docti complures laborem & vires ingenij insumerent: ut explicatam Evangelij renovati historiam haberemus. Mandat Deus populo Israëlitico: ut ne obliviscatur servitutem Aegyptiacam, & memoriam liberationis ex illa primo Decalogi præcepto insculpsit. Majores nostri non corporali sed spiritualì animarum servitute pressi fuerunt sub Pharaone Romano. Vindicavit illos in libertatem præpotens Deus. Quid æquius, quàm vindicationis illius tempus indagare, modum cognoscere, lucentem in ea Dei gloriosam virtutem linguis animisque prædicare ? Consulendum & posteritati: ut ne illa fallatur ā scriptoribus rerum ecclesiasticarum proximi seculi ijs, qui res parum sibi compertas posteris tradere aggressi, falsa pro veris tradiderunt: alij ignoratione & securitate, alij credulitate, nonnulli & mentiendi libidine, quos aut turpis spes lucri, aut gratia, aut odium corrupit. Ac quàm necessaria sit rerum superioribus annis in Ecclesia gestarum annotatio, ex amicis bene multis didici: qui mihi de historiola renati apud se Evangelij sciscitanti, dolenter responderunt: vel, evanuisse istarum rerum memoriam: vel, Annales incendio conflagrasse: vel, in invidorum scrinijs hæc talia jacere recondita. Quod igitur ex variorum lectione Scriptorum: quod ex liberali doctissimorum virorum communicatione, quod denique ex annorum propemodum triginta experientia de historia instaurati Evangelij didici, cognovi, observavi: id hisce includendum Annalibus duxi, quorum specimen nunc edo. Atq; huic vestra, viri venerandi, praescribere nomina libuit ideo, quia de historiolae huius veritate omnium optime judicare potestis, quippe qui & proximi fuistis initiis renati Evangelij, & dimidium fere seculum Ecclesiam Filij Dei, quâ voce vivâ, quâ Scriptis eruditis docuistis, & deniq; pars aliqua fuistis eorum, quae in Germanicis & Helveticis Ecclesiis sunt acta. Volui etiam hac θεοφωνήσει posteritati commendare memoriam diutini vestri in me favoris meaeque in vos observantiae, adeoque amicitiae tot annos sanctè inter
units.tr: Accordingly, Jerome also, in his action against Helvidius, says: "Whether Moses wished to be the author of the Pentateuch, or Ezra its restorer, I do not object." Also, among the ancient annals of the Hebrews there were some that were called the Book of the Upright, either because they described the things done in the assembly of God with the most faithful accuracy and order, or because they contained the deeds of the Israelite people, whom Moses in Deuteronomy 32:15 and Isaiah in 24:2 called "upright." Whether this was the same book that is called the Book of the Wars of the Lord in Numbers, or a part of it, or even a different work; or whether Josephus persuades us, who in his Antiquities, in the fifth book, chapter 2, speaks of the Book of the Upright, which is mentioned in the sacred writings, as "writings kept in the temple." We should not rightly regard as anything but fables what the Jewish rabbis, and with them Lyra, babble about the Book of the Upright. In the New Testament, no sane person doubts that the disciples of our Saviour himself recorded his daily sermons in their diaries and annals, from which the evangelical history was later woven together. In the times of the Fathers, Eusebius, Theodoret, Socrates, Sozomen, Orosius and Severus labored at this, so that whatever was done in the Church of God worthy of the remembrance of good men might be consecrated in the monuments of annals and handed down to posterity. Following the example and authority of these men, I have begun to compose the Annals of the Gospel, renewed here and there throughout Europe in the fifteenth century after the birth of Christ Jesus. It is a great and arduous work, I admit; yet no difficulty could deter me from it. Not that I am unaware of my own weakness, but because the pleasant usefulness and useful pleasantness of this labor so occupied me that I believe I shall sufficiently show this purpose to the Church of Christ, if I have given some indication of this will, or if, with this rough and unpolished little work, whatever its quality, I have provided an occasion for more learned men to think more carefully about a matter so holy. And indeed, if things were done according to my wishes, several learned men would devote their labor and mental powers to this, so that we might have a full history of the renewed Gospel. God commands the Israelite people not to forget their Egyptian servitude, and he impressed the memory of liberation from it on the first commandment of the Decalogue. Our forebears were oppressed not by bodily but by spiritual slavery of souls under the Roman Pharaoh, and almighty God delivered them into liberty. What is more fitting than to investigate the time of that deliverance, to learn its manner, and in tongues and minds to proclaim the glorious power of God shining in it? Posterity must also be provided for, so that it is not deceived by those writers of ecclesiastical affairs of the recent age who, undertaking to hand down to posterity matters little known to them, have passed off false things as true: some through ignorance and carelessness, some through credulity, and some through a lust for lying, whom either base hope of gain, or favour, or hatred has corrupted. And how necessary is the recording of things done in the Church in recent years, I have learned from many friends, who, when I inquired of them about the little history of the Gospel renewed among them, sadly replied either that the memory of those things had vanished, or that the annals had been burned in a fire, or that such things lie hidden in the chests of the envious. Therefore what I have learned, observed and come to know from the reading of various writers, from the generous communication of very learned men, and finally from the experience of nearly thirty years concerning the history of the restored Gospel, I have judged should be included in these Annals, of which I now publish a specimen. And it has pleased me to inscribe your names, venerable gentlemen, on this work, because you can judge the truth of this little history better than anyone, since you were both close to the beginnings of the renewed Gospel, and for almost half a century you have taught the Church of the Son of God, by living voice and by learned writings, and finally you were some part of the things that were done in the German and Helvetic Churches. I also wished to commend to posterity, by this divinely inspired dedication [θεοφωνήσει], the memory of your lasting favour toward me and my respect for you, and the friendship held so holily for so many years between

units.la: DEDICATIO.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: inter nos cultæ: quam brevi in beata æternitate in complexu amicissimi Fratris & Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi cum tripudio glorificatorum cordium nostrorum nos continuaturos ut spero, ita confido. Deum veneror: ut renovet sicut Aquilæ annos senectæ vestræ, vosque, ubi certamen illud bonum certaveritis, cursumque stadij vestri consummaveritis, Paulinâ justitiæ corona beet. Scripsi Heidelbergæ Anno millesimo sexcentesimo decimo septimo, mense Augusto, cuius die vicesima quarta annum ætatis meæ ingredior quinquagesimum secundum, quem mihi felicem faustum & salutarem jubeat esse is, qui unicus Annalium horum scopus est Jesus Christus, benedictus in sempiterna secula, Amen.
units.tr: among ourselves cherished. I hope, and am confident, that in the blessed eternity, in the embrace of our most beloved Brother and Saviour Jesus Christ, with the rejoicing of our glorified hearts, we shall continue this friendship. I pray to God that He may renew the years of your old age as the eagle's, and that, when you have fought that good fight and finished the course of your race, He may crown you with the crown of righteousness of Paul. I have written this at Heidelberg in the year 1617, in August, on the twenty-fourth day of which I enter upon the fifty-second year of my life. May He who is the sole aim of these Annals, Jesus Christ, blessed for ever and ever, grant that it be a happy, fortunate and salutary year for me. Amen.

units.la: Lectori S.
units.tr: To the Reader, S.

units.la: ANalium Evangelij renovati specimen hocce idcirco publico, Lector Christiane, ut quasi manu pulsem amicas doctorum virorum Bibliothecas, atq; inde eliciam historica ad continuandum hoc opusculum necessaria. Absq; his enim subsidiis sit, frustra quis in hoc studio desudet. Ad primam quidem Decadem non invitii symbolam suam contulerunt Nicolaus Henelius J. C. Caspar Cunradus Medicus Uratislaviensis, Caspar VVaserus Tigurinus, Joannes Cunradus Cochius
units.tr: I publish this specimen of the Annals of the Renewed Gospel, kind reader, so that, as it were, I may knock by hand at the friendly libraries of learned men and from them draw out the historical materials needed to continue this little work. For without these aids anyone would toil in vain at this study. Indeed, for the first Decade, not unwilling men have contributed their share: Nicolaus Henelius, doctor of both laws; Caspar Cunradus, physician of Breslau; Caspar Waserus of Zurich; Johannes Cunradus Cochius.

units.la: chius Scaphusianus, Gregorius Richterus Gorlicensis, Theologi: V Volfgangus item Meierus Theologiæ Doctor in inclyta Basilea: cui uni acceptum refero, quod Epistolas MSS. Capitonis, Buceri, Musculi, Oecolampadij, aliorum, novi, quas ut selectas literato orbi communicet per Chalcographorum operam, publicâ illum voce cohortor. Quod si horum liberalitatem alij fuerint imitati, & Deus voluerit animulam hanc in corpusculi hujus ergastulo unum adhuc atq; alterum annum habitare: erunt fortasis, qui suis votis in hoc genere aliqua ex parte satisfactum esse, fatebuntur.
units.tr: Cochius of Schaffhausen, Gregor Richter of Görlitz, theologians; and Wolfgang Meier, Doctor of Theology in the renowned city of Basel, to whom alone I attribute it that he is willing to communicate to the learned world, through the labour of the printers, the manuscript letters of Capito, Bucer, Musculus, Oecolampadius and others, new and selected; I urge him by public voice to do so. If others have imitated their generosity, and God is pleased that this little soul should dwell for one or another year more in the prison of this little body, there will perhaps be those who will confess that their wishes have been satisfied to some extent in this respect.

units.la: ANNALIUM EVANGELII RENOVATI DECAS PRIMA.
units.tr: THE FIRST DECADE OF THE RENEWED ANNALS OF THE GOSPEL.

units.la: Annus M.D.XVI.
units.tr: The Year 1516.

units.la: VT aurora est clari Solis prænuncia: ita oriturum Evangelii lucem instaurata superiori seculo linguarum & artium optimarum studia præsignificârunt.
units.tr: As the dawn is the forerunner of the bright sun, so the revival of letters and of the finest arts, which began in the previous century, foreshadowed the rising of the light of the Gospel.

units.la: Memorabilibus autem mediis Deus usus est, elegantiores literas instauraturus: Typographiâ: Græcorum exilio: Scholarum publicarum apertione.
units.tr: God, however, prepared to restore the more refined letters by means of notable instruments: the printing press, the exile of the Greeks, and the opening of public schools.

units.la: aTypographiam Germania invenit anno Servatoris 1440. primis libris Moguntiæ excusis. bHuius beneficio primùm Erasmi Roterodami, deinde Lutheri libri variis locis
units.tr: Germany invented printing in the year of our Saviour 1440, with the first books printed at Mainz. By its benefit, first the books of Erasmus of Rotterdam and then those of Luther were printed in various places and sent out into all of Europe.

units.la: Græcis exsulibus post expugnatam à Turcis anno 1453 Constantinopolim, asylum in Italia aperuerunt, Hercules Dux Ferrariæ, Nicolaus V. Episcopus Romanus, Laurentius Medices Florentinus, Bessarion, natione Græcus, sed ob excellentem eruditionem ab Eugenio Papa in ordinem Cardinalium adscitus: cui familiares fuerunt Trapezuntius, Gaza, Argyropylus, alii.
units.tr: After Constantinople was taken by the Turks in the year 1453, the Greek exiles opened a refuge in Italy: Hercules, Duke of Ferrara; Nicholas V, Bishop of Rome; Lorenzo de' Medici of Florence; and Bessarion, a Greek by birth, who was admitted by Pope Eugenius into the college of cardinals on account of his outstanding learning. Among his intimates were Trapezuntius, Gaza, Argyropylus, and others.

units.la: Ex hoc velut emporio Italiæ præclaras literarum merces in Germaniam importârunt nostri homines, quorum primus fuit Rodolphus Agricola, qui Ferrariam & Lutetiam profectus, tantos subito fecit in Græca lingua progressus: ut cum Guarino solutâ oratione, cum Strozis carmine, cum Gaza in Philosophia contenderet, &, quod Germanis semper difficilimum fuit, Italis in Græcorum & Latinorum Authorum enarratione admirationem moveret.
units.tr: From this, as it were, emporium of Italy, our countrymen imported the splendid wares of literature into Germany. The first of them was Rudolf Agricola, who, travelling to Ferrara and Lyons, made such sudden progress in the Greek language that he could compete with Guarino in prose, with the Strozzi in verse, and with Gaza in philosophy. And, what was always most difficult for Germans, he aroused admiration among the Italians in the explanation of Greek and Latin authors.

units.la: Proximus ab hoc fuit Joannes Capnio, qui Hieronymum Spartiatam, Georgii Tifernatis in Græca professione successorem, tam feliciter Lutetiæ audivit: ut à Philippo Palatino Electore legatus Romam missus, & Argyropyli, Thucydidem enarrantis, auditorium ingressus, edito sui in Græca lingua profectûs specimine, lacrymas pene excusferit. ferit Argyropylo, exclamanti, Græciam exilio doctorum transvolasse Alpes.Horum vestigia secutus est magnus ille Erasmus: unde eiusmodi repentè omnium artium & studiorum lumen effulsit: ut scholæ ceu nova luce de cœlo collustratæ viderentur.
units.tr: Next after him came Johannes Capnio, who heard Hieronymus Spartiata, successor of Georgius Tifernas in the chair of Greek, at Paris so successfully that, sent as an envoy to Rome by the Elector Palatine Philip, and entering the lecture room of Argyropylus while he was expounding Thucydides, he displayed a specimen of his progress in Greek and almost drew tears from Argyropylus, who exclaimed: Greece has flown across the Alps in the exile of her scholars. Following in their footsteps came the great Erasmus. From this, suddenly, a light of all the arts and studies shone forth, so that the schools seemed to be lit up by a new light from heaven.

units.la: Porrò cum in Comitiis VVormatiensibus, quæ prima Maximilianus, Friderici filius, anno 1495 celebravit, omnibus suffragiis decretum fuisset: ut Septemviri, in sua quisque ditione, publicis scholis sedem figerent: Fridericus Saxoniæ Elector 1502 VVittembergæ, Joachimus I. Brandeburgicus Elector 1506. Francofurti ad Viadrum, Academias condidêre.
units.tr: Moreover, when at the Diet of Worms, which Maximilian, son of Frederick, first held in the year 1495, it had been decreed by all votes that each of the seven electors should establish public schools in his own territory, Frederick, Elector of Saxony, founded the university at Wittenberg in 1502, and Joachim I, Elector of Brandenburg, founded one at Frankfurt on the Oder in 1506.

units.la: Et, quod mireris, uno & eodem tempore in diversis mundi regionibus, intermortua pridem studia in vitam revocabant Leo X. Pontifex, Romæ: apud Hispanos Cardinalis Toletanus: apud Anglos Rex Henricus, eius nominis Octavus: apud Belgas Rex Catholicus, Carolus: apud Gallos Rex Franciscus.
units.tr: And, what is remarkable, at one and the same time in different regions of the world, Leo X, Pope, at Rome; among the Spaniards the Cardinal of Toledo; among the English King Henry, the eighth of that name; among the Belgians the Catholic King Charles; and among the French King Francis, began to call back to life studies that had long been dead.

units.la: Nullum igitur disciplinæ genus fuit, quod non excoli cœperit. Medicinam vindicabant Nicolaus Leonicenus, Romæ: Ambrosius Leo Nolanus, Venetiis: Guilielmus Copus, Basiliensis, & Joannes Ruellius, in Gallia: Thomas Linacer apud Britannos. Jus Cæsareum instaurabat
units.tr: Therefore there was no branch of learning that did not begin to be cultivated. Nicolaus Leonicenus at Rome, Ambrosius Leo of Nola at Venice, Guillaume Cop of Basel and Jean Ruel in France, and Thomas Linacre among the British, claimed medicine for themselves. Roman law was restored

units.la: Lutetiæ Guilielmus Budæus : apud Germanos Udalricus Zasius : Mathematicen Glareanus Basileæ. Intra Theologiæ scholasticæ spineta latitabant Monachi complures, quorum postea celebre inter Theologos reformatos fuit nomen.
units.tr: at Paris by Guillaume Budé; among the Germans by Ulrich Zasius; and mathematics by Glareanus at Basel. Within the thickets of scholastic theology there lay hidden several monks, whose name later became famous among the reformed theologians.

units.la: In gemina literatura celebrabantur, Erasmus apud Germanos, Budæus apud Gallos, Antonius Nebrissensis apud Hispanos. Reuchlinus Hebraeas literas in Germaniam, Marcus Masurus Graecas Venetias inferebat.
units.tr: In both kinds of literature the following were celebrated: Erasmus among the Germans, Budé among the French, and Antonio de Nebrija among the Spaniards. Reuchlin brought Hebrew letters into Germany, and Marcus Musurus brought Greek letters to Venice.

units.la: Virebant hoc tempore Jacobus Wimphelingus, Ludovicus Vives, Longelius, Hermannus Buschius, Conradus Goclenius, Petrus Mosellanus, Thomas Morus. In spem vero novi seculi efflorescebant, Beatus Rhenanus, Simon Grynæus, Brentius, Frechtus, & Philippus ille Melanchthon : de quo hoc legimus Erasmi præsagium : At Deum immortalem, quam non spem de se præbet etiam adolescens, & penè puer, Philippus ille Melanchthon, utraque literatura penè ex æquo suspiciendus ? quod inventionis acumen? quæ sermonis puritas? quanta reconditarum rerum memoria? quàm varia lectio, quàm verecunda, regiaque prorsus indolis festivitas?
units.tr: At this time there flourished Jakob Wimpfeling, Ludovicus Vives, Longolius, Hermann Busch, Konrad Goclenius, Peter Schade (Mosellanus), and Thomas More. Those who were growing in hope for the new century were Beatus Rhenanus, Simon Grynaeus, Brenz, Frecht, and that Philip Melanchthon, of whom we read this prophecy of Erasmus: But, immortal God, what hope does even a young man, almost a boy, Philip Melanchthon, give of himself, who is to be admired almost equally in both literatures? What acuteness of invention! What purity of speech! What a memory of hidden things! How varied his reading, how modest, and how wholly of royal character in its graciousness!

units.la: Sic igitur literæ & artes instaurari, & cum illis totus penè mundus, ipsaque inprimis Religio renovari coepit. Nam Biblia Ebraica (vulgo Complutensia) cum translationibus, Chaldaicâ, Græcâ, & Latinâ, Francisci Ximenii Cardinalis, Archiepiscopi Toletani curâ, typis descripta, publicantur, anno millesimo quingentesimo, decimo quinto.
units.tr: Thus, then, letters and arts began to be restored, and with them almost the whole world, and above all Religion itself. For the Hebrew Bible (commonly called the Complutensian) with the translations, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin, was printed under the care of Cardinal Francisco Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo, and published in the year one thousand five hundred and fifteen.

units.la: Hęc proximo anno 1516. excipit Novum Testamentum, ab Erasmo quinquagenario Latinè conversum, & permissu Papæ ex fontibus correctum: quo labore ut omnes bonos in perpetuum sui amorem, ita ignavos Monachos in implacabile sui odium convertit.
units.tr: In the following year, 1516, the New Testament followed, translated into Latin by Erasmus when he was fifty, and corrected from the sources with the permission of the Pope. By this labour he won all good men to a lasting love of himself, while he turned the lazy monks to implacable hatred of him.

units.la: Hic est ill'z annus: quo Joannes Hilten, Isennaci Franciscanus, initium fore inclinantis Pontificiæ potentiæ prædixerat. Melanchthon vidisse se enarrationem Danielis manu Hiltenii, & in ea vaticinium hoc scriptum, refert in libello altero epistolarum. pag. 81.
units.tr: This is that year in which John Hilten, a Franciscan of Isenach, had foretold that the decline of Papal power would begin. Melanchthon reports in the second booklet of his letters, page 81, that he had seen an exposition of Daniel in Hilten's hand, and that this prophecy was written in it.

units.la: Præsagio respondit eventus. Hoc ipso 1516 anno Leo Decimus (qui Pontificatus autoritate nimis licenter abutebatur, & exactionum suarum emolumentum Magdalenæ sorori, fœminæ cupiditatem expleturus, dabat) Campeium Cardinalem in Angliam, Angelum Arcomboldum in Daniam & Suetiam, Samsonem Mediolanensem in Helvetiam, Joannem Tecelium in Germaniam misit, cœlumq; vel maximis sceleribus inquinatis turpissimo mercatu vendendis.
units.tr: The outcome answered the prediction. In this same year, 1516, Leo X (who abused the authority of the Papacy too licenly, and who gave the profit from his exactions to his sister Magdalena, a woman about to satisfy her desires) sent Cardinal Campeggio to England, Angelo Arcimboldi to Denmark and Sweden, Samson of Milan to Switzerland, and Johann Tetzel to Germany, to sell heaven, which had been defiled even by the greatest crimes, in a most shameful trade.

units.la: a Guicciardinus lib. 13. hist.
units.tr: a Guicciardini, History, book 13.

units.la: b Antiquitates Britannicæ.
units.tr: b British Antiquities.

units.la: c Chronico Lubecense Bonni.
units.tr: c Lübeck Chronicle of Bonnus.

units.la: d Chronicon Bullingeri M.S.
units.tr: d Bullinger's Chronicle, manuscript.

units.la: e Sleidan. nale proposuit. Ad quos cum maximus hominum fieret concursus, erant qui id ægerrimè ferrent, & inter hos *Martinus Lutherus Saxo Islebius, Monachus Augustinianus, Theologiæ Doctor VVittembergæ in Saxonia Septemvirali, qui in monasterio suo homines monere cœpit: agerent prudenter, neque merces istas, Iuterboci oppido VVitembergæ vicino à Tecelio expositas tanti emerent: præstare facultatibus suis sublevare pauperes, quam incertam gratiam certâ pecuniâ redimere. Quæ prima fuit occasio immutandæ Religionis Pontificiæ.
units.tr: e Sleidan. They proposed these things for sale. Since a very great crowd of people came to them, there were some who took this very badly, and among these was Martin Luther, a Saxon from Eisleben, an Augustinian monk and Doctor of Theology at Wittenberg in Saxony, a Septemvir, who began to warn the people in his monastery that they should act prudently and not buy such wares, which Tetzel was offering at Jüterbog, a town near Wittenberg, at such a price. It was better, he said, to relieve the poor with their means than to redeem an uncertain grace with certain money. This was the first occasion for changing the Papal religion.

units.la: Hunc eundem annum centum annis antè quasi nominarunt gloriosissimi Christi Martyres, Joannes Hussus, & Hieronymus Pragensis: quorum ille in mediis flammis 1415. sexta Julii Constantiæ , Hodie, inquit, Hußum (Anserem Boëmis notat) crematis: post centum annos Cygnus veniet, quem comburere non poteritis: Hic 1416. trigesimo Maij contentâ voce professus est: carnifices suos post centum annos sibi responsuros. Nec ex eventu hæc illis ab Evangelicis affinguntur. Bohemos enim desiderio Hussi numismata cudisse, inscriptione postremorum eius verborum: post centum annos respondebitis Deo & mihi, & his exactis apparuisse Lutherum, auauthor est Catholicissimus Historiographus.
units.tr: A hundred years earlier, the most glorious martyrs of Christ, John Hus and Jerome of Prague, had almost named this very year. Hus, in the midst of the flames at Constance on the sixth of July 1415, said: Today you burn a goose (Hus means goose in Bohemian), but after a hundred years a swan will come, whom you will not be able to burn. Jerome, in 1416 on the thirtieth of May, professed with a steady voice that his executioners would answer to him after a hundred years. Nor do the Evangelicals invent these things after the event. The Catholic historian is the authority for the claim that the Bohemians, out of longing for Hus, struck coins bearing the inscription of his last words: After a hundred years you will answer to God and to me, and that when these years had run out, Luther appeared.

units.la: Edidit tum Lutherus etiam disputationum aliquid contra traditiones humanas, & alia quædam Pontificia dogmata. Scripsit idem præfationem in libellum, Theologia Germanica, dictum. Ac quid iam tum senserit de justitia fidei, ex epistola ipsius ad Eremitam quendam videre est: ubi plenus spiritu, ait: Cæterum quid agat anima tua, scire cupio: utrum ne tandem suam pertæsa propriam iustitiam, discat in iustitia Christi respirare atque confidere. Fervet enim nostra ætate tentatio præsumptionis in multis, & iis præcipuè, qui justi & boni esse omnibus viribus student, ignorantes iustitiam Dei, quæ in Christo est nobis effusissimé, & gratis donata, quærunt in seipsis tam diu operari benè, donec habeant fiduciam standi coram DEO, veluti viribus & meritis ornati, quod est impossibile fieri. Fuisti tu apud nos in hac opinione, imo errore; fui & ego, sed & nunc quoq; pugno contra istum errorem, sed nondum expugnavi. Igitur, mi dulcis Frater, disce Christum, & hunc crucifixum: disce ei cantare, & de te desperans, dicere ei: tu, Domine Iesu, es iustitia mea, ego autem sum peccatum tuum: tu assumpsisti meum, & dedisti mihi tuum: assumpsisti quod non eras, & dedisti mihi quod non eram. Cave ne aliquando ad tantam puritatem aspi-
units.tr: Luther then also published some disputations against human traditions and other Papal dogmas. The same man wrote a preface to the little book called the German Theology. And what he then thought about the justice of faith can be seen from his letter to a certain hermit, where, full of the Spirit, he says: For the rest, I want to know what your soul is doing: whether at last, weary of its own righteousness, it learns to breathe and trust in the righteousness of Christ. For in our age the temptation of presumption rages in many, especially in those who strive with all their strength to be righteous and good, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, which is in Christ and given to us most abundantly and freely, and who seek to work well in themselves for so long until they have confidence to stand before God, as if adorned with their own powers and merits, which is impossible. You were among us in this opinion, indeed in this error; I was too, but even now I still fight against that error, though I have not yet overcome it. Therefore, my sweet brother, learn Christ, and him crucified: learn to sing to him, and, despairing of yourself, to say to him: You, Lord Jesus, are my righteousness, but I am your sin; you have taken on mine and given me yours; you took on what you were not, and gave me what I was not. Beware lest at some time you aspire to such purity

units.la: Tom. I. Opist. Lutheri. res : ut peccator tibi videri nolis , imò esse. Christus enim nonnisi in peccatoribus habitat. Ideo enim descendit de cælo: ubi habitabat in iustis : ut etiam habitaret in peccatoribus. Iflam charitatem eius rumina , & videbis dulcissimam consolationem eius. Si enim nostris laboribus & afflictionibus ad conscientia quietem pervenire oportet : ut quid ille mortuus est? Igitur npn nisi in illo per fiducialem desperationem tui , & operum tuorum , pacem invenies: disces insuper eo ipso, ut sicut ipse suscepit te , & peccata tua fecit sua, & suam iustitiam fecit tuam.
units.tr: Vol. I, Letters of Luther: "...that you do not wish to appear a sinner to yourself, but rather to be one. For Christ dwells only in sinners. For this reason he came down from heaven, where he had dwelt among the righteous, so that he might also dwell among sinners. Chew over this love of his, and you will see his most sweet consolation. For if we must attain peace of conscience through our labours and afflictions, why then did he die? Therefore you will find peace only in him, through a trusting despair of yourself and of your works. You will learn moreover, by that very means, that just as he took you up and made your sins his own, so he made his righteousness yours."

units.la: Etsi autem Lutherus primus in disputationis Pontificiæ arenam protractus est: non tamen unus ex omnibus fuit, qui fraudes Romanæ curiæ agnosceret. Erant enim iam tum in Helvetia quoque & Germania superiori vitæ & doctrinæ probatæ viri aliquot, qui, missis hominum commentis, decreta Dei auditoribus suis annunciabant, Udalricus Zwvinglius , VVolffgangus Fabritius Capito, Joannes Oecolampadius, Joannes Creutzer, alii.
units.tr: Although Luther was the first to be dragged into the arena of the Papist dispute, he was not the only one who recognised the frauds of the Roman curia. For already at that time there were several men in Switzerland and Upper Germany, approved for their life and teaching, who, setting aside the inventions of men, announced the decrees of God to their hearers: Ulrich Zwingli, Wolfgang Fabricius Capito, Johannes Oecolampadius, Johannes Creutzer, and others.

units.la: Udalricus Zwvinglius Helvetius, in pago Toggiorum , quem ad domum Sylvestrem (<bl>zum</bl> <bl>wilden Hauß</bl>) vocant, anno 1484. Kal. Januarii natus, & in liberalibus studiis Bernæ, Viennæ, Basileæ enutritus, hoc decimo sexto supra millesimum quingentesimum anno Glaronæ Evangelium prædicat, cum Lutheri nomen in istis locis nec dum fuisset auditum. ª Is à præceptore suo Thomma VVittenbachio Theologo Professore Basiliencи anno 1505. didicerat: solam mortem Christi esse λύτρον pro peccatis: indulgentias Papæ figmentum esse.
units.tr: Ulrich Zwingli, a Swiss from the district of the Toggenburg, called to the house of Sylvester "zum wilden Hauß," was born on 1 January 1484. Brought up in the liberal studies at Bern, Vienna and Basel, in the year 1516 he preached the Gospel at Glarus, when the name of Luther had not yet been heard in those parts. He had learned from his teacher Thomas Wittenbach, professor of theology at Basel, in the year 1505, that the death of Christ alone is the ransom for sins, and that indulgences are the Pope's fiction.

units.la: VVolfgangus Fabritius Capito Haganoæ in Alsatia anno 1478. nascitur: ᵇ à studio Theologico per parentem, impiam sacrificulorum vitam abominantem, avocatur: Medicinæ Doctor creatur circa annum 1498. Defuncto patre ad Theologiam redit, summos in ea honores consequutus anno 1504.
units.tr: Wolfgang Fabricius Capito was born at Haguenau in Alsace in the year 1478. Drawn away from the study of theology by his father, who abhorred the impious life of the priestlings, he was made a Doctor of Medicine about the year 1498. After his father's death he returned to theology, and obtained the highest honours in it in the year 1504.

units.la: ᶜ Friburgi in Brisgoia Scoticas subtilitates profitetur: harum pertæsus sacris initiatus: à Philippo Rosenbergio Episcopo Spirensi vocatur Brusellam (agri Spirensis oppidulum est) triennium ibi concionatur: inde Basileam à senatu tertio nuntio invitatus, summo templo aliquot annos præest, ubi docendo disputandoq; prima Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ in inclyta illa urbe semina jecit: id quod non solùm epistolæ Capitonis, sed etiam versus, auditorio Theologico Basiliencи inscripti, testantur.
units.tr: At Freiburg in the Breisgau he lectured on the Scotist subtleties; wearied of these, he was ordained to the sacred ministry. Called by Philip Rosenberg, Bishop of Speyer, to Bruchsal (a small town in the territory of Speyer), he preached there for three years. Then, invited to Basel by the council after the third messenger, he presided for some years over the great church, where by teaching and disputing he sowed the first seeds of the evangelical Church in that famous city. This is attested not only by the letters of Capito but also by the verses inscribed in the theological lecture hall at Basel.

units.la: Joannes Oecolampadius (Hausschein Germanis) anno 1482. in oppido Cherufcorum VVinfperga natus, Heilprunnæ & Heidelbergæ adolescens eos in studiis fecit progressus: ut illum Philippus quidem Elector Palatinus liberorum suorum natu minorum praeceptorem, V Vinsperga vero non ita multo post sibi verbi praeconem deligeret.
units.tr: Johannes Oecolampadius (called Hausschein in German) was born in the year 1482 in the town of Weinsberg in the land of the Chatti. As a young man at Heilbronn and at Heidelberg he made such progress in his studies that Philip, Elector Palatine, chose him as tutor to his younger sons, and not long afterwards the people of Weinsberg chose him as herald of the Word.

units.la: a Is circa annum 1514. patriae suae Christū, cum omnium verè spiritualium & eruditorum admiratione, praedicavit, quanquam adhuc multa veteris superstitionis admixta essent. b Annitente autem Capitone per Christophorum ab Uttenheim Episcopum, Basileam vocatus, & parœciae primi templi praefectus, Erasmum Annotationes in N. T. edentem, multum juuit, & à Capitone hoc 1516. anno Theologiae Doctor renunciatus est.
units.tr: About the year 1514 he preached Christ to his fatherland, to the admiration of all who were truly spiritual and learned, although many remnants of the old superstition were still mixed in. Summoned to Basel by Christoph of Utenheim, Bishop, and made head of the parish of the first church, with the help of Capito he greatly assisted Erasmus in publishing his Annotations on the New Testament. In the year 1516 Capito had him proclaimed Doctor of Theology.

units.la: c ARGENTINÆ JoannesCreutzer, Theologiae Doctor, etsi ritus Papisticos pro ratione temporum illorum retinebat, tamen pure Evangelium docebat, cum non paucis aliis: praesertim ad Carmelitas & Augustinianos: nec aliud tum audiebatur ibi, quàm quod confessione postea anni tricesimi descriptum. Viam ad reformationem muniverat D. Keisersberger anno 1508. qui collegam & successorem Joannem hunc habuit. Itaq; inter Germaniae urbes Argentina prima fuit, quae caeteris exemplo esset.
units.tr: At Strasbourg, Johannes Creutzer, Doctor of Theology, although he retained the Papist rites in view of the circumstances of that time, nevertheless taught the Gospel purely, together with not a few others, especially among the Carmelites and Augustinians. Nothing else was heard there at that time than what was later set down in the Confession of the year thirty. Dr Keisersberger had paved the way to the reformation in the year 1508, and he had this Johannes as colleague and successor. Thus among the cities of Germany Strasbourg was the first that became an example to the others.

units.la: Atq; haec Ecclesiae per Europam renascituræ primodia fuerunt in Germania.
units.tr: These were the beginnings in Germany of the Church that was about to be reborn throughout Europe.

units.la: Estq; hic
units.tr: And here

units.la: ANNUS M D XVI.
units.tr: The Year 1516

units.la: Trecentesimus quinquagesimus sextus à prima reformatione doctrinæ Papisticæ in Gallia, per Valdenses.
units.tr: The 356th year since the first reform of Papist doctrine in Gaul, by the Waldensians.

units.la: Centesimus quadragesimus sextus à prima cōfutatione errorum Pontificiorum in Anglia, per Joannem VVicleff.
units.tr: The 146th year since the first refutation of Papist errors in England, by John Wycliffe.

units.la: Centesimus decimus sextus à primo anno Ministerii Joannis Hussi, receptas seculi sui opiniones & dogmata impugnantis in Boëmia.
units.tr: The 116th year since the first year of the ministry of John Hus, who attacked the opinions and dogmas accepted in his age, in Bohemia.

units.la: Tricesimus sextus à condemnatione Joannis VVesselli Gröningensis, qui VVormatiæ ante Lutherum natum eadem quæ postea Lutherus, docuit.
units.tr: The 36th year since the condemnation of John Wessel of Groningen, who taught at Worms, before Luther was born, the same things that Luther later taught.

units.la: Sexagesimus ab eo tempore, quo Boëmi nonnulli à fide Hussitarum, (qui inter varia bella & certamina nil nisi nomen Hussi & calicem in cœna sacra retinuerant) discesserunt, peculiares cœtus collegerunt, cum doctrinæ puritate disciplinæ Apostolicæ severitatem conjunxerunt, & amabili FRATRUM nomine mutuò se salutarunt. Qui quidem FRATRES, falsò PICCARDI dicti, annos jam centum sexaginta & amplius inter varios motus, persequutiones, pericula, mortes, non solùm conservati, sed in Moraviam etiam & Poloniam non sine miraculo diffusi, hocipso quo hæc scribimus tempore gaudent Patronis quidem, inter alios multos RAPHAELE, Comite à Lesno Castellano Vislicienſi, in Polonia, Carolo Zerotinio in Moravia, VVenceslao à Budowitz in Boëmia, heroibus illuſtribus: Doſtoribus verò primariis, Matthæo Koneczny & Matthia Cyro, in Boëmia, Joanne Lanetio & Georgio Erasto in Moravia, Martino Gratiano & Joanne Turnovio, in Polonia, viris innocentis vitæ & eruditæ doſtrinæ laude florentibus, fratribus in Domino carissimis.
units.tr: The 60th year since the time when some Bohemians, who had departed from the faith of the Hussites (who, amid their various wars and conflicts, had retained nothing but the name of Hus and the chalice in the Lord's Supper), gathered separate assemblies. They joined purity of doctrine with the strictness of apostolic discipline, and greeted one another with the dear name of BROTHERS. These Brothers, falsely called Picards, have now survived for more than 160 years amid various upheavals, persecutions, dangers and deaths. They have not only been preserved but, not without a miracle, spread also into Moravia and Poland. At the very time in which we are writing this, they rejoice in patrons, among many others: Raphael, Count of Lesno, Castellan of Wislica in Poland; Charles of Žerotín in Moravia; and Wenceslaus of Budowitz in Bohemia, illustrious heroes. Their leading teachers are Matthew Konečný and Matthias Cyrus in Bohemia, John Lanetius and George Erastus in Moravia, and Martin Gratian and John Turnovius in Poland, men flourishing in the praise of blameless life and learned doctrine, most dear brothers in the Lord.

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXVII.
units.tr: The Year of Christ 1517

units.la: MArtinus Lutherus ubi refcivit, Tecelii moderata fua ad populū monita de vanitate Indulgentiarum, indignè ferre, in publico Academiæ Wittebergensi theatro contra impoſturas iſtas Pontificias ſibi diſputandum duxit.
units.tr: Martin Luther, when he learned that Tetzel, in his moderate admonitions to the people about the emptiness of indulgences, had taken offence, resolved to dispute publicly against these Papist impostures in the public hall of the Academy of Wittenberg.

units.la: Itaque Theses numero nonaginta quinq; pridie Kal. Novembris anni decimi ſeptimi ſupra millesimum quingentesimum foribus templi arcis affixit, quibus institorum Romanensium menſas evertit.
units.tr: Accordingly, on the eve of the Kalends of November in the year 1517 after the thousand five hundred, he fixed to the doors of the castle church ninety-five theses, by which he overturned the tables of the Roman hawkers.

units.la: Hic eſt ille Lutherus, qui duorum Martyrum & homologetarum, VViclefi & Huſfi dosi doctrinam sibi centum post annis assumpsit in Saxonia Septemvirali, & resumpsit, quæ contra corruptelas Pontificias ambo illi scripserunt, atq; expolivit etiam & auxit luculentè, docuitq; de conversione hominis peccatoris, pœnitentia & justificatione, perfectissime, & sacramentum etiam integrum, exemplo Hussi, suis popularibus recuperavit. Quo cum non ita multò post in Helvetia Zwinglius & Oecolampadius tum cætera omnia contra Romanenses utriusque illius, VViclefi & Hussi prosecuti sunt: à VViclefo autem peculiariter contra idolum corporalis præsentiæ corporis Christi in cœna sacra, jacta semina, sibi excolenda sumpserunt: de quo minor fuit Hussi scientiæ plerophoria, sed Lutheri inprimis, vel nulla potiùs huius prorsus, sicut ipse post-ea de se scriptis suis probavit; qui & prositetur hoc de se in quodam scripto suo: so potiùs dogma de transubstantiatione admissurũ, quàm de corporali præsentia quidquam remissurum. Meminerit autem lector: etiam Prophetarum priscorum vocationis dona & beneficia fuisse imparia. Unus vitulos sustulit: & pseudolatriam in montibus intactam reliquit: alius contrà excelsa sustulit;& vitulos reliquit.
units.tr: This is that Luther who, a hundred years after them, took up in Saxony the doctrine of the two martyrs and witnesses, Wycliffe and Hus, and took up again what those two had written against Papist corruptions. He also polished and greatly enlarged it, and taught most perfectly about the conversion of the sinful man, repentance and justification. He also restored the whole sacrament to his fellow countrymen, following the example of Hus. Not long afterwards, Zwingli and Oecolampadius in Helvetia followed up everything else against the Romanists, taken from both of those men, Wycliffe and Hus. From Wycliffe in particular, they took up as their own to cultivate the seeds he had sown against the idol of the bodily presence of Christ's body in the Lord's Supper. In this matter, Hus's knowledge was less full in its assurance, but especially Luther's, or rather, he had none of it at all, as he himself later proved from his own writings. He also professes this about himself in a certain writing of his: that he would sooner admit the dogma of transubstantiation than give up anything of the bodily presence. The reader should remember, however, that even the gifts and benefits of the calling of the ancient prophets were unequal. One removed the calves, but left the false worship in the high places untouched; another, on the contrary, removed the high places, but left the calves.

units.la: Lutheri propositionibus contra indulgentias Papales lectis mira animorum immuta-tio tio per totam Europam facta est.
units.tr: After Luther's propositions against the papal indulgences were read, a remarkable change of minds took place throughout Europe.

units.la: {a} Albertus Crantzius, Vandalorum Historicus dixisse fertur: Frater, vade in cellam, & dic: miserere mei, Deus. Subinnuens, frustra Monachum Augustinianum adversus Pontificem disputaturum.
units.tr: {a} Albert Krantz, the historian of the Vandals, is reported to have said: Brother, go into your cell and say: have mercy on me, O God. He hinted that the Augustinian monk would dispute in vain against the Pontiff.

units.la: {b}VVitteberga Prior & Supprior metu perculsi Lutherum adeunt, rogantque: parcat ordini, nec illum ludibrio hominum exponat. Jam nunc in sinu gaudere Franciscanos, in ignominiae suae societatem Augustinianos venisse. Quibus respondit Martinus: totum hoc statim concidet, si in nomine Domini coeptum non est. Sin autem; Deo rem committite perficiendam.
units.tr: {b} The Prior and Subprior of Wittenberg, struck with fear, approached Luther and asked him to spare the order and not expose it to the mockery of men. Already, they said, the Franciscans were rejoicing in their bosom, and the Augustinians had come into the fellowship of his disgrace. Martin answered them: "All this will immediately collapse if it has not been begun in the name of the Lord. But if it has, commit the matter to God to bring to completion."

units.la: {c}Monachus quidam in Saxonibus prope Bitterfeld, conversus ad sacrificulos, Ha, ha, ha, inquit, venit jam is, qui vos recte tractabit.
units.tr: {c} A certain monk in Saxony, near Bitterfeld, turned to the priests and said, "Ha, ha, ha! The one who will treat you rightly has now come."

units.la: Complures alii in claustris monasticis, tyrannide humanarum superstitionum pressi, Deo gratias agebant pro liberatore. Neque verò mirum, cupidè fuisse Lutherum auditum. Theologia, conciones, vita Papalium Ecclesiasticorum bonis omnibus erat exosa.
units.tr: Many others in the monastic cloisters, oppressed by the tyranny of human superstitions, gave thanks to God for the liberator. Nor is it any wonder that Luther was eagerly heard. Theology, sermons, and the life of the Papal clergy were hateful to all good people.

units.la: THEOLOGIA qualis fuerit, docet Joannis Keisersbergii, Ecclesiastae primae aedis Argentinae, ad Jacobum VVimpfelingum, circa annum 1502. perscripta epistola: Quid dicam de mea gente? Multos Theologos, Theophilos philos producit paucissimos. Si tamen aliquos, acutos nimirum disputatores, proximorum & Dei dilectores nullos. Deus misereatur nostri, qui omnem absumimus nostram aetatem in nugis non solum humanorum studiorum, sed & divinorum, in quibus utique nugae sunt, dum Dei scrutamur majestatem, & nostram negligimus considerare infirmitatem, ignorantias & malitias. Nihil de virtutibus, quemadmodum efficiamur boni, casti, mansueti, humiles, liberales, modesti, temperati, charitativi, misericordes, patientes. De hoc quis se Theologorum etiam religiosorum intromittit?
units.tr: What theology was like is shown by the letter written by John Geiler of Kaysersberg, preacher of the first church of Strasbourg, to Jacob Wimpfeling, around the year 1502: "What shall I say about my own people? They produce many theologians, but very few lovers of wisdom. If there are some, they are surely clever disputers, but none who love their neighbours and God. May God have mercy on us, who spend our whole lives on trifles, not only of human studies but also of divine ones, in which surely there are trifles, while we investigate the majesty of God and neglect to consider our own weakness, our ignorance and our wickedness. Nothing about the virtues, how we may become good, chaste, gentle, humble, generous, modest, temperate, loving, merciful and patient. Who among even the religious theologians concerns himself with this?"

units.la: aCONCIONUM materies aniles fuerunt fabulae: de Vespasiano, Veronicae sudario, a vespis liberato: de purgatorio Patricii: de lepra Constantini Magni: de colloquio Sibyllae cum Augusto.
units.tr: {a} The subject matter of sermons was old wives' tales: about Vespasian, healed of a plague of wasps by Veronica's cloth; about St Patrick's purgatory; about the leprosy of Constantine the Great; about the conversation of the Sibyl with Augustus.

units.la: bVITA religiosorum ita foetebat ad vulgus: ut Carolus V. Imperator, Ecclesiasticis de Luthero conquerentibus in Comitiis Augustanis, responderit: Weret ihr Pfaffen from / so hettet ihr keines Luthers bedorft. Si vos sacrificuli pij essetis, non indiguissetis censore, & morum correctore Luthero.
units.tr: {b} The life of the religious stank so much before the common people that Emperor Charles V, when the clergy complained to him about Luther at the Diet of Augsburg, answered: "If you priests were pious, you would not need Luther as a censor and corrector of morals." If you priests were pious, you would not have needed Luther as censor and corrector of morals.

units.la: Jam superstitionibus ita erant omnia Oppleta: ut celebris monasterii Neuhusani in Vangionibus Abbas dixerit: (vera narro) Wann Lutherus nicht kommen were / sie hetten die leute vberzeden wollen / daß sie hew gefressen hetten. hetten. Hoc est: Si Lutherus non venisset: se persuasuros fuisse populo: ut fæno latrantem stomachum placarent.
units.tr: Superstitions had already filled everything to such a degree that the Abbot of the famous monastery of Neuhausen in the Vangiones said (I tell the true story): "If Luther had not come, they would have persuaded the people that they had eaten hay." That is: If Luther had not come, they would have persuaded the people to appease their barking stomach with hay.

units.la: a Itaque Joannes Misnensium Episcopus tum fassus est: se sacra Biblia legentem, Religionem præsenti valdè dissimilem invenire. Qui idem cum paulò ante obitum à Teccelio indulgentias denuò vendi audiisset, dixit: hunc fore institorem indulgentiarum ultimum: quod nimia ipsius, & intoleranda esset impudentia.
units.tr: {a} So John, Bishop of Meissen, then confessed that when he read the holy Bible, he found a religion very unlike the present one. When he had heard shortly before his death from Tetzel that indulgences were being sold again, he said that this man would be the last indulgence-hawker, because his shamelessness was excessive and intolerable.

units.la: b Certè nequissimus Monachus Magdeburgi opulentam fœminam, peccata sua cõsitentem, absolvere noluit; nisi centum florenis ab ea numeratis. Super qua re cum illa ordinarium suum confessionarium, Monachum Franciscanum consuluisset, respondit ille: Deum peccata gratis remittere, non institorum more vendere. Rogavit autem fœminam: Teccelio ut ne aperiret, à quo hoc responsi tulisset. Et sanè cum causam non numeratæ pecuniæ Teccelius audiisset, aut igni aut exilio adjudicandum huius consilii autorem dixit.
units.tr: {b} Certainly a most wicked monk at Magdeburg was unwilling to absolve a wealthy woman who confessed her sins, unless she first counted out a hundred florins. When she consulted her regular confessor, a Franciscan friar, about this matter, he answered: "God forgives sins freely, not for sale like the hawkers." He asked the woman, however, not to reveal to Tetzel from whom she had received this answer. And indeed, when Tetzel heard of the refusal of the money, he said that the author of this advice should be condemned either to the fire or to exile.

units.la: Ab hoc tempore universæ Europæ oppidulum VVittemberga innotuit. Audivimus à præceptoribus nostris: diversarum gentiū studiosos, Lutheri & Melanchthonis audiendi gratiâ, VVittembergam profectos, ad primum oppidi conspectum complicatis manibus Deo gratias egisse: quod sicut olim è Sione, ita isto seculo è VVittemberga Evangelicæ veritatis lucem in remotissima regna voluisset diffundi.Compertumq; est,
units.tr: From this time the little town of Wittenberg became known throughout all Europe. We have heard from our teachers that scholars of various nations, travelling to hear Luther and Melanchthon, on first catching sight of the town folded their hands and gave thanks to God that, as once from Zion, so in this age from Wittenberg, He had willed the light of evangelical truth to be spread to the most distant kingdoms. And it is well established that…

units.la: Cæterùm Lutherus propositiones suas misit ad Albertum Archiepiscopum Moguntinum, itemq; ad Hieronymum Episcopum Brandeburgicum. Ab illo nihil responsi tulit: erat enim (quod Lutherus ignorabat) particeps rapinarum Tecelianarum: hic Luthero per literas & Abbatem quendā significat: optare se, & petere, ut paululùm differat editiones probationum suarum: de indulgentiis etiam sermonem vulgarem editum valdè nolle. Ad quæ Lutherus: Benè sum contentus: malo obedire, quàm miracula facere, etiamsi possem.
units.tr: Moreover, Luther sent his propositions to Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, and likewise to Jerome, Bishop of Brandenburg. He received no answer from the former, for he (which Luther did not know) was a partner in the Tetzelian plunder. The latter signified to Luther through letters and a certain abbot that he wished and asked that he delay somewhat the publication of his proofs, and that he very much disliked the vernacular sermon published on indulgences. To this Luther replied: "I am quite content. I prefer to obey rather than to work miracles, even if I could."

units.la: Francofurti ad Viadrum Teccelius Lutheri Thesibus contrarias opponit, à Doctore Conrado VVimpina confectas: quibus Papam Petro; crucem à Papa erectam, cruci Christi comparat. Disputationi illi trecenti Monachi interfuerunt.
units.tr: At Frankfurt on the Oder, Tetzel set against Luther's Theses the counter-theses drawn up by Doctor Konrad Wimpina. In them he compared the Pope with Peter, and the cross set up by the Pope with the cross of Christ. Three hundred monks took part in that disputation.

units.la: Annum hunc quidam in hoc Cantici Ambrosiani versu comprehendi observavit:
units.tr: Someone has observed that this year is contained in this verse of the Ambrosian hymn:

units.la: TIbI CHERVBIN & SERAPHIN INCESSABILI VOCE PROCLAMANT.
units.tr: To you the Cherubim and Seraphim proclaim with unceasing voice.

units.la: Et sane eventibus etiam aliis insignibus annus hic est memorabilis.
units.tr: And indeed, this year is also memorable for other remarkable events.

units.la: {a} Fridericus Saxoniae Elector cum fratre Duce Johanne, & nepote Johanne Friderico, Vinariae in pervigilio natalis Christi ad sacra frequenti comitatu iturus, videt supra arcem, coelo sereno, fulgentem crucem purpuream satis magnam, & perspicue expressa figura. Stant aliquandiu attoniti spectatores: At Fridericus cum fratre de religione colloquens, eo signo futura certamina de doctrina, & domus Saxonicae pericula portendi vaticinatur.
units.tr: (a) Frederick, Elector of Saxony, was about to go with his brother, Duke John, and his nephew John Frederick, to Weimar for the sacred service on the eve of Christ's birth, with a large retinue. He saw above the castle, in a clear sky, a purple cross, quite large and clearly formed. The onlookers stood astonished for some time. But Frederick, talking about religion with his brother, prophesied from that sign that conflicts over doctrine lay ahead and that dangers threatened the house of Saxony.

units.la: {b} Joannes Franciscus Picus Mirandula Romae in Concilio illustri Pontificem ad reformationem Ecclesiae splendida oratione hortatur. Et consensum tum est in hanc sententiam: Ecclesiae Romanae mores esse reformandos.
units.tr: (b) Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, at the famous Council in Rome, urged the Pontiff with a brilliant speech to reform the Church. And at that time agreement was reached on this view: the morals of the Roman Church must be reformed.

units.la: {c} Neapoli nascuntur duo insignes Fidei confessores, Galeacius Caracciolus Marchio Vici, Pauli IV. Pontificis sororis filius, Januario, & Joannes Bernhardinus Bonifacius, Marchio Oriae, & Dominus terrarum Francouillae & Casalis novi, Februario mense: quorum uterq; agnita doctrina Evangelii, ministerio Lutheri repurgata, perpetuo exilio docuit: Christum omnibus huius vitae bonis esse praeferendum.
units.tr: (c) At Naples, in February, were born two outstanding confessors of the faith: Galeazzo Caracciolo, Marquis of Vico, son of the sister of Pope Paul IV, was born in January; and Giovanni Bernardino Bonifacio, Marquis of Oria and lord of Francavilla and Casale Nuovo. Each of them, once he had come to know the doctrine of the Gospel and had been cleansed by Luther's ministry, taught in lifelong exile that Christ is to be preferred to all the goods of this life.

units.la: In Helvetia Zwinglius Glaronâ ad famosum illud Virginis Eremitanæ templum (zum Einsiedeln) evocatur: quo cupidè profectus est, tum quod maximus illuc hominum ex omnibus ferè mundi partibus esset confluxus, quâ occasione existimabat se Christum & eius veritatem in regiones & varias & remotas divulgare posse: tum quod Abbas loci esset Nobilissimus Cunradus à Rechenberg, superstitionum osor, & missatici sacrificii non obscurus hostis: qui aliquando Visitatoribus, ut missam celebraret, hortantibus, respondit: Si vere Christus est in hostia, indignus sum, qui illum intuear, indignior, qui Patri offeram. Si non est in hostia, væ mihi, si panem pro Deo populo adorandum proponam.
units.tr: In Switzerland Zwingli was summoned from Glarus to that famous shrine of the Hermit Virgin at Einsiedeln (zum Einsiedeln). He went there eagerly, both because a very great crowd of people had gathered there from almost every part of the world, an occasion through which he thought he could spread Christ and his truth into many distant regions, and because the abbot of the place was the most noble Konrad von Rechberg, a hater of superstitions and no secret enemy of the Mass. When the visitors urged him to celebrate Mass, he replied: "If Christ is truly in the host, I am unworthy to look upon him, and even more unworthy to offer him to the Father. If he is not in the host, woe to me if I set before the people bread to be adored as God."

units.la: Thuringiæ suscitavit Deus Evangelistam Fridericum Myconium Francum. Is cum ordinem Fratrum minorum aliquandiu sectatus fuisset Annæbergæ, Lipsiæ, Vinariæ, & anno superiore, ætatis vigesimo quinto, ipso die Pentecostes, præsentibus Joanne, & Joanne Friderico, Ducibus Saxoniæ, Vinariæ sacris initiatus fuisset, hoc anno ad ministerium docendi à Vinariensibus vocatur.
units.tr: God raised up in Thuringia the evangelist Friedrich Myconius, a Franconian. After he had for some time followed the Franciscan order at Annaberg, Leipzig and Weimar, and in the previous year, at the age of twenty-five, had been ordained at Weimar on Pentecost day in the presence of John and John Frederick, Dukes of Saxony, he was called this year by the people of Weimar to the ministry of teaching.

units.la: Papisticum quid olebant initiò Sermones ad populum ab illo habiti. At ubi illi Deus intùs, Lutherus foris concionatus est, primus in Thuringia Papatui contradixit, & concredita sibi fidei mysteria volentibus auditoribus pervulgavit.
units.tr: At first his sermons to the people smelled of something Papist. But when God was within him and Luther without, he preached, and he was the first in Thuringia to speak against the Papacy, and, as his hearers wished, he made known the mysteries of the faith entrusted to him.

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI M D XVIII.
units.tr: The Year of Christ 1518

units.la: LUTHERI, mandato Præsulis Brandeburgici, parituri, & quieturi, pennam novi acuunt adversarii, Joannes Eccius Ingolstadiensis, Sylvester Prieras Romanus, Jacob Hochstrat Lovaniensis, Theologi. Ille respondens Hochstrato animum crudelem & sanguinarium exprobrat: Eccii Obeliscos suis Asteriscis configit: Sylvestri verò Dialogo, verè, ut ait, Sylvestro, solius Thomæ autoritate pugnanti, sacram scripturam opponit: & , quò magis illi furunt, eò amplius, inquit,procedo: relinquo priora, ut in illis latrent: sequor posteriora, ut & illa allatrent.
units.tr: At the command of the Bishop of Brandenburg, Luther was to submit and keep quiet, but his new adversaries sharpened their pens: John Eck of Ingolstadt, Sylvester Prierias of Rome, and Jacob Hochstraten of Louvain, theologians. Luther replied to Hochstraten by charging him with a cruel and bloodthirsty spirit. He pierced Eck's obelisks with his own asterisks. Against Sylvester's dialogue, which, as he said, fought truly "for Sylvester" on the sole authority of Thomas, he set Holy Scripture. And he added: "The more these men rage, the further I advance. I leave my earlier points so that they may bark at them, and I pursue my later ones so that they may bark at those too."

units.la: Sylvester non ita multò post epitomen responsionis ad Lutherum edit: ad quam epistolâ respondet Martinus, Sylvestri scriptum Satanicum appellat: Romam, si idem quod Sylvester sentiat, ipsissimam Antichristi sefti sedem pronuntiat : quæ causa fuit, cur silentium Prierati fit indictum.
units.tr: Not long after, Sylvester published an abridged reply to Luther. Martin answered this letter, calling Sylvester's writing Satanic, and declaring that Rome, if it thought as Sylvester did, was the very seat of Antichrist. This was the reason why Prierias was ordered to be silent.

units.la: Vivebat tum VVitteberga Andreas Bodensteinius , patria Carolostadius , gente Francus Germanicus , qui Romæ studiis Theologiæ operam dederat , & in Germaniam reversus VVitteberga Doctor Theologus creatus , in Professorum sacrorum ordinem adscitus , & in templo Arcis Canonicus ac Archidiaconus fuerat declaratus. Cuius sub Decanatu Lutherus Theologiæ Doctor est renunciatus. Hic inter primos fuit VVitteberga , qui Lutheri doctrinæ adstipularetur , & eam etiam scriptis nonnullis defendere non dubitaret. Saxo Elector Carolostadii huius & D. Lutheri patrocinium non rogatus suscipit : nec patitur , ut Lutherus ad Urbem trahitur : studiosi VVittembergenses positiones Teceliianas , Halâ Saxonum allatas , in foro cremant: Lutherus , omnibus dissuadentibus , tamen obedientiæ satisfacturus ad Capitulum Heidelbergense proficiscitur.
units.tr: At that time Andreas Bodenstein, born at Carlstadt, of Frankish German stock, was living at Wittenberg. He had studied theology at Rome, and on returning to Germany he was made a doctor of theology at Wittenberg, admitted to the order of sacred professors, and appointed canon and archdeacon in the castle church. Under his deanship Luther was proclaimed doctor of theology. He was among the first at Wittenberg to support Luther's teaching, and he did not hesitate to defend it in several writings. The Elector of Saxony took up the patronage of this Carlstadt and of Dr Luther without being asked. He would not allow Luther to be dragged to Rome. The Wittenberg students burned the Tetzelian theses, which had been brought from Halle in Saxony, in the marketplace. Luther, though all advised against it, set out for Heidelberg to the chapter, in order to satisfy obedience.

units.la: Ut Herbipoli ab Episcopo , ita Heidelbergæ à Comite Palatino Wolfgango ., honorificè excipitur: apud Augustinianos (Collegium sapientiæ indigetatur hodiè) disputat: paradoxis xxviiii.ex Paulo de justificatione fidei propositis : inter quæ eminent ista: Liberum arbitrium post peccatum res est de solo titulo.
units.tr: At Würzburg he was received with honour by the bishop, and at Heidelberg by the Count Palatine Wolfgang in the same way. At the Augustinians' house (now called the College of Wisdom) he held a disputation on twenty-nine paradoxes concerning justification by faith, drawn from Paul. Among them stand out these: "Free will after sin is a thing in name only."

units.la: Non ille justus est, qui multum operatur sed qui sine opere multum credit in Christum.
units.tr: "He is not righteous who works much, but he who, without works, believes much in Christ."

units.la: Interfuit disputationi Martinus Bucerus. Is quâ potuit manus celeritate excepit, quae inter disputandum à Luthero dicta, eaque cum Beato Rhenano communicavit, addito hoc Lutheri elogio.
units.tr: Martin Bucer attended the disputation. As quickly as he could, he took down in writing what Luther said during the debate, and he shared these notes with Beatus Rhenanus, adding this praise of Luther:

units.la: Lutherus in suorum Fratrum apud nos celebrata Synodo literaria pugna solenni more praefectus, ea disputavit paradoxa, qua non modo opinionem omnium superarent, sed etiam pleraque visa sunt haretica. Mira eius in respondendo suavitas, in audiendo incomparabilis longanimitas, in dissolvendo Pauli agnovisse acumen, non Scoti, adeo brevibus, eque divina scriptura penu depromptis responsis in sui admirationem facile cunctos adduxit. Cum Erasmo illi conveniunt omnia, uno hoc hic praestat, quod, qua ille tantum insinuat, hic aperte docet.
units.tr: "Luther, appointed in the customary manner to conduct the solemn literary contest held among our brothers here at the Synod, put forward paradoxes which not only surpassed the opinion of all, but also seemed to many to be heretical. His gentleness in answering was remarkable, his incomparable patience in listening was remarkable, and in resolving the arguments he showed the sharpness of Paul, not of Scotus. With such brief answers, drawn from the store of divine Scripture, he easily brought everyone to marvel at him. He agrees with Erasmus in everything; he surpasses him in this one respect, that where Erasmus only hints, he teaches openly."

units.la: In reditu Erfurti literas dedit ad Judocum Isennacensem Theologum, praeceptorem suum: quibus scribit: in doctrina gratia & operum secum sentire totam Universitatem VVittembergensem, excepto uno fermè Licentiato: sed & Principem, & Episcopum ordinarium suum, multos Pralatos, & ingeniosiores cives uno uno ore dicere: sese prius non novisse Christum & Evangelium. Fatetur etiam, se ex Iudoco primo omnium audivisse: solis Canonicis libris deberi fidem, caeteris omnibus iudicium.
units.tr: On his way back through Erfurt he wrote a letter to Jodocus of Eisenach, a theologian and his own teacher, in which he writes: "In the doctrine of grace and works, the whole University of Wittenberg thinks with me, except for almost one licentiate. But the Prince, and his ordinary bishop, many prelates, and the more gifted citizens all say with one voice that they did not previously know Christ and the Gospel." He also confesses that he first heard this from Jodocus: "Faith is owed to the canonical books alone; all other writings are subject to judgement."

units.la: Domum reversus Lutherus, edit propositionum suarum de indulgentiis resolutiones & declarationes, quas Leoni X. dicat Dominicâ Trinitatis. Causas editionis aperit, partim ad Leonem, partim ad Episcopum Brandeburgicum, epistolis: ut mitiget adversarios: ut desideria multorum expleat:
units.tr: On returning home, Luther published the resolutions and explanations of his propositions on indulgences, which he dedicated to Leo X on Trinity Sunday. He sets out the reasons for publishing them, partly in a letter to Leo and partly in a letter to the Bishop of Brandenburg: to soften his adversaries, and to satisfy the wishes of many,

units.la: ut ne errare sinat eos, qui putant omnia esse asserta. Inter quae sunt, inquit, de quibus dubito, nonnulla ignoro: aliqua etiam nego, nulla vero pertinaciter affero. Obsecrat Brandeburgicum; ut arrepto calamo, quaecunque visum, aboleat, aut igne facto, universa comburat: protestatur se disputare, non determinare. Sic ad Leonem X: prostratum, inquit, pedibus me offero Beatittua cum omnibus quae sum & habeo: vivifica, occide, voca, revoca, approba, reproba: vocem tuam vocem Christi, in te praesidentis & loquentis, agnoscam.
units.tr: and so as not to let those who think that everything has been asserted go astray. "Among these things," he says, "there are some about which I have doubts, some I do not know, and some I even deny, but I stubbornly assert none." He begs the Brandenburger that, taking up his pen, he should annul whatever seems fit, or, lighting a fire, burn the whole thing. He protests that he is disputing, not determining. So to Leo X: "Prostrate at your feet, Most Blessed Father, I offer myself, with all that I am and have. Make me alive, kill me, call me, recall me, approve me, reject me. I will recognise your voice as the voice of Christ, who presides in you and speaks through you."

units.la: Maximilianus Caesar de eventu harum disputationum solicitus, Pontificem officii admonet. Is Lutherum Romam evocat. Hic in Germania se audiri petit, loco & judicibus idoneis: Saxo Elector à Caietano, Pontificis legato hoc impetrat Augustæ in Comitiis, quæ Maximilianus postrema celebravit.
units.tr: The Emperor Maximilian, worried about the outcome of these disputations, reminded the Pope of his duty. The Pope summoned Luther to Rome. Luther asked to be heard in Germany, in a suitable place and before suitable judges. The Elector of Saxony obtained this from Cajetan, the papal legate, at the Diet of Augsburg, which Maximilian held last.

units.la: Interea Luthero associatur fidus in negotio Evangelico promovendo parastates Philippus Melanchthon. Is in oppido Archipalatinatus Bretta anno 1497. 16. Februarii natus, & in bonarum artium ac linguarum studiis Heidelbergæ & Tubingæ educatus, à Friderico Saxoniæ Electore ex Academia Tubingensi vocatur Vvittembergam ad docendas Græcas literas. Ac Capnio autor est Philippo, ut conditione oblatâ utatur, ac in literis ad Philippum inter alia sic scribit, vaticinans: Ecce adsunt literæ piissimi Principis, manu ipsius subsignatæ, quibus pollicetur tibi beneficium & propitium se fore. Quare nunc haud affabor te poëticè, sed verâ utens promissione, Abrahæ fideli facta: egredere de terra tua, & de cognatione tua & de domo patris tui: & veni in terram, quam monstravero: faciamque te in gentem magnam, & benedicam tibi, & magnificabo nomen tuum, crisq; benedictus. Hæc Geneseos 12. Ita mihi præsagit animus, ita spero futurum de te, mi Philippe, meum opus & meum solatium. Hactenus Capnio.
units.tr: Meanwhile, Philip Melanchthon, a faithful helper in promoting the Gospel, joined Luther. He was born in the Lower Palatinate town of Bretten on 16 February 1497, and educated in the study of the liberal arts and languages at Heidelberg and Tübingen. Frederick, Elector of Saxony, called him from the University of Tübingen to Wittenberg to teach Greek. Capito advised Philip to accept the offered post, and in a letter to Philip he writes, prophesying: "Behold, here is a letter from the most pious Prince, signed by his own hand, in which he promises you a benefice and says that he will be favourable to you. So now I will not speak to you poetically, but using a true promise made to the faithful Abraham: 'Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father's house, and come into the land that I shall show you; and I will make you a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be a blessing.'" These are the words of Genesis 12. "So my spirit foretells, and so I hope it will be concerning you, my Philip, my work and my comfort." So far Capito.

units.la: Discedente Philippo Tubingâ, Simlerus præceptor, vir eruditione præstans, deplorandum esse toti civitati eius abitum,
units.tr: When Philip left Tübingen, Simler, his teacher, a man outstanding in learning, said that his departure was to be lamented by the whole city.

units.la: Integra epistola excitat in tertio libello epistolarum Eobani Hessi per Camerarium editarum epistola 8. p. 187. Tom. 5. Declamat. Philippi, pag. 187. abitum, dixit: & subiecit: Quotquot ibi essent docti homines, non esse tam doctos, ut intelligerent, quanta esset doctrina eius, qui inde evocatus discederet. Venit autem VVittembergam 25 Augusti, qui fuit dies Mercurii aetatis anno 22.
units.tr: The whole letter is given in the third little book of Eobanus Hessus's letters, edited by Camerarius, letter 8, p. 187, vol. 5 of the Declamations of Philip. He said: "Whatever learned men there were there, they were not so learned as to understand how great the learning was of the man who was leaving them, having been called away from there." He came to Wittenberg on 25 August, which was a Wednesday, in the twenty-second year of his age.

units.la: De Philippo ita Lutherus ad Spalatinum: Habuit orationem quarto die postquam venerat, plane eruditissimam & terssissimam, tanta gratia & admiratione omnium, ut iam non tibi id cogitandum sit: qua ratione eum nobis commendes. Abstraximus cito opinionem & visionem staturae & personae, & rem ipsam in eo gratulamur & miramur.
units.tr: Luther wrote about Philip to Spalatin as follows: "He gave a speech on the fourth day after he arrived, most learned and most polished, with such grace and admiration from everyone that you need no longer consider how you should recommend him to us. We quickly laid aside our opinion and mental picture of his stature and person, and we rejoice and marvel at the man himself."

units.la: Et alia epistola ad eundem: Philippum Graecissimum, eruditissimum, humanissimum, habe commendatissimum. Auditorium habet refertum auditoribus: inprimis omnes Theologos summos, cum mediis & infimis, studiosos facit Graecitatis. Et ad Joannem Langum: Eruditissimus & Graecanissimus Philippus Melanchthon apud nos Graeca profitetur, puer & adolescentulus, si aetatem consideres, caeterum noster aliquis, si varietatem, & omnium fere librorum notitiam spectes: tantum valet non solum in utraque lingua, sed utriusque lingua eruditione. Ebraeas quoque non incognitas habet literas.
units.tr: And in another letter to the same man: "Keep in mind Philip, most Grecian, most learned, most humane. His lecture hall is full of students; above all, he makes all the leading theologians, along with the middling and lowest students, into students of Greek." And to John Lang: "Philip Melanchthon, most learned and most Grecian, professes Greek among us. If you consider his age, he is a boy and a young man; but if you consider his range and his familiarity with almost all books, he is one of ours. Such is his power, not only in both languages, but in the learning of both. He is not unacquainted with Hebrew letters either."

units.la: Erasmus ad Oecolampadium hoc anno. De Melanchthone & sentio praeclare, & spero magnifice, tantum ut cum iuvenem nobis Christstus diu velit esse superstitem. Is prorsus obscura-bit Erasmum.
units.tr: Erasmus, writing to Oecolampadius this year: "I think very highly of Melanchthon, and I hope great things of him, provided that Christ wishes this young man to survive us for a long time. He will utterly overshadow Erasmus."

units.la: Augustam venit Lutherus sub initium Octobris, Caietano se sistit duodecimâ Octobris: humaniter ab eo accipitur: ad palinodiam sive revocationem, & promissum de abstinendo imposterum ab his & aliis, primûm blanditiis, deinde minis solicitatur. Ille errores sibi demonstrari petit. Cardinalis nullam syllabam ex sacris literis producit: tantùm decretum quoddam Clementis Pontificis de Indulgentiis, quod exstat in extravagante, urget: quod Lutherus cum scriptura pugnare docet, si secundum literam intelligatur: atque post aliquot dierum conflictationculas graviora veritus, & ut Polydorus Virgilius loquitur, metuens, ne Cardinalis rem omnem magis imperio quàm disputatione definiret, datis ad Cardinalem literis, & dispositâ Appellatione à Cardinali ad Papam, publicè affigendâ, Augustâ discedit vigesimo Octobris, reversus Witebergam 30. Octobris: quo die Tecelium ante annum adortus fuerat.
units.tr: Luther came to Augsburg at the beginning of October and presented himself to Cajetan on 12 October. He was received kindly by him, but was pressed, first with flattery and then with threats, to recant, and to promise to abstain henceforth from these and other such matters. He asked to be shown his errors. The cardinal produced not a single syllable from Holy Scripture; he merely pressed a certain decree of Pope Clement concerning indulgences, which is found in the Extravagantes, and which Luther taught was contrary to Scripture if it were understood according to the letter.
