After some days of little skirmishes, and fearing more serious consequences, and, as Polydore Vergil puts it, fearing that the cardinal would settle the whole matter by authority rather than by disputation, Luther gave letters to the cardinal and drew up an appeal from the cardinal to the Pope, to be posted publicly. He left Augsburg on 20 October and returned to Wittenberg on 30 October, the day on which he had attacked Tetzel a year before.

units.la: Caietanus ad Saxonem scribit, consulens, ut Lutherum vel ad Urbem mittat, vel ditione suâ eiiciat. Lutherus cogitat in Galliam: amici suadent: ut se Saxoni captivum det: Saxo veluti captum alicubi custodiret, scriberetque Legato: Lutherum captum, ptum, & sistendum in loco tuto ad respondendum.
units.tr: Cajetan writes to the Elector of Saxony, urging him either to send Luther to Rome or to expel him from his territory. Luther considers going to France; his friends advise him instead to surrender himself as a captive to the Elector, who would keep him in some safe place as though he were a prisoner, and would write to the Legate that Luther had been taken and would be held in a safe place to answer.

units.la: Saxo respondet Legato: se nec Romam, nec in exilium posse mittere Lutherum: cum nullius erroris convictus sit: & Academiæ utiliter inserviat. Petit ut eausa eius in publicâ disputatione in locis tutis cognoscatur: & errores eius ostendantur. Lutherus 29. Novembris per epistolam Saxoni valedicit, pro patrocinio gratias agit, abitum in alia loca parat. Saxo hanc Legato Pontificis mittit. Lutherum V Vittembergę manere iubet: qui pridie huius diei, id est 28 Novembris (cum audiislet Leonem X. Indulgentias novo edicto sanciisse: & videret hoc agi, ut violenter ipse opprimeretur ) appellavit à Papa ad Concilium, præmissâ & expressâ solenni protestatione: quod contra unam, sanctā, & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, quam totius orbis esse magistram non ambigat, sanctæ sedis autoritatem, ac sanctissimi Domini Papæ bene consulti potestatem, nihil dicere intendat.
units.tr: The Elector replies to the Legate that he can send Luther neither to Rome nor into exile, since he has not been convicted of any error, and since he is usefully serving the University. He asks that Luther's case be examined in a public disputation in safe places, and that his errors be shown. On 29 November Luther bids farewell to the Elector by letter, thanks him for his protection, and prepares to leave for other places. The Elector sends this letter to the Legate of the Pontiff, and orders Luther to remain at Wittenberg. Luther, on the day before this (that is, 28 November), having heard that Leo X had confirmed the indulgences by a new edict, and seeing that the aim was to crush him by force, appealed from the Pope to a Council, prefacing this with a solemn and express protestation: that he intended to say nothing against the authority of the holy see, or against the power of the most holy Lord Pope when well advised, against the one, holy, and apostolic Church, which he does not doubt is the teacher of the whole world.

units.la: Memoratu dignū est, quod inter tot támque graves conflictus Lutherus ad V Venceslaum Linckium scripsit sub finem huius anni: Mitto ecce acta mea acutius, quàm speraverit D. Legatus, edita: sed longè maiora parturit mihi iam calamus: nescio unde veniant ista meditationes: res ista nec dum habet initium, meo iudicio: tantum abest, ut finem
units.tr: It is worth recording that, amid so many and such grave conflicts, Luther wrote to Venceslaus Linck near the end of this year: "Behold, I am sending you my writings, published more sharply than the Lord Legate may have hoped; but my pen is already bringing forth far greater things. I do not know where these meditations come from; in my judgment this matter has not yet even begun, so far is it from an end

units.la: Tom 1. epist. Luth. nem possint sperare Romani Proceres. Mittam ad te nugas meas: ut videas: an recte divinem, Antichristum illum verum, iuxta Paulum, in Romana curia regnare: peiorem Turcis esse hodie puto me demonstrare posse.
units.tr: (Tom. 1, Epist. Luth.) that the Roman magnates can hope for one. I will send you my trifles, so that you may see whether I rightly conjecture that the true Antichrist, according to Paul, reigns in the Roman curia; I think I can now show that it is worse than the Turks."

units.la: Hac de re cogitanti mihi saepenumero in mentem venire solet fabula, cuius titulus est: Malum irritatione auctum: Quodam in oppido solebant de certis caeteribus excludi omnes vitiati quacunque corporis parte: erantque constituti, qui de illorum (si qui forte obrepsisse comperirentur) singulis vitiis singulos nummos exigerent. Hi aliquando claudo conspecto, cum exigerent ab eo multam, & renitentem invaderent, scabiem in eo etiam deprehendunt. Ergo postulant iam nummos duos. Etiam tunc illo refragante, apparet lippitudo oculorum. Tum isti, iam tres dabis nummos, inquiunt. Egone? inquit ille. Pugnabo potius. In lucta igitur ea apparet hernia quoque. Tum exegere tandem nummos quatuor ab eo: qui se uno liberare potuisset. Fabula narratur contra pertinaces, & propugnatores vitiorum suorum. Narratur & contra eos, qui renitendo & resistendo malis levibus, graviora sibi ipsi accersunt. Quid mollius dici potuisset: quam quod contra impudentissimas conciones de indulgentiis a Luthero tantum dicebatur?
units.tr: While I am considering this matter, a fable often comes to my mind, whose title is "Evil increased by irritation." In a certain town, all those afflicted in any part of the body were in the habit of being excluded from certain offices, and there were appointed officials who would exact from each of them one coin for each defect (if any were found to have slipped in). Once, on seeing a lame man, they demanded a fine from him, and as he resisted and they pressed him, they discovered a scab on him as well. So they now demand two coins. When he still objects, a dimness of the eyes appears. Then they say, "Now you must give three coins." "Me?" says he. "I'd rather fight!" In that struggle a hernia also appears. At last they extracted four coins from him, though he could have freed himself with one. The fable is told against the obstinate and the champions of their own vices. It is also told against those who, by resisting and opposing light evils, bring upon themselves graver ones. What could have been said more mildly than what was said by Luther against the most shameless sermons on indulgences?

units.la: Magnus omninò animus fuit in Luthero. Augustam profecturus, pedester venit Vinariam, in monasterioque pernoctat. Jo- annes Kestnerus, Monachorum Vicarius & Administrator, inter alia ad Lutherum: Mi frater, habebis Augusta Italos, homines doctissi-mos & acutissimos, & antagonistas acerrimos, qui plurimum tibi facessent negotii: valde metuo, ne causa excidas: profectò in ignem te coniicient, & flammis exurent. Cui Luthetus periocum respondit: si urticis me usserint: aliquo modo tolerabile erit: sin igne, nimiùm grave & intolerabile, addens hanc exhortationem: interpone quaeso tuas preces apud Deum pro me: & ora Christum filium eius, cuius est causa hac: ut mihi adsit: quàm si obtinuerit; mihi obtenta erit: sin verò causâ exciderit: nec ego eam obtinere potero: atq; ita ipse solus ignominiam reportabit.
units.tr: Luther had a truly great spirit. Setting out for Augsburg, he went on foot to Weimar, and spent the night in the monastery. John Kestner, Vicar and Administrator of the Monks, wrote to him, among other things: "My brother, you will have at Augsburg Italians, men most learned and most keen, and very fierce antagonists, who will cause you a great deal of trouble. I greatly fear that you will fail in your cause; surely they will cast you into the fire and burn you with flames." To this Luther replied with a jest: "If they burn me with nettles, it will be somewhat tolerable; but with fire, it will be too grievous and intolerable," adding this exhortation: "Please interpose your prayers with God on my behalf, and beseech Christ, His Son, whose cause this is, to stand by me. If He obtains it, it will be obtained for me; but if the cause fails, I too shall be unable to obtain it, and so He alone will bear the disgrace."

units.la: Oratori Principis Montis ferratensis Augustæ rogatus: ubinam locorum mansurus sit tutò? sub cælo, respondet.
units.tr: When asked by the envoy of the Prince of Montferrat at Augsburg where he would remain safely, he answered: "Under heaven."

units.la: Profecturus Augustam, cum ab Alberto Comite Mansfeldico de periculo moneretur: quanto magis, inquit, illi minantur: tanto magis ego confido: uxor mea & liberi mei provisi sunt: agri, domus, substantia, cuncta disposita: gloria & nomen iam discerpitur: unum superest, imbecille &, fractum corpusculum: quod si abstulerint, forte duabus, vel unâ vivendi horâ me pauperiorem facient: animam verò non auferent. Canto cum Ioanne Reuchlino, qui pauper est, ni-hil timet: nihil perdere potest: sed spe bonâ latus sedet: nam sperat acquirere.
units.tr: When about to set out for Augsburg, and warned of the danger by Count Albert of Mansfeld, he said: "The more they threaten, the more I trust. My wife and children are provided for; fields, house, property, everything is arranged. My glory and name are already being torn to pieces; one thing remains, my feeble and broken little body; if they take that, they will make me poorer by two or one hours of life, but they will not take my soul. I sing with John Reuchlin, who is poor and fears nothing; he can lose nothing, but sits cheerfully with good hope, for he hopes to gain."

units.la: Ubi Augustæ intellexit: Caietanum Cæsaris & Principum animos à se abalienare, sic ille ad Spalatinum: Ego in his omnibus nihil timeo: quod si etiam obtinuerit eorum vel adulatio, vel potentia: ut omnibus me odiosum faciant: id mihi reliquum est & cordis & conscientiæ: quod omnia quæ habeo, quæq; ipsi impugnant, ex Deo me habere agnoscam & confitear: cui & ea ipsa libens & sponte refero & offero: si aufert, sint ablata: si servat, sint servata; & nomen eius sanctum & benedictum in secula, Amen.
units.tr: When he learned at Augsburg that Cajetan was alienating the minds of the Emperor and the Princes from him, he wrote thus to Spalatin: "In all these things I fear nothing. Even if their flattery or their power were to obtain for them that they make me hateful to everyone, there remains for me this comfort of heart and conscience: that I acknowledge and confess that all I have, and all that they attack, I have from God; and to Him I freely and willingly refer and offer even these things. If He takes them away, let them be taken; if He preserves them, let them be preserved; and His name is holy and blessed for ever. Amen."

units.la: Et ad Philippum Melanchthonem: Tu age virum, sicut & agis: & adolescentes recta doce: ego pro illis & vobis vado immolari, si Deo placet. Malo enim perire; &, quod unum mihi gravissimum est, vestrâ dulcissimâ conversatione carere in æternum; quàm ut revocem bene dicta, & studiis optimis perdendis occasio fiam. Augustâ, Feria 2. post Dionysii.
units.tr: And to Philip Melanchthon: "You play the man, as you are doing; and teach the young people aright. I go to be sacrificed for them and for you, if it pleases God. For I prefer to perish; and, what is the heaviest thing for me, to be deprived for ever of your most sweet company, rather than to recall what has been well said and become an occasion for the ruin of the best studies." At Augsburg, Monday after Dionysius.

units.la: E R A S M U S in caula Lutherana vario fuit animo. Hoc quidem anno sic ille de Luthero: Lutherus tam ignotus est mihi, quàm cui ignotissimus: nec adhuc vacavit hominis libros evolvere praeter unam & alteram pagellam: non quod fastidierim, sed quod per studiorum occupationes non datum sit ocium: & tamen hunc quidam, ut audio, mea confingunt adiutum opera. Si recte scripsit, mihi nihil debetur laudis: sin secus, nihil mereor probri, quando in omnibus illius lucubrationibus ne apiculus quidem illus est meus. Id verissimum esse comperiet, quisquis volet vestigare. Hominis vita magno omnium consensu probatur: iam id non leve praeiudicium est: tantam esse morum integritatem: ut nec hostes reperiant quod calumnientur. Quod si maximè vacasset legere: mihi non tantum arrogo: ut de tanti viri scriptis velim pronunciare: etiamsi nunc passim pueri magna temeritate pronúcient: hoc erroneum, illud haereticum. Imò adversus Lutherum aliquando fuimus iniquiores: ne quid invidia recideret in bonas literas: quas nolebam amplius onerari.
units.tr: Erasmus was of varying mind about the Lutheran cause. This year he spoke thus of Luther: "Luther is as unknown to me as anyone can be; nor have I yet had leisure to read the man's books, apart from a page or two, not because I scorn them, but because no free time has been given me amid the occupations of study. And yet, as I hear, some people are fabricating that he has been helped by my work. If he has written rightly, I deserve no praise; if otherwise, I deserve no reproach, since in all his writings not even a little bit of mine is found. Whoever wishes to investigate will discover this to be most true. The man's life is approved by the general consent of all; now this is no slight presumption: that his moral integrity is so great that not even his enemies can find anything to calumniate. But even if I had had the greatest leisure for reading, I do not claim so much for myself as to wish to pronounce upon the writings of so great a man, even though boys now everywhere pronounce with great rashness: this is erroneous, that heretical. Indeed, at times we have been more unfair to Luther, lest any envy should rebound upon the good letters, which I did not want to be burdened further."

units.la: Et alibi: eò vanitatis processerat frigida illa disputatrix Theologia: ut necesse fuerit ad fontes revocare. Sed tamen illa quoque corrigi malim, quàm explodi: aut certè tolerari: donec potior aliqua Theologiae ratio fuerit parata. Multa praeclarè monuit Lutherus: sed utinam civilius admonuisset. Plures haberet & fautores & propugnatores, & uberiorem messem demeteret Christo. Et tamen impium sit, illu in his, quae recte dixit, prorsus indesensum relinquere: ut posthac nemo sit, qui verum ausit proloqui. Non est huius conditionis, nec huius ingenii, de illius doctrina pronuntiare. Hactenus certè profuit mundo. Nonnulli sunt adacti ad evolvendos veterum Theologorum libros: alii, quo sibi consulerent: alii, quò Lutherò negotium facesseret. Iterum.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "That cold disputatious theology had gone so far into vanity that it was necessary to recall it to the sources. Yet I would rather have it corrected than exploded, or at least tolerated, until some better system of theology had been prepared. Luther admonished many things admirably, but would that he had admonished more courteously! He would have had more both supporters and defenders, and would have reaped a richer harvest for Christ. And yet it would be impious to leave him wholly undefended in those things which he has rightly said, so that henceforth no one would dare to speak the truth. It is not of my condition or my talent to pronounce on his teaching. Thus far at least he has profited the world. Some have been driven to unroll the books of the old theologians; others, in order to look to their own interests; others, so that they might give Luther trouble. Again."

units.la: Epistolarum lib. II. ad Rectorem Acad. Erfurtensis.
units.tr: Letters, Book II, to the Rector of the University of Erfurt.

units.la: Iterumque: Ego Lutherum nec accuso, nec defendo. Sic esse, res ipsa docebit. Quare nolim me horum negotiis admisceri.
units.tr: And again: "I neither accuse Luther nor defend him. The matter itself will show how things stand. For that reason I would not want to be mixed up in their affairs."

units.la: Contrà Lutherus hoc eodem anno sic de Erasmo: Ego apud eos (id est, omnes) qui bonas literas vel oderunt studio, vel nesciunt ignaviâ, Erasmum summis laudibus semper essero, atque tueor, quoad possum, omni industriâ cavens: ne evomam ea, in quibus dissentio: ne mea quoque voce suam invidiam in illum confirment. Quanquam sunt quam multa in Erasmo, quæ mihi ad cognitionem Christi longè aliena videantur: si tamen ut Theologus, non ut Grammaticus, loqui debeo: alioqui nihil eruditius, nihil ingeniosius viderit vel ipse Hieronymus, tanto prædicatus ab Erasmo præconio. Atq; hoc meum de Erasmo iudicium, si alteri feceris notum: tum scias amicitiæ iura te violasse.
units.tr: On the other hand, Luther this same year wrote of Erasmus as follows: "Among those who either hate good letters from zeal or are ignorant of them from laziness, I always praise Erasmus with the highest praise and defend him as far as I can, taking all care to avoid spitting out those points on which I disagree, so that they may not strengthen their own ill will toward him by my voice as well. And yet there are many things in Erasmus which seem to me quite alien to the knowledge of Christ, if indeed I ought to speak as a theologian and not as a grammarian. Otherwise, not even Jerome himself, so highly praised by Erasmus, will have seen anything more learned or more ingenious. And if you make known to another this my judgment of Erasmus, then know that you have violated the laws of friendship."

units.la: VVolffgangus Fabritius Capito quid ex consilio Erasmi, Lutherum hoc tempore monuerit, non est reticendum. Vidi, inquit, concionem tuam de pœnitentia, & alteram de condonationibus, utramque contra receptos huius ætatis mores apertis figuris militantem. Obstupui, de amici salute anxius, qui densis hostium turmis ita nudum obiicis latus, quamvis instrutissimus videre armis veritatis. Tu tamen longè aliis, male metuo, impugnaberis & periculum est, ne vi res geratur. Quod si ex fide consulenti aures dignaris, expertus moneo, Sertorii consilium ampleamplectaris. Crede mihi, carptim facies, quod viribus ne labefactare quidem potuisses. Arcem, ut vides, undiq; munitam occupant, triplici vallo septi, velut extra tela. quod dicitur, stertunt, authoritate Pontificiâ, hoc est, universalis Ecclesiæ potentiâ, tyrannorum, & omnium Scholarum pertinaci consensu. Profecto triplicem hunc Cacodæmonis funem crassissimum haud facile unquam rumpes. Opus est Alexandro quodam, ceu Gordii vincula gladio confidenter dissolvente: ingenio aut ratione fieri difficultas est: piorum simplicitas à nutu & renutu pendet huius factitiæ Ecclesiæ, argutioribus animum tyrannis adimit. Porro qui omnibus vero maiorem sanctimoniam peririamq; Christi venditamus Theologi, superstitio nostro committimus Christum, Religionis omnes invehimus sordes, pretextúque pietatis nostrum probè compendium curamus. Proinde ne in irritum conatus iste egregius vergat, obtegas, oro, quemlibet fucum, quò hamum queas infigere citiùs lectori, quàm sibi putet insidiæ fieri. Sic Apostoli nihil subitò, nihil suapte urgebant. Vbiq; decoram humanitatem custodierunt. Per quos enim Paulus ingreditur caniculos in epistola ad Romanos, quid non facit, quò gratiam apud eos tueatur? simulat, dissimulat, inducit, educit, ostendit procul divitem supellectilem, continuò celat, prorsusque sic sermonem librat, ne vel odium, vel fastidium suboriatur. Eius ingenij exemplis acta Apostolorum redundant. Sic Divus Paulus in tumultu, similis tergiversanti, respondet: Non dicit: nihil loquor contra legem: sed, de resurrectione iudicor, interea reddens de observata lege rationem mirâ dicendi prudentiâ: siquidem obliquo ductu magna res securè conficiuntur. Quam vellem semper aliquam servares fenestram, quâ effugias, vel disputatione vexatus. His diebus à Roma libellum Sylvestri de Prioratis accepi, quem satis inepte in tuas Venias edidit: cui si respondendum, perpetuâ velim id fieri oratione, atque Christi veram ex Evangelis imaginem præbeas. Natum & auctam religionem, consuetudinem priscorum, rationem induere erroris, & variata Pontificum, adeoque Conciliorum decreta narres, expressâ notatione, ut oratio fidem sibi sensibus confirmet, quasi hausta ex fonte veritatis. Deinde singula deliramenta risu eleves frequentius, quàm serio conatu. Sedulò à Pontifice ladendo abstineas, quin omnem detorqueas invidiam in illum, tanquam impudenter adulantem, tanquam indigna affingentem Pontificis dignitati, tantùm ventris causâ: te apertis obsistere sycophantis, ansam mali præcidere conantem: passim ut tulerit facultas, inter agendum respondendi aditus præsepias, ut nequeat nisi incassum referire.
units.tr: It must not be passed over what Wolfgang Fabricius Capito advised Luther at this time, on the counsel of Erasmus. "I have seen your sermon on repentance and the other on indulgences, both fighting openly with figures against the accepted customs of this age. I was astonished, anxious for my friend's safety, that you expose your flank so bare to the dense squadrons of enemies, although you are most fully equipped with the weapons of truth. Yet you will be attacked from quite other directions, and I fear badly, and there is danger that the matter will be carried by force. But if you deign to listen to a counsellor who speaks in good faith, I advise you from experience to embrace the plan of Sertorius. Believe me, you will do piecemeal what you could not have shaken even with full strength. As you see, they occupy the citadel, fortified on all sides, enclosed by a triple rampart, as they say, safe beyond the reach of missiles: they snore, relying on Papal authority, that is, the power of the universal Church, on the stubborn consent of tyrants and of all the schools. Truly, you will not easily ever break this triple, very thick cord of the Evil Spirit. What is needed is some Alexander who will confidently loosen the knots of Gordius with his sword, not by cleverness or reason, for difficulty is the result of those. The simplicity of the pious depends on the nod and the refusal of this made-up Church, which takes the spirit away from the more clever tyrants. Moreover, we theologians who sell to all the greater holiness and the true Christ, commit Christ to superstition, bring all the filth of religion upon ourselves, and under the pretext of piety we carefully look after our own profit. Therefore, lest this excellent attempt turn to nothing, I beg you to cover over whatever pretence you can, so that you may more quickly fix the hook in the reader, rather than he think that a trap is being set for him. So the Apostles never pressed anything suddenly, nothing on their own account. Everywhere they kept a becoming humanity. For through what tunnels Paul enters in his Epistle to the Romans, what does he not do to preserve favour with them? He pretends, he dissembles, he introduces, he leads out, he shows from afar his rich furnishings, he keeps hiding them at once, and so balances his speech that neither hatred nor disgust may arise. The Acts of the Apostles overflow with examples of this talent. So the divine Paul, in the tumult, answers like one who evades: he does not say, 'I say nothing against the law,' but, 'I am judged concerning the resurrection,' meanwhile giving an account of his observance of the law with wonderful prudence in speaking; for great matters are carried out safely by an oblique approach. I would wish that you always keep some window by which you may escape, even when harassed in disputation. These days I have received from Rome the little book of Sylvester on the Priories, which he has published rather foolishly against your Indulgences. If it must be answered, I would wish it done in a continuous oration, and that you present the true image of Christ from the Gospels. Set out how religion was born and grew, the custom of the ancients, the reasoning by which error put on its form, and the varying decrees of the Popes and so of the Councils, with explicit annotation, so that the discourse confirms its faith to the senses, as if drawn from the fountain of truth. Then ridicule each single piece of nonsense with laughter more often than with serious effort. Be careful to refrain from wounding the Pope, but turn all the odium away from him, as one who shamelessly flatters, as one who ascribes unworthy things to the dignity of the Pontiff only for the sake of his belly; while you, opposing the open sycophants, try to cut off the source of the evil, let there be everywhere, as far as opportunity allows, a way of replying placed in the midst of the action, so that they can only retort in vain."

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXIX.
units.tr: The Year of Christ 1519

units.la: SUB initium anni Leo X. Carolum Miltitium ex nobilitate Misnica Brevibus Apostolicis LXX. & amplius armatum, in Germaniam mittit, & Fridericum Saxonem aurea rosa, nescio quibus ceremoniis consecrata, singularis benevolentiae ergo donat, & Degenhartum Pfeffingerum, virum nobilem ex Friderici Consiliariis per literas rogat: ut Miltitio operam navet in expellendo Luthero, Satanae filio. Scribit in hanc sententiam etiam ad Georg. Spalatinū.
units.tr: EARLY in the year Leo X sent Carl von Miltitz, a nobleman of Meissen, into Germany, armed with more than seventy apostolic briefs. As a special mark of goodwill he gave Frederick of Saxony a golden rose, consecrated with I know not what ceremonies. He also wrote to Degenhart Pfeffinger, a nobleman and one of Frederick's counsellors, asking him to help Miltitz in driving out Luther, the son of Satan. He wrote to the same effect to Georg Spalatin.

units.la: Interea Maximilianus 12. Januar. moritur: gubernatio Imperii in Saxonicis partibus, lege Carolina ad Fridericū devolvitur: unde, cohibitis nonnihil adversariorum furoribus, aura mitior Lutherum afflat.
units.tr: Meanwhile Maximilian died on 12 January, and under the Carolingian law the government of the Empire in the Saxon territories passed to Frederick. Because the fury of his opponents was now somewhat restrained, a milder breeze began to blow upon Luther.

units.la: Miltitio autem negotium sibi commissum strenuè agente, Lutherus, Altēburgi cū eo colloquutus, duo promittit; silentium, si adversariis idem iniungatur: & palinodiā, si erroris convincatur. Deinde in eandē sententiam tertiā Martii dat literas ad Pontificem, valde demissas: quib. indicat: à palino-
units.tr: Miltitz, meanwhile, pursued the business entrusted to him with vigour. Luther met him at Altenburg and offered two things: silence, if the same were enjoined on his opponents; and a recantation, if he were convicted of error. Then, on 3 March, he wrote to the Pope to the same effect, in very humble terms, by which he shows that he shrinks from a recan-

units.la: cem, valde demissas: quib. indicat à palinodia... dia se prorsus abhorrere, aspersurâ aliquid maculæ ipsi sedi Apostolicæ: quod in Germania complures sint præstanti ingenio & eruditione viri, qui de tota controversia rectè iudicare possint. De indulgentiis se posthac nihil moturum: modò sileant etiam adversarii.
units.tr: tation utterly, since it would cast some stain on the Apostolic See itself; for in Germany there are many men of outstanding talent and learning who can judge the whole controversy rightly. He would hereafter move nothing concerning indulgences, provided that his adversaries also kept silent.

units.la: Quinto Kal. April. Lutherus literis ad Erasmum datis, amicitiam illius ambit. Cui Erasmus Lovanio valde amanter respondet: & laudatis Lutheri commentariis Psalmicis, expositóque iudicio clarorum per Angliam virorum de lucubrationibus ipsius honorifico, ad civilem in scribendo & disputando modestiam Martinum revocat.
units.tr: On the fifth day before the Kalends of April Luther wrote to Erasmus and sought his friendship. Erasmus replied most affectionately from Louvain, praising Luther's commentaries on the Psalms and reporting the honourable judgement on his writings of distinguished men throughout England. He called Martin back to a civil moderation in writing and disputing.

units.la: Idem Erasmus XVIII. Kal. Maias ad Fridericum Saxoniæ Ducem scribit; eumq; rogat: ne committat, ut se iustitiæ præsidé, quisquam innocens, prætextu pietatis, aliquorum impietati dedatur. Lutheri vitam innocentiæ nomine commendari: nec protinus hæreticum esse, qui huic aut illi displicet: plerosque illius accusatores suum agere negotium, vel quæstui suo consulentes, vel tyrannidi: nec facilè hæreseos suspicione onerandum eum, qui vitam Christo dignam agit.
units.tr: On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May Erasmus wrote again, this time to Frederick, Duke of Saxony, and asked him not to allow an innocent man to be handed over to the impiety of certain persons, under the pretext of piety, while he himself presides over justice. Luther's life, he said, was commended for its innocence, and a man is not at once a heretic because he displeases this person or that. Most of his accusers were pursuing their own business, either looking to their profit or serving their tyranny; and a man who lives a life worthy of Christ should not easily be burdened with the suspicion of heresy.

units.la: Menses Junius & Julius huius anni disputatione Lipsicâ nobilitati sunt. Superiore anno sententias, quas Lutherus de indulgentiis proposuit disputandas, Eccius obeliscis notavit,ijsque valde amarulentis. Ex illis refellit aliquot Carolostadius in conclusionibus suis, quæ exstant. Carolostadio respondit Eccius per Apologiam satis mitem. Apologiam edito libello Carolostadius confutavit: contentio hæc ut componeretur, egit cum Ec-cio Lutherus Augustæ, ut cum Carolostadio Lipsiæ, assentiente Georgio Saxoniæ Duce, congrederetur. Dies disputationi dicta XXVIII. Junii. Acta disputationis invenies de-scripta Tom. I. operum Latin. Luth. Ienen. pag. 242. Et ibidem per Melanchthonem ad Oecolampadium epistolâ pag. 361. Tomo item primo epistolarum Lutheri ad annum XIX. epistolâ ad Ioannem Langum pag. 161. & ad Spalatinum pag. 180. Descripsit eadem eleganti stylo Petrus Mosellanus epistolâ ad Bilibaldum Pirckamerum, quam M. S. ex Bibliotheca Pirckameri erutam, ut fidissimam rei gestæ nunciam, in gratiam lectoris adscribam: Sic igitur ille: Editum est nobis hisce diebus Lipsiæ rarum omninò & iucundum spectaculum. Nempe Theologorum insignium disputatorium congressus: de quo non dubito, quia plura scire gestias. Sed gravissimi morbi, qui me totos quatuordecim dies decumbere coëgit, reliquiæ, non sinunt rem accuratius perscribi. Tum itineris molestiæ, quod ex rei familiaris negotiis ad Treviros institui, mul-tum quoq; alacritatis adimunt. Itaq; capita rerum paucis tibi signabo. XVIII. Iunii, qui dies condictus erat, Illustrissimi Principis mei Georgii iussu & sumptu, magnificum sacrum mane, omnis generis musicâ adhibitâ, in honorem sancti Spiritus cæptum. Quo peracto, Doctores peregrini, qui disputaturi erant, honestissimâ totius scholæ nostræ pompâ in arcem deducebantur.
units.tr: The months of June and July of this year were made famous by the disputation at Leipzig. In the previous year Eck had marked with very bitter obelisks the theses which Luther had put forward for debate concerning indulgences. Some of them Carlstadt refuted in his conclusions, which still survive. Eck answered Carlstadt with a fairly mild Apologia. Carlstadt replied to the Apologia in a published pamphlet. To settle this quarrel, Luther at Augsburg arranged that he should meet Eck, just as Carlstadt was to meet him at Leipzig, with the assent of George, Duke of Saxony. The day fixed for the disputation was 28 June. You will find the acts of the disputation described in vol. I of Luther's Latin works, Jena edition, p. 242; and in the same place, by Melanchthon, in his letter to Oecolampadius, p. 361; likewise in vol. I of Luther's Letters, for the year 1519, in his letter to Johann Lang, p. 161, and to Spalatin, p. 180. Peter Mosellanus described the same events in an elegant style in a letter to Bilibald Pirckheimer. I shall copy it out for the reader's benefit, since it was taken from a manuscript in Pirckheimer's library and is a most faithful report of the affair. It runs thus: "There has been held for us in these days at Leipzig a rare and altogether delightful spectacle, namely a meeting for disputation of distinguished theologians. Of this I have no doubt you are eager to hear more. But the remnants of a very grave illness, which kept me in bed for a full fourteen days, do not allow me to write it out more carefully. The hardships of the journey, which I undertook to Trier on business concerning my estate, also take away much of my cheerfulness. So I shall indicate the main points to you briefly. On 18 June, the day that had been appointed, a magnificent sacred service was begun in the morning, at the command and expense of my most illustrious prince George, in honour of the Holy Spirit, with music of every kind. When this was finished, the visiting doctors who were to dispute were led to the castle in the most honourable procession of our whole school.

units.la: Ibi enim spatiosissimus locus in auditorium erat, aulaeis ac tapetis, pulpitis, suggestisq; instructus. Hunc locum armatorum civium manus ita obsedit, ut non cuivis gregario (confluxit enim ad illud spectaculum magna vis hominum, doctorum pariter & indoctorum) aditus pateret. Huc ubi ingressum est & consensum: ipse, consenso suggestu, Illustrissimi Principis mei nomine disputatores commonui sui officij, longâ oratione differens de disputandi ratione, praesertim in re Theologica. Quam partem liberius fortasse tractavi, quàm ut omnium auribus grata fuerit, Princeps ipse, lectam orationem, antequam pronunciaretur, vehementer probavit. Hoc unum mirabatur: esse tam stultos Theologos, imo malos, ut locum facerent eiusmodi reprehensionibus. Eam orationem, Principis iussu editam, hic unà mitto. Tu, si quando vacabit, lege, & iudica. Sed ad rem. Postea quam ipse perorâram, tibicines pariter, & litici nes, tum Cantores dulcissimo concentu canticum illud; Veni sancte Spiritus, ter modulabantur. Quod ipsum ex meo consilio Princeps demandârat.
units.tr: "For there was a very spacious hall prepared for the audience, furnished with hangings and carpets, with pulpits and platforms. This place was so beset by bands of armed citizens that no ordinary member of the crowd (for a great number of people, learned and unlearned alike, had gathered for that spectacle) had access to it. When the company had entered and taken their seats, I myself, having mounted the platform, addressed the disputants in my illustrious prince's name, reminding them of their duty in a lengthy speech on the manner of disputing, especially in theological matters. I may perhaps have treated this part rather too freely for it to please every ear, but the prince himself, having read the speech before it was delivered, greatly approved of it. He wondered at this alone: that there should be theologians so foolish, indeed so wicked, as to give occasion for such rebukes. I am sending you the speech here with this letter, published by the prince's command. Read it and judge when you have leisure. But to the matter. After I had finished my oration, the trumpeters and the pipers, and then the singers, sang that hymn, "Veni, sancte Spiritus," three times in the sweetest harmony. The prince had ordered this on my advice.

units.la: Hic finis apparatus. Iam prandij tempus appetebat. bat. Quare disputationis serium initium in horâ secundam dilatum est. Quod tempus ubi advenit: partes utrinque, pro more theologico, simplicitatem suam protestabantur. Martinus hoc adiecit: se hoc gravatim ferre, quod ex fratribus Praedicatoribus, qui eam tragœdiam primi excusitassent, nemo disputaturus adesset: cum tamen in singulis suis concionibus graviter Martinianos errores in invidiam vocassent. Commissi sunt primùm Carolostadius & Eccius, par omnino dissimile. Nam Carolostadius voce, vultu, gestu, incessuque modestiâ Theologicam prae se ferebat: disputabatque non ad ingenij gloriam, aut victoriam, sed veri, rectique inquisitionem: quare nihil nisi adhibitis libris asserebat, nihil item ab adversa parte adductum, admittebat, nisi sententiâ scriptoris ex praecedentib. & sequentibus collegisset. Quâ diligentiâ doctis se vehementer commendavit: indocti timorem & tarditatem interpretabantur. Eccius contra clamore, vultu militari ac truci, gestu histrionico penè, & incessu impetuoso, feroculus quispiam apparebat. Omnia illa externa corporis signa animum parùm Theologicum declarabant. Dixisses Gorgiam quempiam disputare, non Theologum. Adeo leviter & impudenter subinde se iactabat: magnam adeo iacturâ nominis sui apud nos fecit. Levissimè asserit, quae falsa sunt: impudentissimè negat, quae pro serto vera, idque cum iactatione sui, quo res fit odiosior.
units.tr: "That was the end of the preparations. By now the time for dinner was approaching, so the serious beginning of the disputation was postponed until two o'clock. When that hour came, the parties on each side, according to theological custom, protested their sincerity. Martin added this: that he took it hard that no one from the Dominican friars, who had first stirred up this tragedy, was present to dispute, although in their individual sermons they had bitterly brought Martin's errors into odium. Carlstadt and Eck were the first to be matched, a pair altogether unlike. For Carlstadt, in voice, look, gesture and bearing, showed a theological modesty; and he disputed not for the glory of his wit or for victory, but for the inquiry into truth and right. Hence he asserted nothing except with books at hand, and admitted nothing brought forward by the other side unless he had gathered the author's meaning from what came before and after. By this diligence he commended himself strongly to the learned; the unlearned interpreted it as fear and slowness. Eck, on the other hand, appeared as a rather bold and fierce fellow, with shouting, a soldierly and grim face, a gesture almost like an actor's, and a headlong stride. All those outward signs of the body showed a mind little given to theology. You would have said that some Gorgias was disputing, not a theologian. So lightly and shamelessly did he keep boasting of himself that he did great harm to his own reputation among us. He very lightly asserts what is false, and most shamelessly denies what is certainly true, and does so with boasting of himself, which makes the matter the more hateful.

units.la: Res fuit Eccio cum Carolostadio de libera arbitrio: omnéne bonum opus proficiscatur è divina gratia, an verò nonnihil etiam de suo conferat humani arbitrii actio? Priorem sententiam Carolostadius, posteriorem Eccius tuebatur. Tum illud iactatum: sitne omnis Christianorum vita pœnitentia? unde fluit, in opere suo hominem peccare. Contra quæ nisus est Eccius. Porro Martinus negavit Romani Pontificis potestatem primariam iure divino, hoc est, sacra scriptura testimoniis posse comprobari. Imò sacerdotem quemvis ex æquo (quod ad Pauli Theologiam attinet) Apostolis succedere, habereq; facultatem & culpæ & pœnæ remittenda, si necessitas ita ferat. Hic Eccius in adversum multa decreta, multas Patrum authoritates congessit, cum iure divino tantùm Primatus Pontificis esset asserendus. Ventum tandem est ad sacram ancoram, nempe illud Matth. xvi. Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam &c. Hic Martinus PETRAM solidam fidei confessionem interpretabatur, & totum corpus Ecclesiæ cum Origene, aut Christum ipsum cum Augustino. Eccius cum recentioribus, hominem Petrum, & eius successores. Eamq; expositionem aliquot Bernhardi & Hieronymi verbulis decerptis firmavit. Quæ omnia Martinus mirè elusit, per hoc: quod toties Ecclesia redderetur ἀνέφαλον, quoties Episcopus Romanus aliquis moreretur. Nam eo tempore, quo necdum surrogatus sit in sedem alius Pontifex, dubio procul ἀνέφαλον reddi Ecclesiam. Nam quod de Cardinalium cætu, qui interim agat Pontificem, respondeatur, duplici de causa frivolum esse. Primùm quia Cardinales haud ita multa ante secula esse cœperint, qui tamen multa capita faciant, non unum. Deinde quod, quæ jure divino statuantur, nullius hominis morte, imò ne cœlorum ruinâ interpellari possint. Iactata item in disputationis aleam indulgentia, sed magis pro luco, quam re seria. De purgatorio item disceptatum: non quod non esset, sed quomodo erga Deum afficerentur anima in illo supplicio detenta. Ejusmodi contentionibus tres penè hebdomades sunt consumptæ, certè, (quantum mihi judicare licet) maiore expectatione quàm fructu. Neque enim quidquam est decretum: nec ulla de re partes consenserunt. Res tota notariorum fide est excepta. Iudices disputatis sunt delecti Erphurdienses ac Parrhisienses: Erphurdienses, quantum privatim ex quorundam colloquio conjicere potui, gravatim tanti oneris sarcinam in humeros suos recipient: cum ob alias causas, tum maximè, quod Eccius optimos quosque & doctissimos Theologici ordinis, ut sibi suspectos, à judicio submovit. Hoc prajudicium vulgo jactatur: in primatu Pontificis asserendo Eccium se turpiter daturum. Vt ut est futurum, meâ nihil refert. Mihi hoc disceptandi genus theatricum nunquam visum est mansuetissimâ Christi doctrinâ dignum. Nec adduci possum, ut credam: spiritum sanctum, pacis authorem, ad eiusmodi pugnas unquam sese demittere. Christiana Theologiæ veritas citiùs impetratur orando, quàm inveniatur disceptando. Habes totam hanc disceptationem, ex tempore à me, & negligentissimè descriptam. Si qua reliqua sunt, fama ad te pertulit. Sed vide ne fidas. Tam est ficti quàm veri tenax: & sicut ut πολλὰ τῶ πλέμῳ κενὰ. Er-furti quinto nonas Augustas An. MDXIX. Ha-ctenus Mosellanus.
units.tr: The dispute between Eck and Carlstadt concerned free will: whether every good work proceeds from divine grace alone, or whether the action of the human will also contributes something of its own. Carlstadt defended the former view, Eck the latter. Then Eck put forward the claim that the whole life of Christians is repentance, from which it follows that a man sins in his own work. Against this Eck laboured. Further, Martin denied that the primacy of the Roman Pontiff can be proved by testimonies of Scripture to be by divine right. Indeed, any priest whatever (so far as Paul's theology is concerned) equally succeeds the Apostles and has the power of remitting both guilt and punishment, if necessity so requires. Here Eck heaped up many decrees against him and many authorities of the Fathers, whereas the primacy of the Pontiff ought to have been asserted by divine right alone. At last they came to the sacred anchor, namely that passage of Matthew 16: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church," and so on. Here Martin interpreted the ROCK as the solid confession of faith, and the whole body of the Church with Origen, or Christ himself with Augustine. Eck, with the more recent writers, took it as the man Peter and his successors, and he confirmed this exposition with a few words snatched from Bernard and Jerome. Martin cleverly mocked all of this by pointing out that the Church would be made headless [ἀνέφαλον] as often as any Roman bishop died. For at the time before another Pontiff had been put in the See, the Church without doubt became headless. As for the answer that a college of Cardinals acts in the meantime as Pontiff, it is, he said, frivolous for two reasons. First, because the Cardinals have not begun to exist for so many centuries, and yet they make many heads, not one. Second, because what is established by divine right cannot be interrupted by the death of any man, nor even by the collapse of the heavens. Indulgences were also tossed into the lottery of the disputation, but more for show than as a serious matter. Purgatory was also debated: not whether it exists, but in what way souls detained in that punishment stand towards God. Almost three weeks were spent in contentions of this kind, certainly (as far as I am able to judge) with more expectation than fruit. For nothing has been decided, and the parties have not agreed on any point. The whole affair has been taken down on the good faith of notaries. The judges chosen for the disputation are the Erfurt and Paris men. The Erfurt men, as far as I could guess from private conversation with some of them, will take up the burden of so great a task reluctantly, partly for other reasons, but chiefly because Eck removed from judgement, as suspect to himself, all the best and most learned men of the theological order. A prejudgement is spread among the common people: that Eck will disgracefully give way in asserting the primacy of the Pontiff. However it turns out, it makes no difference to me. This theatrical kind of debate has never seemed to me worthy of the most gentle doctrine of Christ. Nor can I be brought to believe that the Holy Spirit, the author of peace, ever lowered himself to such battles. The truth of Christian theology is obtained more quickly by prayer than found by disputing. You have the whole of this disputation, written down by me from memory and very carelessly. If there are any remaining details, rumour has carried them to you. But take care not to trust it: it is as tenacious of falsehood as of truth, and, as the proverb goes, many things are empty in war [πολλὰ τῷ πολέμῳ κενά]. At Erfurt, on the fifth day before the Nones of August, 1519." So far Mosellanus.

units.la: Hæc una disputatio plura alia scripta peperit: Luthero & Melanchthone de fide editorum à se Actorum huius colloquii cum Eccio disceptantibus.
units.tr: This one disputation gave rise to several other writings, in which Luther and Melanchthon debated the faithfulness of the editions of the Acts of this colloquy with Eck that they had published.

units.la: Carolostadius deinde & Eccius hoc & sequenti anno publicis scriptis mirè se mutuò deformarunt. Atq; hic fructus fuit disputationis Lipsicæ.
units.tr: Carlstadt and Eck then, in this year and the next, tore each other apart with public writings. This was the fruit of the Leipzig disputation.

units.la: Interfuit Disputationi Philippus quoq; Melanchthon, ad quem interloquentem iste auditus est Eccii sermo: Tace tu, Philippe, ac tua studia cura: ne me perturba.
units.tr: Philip Melanchthon also took part in the disputation, and Eck's remark was heard by him when he interjected: Be quiet, Philip, and attend to your own studies, and do not disturb me.

units.la: Georgius verò Saxoniæ Dux audità disputatione de potestate Romani Pontificis, Eccii & Lutherum manu pulsans dixit: sive hoc sit jure divino, sive humano, Romanus Pontifex est & manet summus Pontifex.
units.tr: Duke George of Saxony, having heard the disputation on the power of the Roman Pontiff, struck the table with his hand, turning to Eck and Luther, and said: whether this rests on divine or human law, the Roman Pontiff is and remains the supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Dum Lutherus & Eccius Lipsiæ de Indulgentiis disputant, ibidem in monasterio Dominicanorum moritur insatiabilis ille curiæ Romanæ Circitor & propola Joannes Teccelius: qui cum in disputationem Lipsicam consensum esse audissęt, dixisse fertur:
units.tr: While Luther and Eck were disputing at Leipzig about indulgences, the insatiable agent and retailer of the Roman court, Johann Tetzel, died in the Dominican monastery there. It is said that when he heard that the Leipzig disputation had been agreed upon, he said:

units.la: Das walt der Teuffel / id est, hoc faxit Diabolus.
units.tr: That would be the devil's doing! That is, Diabolus hoc faxit.

units.la: Lutherus edidit sermones, De duplici justitia: De salutari meditatione passionis Dominicae ; De baptismo: De praeparatione ad mortem,
units.tr: Luther published the sermons: On the Twofold Righteousness; On the Salutary Meditation on the Lord's Passion; On Baptism; On Preparation for Death.

units.la: Item: Resolutiones, sive declarationes propositionum suarum, Lipsiae disputatarum, de primatu Papae.
units.tr: Likewise: Resolutions, or explanations of his propositions on the primacy of the Pope, which were debated at Leipzig.

units.la: Confutationem antidotorum, falsò sibi à Monachis Iutrebocensibus impositorum.
units.tr: A refutation of the antidotes, which the Monks of Dutrebotz had falsely attributed to him.

units.la: Deniq; enarrationem epistolae ad Galatas: in quam praefatus distinguendum esse docet, inter decreta Romanae Ecclesiae, & Romanae curiae : quemadmodum in nuperis Comitiis Augustae ipsi Principes distinxerint : cum recusarent decimas, & vigesimas, & quinquagesimas, in Concilio Romano sancitas.
units.tr: Finally, an exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, in whose preface he teaches that a distinction must be made between the decrees of the Roman Church and those of the Roman Curia, just as the princes themselves made this distinction at the recent Diet of Augsburg, when they refused the tithes, the twentieths and the fiftieths sanctioned in the Roman Council.

units.la: PRAGA Bohemorum mense Octobri Hussitici sacerdotes scribunt ad Lutherum, eumque adhortantur ad Constantiam & patientiam, & esse hanc Theologiam puram, quam doceat, affirmant.
units.tr: At Prague, in the city of the Bohemians, in October, Hussite priests wrote to Luther, urging him to constancy and patience, and affirming that this is the pure theology which he teaches.

units.la: Joannes Oecolampadius in Suevico theatro, urbe Augustâ, sacrum panegyristen agit, & ut Theologicae literae purè ac simpliciter cadoceantur, adnititur.
units.tr: John Oecolampadius, in the Swabian theatre, the city of Augsburg, delivers a sacred panegyric and strives that theological literature be taught purely and simply.

units.la: WOLFGANGUS FABRITIUS Capito de suo & aliorū in Lutheri causam & personam animo Basileâ xii. Kal. Martii hæc scribit: Helvetia & Rhenana regio ad Oceanum usque solidos amicos fovet Lutherio, eosq; potentissimos, neque omnino alienos à bonis studiis. Cardinalis Sedunensis, Comes de Gerorlseck, Episcopus quidam eruditus ac prima honestatis, aliique ex nostris non pauci, cum nuper audierant te periclitari, non tantùm sumptum, sed etiam tuta loca pollicebantur: quibus aut latere, aut aperte degere posses. Cum peregrè constitutum fama prædicaret & summâ rerum difficultate laborare, fuerunt, qui per me submittere nitebantur largissimum sumptum, & submisissent utique. Verùm hoc vespere nuncium accepimus aureum: vivere Lutherium, & semper victurum. Deindè vidimus exemplum literarum Ducis Illustrissimi, & verè Principis ad D. Cardinalem, unde cognoscimus, quàm nihil opellâ nostrâ indigeas. Favore tamen si quid possumus, aderimus ubique. Monimenta tua junctim expressimus, sicut ex dono Frobenÿ cognosces statim post nundinas Francofordianas, simulq; per Italiam, Galliàs, Hispanias, Angliam intra sesqui mensem bonâ fortunâ publicavimus, in hoc videlicet communi causa consulentes, cui maximè consultum putamus, si veritas quàm latissimè declaratur. Natura enim veri gratiâ vel invitum in amorem sui pellicit. Ignosce quod nuper monitus es ex sententia Erasmi, hoc est, quod noctuas Athenæ intuli.
units.tr: Wolfgang Fabritius Capito, writing from Basel on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, sets out his own and others' feelings concerning Luther's cause and person as follows: Helvetia and the Rhenish region as far as the Ocean cherish firm friends of Luther, and very powerful ones, and not at all alien to good studies. The Cardinal of Sion, the Count of Gerolzeck, a certain learned bishop of the first rank of honour, and others of our people, not a few, when they lately heard that you were in danger, promised not only expenses but also safe places where you could either hide or live openly. When rumour reported that you had settled abroad and were labouring under great difficulty, there were those who tried through me to send a very generous sum, and indeed they would have sent it. But this evening we received the golden news that Luther is alive and will always live. Then we saw a copy of the letter of the most illustrious Duke, truly a Prince, to the Lord Cardinal, from which we learn how little you need our help. Nevertheless, if we can do anything by our favour, we will be present everywhere. We have printed your works together, as you will learn from Frobenius's gift immediately after the Frankfurt fair; and at the same time, within a month and a half, by good fortune, we have published them throughout Italy, France, Spain and England, plainly consulting the common cause, which we think is best served if the truth is declared as widely as possible. For the nature of truth draws even the unwilling into love of itself. Forgive me that, having recently been warned in Erasmus's opinion, I have carried owls to Athens.

units.la: Idem
units.tr: The same.

units.la: ANNUS MDXIX.
units.tr: The Year 1519.

units.la: Idem Capito vi. idus Aprilis ad Erasmū in hanc sententiam scribit: Martini, obsecro, negotium, in publicum nihil eleves. Nosti quantum valet calculus tuus. Ex animo loquor. Expedit superesse famam Lutherio, dabitur animus reliquae juventuti ut aliquid audeant pro libertate Christi: quanquam ipse multa in eo desidero. Curato Lovanium ne obsit. Nos tibi in officio continebimus Germaniam & Saxoniam, ubi Princeps potens, Lutherij patronus, & florentissima Academia VVittembergensis, tot illustres viri qui ex aequo favent Erasmo & Lutherio. Nihil in votis potius habent adversarij, quàm tuum in illum stomachum videre. Tibi cum suis addictissimus est. Omnes praestat infestos habere Theologos, quàm illius propugnatores. Sunt enim Principes aliqui, Cardinales, Episcopi, & clarissimi quique Ecclesiasticorum, quibus cordi est negotium.
units.tr: On the sixth day before the Ides of April, Capito wrote to Erasmus to this effect: I beg you, let the Martin affair go, and do not bring anything into the open. You know how much your opinion counts. I speak from my heart. It is useful that Luther's reputation survive; this will give courage to the rest of the young to dare something for the freedom of Christ, although I miss many things in him. Take care that Louvain does no harm. We shall keep Germany and Saxony loyal to you: there is a powerful prince, Luther's patron, and the flourishing Academy of Wittenberg, and many distinguished men who favour Erasmus and Luther alike. Your opponents have nothing they desire more than to see your anger against him. He is entirely devoted to you and yours. It is better to have all the theologians hostile than his defenders. For there are some princes, cardinals, bishops, and the most distinguished of the churchmen, to whom the affair is close at heart.

units.la: Udalricus Zwinglius ipsis Kalendis Januariis Ecclesiae Tigurinae Antistes declaratur. Quid primis quatuor annis docuerit, memorat ipse anno vicesimo secundo, mense Augusto: Anno ab hinc quarto (ut rationem praedicationis nostrae Tiguri promulgata habeatis) solidum Evangelium secundum Matthaeum praedicavi, quo tempore illorum nomina ne nominari quidem audieram, quorum factionis me insimulatis. Adjunxi Evangelio protinus Apostolorum acta: ut Tigurina Ecclesia videret, quo pacto, quibusve autoribus Evangelium propagatum esset ac promulgamulgatum. Successit mox prior Pauli ad Timotheum epistola, quod mirè videretur conducere optimo gregi, in ea enim veluti canones quidam morum, Christiano dignorum continentur. Hic cum de fide quidam scioli non rectè sentirent, secundam epistolam ad Timotheum distuli: donec eam quæ Gallogracis scripta est, enarrassem, tum illam quoq; adjùxi. Cùm jam dicti scioli eò insaniæ at impietatis processissent: ut Pauli nomè tantùm, non infame rederet, jactantes hæc pia scilicet, quæ neminem offendunt. Quis tandem Paulus? nonne homo est? Apostolus est, sed suburbanus tantùm, non ex duodecim viris, cum Christo non est conversatus, articulũ fidei non composuit: ego tam cuivis Thomæ vel Scoto Credo, quàm Paulo. Enarravi etiam Petri utramq; epistolam, Apostolorum antesignani, ut liquidò viderent: an eodem imbuti spiritu, eadem ambo locuti essent. His absolutis, epistolã ad Hebræos orsus sum: ut Christi beneficiũ clarius agnoscerent, ac gloriam.
units.tr: Ulrich Zwingli was proclaimed chief pastor of the Church of Zurich on the very Kalends of January. What he taught in his first four years he recalls himself in August of the twenty-second year: Four years ago (so that you may have the account of our preaching as it was published at Zurich), I preached the pure Gospel according to Matthew, at which time I had not even heard the names of those men whose faction you accuse me of belonging to. I joined the Acts of the Apostles straight after the Gospel, so that the Church of Zurich might see how and by whose authors the Gospel was spread and published. Next came the first epistle of Paul to Timothy, which seemed wonderfully suited to the best flock, for in it are contained, as it were, certain rules of morals worthy of a Christian. Here, since certain half-learned men held wrong views about the faith, I postponed the second epistle to Timothy; but when I had expounded the one written to the Gallo-Greeks, I added that one too. When the said half-learned men had gone so far in madness and impiety that they made Paul's name a disgrace, boasting of these pious things, which of course offend nobody: "Who, after all, was Paul? Is he not a man? He is an apostle, but only a suburban one, not one of the twelve, he did not live with Christ, he did not compose an article of faith. I believe every Thomas or Scotus just as much as Paul." I have also expounded both epistles of Peter, the foremost of the Apostles, so that they might clearly see whether both spoke the same things, being imbued with the same Spirit. When these were finished, I began the epistle to the Hebrews, so that they might recognise more clearly the benefit of Christ and his glory.

units.la: Hic distent: Christum summũ esse sacerdotẽ, ac jam ferme didicerunt. Nec est, ut me quorũdam scriptorum insimuletis: nam antequam ea ad manus nostras venerint; orsi eramus negotium, imo ante annum fere polliciti sumus id facturum. Discent item, Christũ unà ac semel tantùm oblatâ hostiâ in æternum consummasse sanctificatos. Hæc plantavimus: Matthæus, Lucas, Paulus, Petrus rigaverunt: Deus autem incrementum dedit admirabile: quod ipse non ebuccinabo: ne videar meam, non Christi gloriam ambire.
units.tr: Let them learn here that Christ is the supreme priest; indeed they have almost learned it already. Nor is it true, as you accuse me of certain writers, for before those writings came into our hands we had begun the work; indeed, about a year ago we promised that we would do it. Let them also learn that Christ, by one offering of the victim, once for all, has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. We have planted: Matthew, Luke, Paul and Peter have watered; but God gave the wonderful increase. This I will not trumpet abroad, lest I seem to seek my own glory rather than Christ's.

units.la: ANNUS MDXIX.
units.tr: ANNUS MDXIX.

units.la: Ut autem Zwinglius doctrinam fidei dilu- cidè explicuit: ita in vitia acriter invectus est, hac semper interjecta clausulâ: Frommermann nimmdichs nicht an: h.e. probe vir, hac nihil ad te.
units.tr: But just as Zwingli set out the doctrine of faith clearly, so he also attacked vices fiercely, always inserting this refrain: Frommermann, don't take it to heart: that is, good man, this has nothing to do with you.

units.la: Venerat superiore anno in Helvetiam missu Pontificis, Frater Bernhardus Samson Mediolanensis, Franciscanus, Pontificiarum remissionum praeco: adversus quae merces Romanas Suitiae exponentem Zwinglius in Eremo graviter concionibus suis detonuit. Hoc vero anno admonitus ab Episcopo Constantiensi, Hugone, ut Samsonem Tiguro excluderet, qui Pontificis iussa non aperuisset Episcopo, officium fecit fortiter. Ad portam urbis, in urbem non venit impostor ille, usque adeo impudens, ut Badenae venialibus Pontificiis diplomatis propositis, exclamare non dubitârit: Ecce volant, ecce volant: perinde ac si oculis cerneret demortuorum animas, à se liberatas in coelum volitare.
units.tr: In the previous year, Brother Bernhard Samson of Milan, a Franciscan and preacher of the papal indulgences, had come into Helvetia, sent by the Pope. Zwingli thundered vigorously against him in his sermons at Einsiedeln, against the one who was displaying Roman wares in Switzerland. In this year, admonished by Hugo, the Bishop of Constance, to shut Samson out of Zurich because he had not shown the Pope's orders to the bishop, Zwingli performed his duty bravely. That impostor did not enter the city through the gate, so shameless that at Baden, with the papal indulgence documents on display, he did not hesitate to cry out: Behold, they fly, behold, they fly! as though he could see with his eyes the souls of the dead, freed by him, flying up to heaven.

units.la: Praestitit eandem Ecclesiae fidem M. Henricus Bullingerus, Bremgartensis Pastor & Decanus: qua de causa bruto fulmine à Samsone impostore est percussus.
units.tr: Master Henry Bullinger, pastor and dean of Bremgarten, maintained the same faith of the Church, and for that reason was struck by a thunderbolt from the impostor Samson.

units.la: De Antuerpia sic Erasmus ad Lutherum. Est Antuerpiae Prior ejus monasterij, vir purè Christianus, qui te unicè deamat, tuus olim discipulus, ita enim praedicat. Caeteri fere aut hominum fabulas, aut suum quaestum praedicant.
units.tr: Erasmus wrote to Luther about Antwerp as follows: There is at Antwerp the prior of its monastery, a man purely Christian, who loves you alone, once your pupil, for so he preaches. Almost all the others preach either men's fables or their own gain.

units.la: Pfortzhemii purius Evangelium docere coepit Joannes Schwebelius. Quod cum Marchiones Badenses non ferrent, ad patronum Evangelicorum nobilissimum, Franciscum à Sickingen se recepit.
units.tr: John Schwebel began to teach the purer Gospel at Pforzheim. When the Margraves of Baden would not tolerate this, he withdrew to Franz von Sickingen, a most noble patron of the evangelicals.

units.la: Colonienses 30. mensis Augusti die, Lovanienses 7. Novembris Lutheri libros flammis dignos pronunciant.
units.tr: On 30 August the Cologne authorities, and on 7 November the Louvain authorities, declared Luther's books worthy of the flames.

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXX.
units.tr: ANNO CHRISTI MDXX.

units.la: NOvum incendium ex concione Lutheri de Eucharistia oritur, in qua scripserat: bonum sibi videri, si utraque species in cœna communicantibus exhibeatur. Georgius Saxoniæ Dux ad Fridericum Electorem Bohemicæ hæreseos Lutherum accusat: Episcopus Misnensis sermonem Lutheri Eucharisticum, edita schedula supprimit: alii adversarii Lutherum etiam natione Boëmum esse clamant.
units.tr: A new fire arose from Luther's sermon on the Eucharist, in which he had written that it seemed good to him if both kinds were given to those communicating at the Lord's Supper. George, Duke of Saxony, accused Luther to Elector Frederick of Bohemian heresy. The Bishop of Meissen suppressed Luther's Eucharistic sermon by issuing a notice; other adversaries cried out that Luther was also a Bohemian by birth.

units.la: Elector Georgio Duci respondet: causam Lutheri nondum esse legitime cognitam. Ad schedulam Episcopi Misnensis inhibitoriam Lutherus respondet: se probare utramque speciem, si Concilii generalis autoritate detur: interim obediendum esse novissimi Cōcilii decretis: & Laicis unam tantùm speciem porrigendam: placere & illud, esse eundem Christum non partialiter, sed integrum sub qualibet seorsim specie tam panis quam vini. Contra alios adversarios probat: se non in Boëmia, sed Islebiæ in Comitatu Mans- feldico esse natum.
units.tr: The Elector answered Duke George that Luther's cause had not yet been lawfully examined. In reply to the Bishop of Meissen's prohibitory notice, Luther answered that he would approve both kinds if they were granted by the authority of a general council; meanwhile the decrees of the most recent council had to be obeyed, and the laity was to be given only one kind; he also held that it was true that the same Christ is present, not partially but entire, under either kind separately, both of bread and of wine. Against other adversaries he proves that he was born not in Bohemia but at Eisleben, in the County of Mansfeld.

units.la: Decimâ quintâ Januarii ad Carolum Cæsarem, quartâ autem Februarii ad Albertum Præsulem Moguntinum, itemq; ad Episcopum Merseburgensem dat literas Lutherus: quibus causam suam illis commendat, &, ne inauditus damnetur, rogat. Moguntinus & Mersburgensis Lutherum, ut amore Jesu calamum temperet, & de aliis potiùs, caritati & pietati proficuis, quàm de Pontificis autoritate disputet, monent.
units.tr: On 15 January Luther wrote letters to Charles the Emperor, and on 4 February to Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, and likewise to the Bishop of Merseburg, commending his cause to them and asking that he not be condemned unheard. The Mainz and Merseburg prelates advised Luther, for the love of Jesus, to temper his pen, and to dispute about other matters that are profitable to charity and piety rather than about the authority of the Pope.

units.la: Mense Mart o respondet Lutherus ad articulos, quos Colonienses & Lovanienses Theologi ex propositionibus de Indulgen- tiis, & earundem Resolutionibus excerpserant, & velut hæreticos superiori anno damnârant.
units.tr: In March Luther replied to the articles which the theologians of Cologne and Louvain had extracted from the propositions on indulgences and their Resolutions, and had condemned as heretical the previous year.

units.la: Fridericus etiam Saxoniæ Elector cum à Valentino Ditlebio, Romæ tum agente, moneretur, minùs benignè in ipsum affectam esse aulam Romanam, Kalendis Aprilis respondit: se doctrinam Lutheri necdefendere, nec aboleri pati, priusquam convincatur. A doctis viris illam probari: Lutherum paratum esse ad reddendam fidei rationem, &, si demonstretur error, ad palinodiam, etiam ad exilium, quod ipse Miltitius dissuadeat: multa dixisse liberius, lacessitum ab Eccio & aliis: alte doctrinam illius multorum animis insedisse: ut, si vi res agatur, metuendum sit: ne motus longe maiores sint oriturí.
units.tr: Frederick, Elector of Saxony, also, when Valentin Ditleb, then acting in Rome, warned him that the Roman court was rather ill-disposed toward him, replied on 1 April: he neither could defend Luther's doctrine nor allow it to be abolished before it was refuted. It was approved by learned men; Luther was ready to give an account of his faith and, if an error were shown, to retract, even to go into exile, which Miltitz himself advised against. He had said many things rather freely, provoked by Eck and others; his doctrine had sunk deep into the minds of many, so that, if the matter were pushed by force, it was to be feared that far greater disturbances would arise.

units.la: Sexto deinde Aprilis Lutherus de consilio Caroli Miltitii literas dat ad Leonem, quibus se Pontifici purgat: quod non in ipsius personam, sed in impias doctrinas & doctores, tum in Curiam, quovis genere vitiorum & impietate perditissimam, sit invectus, omni culpa in Caietanum & Eccium translata.
units.tr: Then, on 6 April, Luther, on the advice of Charles Miltitz, wrote a letter to Leo, in which he cleared himself before the Pope: he had attacked not the person but the impious doctrines and teachers, and the Curia, most ruined by every kind of vice and impiety; all blame had been transferred to Cajetan and Eck.

units.la: Interim Eccius Romam proficiscitur, successurus, ut loquitur Lutherus, saltum Libani & abyssos abyssorum, hoc est, Bullam adversus Lutherum a Pontifice impetraturus. Terretur nonnihil aula Saxonica: Lutherus de angulo aliquo Boëmico cogitat, in quo se abdat. Rescisci nt hoc Nobiles nonnulli Germani, Lutheri doctrina jam tu imbuti. Offert igitur ipsi hospitium & patrocinium Franciscus a Sickingen, Huldericus ab Hutten, Eques Francus: Sylvester etiam de Schavenberg Nobilis Francus, datis ad Lutherum literis, rogat, ne in Boëmiam aut alio, sed ad se confugiat: si diræ Romanenses prævaluerint: policitus tutelam eximiam centenorum nobilium Equitum Franciæ. Crescit animus Luthero. Itaque Georgio Spalatino autor est: ut literis Friderici Electoris ad Cardinalem S. Georgii hoc subindicetur: etiamsi pellatur diris Pontificis è VVittemberga, nihil effecturos, nisi ut rem peiorem è mala reddant: quandoquidem jam non in Boëmia, sed media quoque Germania sint, qui expulsum tueri possint & velint, invitis ipsis, contra omnia sua fulmina. Vbi periculum est, inquit, ne iis protectoribus tutus, saevius in Romanenses sim grassaturus: quàm si sub, Principis imperio publicis militarem officiis docendi: id quod sine dubio, nisi Deus obsistat, futurum est: Principem vero ut hactenus in multis suspexi, etiam irritatus, tunc certè non necesse erit suspicere.
units.tr: Meanwhile Eck set out for Rome, about to climb, as Luther puts it, the mountain of Lebanon and the depths of the depths, that is, to obtain a bull against Luther from the Pope. The Saxon court was somewhat alarmed, and Luther considered some corner of Bohemia in which to hide. Some German nobles, already imbued with Luther's doctrine, learned of this. Franz von Sickingen and Ulrich von Hutten, a Franconian knight, therefore offered him hospitality and protection; Sylvester von Schaumberg, a Franconian nobleman, also wrote to Luther, asking him not to flee into Bohemia or elsewhere but to take refuge with them, should the dire Romanists prevail, promising the outstanding protection of a hundred noble knights of Franconia. Luther's courage grew. And so he advised Georg Spalatin that this be hinted in a letter of Elector Frederick to Cardinal of St. George: Even if the Pope's dire threats drive him out of Wittenberg, they will achieve nothing except to make a bad matter worse; for there are now men not only in Bohemia but also in central Germany who can and will protect him when expelled, even against their will, against all the Pope's thunderbolts. Where there is danger, he says, lest under such protectors I should rage more fiercely against the Romanists than if I served under the authority of the Prince, teaching in public offices, which without doubt will happen unless God intervenes; and the Prince, whom I have so far admired in many things, even when provoked, will then certainly not need to be admired.

units.la: Zwinglius ubi de Pontificis audiit animo, suasurum se commissario Pontificio, scribit: Pontificem admoneat, ne excommunicationem ferat: augurari enim se, Germanos cum excommunicatione Pontificem ipsum contempturos.
units.tr: When Zwingli heard of the Pope's intention, he wrote that he would advise the papal commissary to admonish the Pope not to issue excommunication: for he predicted that the Germans would hold the Pope himself in contempt together with the excommunication.

units.la: Fidem dicto eventus fecit. Lutherus à Leone excommunicatur die 15. Junii. Bulla in Mishiam ab Eccio; Coloniam à Marino Caracciola & Hieronymo Aleandro fertur: Ridetur Eccius Lipsiæ: non admittitur Bulla Bambergæ, quod non legitimè,ut loquuntur, insinuata: Rector Academiæ Erfurtensis programmate publicè affixo Academicos hortatur: ut si qui Bullam videant affixam, discerpant, & quo possint modo,Lutheri hostibus se opponant. Obsidetur ab adolescentibus armatis Erfurti Eccius: Bullæ excusæ fructillatim in aquas conjiciuntur, Ulricus Huttenus,nobilis Francus Bullam Leonis cum glossis interlinearibus & marginalibus publicat, non sine magna nominis Pontificii contumelia. Lutherus ipse, antequam Bullam vidisset, librum de Captivitate Babylonica edit: in quo profitetur, se quotidie, velit nolit,doctiorem fieri. Optare se, omnes libros de indulgentiis exustos, & illorum loco supponi unam hanc thesin:
units.tr: The outcome confirmed the prediction. Luther was excommunicated by Leo on 15 June. The bull was carried into Meissen by Eck, and to Cologne by Marino Caracciolo and Girolamo Aleandro. Eck was laughed at in Leipzig; the bull was not admitted at Bamberg, because it had not been properly, as they say, intimated. The rector of the University of Erfurt, by a public notice posted up, urged the students that if any of them saw the bull posted up, they should tear it down and oppose Luther's enemies in whatever way they could. Eck was besieged at Erfurt by armed young men. The bulls, printed, were thrown piece by piece into the waters. Ulrich von Hutten, a Franconian nobleman, published Leo's bull with interlinear and marginal glosses, not without great disgrace to the papal name. Luther himself, before he had seen the bull, published his book on the Babylonian Captivity, in which he professes that he is becoming more learned every day, whether he wills it or not. He wished that all books on indulgences were burned, and that in their place this one thesis be substituted:

units.la: Indulgentiæ sunt adulatorum Romanorum nequitiæ.
units.tr: Indulgences are the wickedness of Roman flatterers.

units.la: Optare item,ut iis exustis, quibus negârit, Papatum esse juris divini: admiserit, esse juris humani, substernatur hæc propositio:
units.tr: He also wished that, when those books in which he had denied that the papacy is of divine right, but had admitted that it is of human right, were burned, this proposition be put in their place:

units.la: Papatus est robusta venatio Romani Episcopi.
units.tr: The papacy is the robust hunting of the Roman bishop.

units.la: Deinde docet, sacramenti altaris captivitatem primam esse: quod speciesaltera Laicis subtracta: alteram, quod Transsubstantiatio firmiter credenda sit: tertiam, quod ex Missa factum sit sacrificium. Oppugnat Sacramentorum numerum: & duo tandem agnoscit tantùm, Baptismum, & Cœnam Domini. Atq; hunc librum vult esse partem suæ revocationis, si per Bullam ad eam adigatur. Ubi autem Bullam accepit, contemptim de ea loquens, Venit tandem, inquit, bulla ista Romana, per Eccium allata: de qua nostri scribunt ad Principem plura: ego eam contemno, & jam invado tanquàm impiam & mendacem, omnibus a modis Eccianam. Vides in ea damnari Christum ipsum: deinde nihil afferri causæ: tandem me vocari, non ad audientiam, sed ad palinodiam: ut scias, eos plenos esse furore, cæcitate, & amentiâ, qui nihil videant, neque cogitent: agam tamen adhuc presso nomine Papæ, tanquam in efficiam, & ementitam bullam, quanquam credam veram & propriam esse eorum. O utinam Carolus vir esset: & pro Christo hos Satanas aggrederetur!
units.tr: Then he teaches that the first captivity of the sacrament of the altar is that the one kind is withheld from the laity; the second, that transubstantiation must be firmly believed; the third, that the Mass has been made into a sacrifice. He attacks the number of the sacraments, and at last acknowledges only two, Baptism and the Lord's Supper. And he wishes this book to be part of his retraction, if he is compelled to it by the bull. But when he received the bull, speaking of it contemptuously: At last, he says, this Roman bull, brought by Eck, has come; our people write more about it to the Prince; I despise it, and now attack it as impious and lying, Eckian in every respect. You see that Christ himself is condemned in it; then no reason is given; finally I am summoned not to a hearing but to a retraction: so that you may know that those men are full of fury, blindness and madness, who see nothing and think nothing. I shall nevertheless still act under the pressed name of the Pope, as if it were a forged and fabricated bull, though I believe it is genuinely and truly theirs. O that Charles were a man, and that Satan would attack these men for Christ!

units.la: Deinde adversus execrabilem Bullam scriptum edit, in quo Bullam ipsam & Bullæ autores excommunicat: assertionem etiam publicat omnium articulorum à Papa damnatorum: à Pontifice iterum ad Concilium provocat: Papam nominat Antichristum: & cum audiret libros suos ab Hieronymo Aleandro, Pontificis legato, Lovanii, Leodii, Coloniæ, frustra renitente Friderico Electore, esse incensos: ipse x. Decembris, convocato omni cœtu scholastico, V Vit-
units.tr: Then he published a written attack on the detestable Bull, in which he excommunicated the Bull itself and its authors. He also published his own statement of all the articles condemned by the Pope, and again appealed from the Pope to a Council. He named the Pope Antichrist. When he heard that his books had been burned at Louvain, Liège and Cologne by Hieronymus Aleander, the Pope's legate, although Frederick the Elector had opposed this in vain, he himself, on 10 December, with the whole body of scholars gathered, at Wit-

units.la: Legantur omnia Tom. 2. operum. Lat. Jenen. tembergæ horâ nonâ, ad portam Orientalé, omnes libros Papæ, Decretum, Decretales, Sext. Clementini Extravagant. & Bullam novissimam Leonis X. Item summam Angelicam, & Eccii quædam, exurit : & facti rationem edito scripto exponit.
units.tr: tenberg at the ninth hour, outside the Eastern Gate, burned all the Pope's books: the Decretum, the Decretals, the Sext, the Clementines, the Extravagants, and the latest Bull of Leo X. He also burned the Summa Angelica and some writings of Eck. He then explained his action in a published writing. (Let all of this be read in vol. 2 of the works, Latin, Jena edition.)

units.la: ERASMUS à Friderico Saxoniæ Electore, Aquisgranum ad coronationem Caroli Cæsaris profecturo, & Coloniæ valetudinis causâ commorante, Lovanio accersitus, &, de Luthero quid sentiret, rogatus, fassus est ingenuè : veram esse Lutheri doctrinam, sed plusculum se desiderare moderationis. Iterum interroganti Principi, cur adeo invisus esset clero Lutherus? Respondit quasi per ridiculum: duo illum peccata magna commisisse ; attigisse coronam Papæ, & Monachorum ventres. Mirum igitur non esse, universum regnum Pontificium in ipsum invehi.
units.tr: Erasmus, who was staying at Cologne for the sake of his health, was summoned to Louvain by Frederick, Elector of Saxony, who was travelling to Aachen for the coronation of Emperor Charles. Asked what he thought of Luther, he admitted frankly that Luther's teaching was true, but said that he himself wanted a little more moderation. When the Prince asked him again why Luther was so hated by the clergy, he answered, as if in jest, that Luther had committed two great offences: he had touched the Pope's crown and the monks' bellies. It was no wonder, then, that the whole Papal kingdom rose against him.

units.la: Altero post colloquium cum Friderico Saxoniæ Duce habitum, die, Erasmus ad Conradum Peutingerum, Cæsaris Consiliarii scribit, & Lutheri causam arbitris doctis, integris, & ab omni suspitione alienis, delegari in suturis VVormatiæ Comitiis, consulit.
units.tr: Two days after the conversation with Frederick, Duke of Saxony, Erasmus wrote to Konrad Peutinger, an adviser of the Emperor, and asked that Luther's case be referred, at the coming Diet at Worms, to learned, upright arbiters free from all suspicion.

units.la: Fuit Lutherus & hoc & superiori anno sæpius ex aula Saxonica monitus: moderatius ut doceret, scriberetq;. At ille, Si perfistendum est, inquit, in docendo, mi Spalatine, non intelligo consilium tuum & tuorum, quos memoras : posse videor videlicet sacram Theologiam sine offensione Pontificum doceri. Scriptura potissimùm sacrorum abusum persequitur, quod non poterunt Pontifices sustinere. Ego tradidi, & obtuli me in nomine Domini. Fiat voluntas ejus. Quis rogavit eum, ut me Doctorem crearet? Si creavit, habeat sibi, aut rursus destruat, si pœnitet creasse. Adeo me non terret ista tribulatio, ut incredibili sinu carbasa cordis mei inflet: ut jam intelligam in me ipso, cur Dæmones ventis aguntur in scriptura.
