Dum enim sese efflant furendo, alios instant patiendo. Id solùm curo, ut Dominus in meis, quas inter me & ipsum habeo, causis, mihi sit propitius, atq; hoc, ut potes, juvare digneris. Istam vero hominum causam fideli oratione Deo committamus, & securi simus. Quid enim facere poterunt? Occident? Nunquid resuscitabunt, ut iterum occidant? Hæreticum infamabunt? At Christus cum iniquis seductoribus, maledictis, damnatus est: cuius passionem si quando intueor, mirè uror, hanc meam tentationem non solùm aliquid, sed etiam maximam videri tam magnis & multis, cum sit revera nihil: nisi quod funditus desuevimus passionibus & malis, id est, Christiana vita. Et iterum: Esto, novum & magnum sit futurum incendium: quis potest Dei consilio resistere? sine, quaeso, rem suis ire motibus: solus Deus in negotio est: rapimur, & agimur, ut video, potiùs, quàm agamus.
units.tr: Both this year and the year before, Luther was often warned from the Saxon court to teach and write more moderately. But he replied: "If I must persist in teaching, my dear Spalatin, I do not understand your advice or that of your friends whom you mention. Evidently you think sacred theology can be taught without offending the Pontiffs. Scripture above all pursues the abuses of holy things, and the Pontiffs cannot endure that. I have put myself forward and offered myself in the name of the Lord. May his will be done. Who asked him to make me a Doctor? If he made me one, let him keep me, or else let him unmake me, if he regrets having made me. I am so little frightened by this tribulation that it swells the sails of my heart with incredible force, so that I now understand in myself why demons are driven by the winds in Scripture. While they blow themselves up in fury, they urge others on by suffering. I care only that the Lord should be gracious to me in my causes between myself and him, and I ask you to help this as you can. Let us commit this matter of men to God in faithful prayer, and be at peace. For what can they do? Will they kill me? Will they raise me up again only to kill me a second time? Will they defame me as a heretic? But Christ was condemned with wicked deceivers, with insults. When I look upon his passion, I am greatly inflamed; this temptation of mine seems to great and many people to be not just something but even the greatest thing, when in truth it is nothing, except that we have utterly lost the habit of sufferings and evils, which is to say, the Christian life. And again: "Granted that the fire will be new and great: who can resist God's counsel? Let the matter go, I beg you, on its own course. God alone is at work in this business. We are carried along and driven, as I see, rather than acting."

units.la: ULRICUS HUTTENUS Nobilis Francus Germanicâ linguâ edit libellum historicum de
units.tr: ULRICH VON HUTTEN, a noble Franconian, published in German a historical booklet on the continual disobedience of the Roman Pontiffs towards the Emperors.

units.la: perpetua Pontificum Romanorum inobedientia adversus Imperatores: in quo sub finem recitat dictum Maximiliani I. de Leone Pontifice, cum fidem non servasset: <bl>Nun ist dieser Bapst auch zu einem bößwicht an mir</bl> <bl>worden: Nu mag ich sagen/daß mir kein Bapst/ so lang ich gelebt/ je trew oder glauben gehalten</bl> <bl>hat: hoffe ob Gott wil/dieser solder letzte seyn.</bl>
units.tr: Near the end he recounts a saying of Maximilian I about Pope Leo, when the Pope had not kept faith: "Now this Pope has also turned into a villain towards me. Now I may say that no Pope, as long as I have lived, has ever kept trust or faith with me. I hope, God willing, that this rascal will be the last."

units.la: Leo Pontifex, ut Albertum Brandeburgicum, Archiepiscopum Moguntinum, eundemq; Cardinalem, cui noverat Huttenum familiarem esse, in fide retineret, sextâ Junii amicas ad illum dat literas, in quibus de sua erga Albertum benevolentia præfatus, quin etiam, subijcit, Rosam aueam, vetere instituto prædecessorum nostrorum Romanorum Pontificum Dominicâ Quadragesimæ Quartâ benedici solitam, à nobis, solenni more benedictam, alicui sæculari Principi mitti solitam, per Marinum Caracciolam ad Circumspectionem tuam donum misimus, ut ad Principem quidem Electorem, veruntamen novo exemplo. Sed omnia indicia benevolentia erga te nostræ satis nobis justa etiam ad innovandum aliquid videntur esse. Quare Circumspectio tua gratum illud munus accipiet: quod etsi mysticum est, magnasq; habet in se rerum sacrarum interpretationes, tamen ad cæteras adjunctum est pignus amoris summi in te nostri.
units.tr: Pope Leo, in order to keep Albert of Brandenburg, Archbishop of Mainz and also Cardinal, whom he knew to be a friend of Hutten, in his allegiance, on 6 June sent him a friendly letter. In it, after speaking of his own goodwill towards Albert, he wrote: "Moreover, we have sent you by Marino Caracciolo, as a gift to your Circumspection, the golden rose, which by the ancient custom of our Roman Pontiff predecessors is wont to be blessed on the Fourth Sunday of Lent by us with the solemn rite, and which has been customarily sent to a secular prince. It is indeed sent to an Elector, but in a new manner. Yet all the tokens of our goodwill towards you seem to us just enough to warrant some innovation. Therefore your Circumspection will receive this welcome gift. Although it is mystical and contains great interpretations of sacred things, it is nevertheless added to the others as a pledge of our highest love towards you."

units.la: Duodecimâ deinde Julii missis aliis ad Albertum literis, cordolium suum ipsi aperit: HutteHuttenum in Sedem sanctam effudisse contumelias: & esse illum Archiepiscopo familiarem: & impressos esse libros eius in civitate Alberti Moguntiâ. Hortatur igitur Albertum, authoritatem suam interponat, & ea in maledicos indicia suæ severitatis edat, quæ & ipsos & alios possint à tanta petulãtia cohercere. Albertus igitur emptione & lectione scriptorum Hutteni omnibus sub excommunicationis sententia interdicit.
units.tr: Then, on 12 July, having sent other letters to Albert, he unburdened his anxiety to him: Hutten had poured insults upon the Holy See, he was a close friend of the Archbishop, and his books had been printed in Albert's city of Mainz. He therefore urged Albert to interpose his authority and to show, by such marks of his severity, that could restrain both these men and others from such great insolence. Albert accordingly forbade, under penalty of excommunication, everyone to buy or read Hutten's writings.

units.la: Hoc anno Lutherus certò definit: Pontificem Romanum esse Antichristum. Sic enim ille: Ego sic angor: ut prope non dubitem: Papam esse proprie Antichristum illum, quem vulgatâ opinione expectat mundus. Adeò conveniunt omnia, quæ vivit, facit, loquitur, statuit.
units.tr: This year Luther firmly settled that "the Roman Pontiff is Antichrist." For he wrote: "I am so troubled that I scarcely doubt that the Pope is properly that Antichrist whom the world awaits by common opinion. So well do all the things he lives, does, says and decrees agree with it."

units.la: Et alibi: Nos hic persuasi sumus, Papatum esse veri & germani illius Antichristi sedem: in cuius deceptionem & nequitiam ob salutem animarum nobis omnia licere arbitramur. Ego pro me confiteor: Papa à me nullam deberi obedientiam, nisi eam, quam Τῶ γνησίῳ Ἀντιχρίστῳ debeo.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "We here are persuaded that the Papacy is the seat of that true and genuine Antichrist, and we think that for the salvation of souls everything is lawful against his deception and wickedness. For my part I confess that I owe the Pope no obedience, except the obedience I owe to τῷ γνησίῳ Ἀντιχρίστῳ [the true Antichrist]."

units.la: ERASMO nec Lutherus, nec Lutheri adversarii satisfaciunt. Video, inquit, rem hactenus multò aliter esse tractatam, quàm viri prudentes putârint esse tractandam. Lutherus etiamsi vera scripsisset omnia, tamen eo modo scripsit, quasi veritati suum fructum inviderit. Contrà, qui se huic negotio transversim ingesserunt, sic gesserunt rem apud populum: ut, etiamsi causam habuissent optimam, tamen illi plurimum obfuerint sinistro patrocinio. Admonitus est Lutherus; ut stylum verteret, & atrocitatem temperaret: scribit indies, ut audio, saviora. Admoniti sunt hi: ut moderatioribus rationibus rem agerent: quidam sic egerunt, ut cum Luthero colludere viderentur.
units.tr: Neither Luther nor Luther's opponents satisfy Erasmus. "I see," he says, "that until now the matter has been handled much differently from how prudent men thought it should be handled. Luther, even if he had written everything truthfully, nevertheless wrote in such a way as if he begrudged truth its fruit. On the other hand, those who have thrust themselves crosswise into this business have so conducted it before the people that, even if they had the best cause, they have been greatly harmed by their unfavourable advocacy. Luther was admonished to change his style and temper his savagery; he writes, I hear, more fiercely every day. These others were admonished to pursue the matter by more moderate methods; some have acted in such a way that they seem to be colluding with Luther."

units.la: Et alibi: Precor, ut Christus optimus maximus Lutheri stylum ita temperet: ut plurimum adferat fructūs Evangelica pietati: mentemq; meliorem det quibusdam, qui cum ignominia Christi suam quærūt gloriam, qui cum illius iactura suum quærunt lucrum. In castris eorum, qui Lutherum oppugnant, multos video, qui mundum spirant magis quàm Christum. Et tamen utrinq; peccatur. Vtinam Huttenus temperasset stylo suo, cuius ingenium amo unicè! Optàrim, Lutherum ab istis contentionibus aliquantisper conquiescere, ac rem Evangelicam tractare purè, non admixtis adfectibus, fortasse res aliquanto melius successerit. Nunc & bonas literas degravat invidiâ, nobis exitiabili, ipsi infrugiferâ. Et periculum est, ne publica morum corruptela, cui nemo non fatetur opus fuisse publico remedio, ceu pestis exagitata, magis ac magis sese confirmet. Nec semper est proferenda veritas.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "I pray that Christ, the best and greatest, may so temper Luther's style that it brings the most fruit to evangelical piety, and gives a better mind to certain people who seek their own glory with the dishonour of Christ, who seek their own gain with his loss. In the camp of those who attack Luther I see many who breathe the world more than Christ. And yet on both sides wrong is done. Would that Hutten had tempered his style, whose genius I love uniquely! I would wish that Luther might rest a little from these contentions, and handle the evangelical matter purely, without mixing in passions; perhaps the affair would have gone rather better. As it is, they weigh down good literature with hatred, which is ruinous to us and barren for itself. And there is a danger that the public corruption of morals, which everyone admits needed a public remedy, will, like a raging plague, establish itself more and more. Nor is the truth always to be put forward."

units.la: CHRISTIERNUS Rex Daniæ, sive bonorum ecclesiasticorum cupidine, sive purioris Religionis studio incensus, ab avunculo Saxoniæ Electore Concionatorem Evangeligelicum ad se mitti petit. Mittitur quidam M. Martinus, vir eruditus, qui Hafniæ Daniç metropoli diebus festis à meridie magno populi applausu docet. Is quia gestum in dicendo minus decorum egit, à Canonicis ad D. Virginem falsè fuit irrisus: inventusque puer est, qui in conviviis & alibi callidè Pastorem novum imitaretur, & M. Martinus vocaretur.
units.tr: Christian, King of Denmark, inflamed either by desire for church revenues or by zeal for a purer religion, asked his uncle, the Elector of Saxony, to send him an evangelical preacher. A certain Master Martin, a learned man, was sent; at Copenhagen, the Danish capital, he taught on feast days at noon to a great crowd who applauded him. Because he used gestures in speaking that were less becoming, he was falsely mocked by the canons of St Mary's; and a boy was found who, at banquets and elsewhere, cleverly imitated the new minister and was called "Master Martin."

units.la: Joannes Thurzo, Episcopus Uratislaviensis, primus fuit Episcoporum Pontificiorum, qui renascenti Evangelio, & huius præconibus favēret. Id quod Lutheri & Melāchthonis ad ipsum epistolę testantur: quas, quia vix alibi reperias, apponendas duxi.
units.tr: John Thurzo, Bishop of Breslau, was the first of the Papist bishops who favoured the reborn Gospel and its heralds. Luther's and Melanchthon's letters to him bear witness to this; since you can hardly find them anywhere else, I thought they should be appended.

units.la: REVERENDISS. ET AM- PLISSIMO IN CHRISTO PA- TRI AC DOMINO, D. JOANNI Epi- scopo Ecclesiæ Uratislaviens. Domi- no suo gratioso, ac patrono unicè colendo.
units.tr: To the most reverend and most distinguished father in Christ and lord, Lord John, Bishop of the Church of Breslau, his gracious lord and patron, to be honoured above all.

units.la: JHESUS
units.tr: JESUS

units.la: SESE commendat. Quanquam ego, Reverendiss. Præsul, rationem mea parvitatis habens, ut ad omnes alios magnates, ita ad tuam magnitudinem præcipuè timidus scribo: animum tamen tamen erexit Venerabilis Vir, Dominicus Sleup-ner, Reverendiss. tua paternitati addictissimus, qui hinc pietate, quâ in suum Episcopum affectus est, solvit, visurus, quid rerum Dominus operetur in mortali corpusculo p. t. Noluit autem sine meis literis ire, persuadens, me rem facturum non ingratam R. p. t. Ego sanè fateor, & me nonnihil, imo multum cum R. p. t. agrescere, quod Ecclesia Dei compatior, cui, proh dolor, rari dantur, qualem R. p. t. dedit, Episcopi, cum nunquam magis eguerit talibus. Caterum confido, quòd manus eius percutiet, & sanabit: atque qui R.p. t. tam insignibus ornavit dotibus, non deerit, ut det virtutem fortitudinémque, omnia constanti Christiano, Episcopali animo ferendi, & standi in omnes sanctas voluntates eius. Si vita negabitur Ecclesia, prosit mors. Potens autem est, tam ex vita quàm ex morte p. t. Ecclesiam suam iuvare, pro divitiis bona voluntatis sua.
units.tr: I commend myself to you. Although, most reverend prelate, I bear my own littleness in mind and write timidly to all other great men, and especially to your greatness, nevertheless the venerable man Dominicus Sleupner, most devoted to your reverend fatherhood, has raised my spirits. Moved by the piety with which he is attached to his bishop, he sets out to see what the Lord is doing in your reverend fatherhood's mortal body. He would not go without a letter from me, persuading me that I would be doing your reverence a welcome service. I confess that I am somewhat, indeed greatly, vexed with your reverence, because I sympathise with the Church of God, to which, alas, such bishops as your reverence has been given are rarely given, when it has never needed such men more. But I trust that his hand will strike and heal, and that he who has adorned your reverence with such outstanding gifts will not fail to give the strength and fortitude to bear all things with a constant Christian and episcopal spirit, and to stand firm in all his holy wills. If life is denied to the Church, let death profit her. For he is powerful to help his Church through your life as well as through your death, according to the riches of his good will.

units.la: Non hoc scribo, quod necessarium arbitrer, animum tuum confortari in Domino (quanquam quis est tam fortis, qui non egeat vel minimi fratris solatio? ) sed quod communia nobis omnia voluit & fecit is, qui pro nobis omnia factus, iussit: ut alter alterius onera portaret; ne ullus fidelis suus solus viveret, aut solus moreretur; sed in communione sanctorum securus per omnia ageret & pateretur. Itaque quantum nos contristat communis T. P. agritudo, aut, si Dominus volet, etiam futura mors: tantum nos rursus latifificat scat, quod nec sola patitur, nec sola vivit anima tua, sed vivimus, & patimur cum illa, & omnibus Iesus Christus, medium cordis nostri, in quo sancte valeat R. P. T. & mea temeritati ignoscat. Litera enim priores P. T. R. animosum me fecerunt, cum sint magnae humilitatis & charitatis: ut eruditionem taceam: plenissima, & inter sacra mea perpetuo monumento servanda. Iterum: valeat R. P. T. in Christo, & me commendatum habeat. Vvittembergae 3. Kalen. Augusti, 1520.
units.tr: I write this not because I think your soul needs to be strengthened in the Lord (though who is so strong as not to need the comfort of even the least brother?), but because he who became all things for us, and who commanded it, willed and made all things common to us, so that one should bear another's burdens, and so that none of his faithful should live alone or die alone, but in the communion of saints should act and suffer securely in all things. Therefore, as much as your reverence's common sickness, or even the death that may follow if the Lord wills it, saddens us, so much again it gladdens us that your soul neither suffers nor lives alone, but we live and suffer with it, and Jesus Christ, the centre of our heart, in whom may your reverence fare well and pardon my boldness. For your reverence's earlier letters made me bold, since they are full of great humility and charity, not to mention their learning; they are most full, and I will keep them among my sacred things as a lasting memorial. Once more: may your reverence fare well in Christ and keep me in your mind. Wittenberg, 3 days before the Kalends of August, 1520.

units.la: T. R. P.
units.tr: Your Reverend Fatherhood's

units.la: filius
units.tr: son

units.la: F. Martinus Luther, Aug.
units.tr: Brother Martin Luther, Augustinian.

units.la: REVERENDISS. ET A- MPLISSIMO PATRI AC DOMINO, D. JOANNI URATISL. Ecclesiae Episcopo, Domino suo ac patrono.
units.tr: To the most reverend and most distinguished father and lord, Dr. John, Bishop of Breslau (Uratislaviensis), his lord and patron.

units.la: SALVE, Reverendiss. Praesul, Optime pr. Quàm grato pectore acceperim, quae de me ad Dominicum nostrum Reverend. p. tua scripsit, multo iam tempore, iusto aliquo & argumentoso opere testari gestio. Sive enim ita de nobis in iis literis iudicabas, sive pro benignitate tua nos istiusmodi laudatiunculâ ad recta studia incitabas, incundissimum fuit his vocibus à tanto principe vel probavi, vel animari. Verùm dum cesso interim, & contor hunc talem animum Reverend. p. tuæ declarare, Dominicus noster, pro officio ad Reverend. p. tuam profecturus, hortatur: ut brevi me epistolio Reverend. p. tuæ commendè. Ego verò ut intelligebam, & quid deberè, & qualia decerent Reverend. p. tuam: ita parum civile arbitrabar, putidâ tatùm epistolâ, ac non potiùs graviore aliquo argumento Reverendiss. p. tuam interpellare: tamen victus hominis amici consilio, hoc, quidquid est, literarum scribo: ac Rever. p. tuæ simul mea studia, & hunc animum, laudibus tuis impensè faventem, addico. Quis enim ei non faveat? qui unus nobis, quod sciam equidem, in Germania Episcopi παραδειγμα absolvisti, autoritate, literis, ac pietate. Qui, si haberet Christiana Respublica, ut ille Rex Homericus ait, decem tui similes συμφράδμονες, non dubitarem, renasci aliquando Christum. Sed hæc alias. Catera Dominicus coram. Huius officium, qui te visurus abit, Reverend. p. tua probabit, cuius salute, ne suam quidem, quæ est hominis dexteritas, qui candor, antiquiorem habet, studia eius pro benignitate tua Reverend. p. tua adiuvabit ac provehet. Dignus est, & quia bonus, & quia tuus est; quem Reverend. p. tua tueatur. Feliciter valeat eadem p. tua. VVitemberga. Kal. Augusti 1520.
units.tr: Greetings, most reverend prelate, most excellent sir. I have long been eager to show, by some substantial and well-argued work, how gratefully I received what your reverence has written about me to our friend Dominicus. For whether you judged us so favourably in that letter, or whether, out of your kindness, you were encouraging us with such a little word of praise to pursue sound studies, it was most delightful to be either approved or spurred on by such words from so great a man. But while I hesitate and struggle to express this disposition of mine to your reverence, our Dominicus, who is setting out to visit your reverence as part of his duty, urges me to commend myself to you in a short letter. Yet I thought it impolite, as I understood both what I owe and what befits your reverence, to trouble your most reverend lordship with a mere trifling letter rather than some weightier matter. Nevertheless, persuaded by the advice of a friend, I am writing this, whatever it is, and at the same time I devote my studies and this mind of mine, which is eagerly favourable to your praises, to your reverence. For who would not favour him? You alone, as far as I know, in Germany have set before us the model of a bishop, in authority, learning and piety. If the Christian commonwealth had, as that Homeric king says, ten counsellors like you (sumphradmones [συμφράδμονες]), I would not doubt that Christ would one day be reborn. But enough of this for now. Dominicus will tell you the rest in person. The business of the man who is leaving to visit you, which your reverence will approve, and whose integrity and candour he values even above his own well-being, your reverence will support and advance with your accustomed kindness. He is worthy, both because he is good and because he is yours, to be protected by your reverence. May your reverence fare well. Wittenberg, 1 August 1520.

units.la: R. P. T.
units.tr: R. P. T.

units.la: Deditissimus
units.tr: Your most devoted

units.la: Philippus Melanchthon.
units.tr: Philip Melanchthon.

units.la: Non vidit autem has literas Episcopus. Obiit enim secunda Augusti huius anni Nisa. Ideo Lutherus gloriatur, Episcopum hunc optimum in fide Evangelica mortuum esse.
units.tr: The bishop, however, did not see this letter. He died on the second of August of this year at Nysa. Hence Luther boasts that this excellent bishop died in the Evangelical faith.

units.la: ULRICUS ZASIUS Jurisconsultus, quid in Luthero laudârit pariter, & deside- ràrit: loquatur illius ad hunc epistola Fribur- go Kal. Septemb. scripta:
units.tr: ULRICH ZASIUS, jurist: what he equally praised in Luther and what he missed. Let his letter to him, written at Freiburg on the Kalends of September, speak:

units.la: Si animi mei affectu, Martine, Theologorum Phoenix (lubet ultra epistolare filum mollius scribere) si, inquam, affectu declarare tibi pergam: nihil secius, quàm Sardos venales exhibeo: ita in te omnia mea, non dico, afficiuntur, sed vel ardent: didici abs te, si quid boni in me sit, quod vel nihil, vel exiguum est, omnia prorsus accepta referre Deo. Indulgentiarum vim, quam à trecentis, & amplius, annis, nemo deprehendit, ita mihi clarè depinxisti: ut non solus ego, sed ipsissimi Romanista, in ordinem redactas esse, confiteri cogantur. De pœnitentia, de Confessionis veritate, de decem præceptorum spirituali medulla, quid poterat tuis opusculis esse, vel verius, vel fundatius? taceo minutiora. Et una à te epistola ad Galatas tradita, præsentibus & posteris utilis esse poterit: in qua tu loca abstrusa, clarissimè elucidas: ut non aliter quàm fide, non ex operibus legis iustificemur, & quod lex peccatum potius augeat, quàm adimat: nec aliter impleatur lex, nisi destruatur: multaque id genus & rara & insignia, & ut verbo dicam, unus es, qui doctus & integer Theologus dici me-rearis. Te sequuntur passim docti omnes: ex te pendet iam non quota pars Christiani orbis. Sunt, quod ausim ex veritate dicere, ex doctissimis, qui eam sortem nullo argento commutarent, quod te non legissent. Equidem cuperem potius extremâ laborare inopiâ, quàm tua non vidisse. Quo tamen nomine non est, quod tibi glorieris, sed DEO (hoc enim tu ipse doces) qui ex te salutem nostram operatur.
units.tr: If I were to go on expressing my feelings toward you, Martin, phoenix of theologians (let me pursue the thread of a letter a little more freely), I would be no less than offering Sardinians for sale. My whole being is not merely affected but set on fire by you. I have learned from you that whatever good there is in me, which is nothing or very little, I must wholly attribute to God. The power of indulgences, which no one has discerned for more than three hundred years, you have depicted so clearly for me that not only I but the most ardent Romanists themselves are forced to confess that it has been reduced to order. On repentance, on the truth of confession, on the spiritual marrow of the Ten Commandments, what could be more true or more solidly founded than your little works? I say nothing of the smaller matters. And the one epistle of yours on the Galatians, handed down, will be useful to the present and to posterity, in which you so clearly illuminate obscure passages: that we are justified not otherwise than by faith and not by the works of the law; that the law rather increases sin than takes it away; and that the law is not fulfilled unless it is destroyed; and many other things of this kind, rare and remarkable. In a word, you are the one who deserves to be called a learned and sound theologian. All the learned follow you everywhere; the whole Christian world now depends on you, to a degree that cannot be measured. There are, I may say with truth, learned men who would not exchange that lot for any amount of money, were they not to have read you. For my part, I would rather suffer the utmost poverty than not have seen your works. Yet you have no cause to glory in this, but in God (for this you yourself teach), who works our salvation through you.

units.la: Sed, si æquo pateris animo, vereor esse in te, quæ desiderentur. Amore enim victoriæ Ecckianæ (quem certè subtrivisse videris) nimium Sedis Apostolicæ authoritatem attenuare, quibusdam iudicaris, quos tamen licet nec approbem, nec improbem, quando id genus controversiæ non est mihi satis perspectum: habeo tamen vel ego, de quibus nonnihil subsistam. Tot enim ætates, quæ summam Pontifici Romano potentiam prærogarunt, & sanctos viros convellere, nisi fortissimis agatur rationibus, non est tutum: & esset in iure nostro, si ulla tibi eius esset authoritas, hac ratio invicta. Quae enim diutissimè sunt iusta visa, nefas putamus everti contendere. Sed tamen dubito, non affirmo, tuam clariorem expectamus elucidationem. Si ita tibi libeat: Si hominem exiguum, auditorem tuum eâ notâ digneris. Sin minùs, tamen brevissimis ad me literis scribito: ut intelligam, te meis nugis non offendi, qui alioquin omnia tua, tanquàm veritatis oraculum, amplector[?], & me eis, prout Deus dederit, confirmo. Vale. Plura scripturum nuncius praepedit, qui iam itineri intentus, negat diutius praestolari posse. Alio tamen tempore plura. Praesentium exhibitorem, iuvenem integrum, devotum, doctum, & tui amantissimum, fac ex humanitate complectare: famulus Ioannis de Schoenaw fuit, viri nobilis, devotissimi, & qui totus ex tuis pendet praescriptis, assiduus & lector & imitator tuarum praeceptionum, qui etiam a decem annis Taulero studuit, & qui ductu praestantissimi Theologi Brisgoici fovetur. Brisgoici, inquam, cui nihil, post sacras literas, nisi Lutherana sapiunt, illic te iuvenis ille colere didicit.
units.tr: But if you bear it with an even mind, I fear there are things in you that are wanting. For through love of Eck's victory (which you seem to have worn down thoroughly) you seem to some to diminish too much the authority of the Apostolic See. Those men I neither approve nor condemn, since I do not sufficiently understand this kind of controversy; yet I too have some points on which I hesitate. For so many ages, which have granted the Roman Pontiff the highest power, it is not safe to overturn holy men unless the matter is pursued with the strongest arguments; and if you had any authority in our law, this argument would be unanswerable. For what has seemed just for a very long time, we think it wrong to try to overturn. But still, I doubt rather than affirm, and we look for your clearer explanation. If you are so inclined, deign to honour a humble man, your listener, with that mark. If not, write to me at least in the briefest letter, so that I may understand that you are not offended by my trifles, I who otherwise embrace all your words as the oracle of truth, and strengthen myself by them as God gives. Farewell. The messenger, who is already intent on his journey and says he can wait no longer, prevents me from writing more. I will write more at another time. Please receive the bearer of this letter, a young man of integrity, devoted, learned, and very fond of you, with kindness. He was servant to John of Schoenau, a noble man, most devoted, who depends entirely on your precepts, a constant reader and imitator of your teachings; for the past ten years he has also studied Tauler, and he is cherished under the guidance of the most distinguished theologian of the Breisgau. Of the Breisgau, I say, where, apart from the sacred writings, nothing tastes of anything but Luther; there that young man learned to honour you.

units.la: Mi dulcissime Martine, nolito moveri; ex syncteritate purissimi amoris ad te scribo, veritus, ne pulcerrima tuae doctrinae hac odiosa & exotica concertatione, quam forte sustinere non possis, dehonestentur. Vale, decus Christiani orbis. Georgium Spalatinum, virum cum doctrina humanissimum, salvum iube, cui scripsissem, nisi nuncius festinasset. Sed proxime scribam. Melanchthona, hominem rarae eruditionis, omnes animae meae vires, saluta.
units.tr: My dearest Martin, do not be troubled. I write to you out of the sincerity of the purest affection, fearing that your most beautiful teaching may be dishonoured by this hateful and foreign controversy, which perhaps you cannot endure. Farewell, glory of the Christian world. Greet Georg Spalatin, a man most cultivated in learning, for whom I would have written had the messenger not hurried. But I will write soon. Greet Melanchthon, a man of rare learning, with all the powers of my soul.

units.la: {a}OECOLAMPADIUS, Ecclesiastes Augustanus, in coenobium Salvatoris, prope Augustam concedit, factus ibi Monachus, cum metueret Reipublicae a Lutheri scriptis; sed inprimis ut otium ei conservaretur ad studia sua Theologica. Antequam au-
units.tr: {a} OECOLAMPADIUS, preacher at Augsburg, withdrew to the monastery of the Saviour near Augsburg, where he became a monk, because he feared for the state on account of Luther's writings; but above all so that leisure might be preserved for him for his theological studies. Before he entered the monastery,

units.la: {a} Capito in vita Occolamp. Et Occolampadius ipse epist. ad amicum quae extat lib. 4. epistolarum Zwinglii & Occolampadii, tem monasterium ingrederetur, studiis suis & fidei libertatem à fratribus stipulatus est. Substitit in eo annum integrum, usque dum libertas verbi divini interdici coepta.
units.tr: {a} Capito in the life of Oecolampadius; and Oecolampadius himself in a letter to a friend, which is extant in book 4 of the letters of Zwingli and Oecolampadius. He stipulated with the brothers for his studies and for freedom of faith. He remained there a full year, until freedom of the divine word began to be forbidden.

units.la: Hoc gravissimè in eo tulit Erasmus. Judicio est epistola ad Pirkhaimerum Nonis Septemb. scripta; ubi inter alia: Quod scribis ab Oecolampadio factum, iam ex illius literis subodorabar futurum: Id sive iudicio fecit, sive animi morbo, quando mutari non potest, precandum est, ut illi as nobis quàm optimè vertat. Video res humanas sic undique corruptas; ut nullis unquam seculis, existimem, plus licuisse impudentia, plus licuisse stoliditati, plus licuisse sceleri. Et nonnunquam libet aliquò profugere: sed vereor: ne, quocunque me vertero, sequatur molestia. Proinde tuus arbitror, mali remedium ab animo petere potiùs, quàm à loco, aut vita instituto. Bene habet, quod Christus in tanta vitiorum caligine nobis Evangelica doctrina scintillas reliquit.
units.tr: Erasmus took this very badly. The judgement is in his letter to Pirckheimer, written on the Nones of September, where, among other things: That you write was done by Oecolampadius, I had already suspected from his letters. Whether he did it by judgement or from a sickness of mind, since it cannot be changed, we must pray that it turns out as well as possible for him and for us. I see human affairs so corrupted on every side that I think at no age has impudence, stupidity and crime been more powerful. Sometimes one feels like fleeing somewhere, but I fear that wherever I turn, trouble will follow. Therefore, I think you should seek a remedy for evil from the mind rather than from place or from a change of life. It is good that Christ, in such darkness of vices, has left us sparks of the Evangelical doctrine.

units.la: VVOLFGANGUS etiam Fabritius Capito ad Melanchthonem: Oecolampadius noster, inquit, ad vitam monasticam secessit, ad monasterium Divi Altonis, quod ab Augusta tertiu lapidem distat. Fecit inconsultè vir alioquin cautus & prudens, qui animum per se parum alacrẽ insueto iugo oneravit, causâ religionis, quasi Christus nostrâ mœstitudine fruatur, & cultus sit ingenuè Christianus refugisse hominum conspectum. Quamlibet infirmum corpus afflicet obstinato silentio, tentio, vigiliis inedia: vita tamen exemplo plu-ribus, inter homines agens, profuisset. Totus paret iam pauculis mulierculis, quibus anxie desudabit, se illis praebens promptum ad omnia, ceu discipulum praeceptoribus, quibus, mi Philippe, opus est praeceptore: & quas iustius ferre, quam exercere imperium dixeris: ut nihil aliud certe propter sexus imbecillitatem. Est enim monasterium, cui se mancipant instituti, D. Brigidae, ubi mulieres viris in caput habentur, ordine praeposters. At ferendum est, quando mutari nequeat.
units.tr: Wolfgang Fabritius Capito also writes to Melanchthon: "Our Oecolampadius, he says, has withdrawn into monastic life, to the monastery of St. Alto, which is three miles from Augsburg. He has acted imprudently, though he is otherwise a cautious and wise man. Burdening his spirit, which was already not very cheerful, with a yoke it was not used to, he has fled from the sight of men for the sake of religion, as though Christ took pleasure in our sadness, and as though it were a truly Christian way of worship to avoid human company. However weak his body is, though he wears it down with obstinate silence, fasting, watching and hunger, a life spent among men would have been more useful to many by its example. He is now wholly given over to a few silly women, for whom he will sweat anxiously, offering himself ready for everything, like a pupil to his teachers. My Philip, these are the very people who need a teacher, and whom you would say it is more fitting to put up with than to rule over, since nothing else can be done because of the weakness of their sex. For the monastery to which he has committed himself is that of St. Bridget, where women are held as heads over men, in an inverted order. But it must be endured, since it cannot be changed."

units.la: CASPAR Hedio Etlingae in Marchionatu Badensi natus, Basileae Theologiae Do-ctor creatur, & summo apud Moguntinos templo praeficitur, Evangelii lumine iam tum collustratus.
units.tr: Caspar Hedio, born at Ettlingen in the Margraviate of Baden, is created Doctor of Theology at Basel, and is placed in charge of the chief church among the Mainzers, already at that time enlightened by the light of the Gospel.

units.la: Quo loco Basileae res Christi fuerit hoc anno, Capito narrat. Hic, inquit, res semper in melius vergit. Theologi & Monachi nobiscum faciunt. Enarranti modo Matthaum operam dat auditorium frequentissimum. Lutherio quidam dira minantur. Sed receptior est opinio, quam quae ulla vi queat evelli. Sunt qui me favoris Luheriani reum agunt: tametsi sedulo dissimulo.
units.tr: Capito tells what the state of Christ's cause was at Basel this year. "Here," he says, "things always move for the better. The theologians and the monks side with us. A very crowded audience attends while I expound Matthew. Some threaten dire things against Luther. But the more common opinion is one that cannot be torn up by any force. There are some who accuse me of being a supporter of Luther, although I dissemble diligently."

units.la: Mense Aprili V Volffgangus Fabritius Capito, favore Ulrici Huttenii ab Archiepiscopo Moguntino in aulam vocatus est, Principis Concionator, & Consiliarius, qua ille conditione ideo suscepit: ut Moguntiae Christianismum plantaret, Sic enim ille ad Huttenum anni superioris mense Novembri : Iuris Pontificii, ut vocant, Doctoratum sus- cipiam : propter auctoritatem videlicet comparandam : scopum suboles±s, pra ceteris multis sacrosanctum. Licet interim sint aliqui, qui vitio vertunt, Theologum esse, & una simul Civilem : quasi Theologus necesse habeat omnem exuere humanitatem.
units.tr: In April, Wolfgang Fabritius Capito was called to the court of the Archbishop of Mainz, through the favour of Ulrich von Hutten, to be the Prince's preacher and counsellor. He accepted this position on the condition that he would plant Christianity at Mainz. For he wrote thus to Hutten in November of the previous year: "I shall take up the doctorate of Pontifical law, as they call it, in order to acquire authority, the aim of which is, to be sure, a most sacred thing above many others. Yet in the meantime there are some who find fault that one man is both a theologian and at the same time a civil officer, as though a theologian must strip off all human feeling."

units.la: Ex Moguntia mense Decembri Capito iterum hortatur Lutherum ad modestiam, ubi inter alia, Cupio, inquit, reflorescere Christum, armis an patientia reflorescat, compertum habes. Nata est Religio: aucta est: firmata est, ab innocentibus, ab imbellibus; tolerantia gladios furiosis e manibus excusserunt inermes. Qua vero gens ab Hoplomachis cruentis candidam Religionem susceperit, non observavi. Quanquam haud ignorem veterem legem, cui nos videmur perfimilimi, assertam esse manu saepius: & a nostris tentatum interdum, non dico, quam feliciter, neq; quam pie, quia interim decrevit res nostra. Idcirco vehementer deterres deditos tibi significantia praesidiorum & armorum, etiamsi intelligam forte rationem consilii tui: qua apud me prope alia est. Nam quod alte haeret, non semel evellitur, sensim est, & subinde labefactandum: ut tandem sequatur trahentis manum.
units.tr: From Mainz in December, Capito again urges Luther to moderation. Among other things he says: "I wish Christ to flourish again. Whether he flourishes by arms or by patience you know well. Religion was born, and has grown and been strengthened, by the innocent and the unarmed; by patience the unarmed have knocked the swords out of the hands of the furious. But what nation has received the pure religion from bloody swordsmen, I have not observed. Though I am not unaware that the old law, to which we seem very much alike, has often been upheld by the hand, and that our side has sometimes attempted it, I do not say how successfully or how piously, since in the meantime our cause has been decided. So I strongly warn you against the devoted hope of protection and arms, even though I perhaps understand the reasoning of your plan, which in my view is almost otherwise. For what clings deeply is not torn out at once; it must be loosened gradually and shaken again and again, until at last it follows the hand that pulls it."

units.la: SENATUS Tigurinus de consilio Zwinglii omnibus ditionis suae concionatoribus mandat: dat: ut, missis hominum commentis, liberè, doceant, quidquid autoritate Propheticarū & Apostolicarū literarū adstrui possit. Cives Tigurini concionibus & libello Zwinglii de discrimine ciborū mense Aprili edito motl, legem Papæ de vetito carnium esu perrumpunt. Hugo Episcopus Constātiensis per edictum publicū singulos, per legatos vero Tigurinos hortatur: in fide Romanæ Ecclesiæ ut maneāt tantisper, dum Conciliū celebretur. Zwinglius ad legatos se suaq; defendit. Tigurini Episcopum orant: ut cogat synodum, in qua viri docti colloquantur, & quid populo credendum, definiant.
units.tr: The Senate of Zurich, on Zwingli's advice, orders all the preachers of its dominion that, having put aside human inventions, they teach freely whatever can be established by the authority of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings. The citizens of Zurich, moved by the sermons and by Zwingli's little book on the distinction of foods, published in April, break the Pope's law on the forbidden eating of meat. Hugo, Bishop of Constance, by public edict urges each man, and through Zurich's envoys urges them, to remain for the time being in the faith of the Roman Church, until a Council is held. Zwingli defends himself and his cause to the envoys. The Zurichers beg the Bishop to call a synod, in which learned men may confer and decide what the people ought to believe.

units.la: Fuit Zwinglio idem animus qui Luthero, fortis nimirum & intrepidus. Sic enim hoc anno ille de se: Ego quod ad me attinet, dudū devotus expecto omne malū ab omnibus, Ecclesiasticis dico & laicis: hoc unum Christum obtestans, ut masculo omnia pectore ferre donet, & me figulinum suū rumpat aut firmet, ut illi placidum sit. Si excommunicabor, memor ero Hilarii doctissimi & sanctissimi viri, qui è Galliis in Africam relegatus fuit: & Lucii, qui à Romana sede exturbatus cum multa gloria redijt: non quod me illis comparē, sed quod hıs me sim solaturus, ut longè meliorib. nobis, ita lõgè indignissima passis: & si forsan gloriari expediret, gaudere pro nomine Christi cõtumeliā pati.
units.tr: Zwingli had the same spirit as Luther, certainly strong and fearless. For this year he speaks thus of himself: "As far as I am concerned, I have long been prepared and expect every evil from everyone, I mean from churchmen and laymen alike. I beseech Christ alone that he grant me to bear everything with a manly heart, and that he either break or strengthen me, his clay, as seems pleasing to him. If I am excommunicated, I shall remember the most learned and most holy man Hilary, who was banished from Gaul to Africa, and Lucius, who was driven from the Roman see and returned with great glory. I do not compare myself with them, but I shall console myself with them, since they suffered things far more deserved than we do, and if perhaps it were expedient to boast, to rejoice in suffering insult for the name of Christ."

units.la: Inter primas regiones, quibus Evangelii lumen affulsit, Frisia Orientalis fuit: in qua
units.tr: Among the first regions upon which the light of the Gospel shone was East Frisia, in which

units.la: Princeps ipse Edfardus, primis Lutheri scriptis magno studio lectis & relectis, hauftisq; inde lucis primitiis, superstitiones abiecit: eadé scripta Lutheri venire in Bibliopoliis, lectitariq; ab omnibus, quib. animus eflet, fine metu ac discrimine ullo sivit: imò exemplo suo ad hoc ipsū præcipuos ex nobilitate patria, atq; alios doctrinâ & iudicio valetes, excitavit. Primi Evangelii doctores fuêre, apud Auricanos Henricus Brunius, apud Leranos Lubbertus Cantius, apud Nordanos Joannes Stephanus, apud VVeneranos Joannes Sculteto, quanquam hic deflexerit postea, sed omnibus prælucēs Georgius Aportanus apud Embdanos. Hic Suollis in ædibus Fratrū, uti nuncupāt, cum minor annis effet, literis imbutus, deinde adultior in docēdis bonis artibus ibidem in schola versatus aliquandiu: inde ab Edfardo vocatus, & instituendis filiis ipsius præfectus, cum veritatis primū lumen hausisset, exarsit studio: ut, quod ipse intelligeret verū, id alios quoq; doceret: ideoq; sacerdotium, ut sibi aditus ad suggestū pateret, iniit. Inde cum Emdanos doctrinæ cupidos, sed bonorum doctorū inopes videret, templis exclusus à Sacerdotibus, quib, odio erat, permissu Comitis, patenti in campo, concurrente magna multitudine, cōciones habuit. Mox civium studio, ne quidq̄ obnitentibus sacerdotibus, in templum urbanū duētus, & in suggesto collocatus est, Principe, ut à se-
units.tr: The prince himself, Edzard, having read and re-read Luther's first writings with great zeal and drunk in from them the first fruits of light, cast off superstitions. He allowed these same writings of Luther to be sold in bookshops and read by all who had the inclination, without any fear or danger. Indeed, by his own example he stirred up to this very purpose the leading men of his country from the nobility, and others strong in learning and judgment. The first preachers of the Gospel were: among the Auricans, Henricus Brunius; among the Leerans, Lubbertus Cantius; among the Nordanians, Johannes Stephanus; among the Weneranians, Johannes Sculteto, although he later turned aside; but excelling all, Georgius Aportanus among the Emdeners. While still a younger man, he was educated in letters in the house of the Brethren, as they call it, at Suollis, and later, as a grown man, he was for some time employed in teaching the liberal arts in the school there. Then, called by Edzard and placed over the instruction of his sons, after he had first drunk in the first light of truth, he burned with such zeal that he wished to teach others what he himself understood to be true; and therefore he took holy orders, so that a way to the pulpit would be open to him. Then, seeing the Emdeners eager for doctrine but short of good teachers, and shut out of the churches by the priests, who hated him, with the Count's permission he preached sermons in an open field, with a great crowd gathering. Soon, through the zeal of the citizens, lest the priests stir up any opposition, he was led into the city church and placed in the pulpit, with the Prince, so that from

units.la: Idem Ubbo lib. 53. hust. Frif. nibus accepi, Bernhardo Campio, publicum munus gerente (scriba enim praetorii praefecturae suburbanae erat) qui apparitoribus stipatus, dabat operam, ne quid turbarum per sacerdotes cōciretur, aut immodeste fieret à populo. Datus Aportano collega primus, Hermānus Henricus, ex sacrificorū oppidanorū numero, abiectâ idolomaniâ ad veritatem cōversus. Reliqui sacerdotes sensim altarib. & suggesto amoti, quotquot eorū concedere alio noluere, retentis censib. suis unà cum civiū parte, quib. Papatus nondū fastidio erat, apud Fraciscanos exercitiū religionis solitæ sustentabāt. In quib. Poppo Manninga locū nomenq; suum tenuit ad annum Christi 1530. & defuncto Unicone Ripperda, qui Hicconi Cankenio in honore succederat, Praepositurae census prioribus quoq; adiecit.
units.tr: The same Ubbo, in book 53 of his Frisian history, tells that I learned from Bernhard Campius, who held a public office (for he was the clerk of the praetorium of the suburban prefecture). Surrounded by attendants, he took care that no disorder was stirred up by the priests, or done immodestly by the people. Hermannus Henricus, from the number of the town's priests, was assigned as the first colleague of Aportanus, having abandoned idolatry and turned to the truth. The remaining priests, gradually removed from the altars and the pulpit, all who were unwilling to go elsewhere, kept their incomes, and together with the part of the citizens who were not yet weary of the Papacy, maintained the accustomed exercise of religion among the Franciscans. Among them Poppo Manninga kept his place and his title until the year of Christ 1530; and when Unico Ripperda died, who had succeeded Hicco Cankenius in the office, he also added the revenues of the provostship to the former ones.

units.la: Nec aliter factum in tota regione, stetitq; aut concidit Papatus, prout plebs, aut sacris initiati, huc illucq; inclinarunt: quippe cum cogeret neminem, neminem loco moveret Edfard°, plebi vero libertatem in hac re, atq; arbitriū omne relinqueret: nisi q; causam piā, quantū poterat, favore iuvaret, atq; hoc praestaret, ne qd immodeste aut turbulente usquā ob religionem fieret. Deniq; fine imperio religionis forma, verbi divini vi, brevi tempore sub ditione Edfardi cōversa est; superstitioq; vetus aut privatis parietib. hic illicq;, aut Monachorum Monachorūq; cœnobiis cōclusa,
units.tr: It was no different in the whole region: the Papacy stood or fell according as the common people, or those initiated into the sacred offices, inclined this way or that. For Edzard compelled no one and moved no one from his place, but left the common people free in this matter and wholly to their own judgment, except that he helped the pious cause with his favour as far as he could, and took care that nothing was done immodestly or tumultuously anywhere on account of religion. Finally, without any command, the form of religion was changed within a short time under Edzard's rule by the power of the divine Word; and the old superstition, shut up either in private houses here and there, or in the monasteries of the monks and nuns,

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXXI.
units.tr: The Year of Christ 1521.

units.la: ANNus vicesimus primus Lutheri consessione coram imperio edită : origine sectæ Anabaptisticæ: Henrici VIII. Anglorũ Regis adversus Lutherum libro: & aliquot in Germania Ecclesiarum reformatione est insignis.
units.tr: AThe twenty-first year is notable for Luther's confession, made publicly before the Emperor; for the origin of the Anabaptist sect; for Henry VIII, King of the English, writing a book against Luther; and for the reformation of several churches in Germany.

units.la: LUTHERUS ut à Cæsare audiretur, Fridericus Saxoniæ Elector effecit. Sexto igitur Martii literis Cæsaris, fidem publicam promittétibus, per Caduceatorē Casparū Sturmium, vocatur VVormatiam: comitantur eŭ Justus Jonas præpositus: D. Hieronymus Schurffius Juriscōsultus, & Nicolaus Ambsdorfius Theologus. Ex scholasticis unum sibi comitem adiunxit, Petrum Suavenium Danum, qui postea in aulam Regis Daniæ Christiani accitus, studia literarum & Ecclesiæ multùm iuvit.
units.tr: Frederick, Elector of Saxony, arranged for Luther to be heard by the Emperor. So, by a letter from the Emperor on 6 March promising public safe conduct, he was summoned to Worms through the herald Caspar Sturm. He was accompanied by Justus Jonas, provost; Dr Hieronymus Schurff, jurist; and Nicholas Amsdorf, theologian. From the scholars he took one companion, Peter Suavenius, a Dane, who later was summoned to the court of Christian, King of Denmark, and greatly helped literature and the Church there.

units.la: Erant qui hominem in itinere dehortarentur: VVormatiam ut ne ingrederetur: alii, qui exustione librorum ipsius iam damnatum Pontificiorum calculo crederent: alii, qui Joannis Hussi, alii, qui Savanorolæ exemplis terrerentur. Franciscus etiam à Sickingen à Cæsaris intimis rogatus, per Martinum Bucerum ad se invitat Lutherum, subinnuens: in arce sua Ebernburga commodiùs, quàm in strepitu Comitiorum causam ipsius posse disceptari. Quibus omnibus acriter Lutherus restitit, & non Ebernburgam sed VVormatiam quia à Cæsare esset vocatus, eò se iturum dixit: etiamsi sciret, tot sibi Diabolos esse oppositos, quot sunt in omnibus urbis tectis tegulæ.
units.tr: Some warned him on the journey not to enter Worms; others, who on the Papists' reckoning believed he was already condemned by the burning of his books, warned him too; others were frightened by the examples of John Hus and Savonarola. Franz von Sickingen, asked by the Emperor's intimates, invited Luther to himself through Martin Bucer, hinting that his cause could be debated more conveniently in his castle at Ebernburg than in the uproar of the Diet. Luther resisted all of these firmly, and said he would go not to Ebernburg but to Worms, since he had been summoned by the Emperor, even though he knew that as many devils were opposed to him as there were tiles on all the roofs of the city.

units.la: Venit VVormatiam xvi. Aprilis, quæ erat dies Martis post Misericordias Domini. Erantq; tum nonnulli autores Cæsari: perinde ut cum Husso, agendum cum Luthero. Sed Cæsar securitatem publicam minimè violandam censuit: & Ludovicus Elector Palatinus dixit: eam rem, si ita fieret, pertinere ad Germanici nominis labem & dedecus sempiternum. Bis comparuit coram Cæsare & Principibus: semel coram Trevirensi.
units.tr: He came to Worms on 16 April, which was the Tuesday after Misericordias Domini. Some advisers of the Emperor then urged that Luther be treated as Hus had been. But the Emperor judged that public safe conduct must not be violated in any way; and Louis, Elector Palatine, said that if it were done, it would bring lasting disgrace and shame upon the German name. He appeared twice before the Emperor and the princes, and once before the Archbishop of Trier.

units.la: Coram Cæsare xvii. Aprilis ad duo respondere jussus est. Primùm. An librorum, qui nominabantur, se profiteretur autorem. Deinde, An quicquam in iis retractare, an omnia vellet tueri.
units.tr: On 17 April, before the Emperor, he was ordered to answer two questions. First, whether he acknowledged himself the author of the books named. Second, whether he would retract anything in them, or wished to defend them all.

units.la: Scripta sua statim agnovit. Ad retractationis quæstionem priusquam responderet, veniâ Cæsaris noctem in consilium adhibuit. Decimâ octavâ igitur Aprilis, non unius generis libros esse à se publicatos, respondit: corum alios de pietate & moribus : alios contra Papam & ejus doctrinam: alios contra privatos adversarios scriptos. Nullos se retractare posse: non primi generis: quia ipsi adversarii eos utiles & innoxios esse fateantur. Non secundi, non tertii generis, quamlibet calidius scriptos : ne tyrannidem Antichristi,& eius asseclarum corroboret. Denique ex scripturis solis se revincendum offert.
units.tr: He at once acknowledged his writings. Before answering the question of retraction, he asked the Emperor's leave and took a night to consider. Then on 18 April he replied that the books he had published were not all of one kind: some dealt with piety and morals; others attacked the Pope and his doctrine; others were written against private adversaries. He could retract none of them. Not those of the first kind, because his opponents themselves admit they are useful and harmless. Not those of the second or third kind, however hotly written, since to retract them would strengthen the tyranny of Antichrist and his followers. Finally, he offered to be refuted from Scripture alone.

units.la: Caesar xix. Aprilis missa in Senatum epistola, se fidem Luthero servaturum, sed finito salvi conductus tempore, proscripturum illum, significat.
units.tr: On 19 April the Emperor sent a letter to the Diet, stating that he would keep faith with Luther, but that once the period of safe conduct had ended he would proscribe him.

units.la: Trevirien sis xxiv. Aprilis primum praesente Electore Brandeburgico, deinde privatim Lutherum tentat. Sed nihil ab eo extorquet, nisi repetitione consilii Gamalielis. Dimissus Lutherus xxvi. Aprilis Wormatia abit. Fridberga scribit ad Caesarem: Acta Vormatiensia repetit: confessionem suam inserit: gratias agit pro data fide publica: vim deprecatur. Eiusdem argumenti literas ad status Imperii exarat.
units.tr: On 24 April the Archbishop of Trier first tried Luther in the presence of the Elector of Brandenburg, and then privately. But he drew nothing from him except a repetition of Gamaliel's counsel. Luther was dismissed and left Worms on 26 April. Friedberg writes to the Emperor, repeats the Acts of Worms, inserts his own confession, gives thanks for the public safe conduct granted, and deprecates violence. He drew up letters on the same subject to the states of the Empire.

units.la: Caesar vi ii. Maij Lutherum proscribit: quem Leo Pontifex 28. Martii die coenae Domini iterato excommunicarat. Omnium animi tum erant arrecti, quid illa Caesaris & Pontificis fulmina essent effectura. Mirare hic mecum bonitatem iuxta & sapientiam Dei. Lutherus Friderici Electoris prudentia ex oculis hominum abripitur, & in arce Vartberg, prope Isennacum ababscöditur: ubi menses deciem circiter latuit.
units.tr: On 2 May the Emperor proscribed Luther, whom Pope Leo had already excommunicated a second time, on 28 March, the day of the Lord's Supper. Everyone's minds were then on edge as to what the thunderbolts of Emperor and Pope would achieve. Marvel with me here at the goodness and the wisdom of God alike. Through the prudence of the Elector Frederick, Luther was snatched from the eyes of men and hidden away in the castle of Wartburg, near Eisenach, where he lay concealed for about ten months.

units.la: LEo Papa Kal. Decemb. moritur. Cæsar in Hispaniâ ob excitatas ibi seditiones vocatur: bello deinde Gallico implicatur. Et sic persequutionū venti sedati, & in turbido renascentis Ecclesiæ mari tranquillitas est facta. Falsus fuit Hieronymus Alcander, qui ad Marinum Caracciolum, legatum Pontificum, fertur dixisse: Eia, mi Caracciole, si nihil adeo praeclari his Comitiis effecimus: tamen certum est, nos magnam hoc edicto in Germania lanienam concitare, qua Alemanni ipsi in viscera sua saevientes, propediem in proprio sanguine suffocabuntur.
units.tr: Pope Leo died on 1 December. The Emperor was called to Spain because of the seditions stirred up there, and then became entangled in the French war. And so the winds of persecution were calmed, and in the troubled sea of the reborn Church there came a calm. Hieronymus Aleander was wrong, who is reported to have said to Marino Caracciolo, the Pope's legate: "Come now, my Caracciolo, if we have achieved nothing so splendid at this Diet, yet it is certain that by this edict we stir up a great slaughter in Germany, in which the Germans, raging against their own vitals, will shortly be suffocated in their own blood."

units.la: De ipsa proscriptione Caesarea diversa diuersorum (ut fieri solet) erant judicia: aliis zelum Caroli collaudantibus: aliis Propheticū illud identidem ingeminantibus: vae terrae, cujus Rex puer est. Erasmus quid de bulla Papae & Caesaris proscriptione senserit: epistola ipsius docet: in qua haec leguntur: Semper in hac fui sententia: tragœdiam hanc nulla ratione melius consopiri posse, quàm silentio. Idem sentiunt, qui sunt inter Cardinales & magnates cordatissimi. Prodijt saevissima bulla à Pontifice. Nihil aliud quàm exacerbavit incendium. Sequutum est etiam saevius Caesaris edictum, qui totus in hanc rem propensus est. Ea res linguas quorundam & calamos coercet, at non mutat animos. Laudatur quidem pius Caesar animus: sed judicium huius rei adscribunt ijs, quibus eruditi non multum tribuunt. Erant
units.tr: As for the Emperor's proscription itself, opinions differed, as usual: some praised the zeal of Charles, while others kept repeating that prophetic saying: "Woe to the land whose king is a child." What Erasmus thought of the Pope's bull and the Emperor's proscription his letter shows, in which these things are read: "I have always been of this opinion: this tragedy can be settled in no better way than by silence. The most sensible of the Cardinals and magnates think the same. The most savage bull has come out from the Pope. It has done nothing but fan the fire. Even more savage was the Emperor's edict, which is wholly bent on this matter. That affair restrains the tongues and pens of some, but does not change their minds. The pious spirit of the Emperor is indeed praised; but the judgment in this matter is ascribed to those whom learned men do not greatly esteem." There were

units.la: Cochlæus in vita Lutheri. Basileæ III. Non. Sept. 1522.
units.tr: Cochlaeus, in the life of Luther. Basel, 3 September 1522.

units.la: Erant qui dicerent: edictum VVormatiense plus profuisse Caesari, quàm nocuisse Luthero. Nam ut edictum illud Papam Caesari, à Gallo alienatum, ita Luthero multorum hominum corda conciliavit.
units.tr: Some said that the Edict of Worms did more good to the Emperor than harm to Luther. For just as that edict won the Pope over to the Emperor, estranging him from the French king, so it won over the hearts of many men to Luther.

units.la: ORIGO fanaticæ Anabaptistarum sectæ huic anno debetur. Cum inter cæteras Martini Lutheri theses liber de libertate Christiana in lucem editus, toto orbe spargeretur, mox Germanicâ linguâ jactari omnium manibus cœptus, incredibili dictu est, quos plausus apud homines literarum ignaros excitârit. Is certè liber materiam vulgo ad memorabilem rusticorum seditionem, sed non bene intellectus, præbere visus fuit.
units.tr: The origin of the fanatical Anabaptist sect is owed to this year. When, among Martin Luther's other theses, the book on Christian liberty was published and spread across the whole world, it soon began to be bandied about in German in everyone's hands; it is hard to say what applause it stirred among men ignorant of letters. That book certainly seemed to provide the common people with material for the memorable rebellion of the peasants, though it was not rightly understood.

units.la: Nicolaus Ciconia (Claus Storch) Marcus Stubnerus, Martinus Cellarius, Thomas Müntzerus, primi huius sectæ nominantur autores.
units.tr: Nicholas Ciconia (Claus Storch), Marcus Stübner, Martin Cellarius and Thomas Müntzer are named as the first authors of this sect.

units.la: CICONIA vagabatur passim, seq; imperitum literarum esse penitus simulabat, prædicans sibi divinitùs scientiam salutarem contingere. Is ex plebe imperita & simplice plurimos deceptos falsitate opinionis perniciosæ complebat.
units.tr: Ciconia wandered about everywhere, pretending that he was wholly unlearned, and preaching that saving knowledge had come to him by divine means. By this pernicious opinion he filled many who were deceived, from among the untrained and simple common people, with falsehood.

units.la: MARCUS literatus erat: & sibi à Deo hoc esse datum tributumque eximium, gloriabatur: ut ipse interpretando explicandoq; scripta sacrarum literarum excelleret. Hûc apud se fovebat VVittembergæ Melanchthon, vel innainnatâ sibi bonitate: vel ut certius cognosceret: quid istud genus doceret.
units.tr: Marcus was learned, and boasted that God had given him this special gift, so that he excelled in interpreting and explaining the writings of Holy Scripture. At Wittenberg Melanchthon kept him close to himself, either from innate goodness or in order to learn more surely what that sort of man taught.

units.la: Martinus Cellarius Suevicæ gentis, cum Philippo Melanchthone Tubingæ usum quendam habuerat: ideo VVittembergam venienti tradidit Melanchthon discipulos instituendos in privata Schola. Hunc Marcus amicum, socium & adiutorem natus, cum patrocinio Andreæ Carolostadii, & favore Melanchthonis niteretur, demoliendum statim censuit, quicquid perperam in Ecclesiam introductum esset.
units.tr: Martin Cellarius, a native of Swabia, had had some dealings with Philip Melanchthon at Tübingen; therefore Melanchthon, when Cellarius came to Wittenberg, handed over pupils to him to instruct in a private school. Marcus, who had been born a friend, partner and helper to him, relying on the patronage of Andreas Carlstadt and the favour of Melanchthon, judged at once that whatever had been wrongly introduced into the Church should be pulled down.

units.la: Thomas Müntzer Saxo erat, homo (ut aiunt) illiteratus, sed, ut apparebat, in libello Lutheri de libertate Christiana egregiè exercitatus, & scripti interpres parum candidus, primum Cygneæ Pastor inventoribus Ciconiâ & Stubuero cœpit res novas moliri: inde profligatus, Alsteti (oppidum est Ducum Saxoniæ in finibus Thuringiæ & Saxoniæ) concionatoris officium sibi arrogavit: ubi editis etiam libris errores suos in universam Germaniam disseminavit. Semel atque iterum cum Luthero VVittembergæ privatim contulit: sed pias Lutheri commonefactiones fusq; déq; habuit. Alsteto igitur ejectus in superiorem Germaniam, & inde in Helvetiam proficiscitur, ubique seminibus furoris sui sparsis. Sed mox in Thuringiam reversus Mulhusium sibi delegit. git, ubi novam conderet Ecclesiam, Luthero frustra Mulhufinos monente, à lupo isto ut sibi caverent.
units.tr: Thomas Müntzer was a Saxon, a man (as they say) unlettered, but, as appeared, very well practised in Luther's little book on Christian liberty, and a not very candid interpreter of it. First, as pastor at Zwickau, he began to plan new things with the originators Ciconia and Stübner; driven out from there, he assumed for himself the office of preacher at Allstedt (a town of the Dukes of Saxony on the borders of Thuringia and Saxony). There, after publishing books, he spread his errors through all Germany. Once and again he conferred privately with Luther at Wittenberg, but he made light of Luther's pious warnings. Expelled from Allstedt, he went off into upper Germany, and from there into Switzerland, scattering the seeds of his frenzy everywhere. But soon returning to Thuringia, he chose Mühlhausen for himself, where he might found a new Church, although Luther warned the people of Mühlhausen in vain to beware of that wolf.

units.la: De Ciconia & Marco quid factum sit, quicquid exitus vitæ eorum fuerint, non constat. Cellarius sectæ isti diu sane adhæsit, cumque anno xxv. in Prussiam venisset, liberam custodiam Principis iussu datus, multa scripsit de doctrina illa. Postea animadvertens, labascere partes, & spem se frustrari, Basileam se contulit, uxorem duxit, quietè vixit, sacra professus est, Latinóque nomine Cellarii in Græcum commutato, se Borrhaum nominavit. Leguntur commentarii eius eruditi in Pentateuchum, & alios Bibliorum libros. Müntzerus, quod notum, in prælio captus, à Duce Saxoniæ ferro percussus est anno xxv. Hoc hominũ genus nil nisi LIBERTATEM in ore habebat: Colloquia cũ Deo jactitabat: in Ecclesiasticos & Politicos detorquebat: omnia esse corrupta, ideoq; instauranda, Ecclesiamque novam condendam, & illius cives denuo Baptismo initiandos, clamabat.
units.tr: What became of Storch and Marcus, whatever their end was, is not known. Cellarius clung to that sect for a good while, and when he came to Prussia in 1525 he was given free custody by order of the Prince and wrote much on that doctrine. Afterwards, noticing that their cause was faltering and that his hopes were being disappointed, he went to Basel, married, lived quietly, professed the sacred faith, changed his Latin name Cellarius into Greek, and called himself Borrhaus. His learned commentaries on the Pentateuch and other books of the Bible are still read. Müntzer, as is well known, was taken prisoner in battle and beheaded by the Duke of Saxony in 1525. This class of men had nothing but LIBERTY on their lips. They boasted of conversations with God, twisted everything against the ecclesiastical and civil authorities, and cried out that everything was corrupt, that it must therefore be restored, that a new Church must be founded, and that its citizens must be baptized anew.

units.la: HENRICUS VIII. Rex Angliæ dogmatum Lutheri commotus novitate, pulcrum simul & honorificum sibi futurum existimabat: si scripto aliquo eruditionem suam & cultus divini piam curam omnibus faceret testatam. Hinc prodiit libellus ille, adeo profectioris ætatis, & exercitato aliquo Theologo dignior, quàm adolescente Rege(cui, quanquam maximè voluerit, non licuerit tamen in literarũ studio ætatem terere) ut alii Thomæ Mori, alii Fisherii Roffensis, plurimi verò alterius alicuius summi viri opus id fuisse, haud sine causa suspicarentur. Ut ut fuerit, edito libello sic respondit Lutherus, ut multi sanè, qui sanctum hominis zelum laudarent, modestiam tamen, spiritu sancto dignam, in eo haud immeritò desiderarent, regiæq; dignitatis magis reverentem. Enimverò Papæ hæc Regis opera navata tam grata fuit: ut eum, successoresq; suos, honorifico titulo (Defensores fidei) postea semper appellandos decreverit, quemadmodum antea Hispanus per Alexandrum sextum Catholici, Gallus per alium, nescio quem, Christianissimi Regis nomine cohonestati sunt, quæ omnia in hunc usq; diem ab eorum singulis usurpantur.
units.tr: HENRY VIII, King of England, was disturbed by the novelty of Luther's doctrines and thought it would be a fine and honourable thing for him to show, in some written work, his learning and his pious concern for divine worship before everyone. Hence appeared that little book, which was more suited to a more mature age and to some experienced theologian than to a young king (who, however much he may have wished it, was not permitted to spend his life in literary study). For this reason some suspected that it was the work of Thomas More, others of Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, and very many of some other great man, and not without cause. However that may be, Luther replied to the published book in such a way that many, who praised the man's holy zeal, nevertheless missed in it, not without justice, a moderation worthy of the Holy Spirit and more respectful of royal dignity. Indeed the Pope was so pleased with this work of the King that he decreed that he and his successors should afterwards always be called by the honourable title "Defenders of the Faith." In the same way the Spanish king had earlier been honoured by Alexander VI with the name "Catholic," and the French king by another, I know not whom, with the name "Most Christian." All these titles are still used by each of their holders to this day.

units.la: Hactenus renascentis Evangelii doctrina intra V Vittembergæ parietes conclusa videbatur. Etsi enim Lutheri scripta non solùm in Germaniam superiorem & inferiorem, sed in remotissima etiam regna fuerunt sparsa: tamen rari coetus alibi erant (Frisiam Orientalem excipio) in quibus abjecto Papismo Evangelium purè doceretur. A Comitiis autem VVormatiensibus, contra quàm Cæsar & Papa existimârant, Ecclesiæ variis in locis suntcœptæ reformari.
units.tr: Up to this point the doctrine of the reborn Gospel seemed to be confined within the walls of Wittenberg. For although Luther's writings had been scattered not only through Upper and Lower Germany but also into the most remote kingdoms, nonetheless there were few assemblies elsewhere (I except East Frisia) in which the Gospel was taught purely with Popery cast aside. But after the Diet of Worms, contrary to what the Emperor and the Pope had thought, the Churches began to be reformed in various places.

units.la: VVORMATIENSES, visâ Lutheri in Comitiis Imperii constantiâ, nil territi horribili Cæsaris edicto, concionatores Evangelicos vocant, quibus cùm aditus ad Pontificiorū templa intercluderetur, portatilem suggestum confici curant, & ad audiendum Dei verbum in aliis atque aliis urbis locis conveniunt. Quod ubi Lutherus rescivit, anno vicesimo tertio scriptâ ad ipsos epistolâ consolatoriâ, mirificè bonorum zelum confirmavit. Anno autem xxv. Pontificii territi metu rusticani belli, liberum Evangelicæ religionis exercitium in omnibus urbis templis civibus permiserunt.
units.tr: The people of Worms, seeing Luther's constancy at the Diet of the Empire and not frightened at all by the Emperor's dreadful edict, summoned Evangelical preachers. When access to the Papists' churches was closed to them, they arranged for a portable pulpit to be made and gathered to hear the Word of God in one and another place in the city. When Luther learned of this, in the year 1523 he wrote a letter of consolation to them and wonderfully strengthened the zeal of the good people. In the year 1525, however, the Papists, frightened by the fear of the Peasants' War, allowed the citizens free exercise of the Evangelical religion in all the churches of the city.

units.la: ERFURTI jubar Evangelicum hoc ipso anno exortum est: Lutherus in itinere VVormatiensi concionem ibi habet in æde Michaëlitana, Dominicâ Quasimodogeniti, de verbis Christi, pax vobis. Facta est paulò post vis in sacerdotum domos, quod Lutherus valde improbat epistolâ ad Melanchthonem scriptâ.
units.tr: At ERFURT the Evangelical light rose in this same year. Luther, on his journey to Worms, preached there in the church of St. Michael, on the Sunday after Quasimodogeniti, on the words of Christ, "Peace be unto you." Shortly afterwards violence was done to the priests' houses, which Luther strongly condemned in a letter written to Melanchthon.

units.la: Primi Evangelii præcones illius urbis laudantur, Doctor Joannes Langus, pastor Michaëlitanus: Georgius Forchemius, qui propinato sibi à Pontificiis veneno, obiit: Joannes Culschamerus, qui in suggestu veneno illito extinctus est: M. Petrus Geltnerus: M. Melchior VVedman: Justus Menius, pastor ad D. Thomam. Totus senatus cum fuit Pontificius: tamen Ministerium Evangelicum & reveritus est, & defendit. Papistici autem Doctores Evangelicos odio Cainico prosequuti sunt, & promotionem etiam Magistrorum suspenderunt, ne Lutheranorum filii gradu Magisterii ornarentur. Crevit autem tantopere Evangelicorum ibi numerus: ut anno 1523. octo templa illis vix sufficerent.
units.tr: The first heralds of the Gospel in that city are praised: Doctor Johann Lang, minister of St. Michael's; Georg Forchheim, who died after the poison given him by the Papists; Johann Culsamer, who was killed by poison smeared on the pulpit; Master Peter Geltner; Master Melchior Wedman; and Justus Menius, minister at St. Thomas's. Although the whole senate was Papist, it nonetheless both revered and defended the Evangelical ministry. The Papist teachers, however, pursued the Evangelical teachers with Cain-like hatred, and even suspended the conferring of master's degrees, so that the sons of the Lutherans might not be honoured with the degree of Master. Yet the number of Evangelicals there grew so greatly that in the year 1523 eight churches scarcely sufficed for them.

units.la: GOSLARIÆ (urbs est Imperialis in Saxonia) primus hoc anno purius Evangelium docere coepit Joannes Kleppen in suburbio in templo ad S.sepulcrum. Cui cum senatus à Clericis instigatus, & Cæsaris indignationem reveritus, silentium indixisset, prodiit Theodoricus quidam Smedeken Goslariensis, & sub dio, in loco quem vocant <bl>den Lin-</bl> <bl>denplan</bl> maximo hominum concursu docuit. Sed captus à Senatu, & Episcopo Hildesiensi missus, diuturniore carceris & vinculorum molestiâ fractus, turpem palinodiam cecinit anno 1523. VI. Octobris. Iterum igitur à civibus in publicum protrusus est Joannes Kleppen, & in ædc D. Jacobi docuit ad annum usque 1524. quo Senatus permissu in illa ipsa ædc Joannes Vvesselus, vir doctus & eloquens, Evangelium liberè profiteri, & sacramenta secundum Christi institutum administrare coepit.
units.tr: At GOSLAR (an Imperial city in Saxony) this year Johann Kleppen first began to teach the purer Gospel, in the suburb, in the church at the Holy Sepulchre. When the senate, stirred up by the clergy and fearing the Emperor's anger, had ordered silence to him, Theodoric Smedeken of Goslar came forward and taught before a large crowd, in the open air, in the place called the Lindenplan. But he was seized by the Senate and handed over to the Bishop of Hildesheim; broken by a long imprisonment and the hardship of chains, he sang a shameful recantation on 6 October 1523. Johann Kleppen was therefore again thrust out into public by the citizens, and taught in the church of St. James until the year 1524, when, by permission of the Senate, Johann Wessel, a learned and eloquent man, began to profess the Gospel freely in that same church and to administer the sacraments according to Christ's institution.

units.la: HALBERSTADII sinceriorem Evangelii doctrinam primi tradiderunt. Joannes VVeselius Brunsvicensis, & Henricus Gebhardus Helmstadiensis, ad S. Martinum. Quibus per Canonicos ejectis, duo Doctores Theologiae, Eberhardus VVidenlee, Praepositus D. Joannis, & Valentinus Musteus Carmelita, pro concione, & VVidenseus etiam in schola sui Monasterii, purius docebant. Et in senatu Henricus scriba Cos. plurimum sua autoritate Evangelium adiuvabat. Hunc Praetor urbis, & Capitaneus Episcopi, captum in salinas ducunt, ubi capitis damnatus aegre tandem se pecunia redemit. D. Valentino Musteo, instinctu suffraganei & Capituli oppresso noctu & ligato virilitas excisa est: qui, sanato vulnere, VVittembergam profectus, in ea vicinia, Lutheri commendatione, functionem accepit. Eberhardus etiam ab Episcopo ad carcerem perpetuum damnatur. Sed in itinere noctu elapsus ea custodia, Magdeburgam pervenit. Ubi ad S. Jacobum pastor factus, fideliter propagationem Evangelii adiuvit: donec ab optimo Principe Christiano, postea Daniae Rege, in Holsatia vocaretur. Halberstadii interea Henricus VVinkelius, & postea Joannes VVimmenstedius usque ad ann. 1529. inter varias persequutiones Ecclesiam puriorem plantarunt.
units.tr: At HALBERSTADT the first to deliver the purer doctrine of the Gospel were Johann Weselius of Brunswick and Henry Gebhard of Helmstedt, at St. Martin's. When they were expelled by the Canons, two Doctors of Theology, Eberhard Widenlee, provost of St. John's, and Valentin Musteus, a Carmelite, taught the purer doctrine in the pulpit, and Widenseus also taught it in the school of his monastery. In the senate, Henry, the city's secretary, supported the Evangelical cause greatly by his authority. The city's Praetor and the Bishop's captain seized him and led him to the salt-works, where, condemned to death, he at last with difficulty redeemed himself with money. Doctor Valentin Musteus, at the instigation of the suffragan and the Chapter, was seized by night and bound, and his virility was cut away. Once his wound had healed, he went to Wittenberg, and in that neighbourhood, on Luther's recommendation, received a ministry. Eberhard too was condemned by the Bishop to perpetual imprisonment, but he escaped that custody by night on the journey and came to Magdeburg. There he became pastor at St. James's and faithfully helped the spread of the Gospel, until he was called to Holstein by the excellent Christian Prince, afterwards King of Denmark. Meanwhile at Halberstadt Henry Winkel and afterwards Johann Wimmenstedt planted a purer Church until the year 1529, amid various persecutions.

units.la: HAMBURGI M. Ordo Stifelius, vel, ut alii, Stemmelius, pastor ad S. Catharinam, primus hoc anno indulgentias vanitatis arguere, fide justificantem hominib. commendare, deque legitimo claviu usu, earundemque Pontificio abusu differere coepit. Sed aetate, morbis, & Cleri persequutionibus fractus, exacto biennio M. Stephano Kempe Ecclesiam erudienda reliquit.
units.tr: At HAMBURG Master Ordo Stifelius, or, as others say, Stemmelius, pastor at St. Catherine's, was the first in this year to begin to expose the vanity of indulgences, to commend justification by faith to men, and to discourse on the lawful use of the keys and their Papist abuse. But, broken by age, illnesses and the persecutions of the clergy, after two years he left the Church to be taught by Master Stephen Kempe.

units.la: VVITTEMBERGAE Augustiniani coeperunt omnium primi Missam privatam abrogare. Lutherus, ut & vacillantes erigeret, & perituros confirmaret, confecit illis in Patmo librum de abrogan da Missa privata. Fridericus Elector totius Academiae sententiam super hac re exquirit: quae Principem orat: ut impietatem Missaticam non in uno solum templo, sed omnibus in locis aboleat, & verum usum coenae juxta Christi & Apostolorum mandatum instituat, & adversariorum calumnias omnes fortiter contemnat. Optima semper placuisse paucis.
units.tr: At WITTENBERG the Augustinians were the very first to begin to abolish private Mass. Luther, both to raise up those who were wavering and to strengthen those who were about to perish, composed for them on Patmos a book on the abolition of private Mass.
