Frederick the Elector sought the opinion of the whole University on this matter, which begged the Prince to abolish the Mass-impiety not in one church only but in all places, to institute the true use of the Supper of the Lord according to the command of Christ and the Apostles, and to despise bravely all the slanders of the adversaries. Good things have always pleased few.

units.la: BASILEAE VVilhelmus Roeblinus Pastor ad S. Albanum impugnat Romanam idolomaniam & in Christi morte vitam quaerendam docet. Ideo sacrificulorum instinctu in exilium pellitur.
units.tr: At BASEL Wilhelm Roeblinus, pastor at St. Alban's, attacked Roman idolatry and taught that life is to be sought in the death of Christ. For this, at the instigation of the priestlings, he was driven into exile.

units.la: In VALLE JOACHIMICA, quae Boemum agnoscit Regem M. Philippus Eberbachius, scholae Rector, in ipso ludo literario adutrinque sexus homines cociones Evangelicas habet.
units.tr: In the VALLEY OF JOACHIM, which acknowledges the King of Bohemia, Master Philip Eberbach, Rector of the school, held evangelical sermons in the literary school itself for men and women of both sexes.

units.la: ANTUERPI A Jacobus Praepositus, Prior Augustinianus, Lutheri discipulus, biennio, & amplius, Christum pure docuerat. Hoc aut anno noducitur Bruxellas, ubi mirè divexatus, metu ignis recantat, & in Flandriam dimissus, Christum iterum praedicat, captus denuo. Brugas primùm, inde Bruxellas missus in carcerem conijcitur, ex quo ope fratris Minoritae elabitur. Edidit ipse historiam lapsûs sui, in qua Bruxellas nominat macellum Christianorum: literas etiam publicat ad auditores suos Antuerpianos: quos rogat, ne lapsum suum doctrinae, sed humanae imbecillitati adscribant: nec ullius hominis, sed solius verbi Dei auctoritatem in negotio religionis respiciant. Hic Jacobus Bremae Saxonum deinceps multos annos fructuosè Evangelium docuit.
units.tr: At ANTWERP Jacob, Provost and Prior of the Augustinians, a disciple of Luther, had taught Christ purely for two years and more. This year he was led to Brussels, where, sorely tormented, he recanted out of fear of the fire; sent back into Flanders, he preached Christ again and was seized once more. First sent to Bruges and then to Brussels, he was thrown into prison, from which he escaped with the help of a Minorite friar. He himself published an account of his fall, in which he calls Brussels the shambles of Christians. He also published a letter to his Antwerp hearers, asking them to ascribe his fall not to the doctrine but to human weakness, and in matters of religion to look to the authority of the Word of God alone and not to that of any man. Afterwards this Jacob taught the Gospel fruitfully for many years at Bremen in Saxony.

units.la: In POMERANIA mutatio religionis alicubi gliscere, & purioris Evangelii doctrinae semina sensim spargi, ac inde in Livoniam & alias gentes propagari ex Collegio sacerdotum Treptoviensi, per Episcopum dissipato, primùm coeperunt. Florebat tum Treptoa ad Regum & Collegio sacerdotum, & scholae literarum celebri, quam Joannes Bugenhagius, & Andreas Cnophius Custrini ad Viadri & VVartae confl. natus, regebant, quorum tantopere in docendo industria, dexteritas & fides celebrabatur: ut nõ solùm ex vicinis oppidis, sed Livonia etiam & VVestphalia exciti scholastici, eò confluerent. Accidit autem anno 1520. excunte: ut inspector Ecclesiae, clesiæ, Otto Slutovius, ex patritia oppidi illius familia natus, cum Rectorem scholæ & collegas convictores aleret, librum Lutheri de captivitate Babylonica, recens ab amico Lipsiâ missum, proferret, & Rectori scholæ Joanni Bugenhagio, cujus præ cæteris ingenium & judicium limatius, & doctrina ac facundia in lectionibus & concionibus sacris spectata probabatur, perlegendum traderet. Qui mox, paginis aliquot inter cænandum prælustratis, præcipitatâ sententiâ, multos à passo Christo salvatore Hæreticos Ecclesiam infestasse, ac duriter exercuisse, sed nullum, eius libri autore, pestilentiorem unquam extitisse, pronunciat: commemorans, quæ adversus recepta Ecclesiæ dogmata ab eo afferrerentur. Post aliquot dies libro attentius lecto & relecto, ac singulis accuratius pensitatis, reversus ad Collegii sodales, & palinodiam canens: Quid ego vobis, inquit, multa dicam? Universus mundus cæcutit, & in Cimmerii tenebris versatur. Hic vir unus & solus verum videt. Ac singulis libri illius capitibus diligenter disputatis ac defensis, plerosque in suam sententiam adduxit: ita ut Collegæ pastores, Joannes Kyrichius, & Joannes Lorichius (qui ad extremam senectam Ecclesiæ illi deinceps servivit) cum Diacono, qui vicini cœnobii Belburgensis frater erat, Christiano Kettelhut, nec non Abbas ipse, Joannes Boldewinus publicè Papatûs præstigias detegere, & à superstitionibus & abusibus traditionum humanarũ, ad dogmata & cultus verbo Dei mandatos, & à fiducia Missæ ac operum humanorũ, ad unicum solius Christi meritum auditores traducere, magno zelo instituerant. Ut autem in articulis mutationum multa incommodiùs ac turbulentiùs, non tam doctorum, dextrâ veram doctrinam tradentium quàm vulgi sinistrâ accipientium, culpâ geruntur: ita tum quoque accidit: ut S. Antonii sacrificulos per plateas usitato more cum nolis vagantes injuriosiùs petulantes quidam juvenes, cœno injecto, tractarent, & ex æde S. spiritus statuas, noctu ablatas, in vicinum puteum conjicerent. Quo comperto Episcopus Caminensis, recens electus, Erasmus Mandùuel, cui in Pomerania Orientali sacrorum cura incumbebat, seditiosâ specie offensus, & zelo avitæ religionis ardens, atrocem persecutionem in multos sacerdotes accives & scholasticos movit: & in vincula multis conjectis, cæteri prærnoniti fugâ sibi consuluerunt. Ac Bugenhagius VVittembergam, absente tum Luthero in Pathmo (Petrus Vincentius oratione de vita Bugenhagii affirmat, ipsum paulo ante iter Lutheri VVormatiense VVittembergam venisse) concessit, & Psalterium privatim legendo scholæ innotuit, & reverso Luthero statim
units.tr: In Pomerania the change of religion first began to stir in some places, and the seeds of a purer doctrine of the Gospel were gradually sown there and spread from there into Livonia and other nations, after the College of Priests at Treptow had been broken up by the bishop. Treptow then flourished, with a royal college of priests and a famous school of letters, which John Bugenhagen and Andreas Cnophius, born at Küstrin on the Oder and the Warthe confluence, ran. Their diligence, skill and faithfulness in teaching were so highly praised that students came flocking to them not only from the neighbouring towns but also from Livonia and Westphalia. Towards the end of 1520 it happened that Otto Slutovius, the inspector of the church, born into a patrician family of that town, was supporting the rector of the school and the fellow teachers who lived with him. He brought out Luther's book on the Babylonian captivity, lately sent from Leipzig by a friend, and handed it to the rector of the school, John Bugenhagen, whose intellect and judgement were considered more polished than the others', and whose learning and eloquence in lectures and sermons were esteemed, to be read through. He, after a few pages had been skimmed over at dinner, rashly pronounced: that many heretics had attacked the Church since the passion of Christ the Saviour and treated it harshly, but that none of them, the author of this book included, had ever been more pestilential. He went on to recall what was being brought forward against the accepted doctrines of the Church. Some days later, having read the book again more attentively and weighed each point more carefully, he returned to his colleagues and, singing a palinode, said: What more shall I tell you? The whole world is blind and lives in Cimmerian darkness. This one man alone sees the truth. Having carefully discussed and defended each chapter of that book, he brought most of them round to his opinion, so that the colleague ministers, John Kyrichius and John Lorichius (who served that church until extreme old age), together with the deacon Christian Kettelhut, who was a brother of the neighbouring monastery at Belbuck, and the abbot himself, John Boldewin, resolved with great zeal to expose publicly the tricks of the Papacy, and to lead their hearers away from the superstitions and abuses of human traditions to the doctrines and worship commanded by the Word of God, and from trust in the Mass and human works to the one merit of Christ alone. But as in matters of change many things are done more awkwardly and turbulently, through the fault not so much of the learned, who hand down true doctrine with the right hand, as of the crowd, who receive it with the left, so it happened then too: certain wanton young men, dragging the priests of St Anthony about the streets as they wandered against their will in the usual way, pelted them with mud and, at night, threw the statues taken from the church of the Holy Spirit into a nearby well. When this came to light, the bishop of Cammin, newly elected, Erasmus Manteuffel, who had charge of religious affairs in Eastern Pomerania, was offended by the seditious appearance of the affair and, burning with zeal for the ancestral religion, stirred up a savage persecution against many priests, citizens and students. Many were thrown into chains, and the rest, forewarned, took thought for their own safety by flight. Bugenhagen went to Wittenberg, where Luther was then absent at Patmos (Peter Vincentius, in his speech on the life of Bugenhagen, affirms that he had come to Wittenberg shortly before Luther's journey to Worms). He made himself known to the school by reading the Psalter privately, and when Luther returned, he was at once

units.la: Tom. 3. Declamat Philippi. latim in defuncti pastoris D. Simonis Beckii locum suffectus est. Joannes Kyrichius, cum Christiano Kettelhut, Sundium migravit. Andreas Cnophius cum Joachimo Mollero, adductis scholasticis Livonis, Rigam ad Fratrem Jacobum, Canonicum profectus, mox ad ministerium illius Ecclesiae in aede D. Petri vocatus est, ubi exemplo pastoris Treptoviensis, acriter in foedas nundinationes, idola & mores sacrificorum Pontificiorum invectus, doctrinam de Justitia fidei, seu remissione peccatorum, & vita aeterna gratis, non propter ulla opera aut merita nostra, sed propter solu Christum pro nobis passum & resuscitatum, credenti donanda, praecipue urgit. Sed ad ritus publicos, & abusus inveteratos aliquantisper connivit, donec per secutos collegas, Sylvestrum Tegetmeier, & alios, turbulentius quaedam isthic quoque in rebus Ecclesiasticis administrata sunt. Sic persequutio Treptoviae mota, in plures civitates ac gentes pios Doctores, inde eiectos, dispersit.
units.tr: Vol. 3. Declamation of Philip. appointed to the place of the deceased pastor, Dr Simon Beck. John Kyrichius went with Christian Kettelhut to Stralsund. Andreas Cnophius, with Joachim Moller and the Livonian students he had brought, set out for Riga to see Brother Jacob, a canon, and was soon called to the ministry of that church in St Peter's. There, following the example of the Treptow minister, he inveighed sharply against the foul trading, the idols and the morals of the Papist priests, and above all urged the doctrine of the righteousness of faith, that is, the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, to be given freely to the believer, not on account of any works or merits of ours, but on account of Christ alone, who suffered and rose again for us. But he connived for a while at the public rites and long-established abuses, until his successors as colleagues, Sylvester Tegetmeier and others, carried out certain matters in ecclesiastical affairs there too with more turbulence. Thus the persecution stirred up at Treptow scattered the godly teachers, who were driven out from there, into many cities and nations.

units.la: In Belgio Carolus Caesar dira edicta contra sectas, quas sic vocant omnes & singulas edit, & quotannis fere renovat, quorum vi imperante Carolo, in solo Belgio capite truncata, submersa, suspensa, defossa, exusta, aliisque mortis generibus exstincta ultra quinquaginta hominum millia scribuntur: primo plurimis ob leves admodum causas (nempe vel car
units.tr: In Belgium Charles the Emperor issued and almost every year renews dire edicts against the sects, as they call all of them without distinction. By the force of these, under Charles's rule, more than fifty thousand people are recorded as having been put to death in the Netherlands alone: beheaded, drowned, hanged, buried alive, burnt and destroyed by other kinds of death; at first, for the most part, for very slight causes (namely, either for eating meat on certain days forbidden,

units.la: ci. ... nium esum diebus certis vetitum: vel servatos aut lectos libellos, quorum tamen doctrinam nonprobarent.) Sacerdotibus quoq; & Monachis ob ductas, fornicationis causâ, uxores, vitâ privatis.
units.tr: or for keeping or reading little books, whose doctrine, however, they did not approve). Priests and monks were also punished with privation of life for having taken wives, for the cause of fornication.

units.la: JOANNES OECOLAMPADIUS quid in coenobio delitescens de Luthero senserit, judicium eius ad amicum loquitur: Iam de Martino liberè loquor, ut sape antehac: quod Evangelica veritati propius accedat quàm adversarii sui. Et poteritne humanus spiritus, vel ab auditu, vel à promulgatione Evangelii suis minacibus mdatis avertere? Mirum, cum meliora non offerant, quod omnibus Sole clarius est, condemnare tamen non verentur, quod improbare, quantum satis est, non possunt. Verè dicit Ennius:
units.tr: JOHN OECOLAMPADIUS, hiding in his monastery, told a friend what he thought of Luther: Now I speak freely about Martin, as I have often done before: that he comes closer to evangelical truth than his adversaries do. And can a human spirit, either by hearing or by the proclamation of the Gospel, be turned away by their threatening edicts? It is strange that, when they offer nothing better, they nevertheless do not hesitate to condemn what, as is clearer than the sun to everyone, they cannot disprove to any sufficient degree. Ennius truly says:

units.la: Pellitur è medio sapientia, vi geritur res.
units.tr: Wisdom is driven from the midst, the matter is managed by force.

units.la: Viderint Episcopi, sive me damnent, aut parcant condemnanti. Non de omnibus, quae scripsit Martinus, loquor: non enim omnia legi. Sed quae legi, adeo immerito reijciuntur: ut fiat etiam injuria sacris literis, quas ipse sincerius exponit: pleraque ab eo dicta tam certa sunt apud me: ut, si etiam coelestes Angeli contradicant, non me sint à sententia mea depulsuri. Vbi articulos condemnatos legero; quid sentiam de quovis, libenter tecum agam.
units.tr: Let the bishops see to it, whether they condemn me or spare the condemned. I am not speaking about everything Martin has written, for I have not read everything. But what I have read is rejected so undeservedly that an injury is done even to the sacred letters, which he expounds more sincerely. Many of his statements are so certain to me that, even if the heavenly angels contradicted them, they would not drive me from my opinion. When I read the condemned articles, I will gladly discuss with you what I think of each.

units.la: Idem Oecolampadius praeter conciones certas, quas edidit, scripsit etiam de confessione librum, quò magis pium, hoc minùs cereceremoniarum nundinatoribus ferendum. Huius enim occasione Glapio Franciscanus, quitum Cesari Carolo à Concionibus, ingens viro periculum creavit. Qua de causa sollicitantibus amicis, & consentientibus fratribus in cœnobio, tutò discessit.
units.tr: The same Oecolampadius, besides certain sermons which he published, also wrote a book on confession, which is all the more pious and all the less tolerable to the traffickers in ceremonies. For on account of it Glapio, a Franciscan who was preacher to the Emperor Charles, created a great danger for himself. For this reason, at the urging of friends and with the agreement of the brothers in the monastery, he withdrew safely.

units.la: MARTINUS BUCERUS Selestadiensis, mense Martio, ætatis trigesimo, hortatu Francisci à Sickingen, & Ulrici Hutteni, relinquit Ordinem Dominicanorum, in quo vixerat annos quindecim, & ad Franciscum Sickingum se confert. Franciscus Friderico Palatino, Præsidi Senatûs Imperii eum commendat: cuius Ecclesiasten aulicum integrum annum egit, donec vacante parœciâ Landstallensi à Francisco volens revocatus fuit, aulæ supra modum pertæsus.
units.tr: MARTIN BUCER of Schlettstadt, in March, in his thirtieth year, at the urging of Franz von Sickingen and Ulrich von Hutten, left the Order of the Dominicans, in which he had lived for fifteen years, and went to Franz Sickingen. Franz recommended him to Frederick the Palatine, president of the Imperial Council. He served as court preacher there for a whole year, until, the parish of Landstuhl being vacant, he was wanted back by Franz, and wearied beyond measure of the court.

units.la: ABSENTE Luthero in Pathmo, Monachi Augustiniani V Vittembergenses Missam privatam abrogandam censent, idque ideo, quia execrabilis sit abusus cœnæ Dominicæ, quæ in Sacrificium propitiatorium commutetur: deinde quia non uno sed duodecim Apostolis præsentibus Christus, & Apostoli conveniente Ecclesiâ, Eucharistiam celebrârint: postremo quia in Missa una tantum species laicis porrigatur, contra institutionem Christi. Elector consilium Academiæ super hac re requirit: Academici, Justus Jonas Præpositus, Joannes Dolcius, D. An-nas Præpositus, Joannes Dolcius, D. Andreas Carolostadius, D. Hieronymus Schurffius, D. Nicolaus Amsdorffius, Philippus Melanchthon, rationes Augustinianorum comprobant. Elector decreta ipsorum rata habet: Missa privata primum in monasterio, deinde in templo parochiali, tandem in templo arcis abrogatur.
units.tr: WHILE Luther was absent at Patmos, the Augustinian monks of Wittenberg judged that the private Mass should be abolished, and that for this reason: because the abuse of the Lord's Supper, which is turned into a propitiatory sacrifice, is execrable; next, because Christ and the Apostles celebrated the Eucharist not with one Apostle present but with twelve, the Church assembling; lastly, because in the Mass only one kind is given to the laity, contrary to the institution of Christ. The Elector asked the opinion of the university on this matter. The academics, Justus Jonas, provost, Johannes Dolcius, Dr Andreas Carlstadt, Dr Hieronymus Schurff, Dr Nicolaus Amsdorf and Philipp Melanchthon, approved the reasons of the Augustinians. The Elector confirmed their decrees: the private Mass was abolished first in the monastery, then in the parish church, and at last in the castle church.

units.la: Mutata deinde sunt & alia, de quibus Melanchthon: Illud, inquit, commemorare hoc loco nolo, qui primi publicè prabuerint utrāq; parte cœna Domini, qui primi omiserint privatas Missas: ubi deserta sint primùm monasteria. Nam Lutherus de his materiis ante convētum, qui fuit in urbe Vangionum anno 1521. tantùm pauca disputaverat. Ritus non mutavit ipse, sed eo absente Carolostadius. Idem Carolostadius templis imagines eiicit, confessionem auricularem tollit, symbola sacra laicis in manus dat, in foro non ex iure humano, sed ex lege Mosis pronunciandum esse contendit: edit librum de coniugio sacerdotum, & de votis monasticis rescindendis, vigesimâ quartâ Junii: qui liber etsi non per omnia Luthero probaretur, scripsit tamen: Sinendum esse Carolostadium, quia nolit forte suum cursum remorari. Vastavit etiam Scholas, literarum cultum abiecit, & ad labores manuum cunctos hortatus est.
units.tr: Other things were changed afterwards, about which Melanchthon says: I do not wish to mention here who first publicly gave the Lord's Supper in both kinds, who first omitted private Masses, where the monasteries were first deserted. For Luther had disputed only a little on these matters before the assembly held in the city of the Vangiones in 1521. He himself did not change the rites, but in his absence Carlstadt did. The same Carlstadt removed images from the churches, abolished auricular confession, gave the sacred symbols into the hands of the laity, and contended that in the market-place sentence should be pronounced not by human law but by the law of Moses. On 24 June he published a book on the marriage of priests and on the annulment of monastic vows. Although this book was not approved by Luther in every respect, he nevertheless wrote: Carlstadt must be allowed to go on, perhaps because he is unwilling to slow his course. He also laid waste the schools, cast off the cultivation of letters, and urged everyone to manual labour.

units.la: ERASMUS offensus periculosis tumultibus
units.tr: Erasmus, offended by the dangerous tumults

units.la: a Ad Georgium Spalatinum 15. Augusti.
units.tr: a To Georg Spalatin, 15 August.

units.la: b Bulcholcerus Dresserus. bus & perniciosis clamoribus, quibus negotium Evangelicum agebatur, aut potius turbabatur, coepit trepidatione quadam nutare ac vacillare, & à causa Lutherana longius se removere atq; subducere, & quasi in locum tutiorem extra telorum iactum secedere. Sentiebat autem, de rebus tam arduis censuram & iudicium deferendum ac permittendum esse Ecclesiae, quae auditâ virorum aliquot piorum & eruditorum sententiâ, communi consilio ac deliberatione de dogmatibus statueret, decreta verbo Dei consentientia coderet, controversias tolleret, & pacem Ecclesiasticam sanciret ac stabiliret. Ut itaque lectori ob oculos ponamus specimen sapientiae huius viri, vel secum luctantis, vel cum utraque parte quodammodo confligantis, verba quaedam eius, ex epistolis, hoc anno scriptis, subiungemus, non ut lectori inde Erasmi de Religione sententiam (quae vel perplexitatibus involuta, non mox cuilibet se pandit, vel suâ quadam lubricitate elabi, mentemq; legentis praetervolare potest) venetur ac discat: sed ut ex his de admirando illius ingenio, dum inter partes ferè medium se gerere studet, coniecturam faciat, & dissidii inter ipsum & alios exorti fontes propius aspiciat. Sic itaq; ille hoc anno scripsit Petro Barbirio 13. Augusti. Initio, inquit, dici non potest, quàm multi, qualesq; viri Luthero faverint. Ego è pauculis pagellis degustatis visus sum mihi subodorari, rem exituram in tumultum. Et mihi sanè adeo est invisa discordia ut veritas etiam displiceat seditiosa. Primus omnium admonui hominem literis: ut rem Evangelicam Evangelicâ mansuetudine moderationeq; tractaret &c. Equidem, ut mihi videre videor, esse quadam in Ecclesia recepta, quae magno Christiana religionis bono mutarentur. Ita nihil placet, quod huiusmodi tumultu geritur. Si communicato inter ipsos consilio, docti obsignatis libellis, utriusq; ditionis Proceres admonuissent, qua iudicassent ad Evangelica doctrina sinceritatem attinere, fortassis & ipse fuissem unus, qui sedulò, quod potuissem, consuluissem. Nunc quid furiosius, quàm rem tantam maledicis libellis & clamoribus agi? Quo quidem in negotio primùm utriusq; peccatum est. Meâ sententiâ, nimiùm calidis consiliis hinc atq; hinc res gesta est, &c. Porro quod dicitur, Lutherum quadam hausisse è libris meis, mihi in manu non erat, praestare, ne quis scriptis meis imposterum abuteretur, quando hoc nec Evangelista, nec Apostoli praestare potuerunt. Scripsi eo seculo, quae tum videbantur ad bonos mores conducere: fortassis quadam scripturus circumspectiùs, si praescissem exoriturum hoc seculum plus quàm Tragicum.
units.tr: b Bulcholcerus Dresserus. Erasmus, offended by the dangerous and destructive outcries with which the Evangelical cause was being carried on, or rather thrown into confusion, began to waver and totter with a certain trepidation. He withdrew and drew himself away from the Lutheran cause, and retired, as it were, to a safer place beyond the range of missiles. He felt, however, that judgment on such weighty matters ought to be referred and entrusted to the Church, which, after hearing the opinion of several pious and learned men, would by common counsel and deliberation settle doctrines, enact decrees agreeing with the Word of God, remove controversies, and sanction and establish ecclesiastical peace. So that we may set before the reader an example of this man's wisdom, whether wrestling with himself or somehow clashing with both sides, we shall append certain of his words from letters written this year. This is not so that the reader may hunt out and learn Erasmus's opinion on religion, which, wrapped in perplexities, does not at once reveal itself to anyone, or can slip away by a certain slipperiness and fly past the reader's mind. Rather, it is so that from these words he may form a conjecture of that man's admirable character, since he strives to stand almost midway between the parties, and may look more closely at the sources of the quarrel that arose between him and others. Thus he wrote this year to Peter Barbirius, 13 August: At the outset, he says, it cannot be said how many and what sort of men have favoured Luther. From a few little pages I tasted, I seemed to smell that the matter would end in tumult. Discord is so hateful to me that even truth displeases me when it is seditious. I was the first of all to admonish the man by letter that he should handle the Evangelical cause with Evangelical gentleness and moderation, etc. Indeed, it seems to me, there are certain things received in the Church which would be changed to the great good of the Christian religion. So nothing pleases me that is done in this kind of uproar. If, after counsel had been shared among them, the learned, by sealed pamphlets, had admonished the leaders of both realms as to what they judged pertained to the purity of Evangelical doctrine, perhaps I too would have been one who diligently did what I could. Now what is more frenzied than carrying on so great a matter with abusive pamphlets and shouting? In this business, first of all, both sides have sinned. In my judgment, the matter was carried on by overly hot counsels on both sides, etc. As for the claim that Luther drew some things from my books, it was not in my power to prevent anyone from misusing my writings in future, since neither Evangelist nor Apostle could have done so. I wrote in that age what then seemed to conduce to good morals. Perhaps I would have written some things more cautiously, had I foreknown that this age would arise more than tragic.

units.la: Idem die 23. Augusti anno eodem. Video tem-
units.tr: On the same day, 23 August, of the same year. I see that the tem-

units.la: Lib. 14. epist. 7. tempestatem esse periculosissimam, in qua mihi sententio cursum sic esse moderandum: ut nec hominibus adulando, Christi negotium deseram: nec me frustra in discrimen aliquod coniiciam. Lutherus veluti malum Eridis misit in mundum, cuius nullam omnino partem non turbatam video. Nemo non fatetur, vehementi quâdam Medicinâ fuisse opus Ecclesiae, nimium collapsis moribus: sed video propemodum usu venire, ut pharmacum parum dextrè adhibitum, morbi vim exacerbârit verius quàm expulerit. Atqui utinam verum esset, quod Danorum Rex Christiernus, mihi simile quiddam dicenti respondit, ludens opinor, levibus pharmacis nihil agi, sed illud esse remediorum efficacium, ut primum corpus omne concutiant. Ego certè nullum exitum video bonum, nisi Christus ipse temeritatem nostram bene vertat, quemadmodum ferunt Minervam δυσβαλίων Atheniensium bene fortunatam solitam.
units.tr: Lib. 14. epist. 7. pest is most dangerous, in which I must so steer my course that I neither desert Christ's cause by flattering men, nor cast myself uselessly into some peril. Luther, like the apple of Eris, has sent a plague into the world, and I see no part of it that is not disturbed. No one denies that the Church needed a strong medicine, its morals having collapsed too far. But I see that it almost commonly happens that a remedy applied rather clumsily exacerbates the force of the disease rather than expelling it. Would that it were true what King Christian of Denmark answered when I said something similar to him, jesting, I suppose, that light medicines accomplish nothing, but that it is the nature of efficacious remedies to shake the whole body at first. Certainly I see no good outcome, unless Christ himself turns our rashness to good, as they say Minerva was wont to be fortunate for the Athenians' ill-counsels [δυσβαλίων].

units.la: Et ad Montioium: Nec cum Luthero, nec cum ullo Lutherano fœdus clancularium inii, & adeo non addidi cuiquam animos, ut omnes, quos potui, deterruerim ab instituto periculoso. Tantùm improbabam quorundam praecipites tumultus, praesertim apud populum, priusquam satis appareret, quorsum iret Lutherus. Nemo non fatetur, disciplinam Ecclesiasticam longè prolapsam esse ã sinceritate Evangelica, populum Christianum multis modis gravatum esse, conscientias hominum variis tricis illaqueatas. His malis Lutherus bonis ac doctis videbatur remedium allaturus. Et passim faventibus omnibus, solus extiti monitor, ut stylum verteret, ac negotium tractaret Evangelicâ mansuetudine. Iactant aliqui, Lutherum quaedam è meis libris hausisse. At quo pacto queam praestare, ne quis meis scriptis abutatur, cum plurimi sint abusi libris Evangelicis? Et tamen, si quis Deus mihi praedixisset, hoc seculum exoriturum, quaedam aut non scripsissem: aut aliter scripsissem: non quod perniciosa scripserim, sed quod non omnia quovis tempore recte dicantur, &c. Nec technis quorundam, nec pollicitis, nec odiis aliorum unquam perpelli potui, aut potero, ut alius sim quàm Christianus. Male sit omnibus, qui gaudent dissidiorum vocabulis.
units.tr: And to Montioius: I have made no secret alliance with Luther or with any Lutheran, and I have not so inflamed anyone's spirits; rather, I have dissuaded all whom I could from their dangerous undertaking. I only disapproved of the headlong tumults of some, especially among the people, before it was sufficiently clear where Luther was heading. No one denies that ecclesiastical discipline has fallen far from Evangelical sincerity, that the Christian people is burdened in many ways, and that men's consciences are ensnared by various snares. Luther seemed to the good and learned about to bring a remedy for these evils. And while all were favouring him everywhere, I alone stood forth as an adviser that he should turn his pen and handle the matter with Evangelical gentleness. Some boast that Luther drew certain things from my books. But how can I guarantee that no one misuses my writings, when very many have misused Evangelical books? And yet, if some God had foretold to me that this age would arise, I would either not have written certain things, or would have written them differently; not because I have written what is harmful, but because not everything is rightly said at every time, etc. Neither by the schemes of some, nor by the promises, nor by the hatreds of others have I ever been, or ever shall be, driven to be anything other than a Christian. Ill befall all who rejoice in the names of divisions.

units.la: PARISIENSIBUS Lutheri libros damnantibus, opposuit Melanchthon scriptū publicum, cuius inscriptio hæc: Adversus tamoforum Parisiensium decretum Philippi Me-lanchthonis pro Luthero Apologia.
units.tr: To the Parisian doctors, who condemned Luther's books, Melanchthon opposed a public writing, with this title: Against the decree of the Parisian doctors, an Apology for Luther by Philip Melanchthon.

units.la: Prodiit item liber à Melanchthone scriptus titulo Didymi Faventini, quo respondit Thomæ Placentino, id est Emsero.
units.tr: A book written by Melanchthon also appeared under the title of Didymus Faventinus, in which he answered Thomas Placentinus, that is, Emser.

units.la: Hoc anno primus Sacerdotum Bartholomæus Bernhardus Feldkirchius, Præpositus in oppido Kemberg, prope VVittembergam, duxit uxorem, & facti sui rationem Archiepiscopo Magdeburgico primùm, deinde Electori Saxonico publicis literis reddidit : quæ Tomo secundo Operum Lutheri Lat. Jen. leguntur, Hunc sequuti sunt, Justus Jonas, Præpositus VVittebergæ, Joännes Bugenhagius, Andreas Carolostadius, cui facetus quidam Morio, Epithalamii loco: ut opinor, scripsit novæ Missæ nuptialis formulam, multo sale respersam.
units.tr: This year the first of the priests, Bartholomew Bernhard Feldkirch, provost in the town of Kemberg near Wittenberg, took a wife. He gave an account of his deed in public letters, first to the Archbishop of Magdeburg and then to the Elector of Saxony; these letters are read in the second volume of Luther's Latin works, Jena edition. Following him came Justus Jonas, provost at Wittenberg, Johannes Bugenhagius, and Andreas Carlstadt. For Carlstadt, some witty fellow, as a wedding song, I think, wrote a formula of a new nuptial Mass, seasoned with much salt.

units.la: Leo Decimus, Kal. Decembrib. moritur, violentiâ, ut creditur, toxici consumptus, ætatis 46. celebrandus iis virtutibus, quæ à Christianis ne nominari quidem debent. Actius Sincerus Sanazarius lusit in eius obitum hoc disticho: Sacra sub extrema, si forte requiritis, hora Cur Leo non potuit sumere? vendiderat.
units.tr: Leo the Tenth died on 1 December, consumed, as is believed, by poison administered by violence, in his forty-sixth year, to be celebrated for those virtues which Christians ought not even to name. Actius Sincerus Sannazaro made a jest on his death in this couplet: "If perchance you ask why Leo could not receive the sacraments in his last hour? He had sold them."

units.la: Sub finem anni nova super indulgentiis tragœdia oritur. Albertus Archiepiscopus Moguntinus post obitum Tecelii novas indulgentiarum Papalium mensas Halæ Saxonum erigi iusserat. Lutherus rei indignitate commotus, ex Patmo vigesimâ quintâ Novembris non solùm acerbas, sed etiam minaces literas ad Albertum scribit, in quibus ipsum hortatur: ut idolum illud veniarum Papalium removeat, nî alia graviora velit experiri. Deinde, ut missos faciat sacerdotes illos, qui vitandæ scortationis ergo matrimonium vel inierunt, vel inire velint. Nî fecerit, ea se de ipso aliisq; Episcopis divulgaturum, quæ perpetuo mallet silentio sepulta.
units.tr: Towards the end of the year a new tragedy arose over indulgences. After Tetzel's death, Albert, Archbishop of Mainz, had ordered new tables of papal indulgences to be set up at Halle in Saxony. Luther, moved by the outrageousness of the matter, wrote from Patmos on 25 November not only harsh but even threatening letters to Albert. In them he urged him to remove that idol of papal pardons, unless he wished to experience other and graver things; and then to dismiss those priests who had either entered marriage, or wished to enter it, to avoid fornication. If Albert did not do so, Luther would publish those things about him and the other bishops which he would rather have kept buried in perpetual silence.

units.la: Commendavit tum Melanchthon hanc ipsam causam Capitoni, Alberti concionatori & Consiliario dignissimâ lectu epistolâ hac: Mittuntur ad vos optimi & sanctissimi hominis, Lutheri, litera, quibus, quod à te fieri oportuit, officii Princeps tuus admonetur: eas quia contemnent, opinor, nonnulli apud vos, non enim ignoro, quid de Luthero sentiat mundus, referre putavi, quod in rem esset Principis tui, tecum privatim commentari. Modis omnibus efficiendum est tibi, ne contemnatur Lutherus, & ut eius hoc tempore litera apud tuos valeant: id quod abs te impetrabit pietas cum erga Evangelium, tum erga Principem tuum. Primùm enim, si Lutherus, id quod multi sentient, divinitus missus est, qui mundum ad Evangelium revocet: cavendum est: ne non tam Lutherum, quam illum, cuius hic Ἀπόστολον agit, contempsisse videamini. Sibi factum interpretatur Christus, quicquid acciderit minimo ex suo grege. Pharisaeos καὶ Νομικὸς, qui Baptistam aspernati erant, Dominus queritur, consilium Dei prævisse. Quid si idem his causetur, ubi contentus fuerit Lutherus? Scio hunc partim stultum, partim malum videri mundo, sed oportet Εναγγέλιον stultitiam esse Gentibus, scandalum Iudaïs. Negare non poteritis, quin Evangelium docet: id reiicitis, si Lutherus reiicitur.
units.tr: Melanchthon then commended this same cause to Capito, preacher and counsellor to Albert, in a letter very worth reading: The letters of that best and most holy man, Luther, are sent to you, by which your Prince is admonished of the duty you ought to have performed. I suppose some among you will despise them, for I am not unaware what the world thinks of Luther. I thought it would be useful to your Prince's interest for you to consider this privately with yourself. By every means you must see to it that Luther is not despised, and that his letters carry weight among your people at this time; piety, both towards the Gospel and towards your Prince, will bring this about from you. For first, if Luther, as many will think, has been sent by God to recall the world to the Gospel, take care that you do not appear to have despised not so much Luther as him whose apostle [ἀπόστολον] he acts. Christ interprets whatever is done to the least of his flock as done to himself. The Lord complains that the Pharisees and lawyers [καὶ Νομικὸς], who had rejected the Baptist, had frustrated God's counsel. What if the same is charged against you, where Luther has been content? I know he seems to the world partly foolish, partly wicked; but it is necessary that the gospel [Εναγγέλιον] be foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews. You will not be able to deny that he teaches the Gospel; if Luther is rejected, you reject that.

units.la: Ex autographo. ġcitur. Nec ignoro, te acerbitate offendi. Sed quid, si divinitus accendatur? εναγγελίσασθαι. Obsecro vide, qui rerum ac temporum status sit, quo sale opus sit istis tam pinguibus Dominis. Nunc tibi contigit qui saliat, vos ne conculcabitis? Paulus cavere praecipit, ne Spiritus extinguatur: quod ne a vobis praestetur, adnitere. Pluribus haec agerem, nisi & Fabritio & Theologo scriberem, ut videri haec quoque nimis multa possint. Deinde, quod privatim ad Principem tuum pertinet: proscindetur acerbissimo scripto, nisi dextre responderitis. Hoc ut prematur, quantillo incommodo efficere potestis. De indulgentiis, credo, agitur, quae cum iam olim deplorata sint, minimo negotio abrogari possunt. Nam vel hinc Lutheri candorem aestimes, qui praeter indulgentias nihil attingit. Quid enim si commoveat reliquam vitiorum ac impostarum ἀρχοντῶν Camarinam, id quod iure queat. Cedite hoc uno loco recta monenti tanto cum commodo vestro, si consultum vultis τῇ ἐπισκόπῳ ἀξιᾷ. Ego hactenus sedulò praestiti, ne quid contra vos ederetur, & porro praestare cupio, modò recta velitis. Vale. VVittembergæ, sub Brumam.
units.tr: From the autograph. Therefore, I am not unaware that you are offended by its harshness. But what if it is kindled by God? Preach the gospel [εὐαγγελίσασθαι]. Please consider what state of affairs and of times there is, and how much salt is needed for those very fat lords. Now you have someone who will leap up; will you not trample him underfoot? Paul gives the warning that the Spirit is not to be quenched; see to it that you do not do this to him. I would say more on these matters, but I am writing also to Fabritius and to the theologian, and these things might seem to be too many already. Next, what concerns your prince personally: he will be torn apart by a most bitter writing, unless you answer skilfully. You can judge how little inconvenience it would take to prevent this. It concerns, I believe, the indulgences, which, though they have long been condemned, can be abolished with the least trouble. For from this one point you may judge the candour of Luther, who touches nothing beyond the indulgences. For what if he should stir up the rest of the vices and the Camarina of impostor rulers [ἀρχόντων], which he would have every right to do? Yield in this one point to one who advises what is right, to your great advantage, if you wish to look after the episcopal dignity [τῇ ἐπισκόπῳ ἀξίᾳ]. So far I have diligently taken care that nothing should be published against you, and I wish to continue to do so, provided you are willing to do what is right. Farewell. Wittenberg, at the approach of winter.

units.la: Favebat Fabritius Evangelio tacitè quidem, sed impensè, & Cardinalem Moguntinum ad favendas Lutheri partes pertrahere satagebat. Huius igitur suasu Archiepiscopus Albertus demisse respondit Luthero vigesimâ primâ Decembris: summa responsi erat : gratiosè se literas Lutheri accepisse, existimareq;, illum causam amplius non habere de se conquerendi : acturum se vitam Christiano Principe dignam, idque tum suarum, tum aliorum precum interventu, quandoquidem agnoscat, solius Dei gratiæ hoc esse : non diffiteri se, miserrimum se esse peccatorem, qui quotidiè peccare & errare posset; adeóque peccet & erret. Scire etiam, absq; gratia Dei nihil in se boni esse, imo se foetidum stercus esse : fraternas admonitiones se ferre posse: Luthero denique propter Christum bene velle.
units.tr: Fabritius favoured the gospel quietly indeed, but earnestly, and he was busy drawing the Cardinal of Mainz to favour Luther's side. Therefore, at his urging, Archbishop Albert replied to Luther humbly on 21 December. The substance of the reply was this: he had received Luther's letter graciously and thought that Luther no longer had cause to complain about him; he would lead a life worthy of a Christian prince, and this through the intervention of his own prayers and those of others, since he acknowledged that this was due to the grace of God alone. He did not deny that he was a most wretched sinner, who could sin and err every day, and so he did sin and err. He also knew that without the grace of God there was nothing good in him, indeed that he was a foul dung-heap. He could bear brotherly admonitions. Finally, he wished Luther well for Christ's sake.

units.la: Addidit his literis Capito suas quoq;, alteras ad Philippum, alteras ad Lutherum. Philippū hortatur, curet, ne subolescentem spiritum Alberti Lutherus lacessendo extinguat: se autore Principem hactenus clam cū Luthero fecisse, illiq; vires atq; autoritatem confirmasse: si quid ille peccet, magis peccare amore religionis, & studio ad verum cultum, quàm malitiâ: videre ipsum, Lutherum non solùm non contemptum, sed illi habitū honorem, tanquam Evangelistæ, cuius reprehensionem ambabus, quod aiunt, amplectantur.
units.tr: Capito added his own letters to this one, two more: one to Philip and one to Luther. He urged Philip to take care that Luther, by provoking him, did not extinguish the young spirit of Albert. He said that, on his authority, the prince had hitherto secretly dealt with Luther and had strengthened his powers and authority; if he should sin in anything, he sinned more from love of religion and zeal for true worship than from malice. He saw that Luther himself was not only not despised but was shown honour, as an evangelist, whose rebuke both parties, as they say, embrace with both arms.

units.la: Lutherū graviter monet: ne nominatim magnatum Ecclesiasticorum vitia notet: quia id sit facturus sine exemplo, multaque præter verum necessariò facturus, cum vel spiritus hominis nesciat quæ sunt in homine: quod si pergat aliorum inservire affectibus, experturum, Moguntinos quoque esse homines, quod sibi serio dictum putare debeat, ne in necessitatem inducat pusillos, ut animum exasperent. Hoc Capitonis responsum, quo animo acceperit Lutherus, sequentis anni historica docebunt.
units.tr: He warns Luther seriously not to name and denounce the faults of the leading churchmen, because he would be doing something without precedent, and would necessarily do many things beyond the truth, since not even the spirit of a man knows what is in a man. But if he persisted in serving the passions of others, he would find that the men of Mainz are also men; he ought to take this as said to himself in earnest, lest he bring the little ones into necessity so as to exasperate their minds. How Luther received Capito's reply the history of the following year will show. ## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1522

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXXII.
IN huius anni historia Ecclesiastica duo, mihi quidem commemoranda, lectori vero observanda. Nempe, quid Pontificii contra Evangelium: quid Deus pro Evangelio fecerit.
units.tr: In the ecclesiastical history of this year there are two things which I indeed ought to recount, but which the reader ought to observe: namely, what the Papists did against the gospel, and what God did for the gospel.

units.la: Quæ Pontificii contra Evangelium hoc anno moliti sunt: hæc habe. Adrianus Pontifex Romanus Principes Imperii Norimbergæ conventum celebrantes, per legatum adversus Lutherum incendit. PRINCIPES Norimbergæ edicta contra Lutherum cudunt. ADRIANUS P. P. ultimo Novembris BREVE, quod vocant, sive literas ad Senatum Bambergensem scribit, quibus illum à Lutheri doctrina dehortatur, &, ne vendi, multo minus imprimi libros ipsius sinat, monet.
units.tr: The things which the Papists undertook against the gospel this year are these. Pope Adrian, when the princes of the Empire were holding a convention at Nuremberg, stirred them up against Luther through a legate. The princes at Nuremberg hammer out edicts against Luther. On the last day of November Pope Adrian VI writes what they call a brief, or letter, to the Senate of Bamberg, by which he dissuades it from the doctrine of Luther, and urges that it not allow his books to be sold, much less printed.

units.la: Idem Adrianus Erasmum Roterodamum hortatur, ut contra Lutherum stylum stringat.
units.tr: The same Adrian urges Erasmus of Rotterdam to take up his pen against Luther.

units.la: FERDINANDUS Austriae Princeps latam adversus Lutherum anno superiori sententia vehementer urgebat, & in Ducatu VVirtembergensi, quem tunc tenebat, gravissimū propositi edictum xxvi die Novembris, ac premium delatoribus constituit, & passim in suis provinciis graviter in eos, qui Pontificiis legibus non parerent, animadvertit.
units.tr: Ferdinand, Prince of Austria, pressed vigorously the sentence pronounced against Luther the year before, and in the duchy of Württemberg, which he then held, on 26 November he issued a most serious edict and set a reward for informers, and everywhere in his provinces he punished severely those who would not obey the papal laws.

units.la: · HENRICUS junior, Dux Brunswicensis: GEORGIUS Dux Saxoniae: PHILIPPUS Episcopus Frisingensis & Naumburgensis, contra Lutherum & eius libros publicis programmatibus fulminant.
units.tr: Henry the Younger, Duke of Brunswick; George, Duke of Saxony; Philip, Bishop of Freising and Naumburg, thunder against Luther and his books with public proclamations.

units.la: LUDOVICUS Rex Hungariae & Bohemiae Uratislavienses vi armata in obedientia Papae & cultu doctrinae Pontificiae retinere nititur.
units.tr: Louis, King of Hungary and Bohemia, strives by armed force to keep the people of Breslau in obedience to the Pope and in the worship of papal doctrine.

units.la: Hugo Episcopus Constantiensis Senatū Tigurinum interpellat, & cuiusmodi querelas audiat de Zwinglio, qui novum doctrinae genus invexerit, ostendit. ( ad iurisdictionem enim illius Ecclesiasticam Tigurini pertinebant. ) Idem Hugo deinde literas dat ad Collegium Canonicorum, in quibus etiam erat Zwinglius, & de novis doctoribus, qui perturbent Ecclesiam, multa loquutus, hortatur ut ab illis diligenter sibi caveant. Cum apud Tigurinos nihil prosiceret literis suis, in conventu Badensi de Tigurinorum inobedientia conquestus est, & omnium pagorum Helveticorum opem, ad tutanda sua de religione publicata mandata, imploravit. Mox igitur Urbanus VVys, pastor in pago VViflitzbach, prope Badenam, qui de nova fide suspectus erat, capitur, Episcopo Constantiensi mittitur, à quo diu in carcere est detentus. Atq; hoc est initium persequutionis Evangelii, à pagis Helveticis suscepta.
units.tr: Hugo, Bishop of Constance, addresses the Senate of Zurich and shows what complaints he has heard about Zwingli, who had introduced a new kind of doctrine (for the Zurich people were under his ecclesiastical jurisdiction). Hugo then also wrote letters to the college of canons, in which Zwingli was also included, and, speaking at length about new teachers who disturb the Church, urged them to be diligently on their guard against such men. Since he achieved nothing at Zurich with his letters, he complained at the convention of Baden about the disobedience of the Zurich people, and implored the aid of all the Swiss villages to uphold the mandates against religion that had been published. Soon afterwards Urban Wys, a minister in the village of Wilfliswil near Baden, who was suspected of the new faith, was seized and sent to the Bishop of Constance, by whom he was kept long in prison. And this is the beginning of the persecution of the gospel, undertaken by the Swiss villages.

units.la: Erant in urbe Tigurina tres Monachorum familiae, Augustinianorum, Franciscanorum, Mendicantium. Hæ ad Senatum accusant Zwinglium, quod illius concionibus in contemptionem adducerentur, rogant, huiusmodi sermonibus Zwinglio interdicat, ne par pari cogantur reddere: & ut sibi ex Thoma & Scoto deinceps quoq; liceat concionari, de quo Senatus recusavit.
units.tr: In the city of Zurich there were three families of monks: Augustinians, Franciscans, and Mendicants. These accused Zwingli before the Senate, saying that by his sermons they were brought into contempt; they asked that he be forbidden such preaching, so that they would not be compelled to repay like with like; and that they too might henceforth be allowed to preach from Thomas and Scotus. The Senate refused this.

units.la: ERASMUS ad Jodocum, Senatus Mechlinensis Præsidem: Ego, inquit, & hic (Basileæ) & ibi (?) partim dictis, partim epistolis, multos alienavi à factione Lutherana. Nec ulla res magis deiecit Lutheranorum animos, quàm quod palam editis libris declaravi: me adhærere Pontifici Romano, & Lutheri negotium improbare.
units.tr: Erasmus writes to Jodocus, president of the Senate of Mechlin: I, for my part, here (at Basel) and there (?), by words and letters, have estranged many from the Lutheran faction. And nothing has cast down the spirits of the Lutherans more than that I have declared openly, in published books, that I adhere to the Roman Pontiff and disapprove of Luther's cause.

units.la: ADMINISTRATOR PRAGENSIS ad Ludovicum Regem Ungariæ & Boëmiæ accusat religionis innovatæ Joannem à Saulhau-sen, Tetschini Dominum.
units.tr: The Administrator of Prague accuses, before Louis, King of Hungary and Bohemia, Johann of Saulhausen, lord of Tetschen, of introducing a new religion.

units.la: In Boëmiæ quoq; conventibus erant, qui Pontificis & Ecclesiæ Romanæ auctoritatem suaderent recipiendam: alioqui dissidiorū & offensionum nullum esse futurum finem.
units.tr: In the assemblies of Bohemia too there were men who urged that the authority of the Pope and of the Roman Church be received; otherwise, they said, there would be no end to dissensions and offences.

units.la: ANTUERPIÆ Frater Henricus Sutphaniensis propter professionem Evangelicam in vincula coniicitur: mulieres vi illum liberant, monasterio expelluntur Fratres, alii aliis locis captivi tenentur, alii, negato Christo, dimittuntur. Vendita omnia vasa monasterii, templum & monasterium ipsum clausum: Sacramentum cum pompa in templum B. Virginis translatum, tanquam é loco haeretico, susceptum honorificè à Domina Margareta: cives aliquot & mulieres vexatæ & punitæ.
units.tr: At Antwerp Brother Henry of Zutphen is thrown into chains on account of his evangelical profession; women forcibly free him, the brothers are expelled from the monastery, some are held captive in various places, and some, when they deny Christ, are let go. All the vessels of the monastery are sold, the church and the monastery itself are closed; the Sacrament is carried with pomp into the church of the Blessed Virgin, as if from a heretical place, and received with honour by the Lady Margaret. Several citizens and women are harassed and punished.

units.la: Hæc contra Evangelium. Pro Evangelio quæ Deus fecerit, videamus.
units.tr: These are the things done against the gospel. Let us look at what God did for the gospel.

units.la: MARTINUS Lutherus Philippum Melanchthonem, per novos Prophetas nonnihil turbatum, erigit epistolâ, in qua docet, quomodo eorum vocatio & Spiritus probari debeat, antequam audiantur: Non probo, inquit, tuam timiditatem, cum & maiori tam spiritu quàm eruditione polleas, quàm ego. Ac primum cum testimonium perhibeant de seipsis, non statim audiendi sunt, sed iuxta consilium Ioannis, spiritus probandi. Habetis consilium Gamalielis. lictis differendi, nihil enim adhuc audio ab eis dici & fieri, quod Satanas non queat praestare vel aemulari. Tu autem ex mea parte hoc explores, an vocatione sua possint probare. Neque enim Deus unquam aliquem misit, nisi vel per hominem vocatum, vel per signa declaratum, ne ipsum quidem filium, Prophetae olim ex lege & ordine prophetali ius habebant, sicut nos modo per homines. Prorsus nolo eos recipi, si nuda revelatione sese vocatos adserat: cum nec Samuelem quidem vellet loqui DEVS, nisi per authoritatem conscientiam Heli. Hoc primum ad publicam docendi functionem pertinet. Iam vero privatum spiritum explores etiam, quaeras, num experti sint spirituales illas angustias, & nativitates divinas, mortes, infernosq;. Si audieris blanda, tranquilla, devota (ut vocant) & religiosa, etiamsi in tertium coelum sese raptos dicant, non approbabis. Quia signum filii hominis deest, qui est Caton, probator unicus Christianorum, & certus spirituum discretor. Vis scire locum, tempus, modum colloquiarum divinorum? Audi, sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Et proiectus sum a facie oculorum. Et repleta est malis anima mea, & vita mea inferno appropinquavit. Non sic loquitur maiestas, (ut vocant) immediate, ut homo videat, imo non videbit me homo & vivet. Et stellam par vae sermonis eius non fert natura. Ideo n. per homines loquitur, quod loquentem ipsum ferre non possumus. Nam & virgine turbavit Angelus, sic & Danielem, sic & Ieremias queritur, corripe me in iudicio, & ne sis tu mihi formidini. Et quid plura? Quasi Maiestas possit cum vetere homine loqui familiariter, & non prius occidere, atq; exsiccare, ne fœteant odores eius pessimi, cum sit ignis consumens. Etiam somnia & visiones sanctorum sunt terribiles saltem postquam intelliguntur. Tanta ergo, & ne Iesum quidem audias gloriosum, nisi videris prius crucifixum.
units.tr: Martin Luther, when Philip Melanchthon was somewhat disturbed by the new prophets, raises him up with a letter, in which he teaches how their calling and spirit ought to be tested before they are heard: I do not approve, he says, your timidity, since you are no less strong in spirit and learning than I am. And first, since they bear witness about themselves, they are not to be heard at once, but, according to the counsel of John, the spirits are to be tested. You have the counsel of Gamaliel. Let them be put off, for I hear nothing yet said or done by them that Satan cannot accomplish or imitate. But you, on my behalf, should examine this: whether they can prove their calling. For God never sent anyone unless either through a man called or declared through signs, not even the Son himself. The prophets of old had the right by the law and the prophetic order, as we now have it through men. I absolutely do not want them received if they assert that they are called by bare revelation, since God would not even speak to Samuel unless through the authority and conscience of Eli. This pertains first to the public function of teaching. Now indeed you should examine also the private spirit, and ask whether they have experienced those spiritual anguishes and divine births, deaths, and hells. If you hear flattering, calm, devout (as they call it) and religious words, even if they say they have been caught up into the third heaven, you will not approve. Because the sign of the Son of Man is lacking, who is Christ, the sole test of Christians and the certain discerner of spirits. Do you want to know the place, time, and manner of divine conversations? Hear: "As a lion he has broken all my bones." And "I have been cast out from before his eyes." And "my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell." Majesty, as they call it, does not speak immediately in this way, so that a man may see; indeed, "man shall not see me and live." Nor can nature bear the star-like power of his speech. For he speaks through men because we cannot bear the speaker himself. For the angel troubled the virgin, and so with Daniel; and so Jeremiah complains, "Contend with me in judgement, and do not be a terror to me." And why say more? As if Majesty could speak familiarly with the old man, and not first kill and dry him up, lest his most wretched odours should stink, since it is a consuming fire. Even dreams and visions of the saints are terrible, at least after they are understood. So great is it that you should not even hear Jesus in glory unless you have first seen him crucified.

units.la: Eundem Lutherū ita Deus in Pathmo animavit: ut nec Principis sui indignatione, nec Cæsaris proscriptione, nec Norici conventus edicta moratus, V Vittebergā revertetur, Epistola, quâ Saxoniæ Electori reditum suum excusat, cùm admirabilem fidei Lutheri πληροφορίαν, & pectus verâ pietate ardens, & instinctu ac impetu plane divino velut ἐνθουσιασμῷ ad gloriam Dei, & Evangelii Christi propagationem inflammatum, & omnia pericula præ pietatis & Evangelii amore, magno & excelso animo cōtemnens, demonstret, digna esse visa est, quæ hoc loci apponeretur. De mea causa, inquit, C.V. novit, aut si ignorat, nunc cognoscat, me Evangelion non ab hominibus, sed tantùm de cœlo per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum habere: ita ut merito potucrim, (ut deinceps facià) me Dei servū & Euangelistam profiteri. Quod autem ad causæ cognitionem me obtuli, & aliorum iudiciis subiecci: id non, quod ego de mea doctrina quidquam dubitarē, sed modestia causâ feci, ut alios invitarē. Postquā verò video,
units.tr: In the same way God also strengthened Luther on Patmos, so that, unmoved by his prince's displeasure, by Caesar's proscription, or by the edicts of the Nuremberg assembly, he returned to Wittenberg. The letter in which he excuses his return to the Elector of Saxony seems worth quoting here, because it shows Luther's remarkable full assurance [πληροφορίαν], his heart burning with true piety, and his spirit inflamed by a prompting and impulse that was plainly divine, as if by enthusiasm [ἐνθουσιασμῷ], for the glory of God and the spread of Christ's Gospel. He shows that he despised all dangers with a great and lofty mind, out of love for piety and the Gospel. Concerning my cause, he says, your Electoral Grace knows, or if he does not know it, let him now learn that I have the Gospel not from men but only from heaven, through our Lord Jesus Christ. So I may rightly profess myself, as I shall henceforth do, a servant of God and an evangelist. As for my having put myself forward for the examination of the case and submitted myself to the judgments of others, I did this not because I doubted anything of my own teaching, but out of modesty, so that I might invite others. But since I see

units.la: Germ. Jen. pag. 57. video, nimiam modestiam meam vergere ad detrimentum Evangelii: & Satanam, cum vix palmum ei cedo, totum campum velle occupare: cogor, conscientiâ meâ urgente, alias rationes inire. Satisfeci, ut spero, C.V. quod hoc anno cessi, tantùm ut C.V. gratificarer. Nam Diabolus bene scit, non metu aut diffidentiâ hoc à me factum esse. Cum enim VVormatiam ingrederer, ita animo constitutus eram: ut etiamsi scivissem tot Diabolos, quot in omnibus adium tectis tegulae sunt, in me intentos collimare: tamen laeto & alacri animo in medium eorum irsiluissem. Et postea. Redeo VVittebergam munitus praesidio multo sublimiore & firmiore, quàm ab Electore Saxonia mihi praestari possit. Neque in animum unquam induxi, a. C.V. defensionem petere. Imò judico C.V. plus à me praesidii & tutelae habituram esse, quàm mihi praestare. Praeterea si scirem C.V. velle & posse me tueri, planè non redirem. Huic causa nullus gladius consulere, aut opem ferre potest. Solum Deum hic gubernare & agere oportet sine ulla sollicitudine & auxilio humano. Itaque in hac causa, qui firmissimè Deo fidit, is fortissimè se & alios defendit. Cum igitur videam C.V. adhuc valde imbecillâ fide praeditam esse, nullo modo tantum tribuere C.V. possum, ut ab illa me defendi aut liberari ex periculis posse statuam. Ego C.V. animâ, corpus, & fortunas, omnis damni & periculi expertes in hac mea causa servabo, sive id credat C.V. sive non credat. Sciat etiam C.V. & nihil dubitet, longè aliter in cœlo quàm Noriberga de hac G ʃ negotio conclusum esse, videbimus enim, eos, qui se jam putant Evangelion totum devorasse, & extinxisse, nondum Benedicite absolvisse. Longè alius & potentior Princeps est, quàm Dux N. cum quo mihi negotium est. Is me, & ego ipsum mediocriter novi. Si crederet Illustrissima C.V. tum magnalia, & gloriam Dei videret. Cum autem nondum credat C. V. nihil etiam eorum vidit. Deo gloria & laus in aeternum.
units.tr: Germ. Jen. pag. 57. see that my excessive modesty is turning to the detriment of the Gospel, and that Satan, when I yield him scarcely a palm, wants to occupy the whole field. My conscience urging me, I am compelled to take other measures. I have, I hope, satisfied your Electoral Grace in that I yielded this year, only so as to do you a favour. For the Devil knows well that this was not done by me out of fear or distrust. When I was entering Worms, I was so resolved in mind that even if I had known there were as many devils as there are tiles on the roofs of all the houses, aimed at me, I would still have leapt into the midst of them with a glad and eager spirit. And afterwards: I am returning to Wittenberg protected by a far higher and firmer defence than the Elector of Saxony could give me. Nor have I ever brought myself to seek your Electoral Grace's defence. Indeed I judge that your Electoral Grace will have more protection and safeguard from me than I from you. Besides, if I knew that your Electoral Grace wished and was able to protect me, I would not return at all. No sword can give counsel or bring help to this cause. God alone must govern and act here, without any anxiety or human aid. Therefore in this cause, he who trusts most firmly in God defends both himself and others most bravely. Since, then, I see that your Electoral Grace is still endowed with very weak faith, I cannot in any way attribute so much to you that I could judge I might be defended or freed from dangers by it. I shall preserve your Electoral Grace, body, soul and property, free from all loss and peril, in this my cause, whether or not your Electoral Grace believes it. Let your Electoral Grace also know, and not doubt, that the matter has been decided in heaven very differently from how it was decided at Nuremberg. For we shall see that those who already think they have wholly devoured and extinguished the Gospel have not yet been dismissed with the blessing. The prince with whom I have to deal is far different and more powerful than Duke N. I know him, and he knows me, to a moderate degree. If your Most Illustrious Grace believed, you would see the great wonders and the glory of God. But since your Grace does not yet believe, you have seen none of them. To God be glory and praise for ever.

units.la: Causas sui ad VVittembergenses reditûs Lutherus ipse commemorat. Vocatus sum, inquit, literis Ecclesia & populi VVittembergensis: deinde, me absente, Satanas irruit in gregem meum, & eas excitavit turbas, quae praesentiam meam necessariò requirunt: praeterea metuo, ne qua magna seditio in Germania oriatur, quam coniunctis cum Ecclesia precibus aut avertere, aut aliquandiu differre cupiat. Ad Melanchthonem literis octavâ Epiphanii huius anni scriptis, aliam causam narrat. Para mihi, inquit, hospitium, quia translatio (Bibliorum) me urgebit ad vos reverti.
units.tr: Luther himself recounts the reasons for his return to the Wittenbergers: I have been summoned, he says, by letters from the Church and the people of Wittenberg. Then, in my absence, Satan has rushed into my flock and stirred up those disturbances which necessarily call for my presence. Besides, I fear that some great sedition may arise in Germany, which he wishes to avert, or at least postpone for a while, by the united prayers of the Church. In a letter written to Melanchthon on the eighth of Epiphany of this year, he gives another reason: Prepare lodging for me, he says, because the translation (of the Bible) will compel me to return to you.

units.la: Rediit autem VVittebergam feriâ quintâ post ESTO MIHI, sextâ Martii.
units.tr: He returned to Wittenberg on the Friday after Esto mihi, the sixth of March.

units.la: Absente Luthero in Patmo Theologi & Professores VVittembergenses, Justus Jonas, Andreas Carolostadius, Melanchthon, Nicolaus Ambsdorfius, D. Schurffius, D. Dolcius, Missam privatam abrogâ-rant, rant, idola removerant, cœnam sacram sub utráq; specie celebrárant, confessionem auricularem, preces ad sanctos, discrimina ciborū, & id genus alia sustulerant. Lutherus domum reversus ilico scribit ad Spalatinum, &, quátopere sibi mutatio ista displiceat, ostendit. Damnare se, ait, Missam Papistarum tanquā βδέλυγμα, imagines, quæ colantur, leges deniq; Papæ, de Confessione auriculari, de jejuniis, festis, invocatione sanctorum: sed damnare hæc omnia per verbum prædicatum, non abrogationem violentam.
units.tr: While Luther was away on Patmos, the theologians and professors of Wittenberg, Justus Jonas, Andreas Carlstadt, Melanchthon, Nicholas Amsdorf, Doctor Schurff, and Doctor Dolcius, had abolished the private Mass, removed the images, celebrated the Lord's Supper under both kinds, and done away with auricular confession, prayers to the saints, distinctions of foods, and other things of that kind. On his return home Luther at once wrote to Spalatin, and showed how much this change displeased him. He says that he condemns the Mass of the Papists as an abomination [βδέλυγμα], the images that are worshipped, the laws of the Pope, auricular confession, fasts, feasts, and the invocation of the saints; but that he condemns all these things by the preaching of the Word, not by violent abolition.

units.la: A Dominica deinde Invocavit usq; ad Reminiscere singulis diebus singulas conciones habet: & quos anno superiori in libello de abroganda Missa privata ob abrogatam Missam collaudárat, eos publicè perstringit, usus inter alia his verbis: Derhalben haben alle die geirret / die darzu geholffen vnnd verwilliget haben / die Meß abzuthun / nicht daß es nicht gut gewest / sondern daß es nicht ordentlich geschehen. Du sprichst: es ist recht / auß der Schrifft. Ich bekenne es auch / wo bleibet aber die ordnung / Dann es ist in einem frevel geschehen / ohn alle ordnung / mit ärgernuß des nechsten. Vnd wann es nicht so ein böß ding were vmb die Meß / wolte ich die wieder auffrichten. Dann ich weiß ewer fürhaben / kan aber dassel dasselbige nicht vertheidigen / vor den Papisten vnd andern vnsinnigen köpffen wüst ichs gleich=wol zuvertheidigen / aber vor dem Teuffel wüste ichs nicht zu suchen. Hoc est: Quamobrem omnes illi errârunt, qui operâ suâ, aut consilio Missarum abolitionem juverunt. Non quòd hoc impium fuerit patrare, sed quòd non recto ordine factum est. Tu quidem obÿcis, hoc rectum esse, ipsâ scripturâ etiam patrocinante. Hoc sanè & ego fateor: at ubi interim ordo locum habet? Nam hac ausu temerario & præcipiti citra omnem ordinem, atque cum proximi offendiculo acta sunt. Quod si non ita abominanda res esset Missa, rursus eam instituere vellem. Nam vestrum factum propugnare & excusare commodè non possum. Coram Papa & inflatis illis turgidisq; capitibus facilè quidem pro vobis causam dicerem. Sic enim istis dicere vellem: Quid scis, an hoc recto spiritu vel secus actum sit, quando opus per se bonum est? Atqui Diabolo vos purgare non ita proclive mihi est.
units.tr: From the Sunday Invocavit to Reminiscere he then preached a sermon every day. He publicly censured those whom he had praised the year before, in his little book on abolishing the private Mass, for having abolished the Mass. Among other things he used these words: "Therefore all those have erred who helped or consented to abolish the Mass, not because it was not good, but because it was not done in good order. You say it is right, from Scripture. I also admit it; but where then is the order? For it was done rashly, without any order, and to the offence of one's neighbour. And if the Mass were not such an evil thing, I would set it up again. For I know your intention, but I cannot defend that deed of yours. I could indeed plead your cause well enough before the Papists and other senseless heads, but before the Devil I would not know how to look for it." This is: Wherefore all those erred who by their labour or counsel helped to abolish the Masses. Not that it was wicked to do this, but that it was not done in proper order. You indeed object that this is right, even with Scripture supporting it. I too admit this indeed; but where, meanwhile, is the order? For these things were done with reckless haste and without any order, and to the offence of one's neighbour. If the Mass were not so abominable a thing, I would wish to institute it again. For I cannot conveniently defend and excuse your deed. Before the Pope and those puffed-up, swollen heads I could easily plead your cause; for I would say to them: How do you know whether this was done with a right spirit or otherwise, when the work is good in itself? And yet it is not so easy for me to purge you before the Devil.

units.la: Concione secundâ docet: impiam Missam non per bipennem, sed Evangelii prædicationem abrogandam, quemadmodum ipse Indulgentias evertrerit Verbo, quod Verbum se dormiente aut cum Philippo suo atque Amsdorsio Zythum VVittembergicum bibente Papatum ita laborare fecerit, ut nullus unquam Principum, aut Cæsar ipse tantum ei derogaverit.
units.tr: In his second sermon he teaches that the impious Mass must be abolished not with an axe but by the preaching of the Gospel, just as he himself overthrew indulgences by the Word. He says that while the Word slept, or while Philip and Amsdorf were drinking Wittenberg beer, the Papacy was made to labour so much that none of the princes, nor Caesar himself, had ever weakened it so much: while the Word slept or while his Philip and Amsdorf drank Wittenberg beer, the Papacy laboured so much that no prince ever, nor Caesar himself, had so much diminished it.

units.la: Concione quartâ inter res liberi usûs refert simulacra. Sie sollen abgestellet seyn/ sagt er/ wann sie angebettet sollen werden/ sonst nicht/ wiewol ich wolte/ sie weren in der gantzen Welt abgethan von wegen des mißbrauchs. Hoc est: Idola, si quis ea adorare velit, abolenda sunt: a- lioquin autem ferenda. Quanquam optarem ex toto orbe ea esse profligata, propter eorum abusum, quem certè dissimulare non possumus. Et paulo pòst: Man kans nicht läugnen/ daß die bilder böse seyn/ wegen ihres mißbrauchs/ noch haben wir sie nicht zuverwerffen. Dann es sind viel menschen/ die die sonne und sterne anbeten/ wolten wir darumb zufahren/ und die sternen vom himmel werffen? Hoc est: Quanquam verum sit, & inficias ire nequeamus: idola noxia esse, quod ijs multi abutuntur, ob id tamen nobis non licet ea damnare. Nam multi sunt homines adeo vecordes, ut Solem & stellas adorent: nosne igitur & hæc cælo deiiciemus?
units.tr: In his fourth sermon, among matters of free use, he mentions images: "They should be removed," he says, "if they are to be worshipped; otherwise not. Although I would wish they had been done away with throughout the whole world, because of their abuse." This is: Images, if anyone wishes to adore them, are to be abolished; otherwise they are to be tolerated. Although I would wish them to have been cast down from the whole world, on account of their abuse, which we certainly cannot overlook. And a little later: "One cannot deny that images are evil because of their abuse; yet we are not to throw them away. For there are many people who worship the sun and the stars; shall we therefore go and cast the stars down from heaven?" This is: Although it is true, and we cannot deny it, that images are harmful because many abuse them, it is nevertheless not lawful for us to condemn them on that account. For there are many people so senseless that they worship the sun and the stars: shall we therefore cast these down from heaven too?

units.la: CAROLOSTADIUS, cuius præcipua nominis, absente Luthero, fuerat auctoritas & celebritas, concionibus istis aculeatis offensus, actiones suas publico scripto contra Lutherum defendere voluit. Rogat illum privatim supplex Lutherus: ne quid contra se edat, ne ipse cogatur invitus mutuis carnibus congredi. Carolostadius nihil se contra Lutherum scribere penè sanctè dejerat, quanquam sexterniones aliud loquerentur, qui tum sub manu Rectoris & Iudicum cum cognoscebantur, & libelli etiam editi per Rec - torem inhibebantur.
units.tr: CARLSTADT, whose reputation and fame had been the chief one while Luther was absent, was offended by those stinging sermons and wished to defend his actions in a public writing against Luther. Luther begged him privately not to publish anything against him, lest he himself be forced, against his will, to engage in a mutual fight. Carlstadt almost solemnly swore that he was writing nothing against Luther, although the printed sheets said otherwise; these were then examined under the hand of the rector and judges, and printed pamphlets were also forbidden by the Rec - tor.

units.la: Hæc fuerunt initia dissensionis illius inter Lutherum & Carolostadium,quæ postea in bellum Eucharisticum exiit.
units.tr: These were the beginnings of that dispute between Luther and Carlstadt, which afterwards broke out into the Eucharistic war.

units.la: Judicatum est tunc à viris prudentibus, utrumq; privatæ studio gloriolæ plusculum indulsisse, & idcirco Lutherum, cum videri vellet modum agendi Carolostadianum tantùm damnare, doctrinam non item, turbine tamen affectuum eò abreptum fuisse, ut RES NIHILI vocaret communionem sub utráque specie, Missam, abolitionem imaginum, & id genus alia, utq; etiam ea auderet dicere inordinatè esse facta, quæ deliberato Theologorum & Jurisconsultorum VVittembergensium consilio facta, & à Principe Electore fuerant approbata. Nec difficile fuerit ex ipsorummet scriptis hoc divinare. Hoc enim nomine Carolostadius Lutherum accusat, quod omnes alios suæ auctoritati quasi mancipatos velit, neque iis permittere, ut aliquid vel scribant, vel faciant, se non præeunte. Lutherus contra: Ille (de Carolostadio loquitur) cupiebat fieri subitò novus Magister, & suas ordinationes in populo, PRESSA AVTORITATE MEA, erigere.
units.tr: Wise men judged at the time that both of them had indulged somewhat in a private zeal for glory. For this reason Luther, while wishing to appear to condemn only Carlstadt's manner of acting and not his doctrine, was nevertheless carried away by the whirlwind of his passions so far that he called communion under both kinds, the Mass, the abolition of images and other such things NOTHING, and even dared to say that they had been done disorderly, although they had been done by the deliberate counsel of the Wittenberg theologians and jurists and had been approved by the Elector Prince. Nor would it be difficult to infer this from their own writings. For on this ground Carlstadt accuses Luther of wanting all others to be, as it were, bound to his authority, and of not allowing them to write or do anything unless he goes first. Luther replies: He (speaking of Carlstadt) wanted to become suddenly a new Master and to set up his own ordinances among the people, with MY AUTHORITY SUPPRESSED.

units.la: Fuerunt è discipulis Martini, quibus minimè ille probaret, quod odio Carolostadii Pontificios ritus & elevationem etiam iam Papisticam aliquam multos annos retineret, quam tamen fassus est, esse nervum illius persuasionis impia, fingentis, sacrificulos offerre Christum pro vivis & mortuis, & hac oblatione mereri sibi & aliis remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: There were some among Martin's disciples whom he by no means approved of, because out of hatred for Carlstadt he for many years kept Papist rites and even an already Papistical elevation of the host. He nevertheless admitted that this was the sinew of that impious persuasion which pretends that little priests offer Christ for the living and the dead, and by this offering merit remission of sins for themselves and others.

units.la: Eodem tempore Lutherus conflixit cum fanaticis hominibus, Nicolao Storck, Thomma Müntzer, & aliis novorum Prophetarum antesignanis, qui jactabant arcanas revelationes Angelicas, &colloquia cum Deo: baptismum quoque parvulorum primi impugnabant. Hæc fuerunt semina doctrinæ Anabaptistarum, sparsa per Prophetas illos, qui ex urbe Cygnæa V Vittembergam, absente Luthero, venerant, & non solùm Carolostadium, sed etiam Melanchthonem nonnihil turbârunt, teste gravissimo viro Joachimo Camerario.
units.tr: At the same time Luther contended with fanatical men, Nicholas Storck, Thomas Müntzer and other forerunners of the new prophets, who boasted of secret angelic revelations and conversations with God. They were also the first to attack infant baptism. These were the seeds of Anabaptist doctrine, sown by those prophets who came to Wittenberg from the city of Zwickau while Luther was absent, and who disturbed not only Carlstadt but also Melanchthon somewhat, as the most serious man Joachim Camerarius testifies.

units.la: POSTHÆC librum edit Lutherus adversus falsò nominatum ordinem Episcoporum. In eo graviter invehitur in Episcopos, quod Evangelii doctrinam damnent & persequantur: neq; tamen toties ab ipso ad controversiarum disceptationem provocati, purâ Evangelii doctrinâ refutare, neq; Pontificios errores defendere possint. Tyrânide nihil ipsos effecturos: neq; se vel Papæ excommunicatione, vel Cæsaris proscriptione moveri, ut veritatis Evângelicæ professionē abiiciat: sed potiùs Evangelicâ doctrinam subinde latius in orbe terrarum propagaturum: idq; tanto animosius, quanto ipsi magis saeviant: neque oppressum iri Evangelion, etiamsi ipsum occidant: Deum autem ipsos, si insanire perrexerint, gravissime punituros.
units.tr: AFTER THIS Luther published a book against the falsely named order of bishops. In it he attacks the bishops severely, because they condemn and persecute the doctrine of the Gospel, and yet, though often challenged by him to a disputation of controversies, they cannot refute it with pure Gospel doctrine nor defend the Papist errors. They would achieve nothing by tyranny. Nor was he moved by the Pope's excommunication or the Emperor's proscription to cast off the profession of evangelical truth. Rather, he would propagate evangelical doctrine ever more widely throughout the world, and all the more boldly the more they raged. The Gospel would not be overcome even if they killed him. God would severely punish them if they persisted in their madness.

units.la: Hoc libro lecto, Episcopi, Abbates, Monachi, totaq; procuratorum Antichristi multitudo, conspiratione facta, ab Electore Brandeburgico petiverunt: hunc, aliosq; Lutheri libros congestos ignis flammis absumeret. Idem sacerdotes Magdeburgenses, Comitem à Stolberg, Cardinalis absentis vicarium, rogarunt.
