After the sermon he met Luther at an inn with the sign of the Black Bear. There, after many not very grave discussions between them, Luther, having given a pledge, challenged Carlstadt to write publicly against him on the sacred Supper, and rashly made a beginning of the Sacramentarian war, which, alas, still lasts. A German account of the meeting of Luther and Carlstadt is inserted in the German volume 2 of Luther's Jena works. Although Luther writes it mixed with lies and truth, he does not deny that he agreed with Carlstadt to dispute about the sacred Supper, and he affirms this elsewhere too. Indeed he boasts that he drew those prophets, who had long been muttering, into battle with a golden coin, and he does not yet repent of that deed.

units.la: ORLAMUNDAM 24. Augusti venit Lutherus: à Carolostadio Pastore loci ne quidē salutari vult: cum auditoribus, aut eius de αὐτονομαχία disceptat, & illis factum suum ex verbo Dei defendentibus, obiectaq; ex eodem verbo refellentibus, penè cōfusus inde abiit.
units.tr: Luther came to Orlamünde on 24 August. He would not even greet Carlstadt, the pastor of the place, but disputed with the hearers, or with Carlstadt's autonomachia [αὐτονομαχία], and when they defended his action from the word of God and refuted his objections from the same word, he went away almost confounded.

units.la: Non ita multò post Carolostadius Lutheri instinctu, & Joannis Friderici Saxoniæ Ducis iussu Thuringiæ finibus exigitur. Iubetur loco cedere Martinus Rheinhardus, prædicator Jenensis, qui Acta Jenensia & Orlamundensia ediderat: mittitur in exilium Egranus.
units.tr: Not long afterwards, at Luther's prompting and by the command of John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, Carlstadt was expelled from the borders of Thuringia. Martin Reinhard, preacher at Jena, who had published the Jena and Orlamünde Acts, was ordered to leave the place; Egranus was sent into exile.

units.la: Carolostadiʼ literas Orlamūdç scribit, alteras viris, alteras fœminis, quç publicè vocatis per cāpanas lectæ sunt, omnib. simul flentibus. Erat autem subscriptio talis: Andreas Bodenstein unverhört / und unüberwunden / durch Martinum Luther vertriebē / h. e. nec auditus nec convictus per Lutherum eiectus. Vides, ait Lutherus ad Ambsdorfium, quòd ego, qui martyr debui fieri, eò perveni, ut martyres ipse faciam. Vix credas, quàm latè serpserit iam etiam dogma Carolostadii de Sacramento.
units.tr: Carlstadt wrote letters from Orlamünde, one to the men and another to the women, which were read publicly after the people had been summoned by the bells, while everyone wept. The subscription was as follows: Andreas Bodenstein, unverhört and unüberwunden, driven out by Martin Luther; that is, neither heard nor convicted, cast out by Luther. You see, Luther says to Amsdorf, that I, who ought to have become a martyr, have come to the point of making martyrs myself. You would scarcely believe how widely the doctrine of Carlstadt on the Sacrament has already spread.

units.la: Deserta Thuringia Carolostadius rectà petit Argetinā, ubi in suas partes pertraxit Ortonem Braunfelsium, quem & solùm ibi allocutus est. Inde tedit Basileā: ubi libellos quos perbreves de Coena Domini confecerat, re cum nemine communicatā, solis Anabaptistis eius loci cōscíis, edēdos curavit. Erasm. ad Henricum Stromerum 4. Idus Decembr. Carolostadius hic fuit, sed vix Oecolampadio salutato. Edidit sex libellos: duo, qui excuderunt, nudiustertius comprehensi sunt in carcere iussu Magistratus, ob id potissimum, quòd ut audio, doceat, in Eucharistia non esse verum corpus Domini. Hoc nemo fert. Indignantur laici sibi eripi Deum suum, quasi nusquam sit Deus nisi sub illo signo. Docti commoventur verbis scriptura sacra, & Ecclesiae decretis. Hac res excitabit nobis magnam tragoediam, cùm tragoediarum plus quàm satis sit.
units.tr: Having left Thuringia, Carlstadt made straight for Strasbourg, where he drew Orto Brunfels to his side, and spoke with him alone. From there he went to Basel, where, without telling anyone, and with only the Anabaptists of that place as his accomplices, he arranged for the publication of some very brief booklets he had written on the Lord's Supper. Erasmus to Henry Stromer, 10 December: Carlstadt was here, but I had scarcely greeted Oecolampadius. He published six booklets. Two of the men who printed them were arrested the day before yesterday in prison by order of the magistrate, chiefly because, as I hear, he teaches that in the Eucharist there is not the true body of the Lord. No one bears this. The laity are indignant that their God is taken from them, as if God were nowhere except under that sign. The learned are moved by the words of holy Scripture and the decrees of the Church. This affair will stir up for us a great tragedy, when there are more than enough tragedies.

units.la: Summa doctrinæ Carolostadianæ de Coena sacra hæc est: corpus Christi nec esse nec comedi in coena oraliter, sed celebrari ibi corporis pro nobis traditi, & sanguinis pro nobis fusi, memoriā. Tropicam igitur locutione in verbis institutionis agnoscit, & vocabulum τῶν non refert ad ἄρτον (cum hoc mascumasculini, illud neutrius generis sit) sed ad ipsum Christi σῶμα sive corpus, ut hæc sit verborū Domini sententia: accipite, edite panem hunc in mei memoriam, hic enim sedet corpus, quod pro vobis traditur. Addit, ad tropum necessariò confugiendum esse; ne cogamur asserere, panem pro nobis crucifixū esse: carnis esum, quod tamē falsum, in scripturis mandatū esse: carnem, quod item falsum, aliquid prodesse: corpus ipsū, quod etiam falsū, in usu Cœnæ frangi & pro nobis tradi. In libello, quem inscripsit, von dem wie derchristlichen mißbrauch des Herren brodt vnd felch/ hoc est; de abusu panis & calicis Domini minimè Christiano, impugnat etiā erroneum dogma, quo iubentur homines remissionem peccatorū in Sacramento quærere.
units.tr: The sum of Carlstadt's doctrine on the Lord's Supper is this: the body of Christ is neither present nor eaten orally in the Supper, but there is celebrated there the memory of the body given for us and the blood shed for us. He therefore recognises a trope in the words of institution, and he does not refer the word touto [τοῦτο] to the bread (since the one is masculine and the other neuter), but to Christ's own sōma [σῶμα], or body, so that the sense of the Lord's words is: take, eat this bread in my memory; for here lies the body which is given for you. He adds that one must take refuge in a trope, lest we be forced to assert that the bread was crucified for us; that eating flesh is commanded in Scripture, which is likewise false; that flesh profits anything, which is false too; and that the body itself is broken and given for us in the use of the Supper, which again is false. In the booklet he entitled Von dem wie der christlichen Missbrauch des Herren Brodt und Kelch, that is, on the abuse of the Lord's bread and cup, which is by no means Christian, he also attacks the erroneous doctrine by which men are bidden to seek the forgiveness of sins in the Sacrament.

units.la: Docet: frequentandā Cœnam sacrā, ut annunciemus ibi mortem Domini: annūciationem mortis Dominicæ ex memoria Christi: memoriā Christi ex vera diiudicatione corporis traditi, sanguinis fusi, fluere: diiudicari corpus, nō panem, sive Sacramentū, quando discernimus corpus & sic sanguinem Christi ab aliis corporib, & sanguinibus: discretionē corporis & sanguinis Christi fieri, quādo cōsideram', corpus Christi pro nobis in mortem traditū, sanguinem pro nobis fusū: qui hæc nō considerat, ḉos fieri reos corporis Christi ḉque ac latrones, à quib. occisus est, p̄sertim quando tales de pane Domini edunt, & de calice bibunt. Itaq; homine seipsum probare debere, an scil. Christi mortem recte secum pensitet, & talis sit, qualem Christus esse vult. Negat etiam, sacramentum esse arrabonem, arram, & pignus redemptionis per Christum, siquidem, quod solius Christi & Spiritus S. proprium est, id pani & vino minime sit tribuendum, nec usquam scriptura testetur, per panem & vinum conscientias tranquillari: quin contra Apostolus, praecipiat: hominem prius se probare, & sic de pane sacro edere debere, quae probatio supervacanea esset, si homo per Eucharistiam de remissione peccatorum suorum certior redderetur.
units.tr: He teaches that the Lord's Supper should be frequented so that we may proclaim there the death of the Lord; that the proclamation of the Lord's death flows from the remembrance of Christ, and the remembrance of Christ from the true discernment of the body given and the blood shed. The body, not the bread or Sacrament, is discerned when we distinguish the body and so the blood of Christ from other bodies and bloods. The discerning of the body and blood of Christ takes place when we consider the body of Christ given to death for us and the blood shed for us; whoever does not consider these becomes guilty of the body of Christ just as the robbers are who killed him, especially when such people eat of the Lord's bread and drink of the cup. Therefore a man ought to examine himself, namely whether he rightly weighs the death of Christ and is such as Christ wills him to be. He also denies that the Sacrament is a pledge, an earnest, and a security of redemption through Christ, since what belongs to Christ alone and the Holy Spirit is by no means to be given to bread and wine; nor does Scripture anywhere testify that consciences are calmed through bread and wine. On the contrary, the Apostle commands that a man must first examine himself and only then eat of the sacred bread; this examination would be superfluous if a man were made more certain of the forgiveness of his sins through the Eucharist.

units.la: Senatus Tigurinus rei novitate turbatus, cavebat, ne publice libelli Caroloftadii in urbe sua venderentur. At Zwinglius & Oecolampadius multo ante in verbis coenae tropu inesse agnoverat, quam videret, quib. verbis eum expedirent. Itaq; Zwinglius pro suggestu hortatus est Senatu, ut libellos illos, sicut & alios, ab omnib. legi pateretur, totaque Ecclesiam ad lectionem eorum incitabat, ut eo magis esset ingenua veritatis victoria: Caroloftadio idem accidisse dicens, quod tyroni, cui animus & arma ad pugnandu non desunt, sed armorum peritia. Qui nescit quae corporis pars, quib. armis munienda sit, ga-leam leam pectori thoracis loco praefigit, armillis crura tegit, ocreis tempora: ex thorace clypeum facit, &c. Ita Carolostadium veritatem quidem agnoscere: sed quia troporum vim non habeat perspectam, verba non recto ordine collocare atq; disponere.
units.tr: The Zurich Senate, troubled by the novelty of the matter, took care that Carlstadt's booklets should not be sold publicly in their city. But Zwingli and Oecolampadius had long before recognised a trope in the words of the Supper, before they saw by which words they might extricate him. So Zwingli, from the pulpit, urged the Senate to allow those booklets, like others, to be read by all, and he urged the whole Church to read them, so that the victory of the truth might be the more open and fair; he said that what had happened to Carlstadt was what happens to a recruit who has spirit and weapons for fighting but lacks skill in arms. Such a man does not know which part of the body is to be armoured with which weapons: he puts a helmet on his chest in place of a breastplate, covers his legs with armbands, his temples with greaves, and makes a shield out of his breastplate, and so on. So Carlstadt indeed recognises the truth, but because he has not clearly grasped the force of the tropes, he does not arrange and set out the words in the right order.

units.la: Oecolampadius vero hinc inde scripsit ad amicos, ne Carolostadium propter libellos suos infamarent. Tametsi enim non assequutus esset quod voluisset: tamen rei summam improbandam non videri.
units.tr: Oecolampadius, however, wrote here and there to friends that they should not defame Carlstadt on account of his booklets. Although Carlstadt had not achieved what he wanted, the substance of the matter did not seem to him to deserve condemnation.

units.la: Anabaptistae quoq;, tametsi Zwinglii sententiam, quam non ignorabant, nequaquam probarent, Carolostadii tamen probabant, & libelles eius longe late
units.tr: The Anabaptists too, although they by no means approved Zwingli's opinion, which they were not unaware of, nonetheless approved Carlstadt's, and they circulated his booklets far and wide.

units.la: q; spargebant. Et Balthasar Pacimontanus Pastor in VValtshut, vir eloquens, quem Thomas Muncerus, ex Thuringia eo veniens, corruperat, Oecolampadio tantum non gratulatur, quod illi non displiceant libelli a Carolostadio super Eucharistia editi. Tametsi, inquit, non est assequutus quod voluit, id tamen res est, quod scripsit. Hanc sententiam jam pridem libens ex te evulsissem: sciebam etenim, aut forte divinabam, te a nobis nihil dissidere. Verum tum semper respondebas mihi sub quodam velamine, & quidem non incircumspecte: nam ita postulabat temporis opportunitas. Sed nunc est hora, qua palam & super tecta praedicamus, qua antehac mussitabamus in penetralibus.
units.tr: Balthasar Pacimontanus, a pastor at Waltshut and an eloquent man, whom Thomas Müntzer had corrupted when he came there from Thuringia, all but congratulates Oecolampadius that the booklets on the Eucharist published by Carlstadt do not displease him. Although, he says, he has not achieved what he wanted, that is nonetheless the substance of what he wrote. I would long since gladly have drawn this opinion out of you: for I knew, or perhaps guessed, that you do not differ from us at all. But then you always answered me under a certain veil, and not without caution, for the opportunity of the time demanded it. But now is the hour in which we preach openly and from the housetops what before we whispered in the inner chambers.

units.la: Zwinglii operum Tom. II. p. 244. b.
units.tr: Zwingli's Works, vol. II, p. 244b.

units.la: Epistola 1. lib. 2. epistolarum Zwinglii & Oecol.
units.tr: Letter 1, book 2 of the letters of Zwingli and Oecolampadius.

units.la: Moxut Carolostadii libri ꝑdierũt, Zwinglius Epistolam scripsit ad Matthæum Alberum,Reutlingensium Ecclesiasten, quem cū fratre quodam de Eucharistia disceptatione instituisse intellexerat: in qua scribit: haêtenus longè à scopo fuisse aberratum: Carolostadii sententiam Leoni Judæ, fratribus aliis & sibi non improbari:sed offendi multos tum obscuritate verborum, tū scommatis intempestivis, Tigurinos imprimis suos eo, quòd ab ea via, quam ipse ingressus fuisset nonnihil Carolostadius abhorreret. Deinde docet: edere Corpus Christi, nihil aliud esse, quàm credere corpus Christi pro nobis esse mortuum,idq; demonstrat:
units.tr: Soon after Carlstadt's books appeared, Zwingli wrote a letter to Matthew Alber, preacher at Reutlingen, whom he had learned was carrying on a dispute about the Eucharist with a certain brother. In it he writes that until now they had strayed far from the goal. Carlstadt's view was not disapproved by Leo Jud, the other brothers, or himself; but many were offended, both by the obscurity of his words and by his untimely jibes, and above all his own Zurich people, because Carlstadt somewhat shrank from the path which Zwingli himself had entered upon. Then he teaches that to eat the body of Christ is nothing other than to believe that the body of Christ was dead for us, and he demonstrates this:

units.la: 1. Ex sexto capite Iohannis, ubi de spirituali manducatione agitur, cujus in cæna sa-cra institutum sit signum.
units.tr: 1. From the sixth chapter of John, where spiritual eating is treated, of which a sign was instituted in the Lord's Supper.

units.la: 2. Ex verbis institutionis, ubi EST exponit per SIGNIFICAT: quia Cæna Domini sit signum corporis Christi pro nobis tra-diti: id quod evincant verba addita: Hoc facite in mei memoriam.
units.tr: 2. From the words of institution, where EST is explained as SIGNIFIES, because the Lord's Supper is a sign of the body of Christ delivered for us; which the added words prove: Do this in remembrance of me.

units.la: 3. Ex verbis Lucæ: Hoc est novum Testamen-tum in meo sanguine. Ergo non ipse sanguis,
units.tr: 3. From the words of Luke: This is the new testament in my blood. Therefore not the blood itself,

units.la: 4. Ex verbis Pauli 1. Cor. 10. qui manifeste docet, quod, qui panem edunt & poculum hauriunt, cum reliquis fratribus in unum corpus coalescant; quod quidem cor-pus Christi sit, eò, quod corpus Christi, hoc hoc est, quòd carnem auctoris sui pro se mactatam, & sanguinem ejus pro se fusum esse credant.
units.tr: 4. From the words of Paul, 1 Cor. 10, which clearly teaches that those who eat the bread and drink the cup grow together with the other brothers into one body; which body is indeed the body of Christ, because they believe that his body was slaughtered for them and his blood poured out for them.

units.la: In calce adjurat Alberum per omnes vivos & mortuos, ut ne cuiquam mortalium hanc epistolam communicet, nisi quem constet in fide Christi Jesu sincerum esse. Tiguri 16. Novembris 1524.
units.tr: At the end he adjures Alber, by all the living and the dead, not to communicate this letter to any mortal unless he is known to be sincere in the faith of Christ Jesus. Zurich, 16 November 1524.

units.la: ARGENTINENSES quoq; Theologi, VVolfgangus Fabritius Capito mense Octobri, & Martinus Bucerus, cui caeteri ministri omnes subscripserunt, mense Decembri huius anni, publicis scriptis docuerunt: mittendas esse contentiones, & cogitandum de usu sacrae coenae, h.e. ut Capito loquitur, fidem nostram pane & vino Domini per memoriam carnis & sanguinis illius tantum pascendam: vel, ut Bucerus nomine omnium Pastorum loquitur: panem ibi edendum, vinum bibendum, & illico ad spirituale deveniendum, memoriam mortis Christi. Sic enim edendum panem, vinum bibendum, ut traditionis corporis & sanguinis semel factae recordemur, atq; ita spiritualiter, verèque carnem illius edamus, sanguinem bibamus.
units.tr: The theologians of Strasbourg too, Wolfgang Fabritius Capito in October, and Martin Bucer, to whose public writing all the other ministers subscribed, in December of this year taught that contentions should be set aside and thought given to the use of the Lord's Supper. That is, as Capito puts it, our faith is to be fed by the bread and wine of the Lord only through the memory of his flesh and blood. Or, as Bucer speaks in the name of all the ministers: the bread is to be eaten there, the wine drunk, and at once one comes to the spiritual, the remembrance of Christ's death. For the bread is to be eaten and the wine drunk in such a way that we recall the body and blood once delivered, and so spiritually and truly eat his flesh and drink his blood.

units.la: LUTHERUS successu doctrinae Carolostadianae perturbatus mense Decembri ad Amsdorffium scribit: Nobis nihil est, nisi unde humiliemur. Nam Carlstadii venenum latissimè serpit, accessit ejus sententia Zwinglius Turegi, & Leo Iudaus, aliíque multi con-
units.tr: Luther, disturbed by the success of Carlstadt's teaching, writes to Amsdorf in December: For us there is nothing but cause for humiliation. For the poison of Carlstadt creeps widely; to his opinion have come Zwingli at Zurich, Leo Jud, and many others con-

units.la: ANNUS MDXXIV.
units.tr: THE YEAR 1524.

units.la: CASPAR Schwenckfeldius Nobilis Silesius Kal. Januarii edidit librum inscriptum Jacobo Episcopo Vratislaviensi, quem hortatur, ut puram Evangelii doctrinam amplectatur. Sed eo tempore adhuc sensit cum Luthero.
units.tr: Caspar Schwenckfeld, a noble of Silesia, published on 1 January a book addressed to Jacob, Bishop of Breslau, urging him to embrace the pure doctrine of the Gospel. At that time, however, he still agreed with Luther.

units.la: Idem undecima Junii scribit ad Fridericum Lignicensem Ducem de abusu Evangelii ad securitatem carnis.
units.tr: On 11 June he wrote to Frederick, Duke of Liegnitz, about the abuse of the Gospel as a license for the security of the flesh.

units.la: LUTHERUS Dominica xx. Trinitatis die nono Octobris deponit cucullum Monasticum.
units.tr: Luther, on the twentieth Sunday after Trinity, 9 October, laid aside his monastic cowl.

units.la: Idem hoc anno edidit, Psalterium Davidis Germanice. Librum contra seditiosos. Epistolam ad Principes Saxonie adversus Iconomachos & Enthusiastas. Librum de exaltatione Benonis, cum ossa Benonis Episcopi Misnensis more solenni Misnae effossa, exaltata atque collocata essent in tumbam marmoream, XIV. Maij: quae res aliis religioni fuit, aliis joco & risui.
units.tr: In this year Luther also published a German Psalter; a book against the seditious; an open letter to the princes of Saxony against the image-breakers and enthusiasts; and a book on the exhumation of Benno. On 14 May the bones of Benno, Bishop of Meissen, were dug up in the customary solemn manner at Meissen, raised up and placed in a marble tomb. This event was a matter of religious reverence for some and of jest and laughter for others.

units.la: THOMAS Müncerus Stolbergensis & Cocionator Alstetensis edidit scripta quaedam adversus Lutheranos, quibus meram effudit rabiem. Liber adversus Lutherum ab eo scriptus, dedicatus & nuncupatus est Christo, Principi, ut ipse loquitur, Illustrissimo, &c. Item Lutherum flagellat, quod Enthusiastico spico spiritu careat, & nihil nisi carnalia sapiat. Idem ad Melanchthonem scribit epistolam feriâ quintâ post Annunciationis, cui hæc verba inseruit: Non in solo pane vivit homo: sed in omni verbo quod procedit de ore Dei. Videte, de ore Dei, & non ex libris proficiscitur. Testimonium quidem verbi veri ex voluminibus est. Nisi enim in corde oriatur, verbum hominis est, damnàs scribas versipelles, qui furantur oracula sancta Ieremia 23. Nunquàm eis Dominus loquutus est, & ipsi usurpât verba ejus. O charissimi, operam navate, ut prophetetis, alioqui Theologia vestra nõ valebit obulum. Considerate Deum vestrum è vicino, & non à longè.
units.tr: Thomas Müntzer of Stolberg, preacher at Allstedt, published certain writings against the Lutherans, in which he poured out pure rage. The book he wrote against Luther was dedicated and addressed to Christ, "the most illustrious Prince," as he himself puts it, and so on. He also lashes Luther for lacking the enthusiastic spirit and savouring only carnal things. On the Friday after the Annunciation he wrote a letter to Melanchthon, in which he inserted these words: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God." Note: out of the mouth of God, and it does not come from books. Indeed the testimony of the true word is in volumes; but unless it arises in the heart, it is the word of man. You scribes, cunning turncoats, who steal the holy oracles (Jeremiah 23), "they have never been spoken by the Lord," and yet they use his words. O dearest men, take pains to prophesy; otherwise your theology will not be worth a penny. Consider your God from close at hand, and not from afar."

units.la: Idem hoc anno edidit protestationem suâ unà cum Apologia de fide & baptismo, ex quibus apparet, eum fuisse hominem fanaticum, qui semina doctrinæ Enthusiastarum sparsit, & incautos homines prodigiosis ξενοφωνίαις fascinavit & dementavit.
units.tr: In the same year he also published, together with his Apology, a protestation concerning faith and baptism. From these it is clear that he was a fanatic, who sowed the seeds of the doctrine of the Enthusiasts and bewitched and maddened unwary people with prodigious "strange utterances" [ξενοφωνίαις].

units.la: ANNVS CHRISTI MDXXV.
units.tr: THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1525.

units.la: CVRSVM doctrinæ Evangelicæ etsi multa sunt hoc anno remorata, tamen sparsa illa subinde latiùs, & ut à multis hostibus oppugnata, ita non paucorum constantiâ quasi de novo fuit confirmata. CurCursum Evangelii remorata sunt in Germania & extra Germaniam, bellum rusticanum & Sacramentarium: in Helvetia & Moravia secta Anabaptistica: in Silesia, secta Schwenckfeldica: in Boëmia, Apostasia Caroli Ducis Monsterbergensis: quibus adde, si placet, nuptias Lutheri, alienissimo tempore celebratas.
units.tr: Although the course of the Evangelical doctrine was much hindered this year, it was nevertheless spread more widely at times, and, though it was assailed by many enemies, it was in a sense confirmed anew by the constancy of not a few. The course of the Gospel was held back both in Germany and outside Germany: in Germany by the Peasants' War and the Sacramentarian controversy; in Helvetia and Moravia by the Anabaptist sect; in Silesia by the Schwenckfeldian sect; in Bohemia by the apostasy of Duke Charles of Münsterberg. To these one may add, if you like, Luther's marriage, celebrated at a most unseasonable time.

units.la: BELLUM RUSTICANUM multum nocuit Evangelio.
units.tr: THE PEASANTS' WAR greatly harmed the Gospel.

units.la: Nam qui in Suevia coïerant rustici, Articulorum Magistratibus propositorum primo liberam Evangelii praedicationem sibi concedi armatis precibus postulabant. Et qui motus in Thuringia plebeios rusticosq; suscitavit Thomas Müncerus, praeco fuerat Evangelicus, sed ab Evangelio Christi ad somnia Diaboli, & a somniis ad seditiones publicas dilapsus. Hinc passim in Germania Pontificiorum in Evangelicos auditae voculae: Hinc nova doctrina, hinc Evangelij Lutheranici fructus? a In Gallia etiam clarissimam Reginam, Francisci Regis captivi matrem, quidam in hanc sententiam pertrahere conatus est, ut obstaret doctrinae Evangelii, tanquam pacis turbatrici. In Germania enim omnia esse mixta, neminem audire Principum imperia, & turbata prorsus esse omnia.
units.tr: For the peasants who had gathered in Swabia demanded, first among the articles presented to the magistrates, that free preaching of the Gospel be granted to them, and they pressed this demand with arms. And Thomas Müntzer, who had stirred up the movement of the common people and peasants in Thuringia, had been an Evangelical herald, but he had slipped from the Gospel of Christ to the dreams of the Devil, and from dreams to open sedition. Hence, throughout Germany, the Papists' taunts against the Evangelicals were heard everywhere: "Here is the new doctrine, here are the fruits of the Lutheran Gospel!" In France too, someone tried to draw the most famous Queen, mother of the captive King Francis, into this opinion, so that she would oppose the doctrine of the Gospel as a disturber of the peace: "for in Germany all things are mixed up, no one hears the commands of the princes, and everything is utterly in turmoil."

units.la: bLUTHERus ut scandalo huic occurreret, glisccente adhuc dissidio, antequam plebei arma sumpsissent, edito scripto, omnes a seditione, velut flagitiosissimo scelere, non solùm externo facto, verùm etiam verbis & cogitationibus fugiendo, dehortatur. Deinde articulis agricolarum respondens, præcipuè sibi postremum caput, quòd verbo Dei meliora edocti, cedere veritati cupiant, probari ostendit. Postea ordine eum verbo Dei plerosqũ pugnare ostendens, concludit: etsi omnia postulata justissima essent: tamen per seditionem & arma, scelerATE adversus Magistratum sumpta, rapi non debere, & gravissimas pœnas, præsentes ac æternas, in proposito perseverantibus, comminatur.
units.tr: Luther, to meet this scandal while the dissension was still growing, before the common people had taken up arms, published a writing dissuading all from sedition, as a most shameful crime, to be avoided not only in deed but also in words and thoughts. Then, replying to the articles of the peasants, he showed especially that the last article, in which they desire to yield to the truth because they have been taught better by the word of God, is to be approved. Afterwards, showing in order how most of the articles were at odds with the word of God, he concluded that even if all the demands were most just, yet they ought not to be seized by sedition and arms, taken up wickedly against the magistrate, and he threatened the gravest punishments, both present and eternal, against those who persevered in this purpose.

units.la: Eodem tempore ad Principes & Nobilitatem scribit: Ipsos Principes esse seditionis hujus causam, Ecclesiasticos inprimis, quippe qui Evangelii sinceram prædicationem impediant, & opprimere atq; eradicare cupiant & subditos onerib. intolerabilibus, & exactionibus iniustis gravissimè premant: quas opes iniquè corrasas, postea luxu turpissimè profundant. Itaq; necesse esse, ut à persequutionibus Evangelii, & ab iniusta oppressione subditorum desinant: & , quæ emendanda sint, corrigant, nisi gravem Dei iram, & vindictam experiri, & impendens à subditis suis exitium incurrere velint. Et monet Principes præterea: ut omnia pacis media priùs quærant, quàm armis decernant: incertos enim esse belli eventus & arma faciliùs sumi quàm deponi.
units.tr: At the same time he wrote to the princes and nobility that the princes themselves were the cause of this sedition, and especially the ecclesiastical princes, who, indeed, hinder the sincere preaching of the Gospel and wish to oppress and root it out, and who sorely burden their subjects with intolerable charges and unjust exactions, which wealth they have wickedly gathered and afterwards squander most shamefully in luxury. Therefore it was necessary that they cease from persecuting the Gospel and from the unjust oppression of their subjects, and that they correct what needs to be amended, unless they wished to experience the heavy wrath and vengeance of God and to incur the ruin hanging over them from their subjects. Luther further advised the princes that they should seek all the means of peace before deciding by arms, for the outcomes of war are uncertain and arms are more easily taken up than laid down.

units.la: Tandem utrisq; sigillatim commonefactis, communem illis epistolà scribit: & quòd malam utriq; causam tueantur, monet, ut ab armis discedant, & disceptatione causam finiant. At rusticis nihilominus progredientibus, & non Pontificiis solùm, sed Nobilitati bellū facientibus, Lutherus alio evulgato scripto, hortatur & instigat omnes, ut velut ad commune restinguendum incendium, sic ad istos consceleratos latrones trucidandos accurrãt. Qui libellus, ut nimis acer, à multis vituperatus, sed à Luthero prolixè fuit defensus.
units.tr: Finally, having admonished both sides separately, he wrote to both together in a letter, and, because each was defending a bad cause, he urged them to lay down their arms and end the dispute by discussion. But since the peasants nevertheless went on, and waged war not only against the Papists but also against the nobility, Luther, by another published writing, exhorted and urged all men to hasten, as if to put out a common conflagration, to slaughter those criminal brigands. This little book, as too harsh, was condemned by many, but Luther defended it at length.

units.la: Prodibant passim & alia Evangelicorū scripta in Germania, quibus retundebantur eorū clamores, qui motuum & seditionum causam in renati nuper Evangelii doctrinam conserebant. Inter alia, nihil novi esse, Evangelici docebant, doctrinæ puræ adscribi, quod hominum peccatis promeritum sit. Romanos temporibus Apostolicis universales calamitates sibi immitti, propter religionem Christianam, putasse; cum tamen ipsi essent rei publicorum incommodorum, & malorum illices, apud quos Deus sperneretur, statuç adorarentur; id quod ex Tertulliani Apologetico, ex Cypriano contra Demetriū, ex Augustino de civitate Dei, ex Orosio deniq; clarū sit.
units.tr: Other Evangelical writings also appeared throughout Germany, by which were repulsed the clamours of those who ascribed the causes of the uprisings and seditions to the doctrine of the Gospel recently reborn. Among other things, the Evangelicals taught that there was nothing new in this: that what had come upon men through their sins was being attributed to the pure doctrine. They showed that the Romans in apostolic times thought that universal calamities were being inflicted on them because of the Christian religion, although they themselves were the authors of the public misfortunes and of the evils, among whom God was despised and idols were worshipped. This is clear from Tertullian's Apologeticus, from Cyprian against Demetrianus, from Augustine's City of God, and finally from Orosius.

units.la: PHILIPPUS quoq; Melanchthon à Ludovico Electore Palatino super articulis Rusticorum consultus, confutationem articulorū illorum scripsit, & consilium adiecit. Incendium hoc Rusticorum non aquâ sed sanguine multorum milliû in bello hoc caesorum, restinctum est.
units.tr: Philip Melanchthon also, consulted by Louis, Elector Palatine, about the articles of the peasants, wrote a refutation of those articles and added counsel. This conflagration of the peasants was extinguished not by water but by the blood of many thousands slain in this war.

units.la: BELLUM SACRAMENTARIUM continuarunt Saxones, Helvetii, Suevi.
units.tr: THE SACRAMENTARIAN WAR

units.la: In Saxonia Lutherus Carolostadium, Joannes autem Bugenhagius Ecclesiae VVittebergensis Pastor, Zwinglium, publicis scriptis adoriuntur.
units.tr: The Saxons, the Swiss and the Swabians continued the war over the sacrament. In Saxony, Luther attacked Carlstadt in published writings, and John Bugenhagius, minister of the church at Wittenberg, attacked Zwingli.

units.la: Lutherus statim sub initium anni respondet ad libellos Carolostadii, libro, quem inscribit, Contra caelestes Prophetas (Prophetas enim tum VVittebergae nominabant Anabaptistarum primitias, de revelationibus arcanis & spiritu prophetico gloriantes, Ciconiam, Muncerum, Cellarium, &qui his familiaris fuerat, Carolostadium) Librum illum Lutherus in duas secat partes: primâ de imaginibus, Carolostadio, & Missa agit, affirmaque Imagines in veteri Testamento prohibitas esse, non in novo: Carolostadium à se non fugatum: Missae nomen etiam ab Apostolis, sacramento tributû, & alia: Alterius materies est Eucharistia: ubi primùm exaggerat expositionem Carolostadianâ pronominis Hoc: deinde respondet ad Carolostadii argumenta: aitq; verba, quod pro vobis traditur, hunc habere sensum, corpus quod in pane editis, paulò post, quando non edetur, pro vobis tradetur. Et sicut non scriptû est, accipiaccipite corpus & edite: ita nec scriptum esse: accipite panem & edite. Dictum Christi, Caro non prodest quicquam, non de carne Christi, sed de sensu carnis, qui mors est, Rom. esse intelligendum. Fractionem esse distributionem corporis: sanguinem Christi, qui pro nobis effusus, nunc sedere ad dextram Dei: sed efficaciam illius effusionis esse perpetui temporis. Deniq; nesciri, quomodo panis fiat & sit corpus Christi. Verbis Christi inhærendum.
units.tr: Luther, at the very beginning of the year, answered Carlstadt's pamphlets in a book which he entitled Against the Heavenly Prophets (for at that time at Wittenberg they called the Anabaptists' first fruits "Prophets," boasting of secret revelations and prophetic spirit: Storch, Müntzer, Cellarius, and Carlstadt, who had been familiar with them). Luther divides this book into two parts. The first deals with images, with Carlstadt, and with the Mass; he affirms that images were forbidden in the Old Testament but not in the New; that Carlstadt had not been put to flight by him; and that the name Mass was also given to the sacrament by the Apostles, and other points. The subject of the second part is the Eucharist. There he first complains of Carlstadt's exposition of the pronoun This; then he replies to Carlstadt's arguments and says that the words which is given for you have this sense: the body which you eat in the bread, shortly afterwards, when it will not be eaten, will be given for you. Just as it is not written take and eat the body, so it is not written take the bread and eat. The saying of Christ, the flesh profits nothing, is to be understood not of the flesh of Christ but of the sense of the flesh, which is death (Romans 8). The breaking is the distribution of the body; the blood of Christ, which was poured out for us, now sits at the right hand of God, but the efficacy of that outpouring is of perpetual duration. Finally, that it is not known how the bread becomes and is the body of Christ. One must cling to the words of Christ.

units.la: Johannes Bugenhagius Pomeranus epistolam Latinè & Germanicè edit de cœna Domini, in qua pro orali manducatione pugnat contra Zwinglium, argumentis: quod Zwinglii doctrina nova sit: ex somniis probetur: Evangelistis nullibi Est pro significat usurpetur: dictum, caro non prodest quicquam, non de carne Christi, sed de carnali intelligentia accipiendum: secundum Paulum 1 Cor. 10. communicetur corpus & sanguis Christi: & indigni rei fiant, non panis sed corporis 1. Cor. 11.
units.tr: Johannes Bugenhagius of Pomerania published a letter on the Lord's Supper in Latin and German, in which he fights for oral eating against Zwingli. His arguments are these: Zwingli's teaching is new; it is shown to be so from dreams; nowhere do the Evangelists use "is" to mean "signifies"; the saying the flesh profits nothing must be understood not of the flesh of Christ but of carnal understanding; and according to Paul, 1 Cor. 10, the body and blood of Christ are communicated, and men become guilty not of the bread but of the body, 1 Cor. 11.

units.la: In Helvetia Zwinglius & Oecolampadius causæ sacramentariæ, à Carolostadio motæ, patrocinium suscipiunt, repudiata tamen violenta interpretatione Carlstadiana particulæ Hoc: quam Carlstadius ipse abjecit Zwinglii & Oecolampadii scriptis lectis.
units.tr: In Helvetia, Zwingli and Oecolampadius took up the sacramentarian cause that Carlstadt had raised. They rejected, however, Carlstadt's violent interpretation of the particle hoc, which Carlstadt himself abandoned after reading the writings of Zwingli and Oecolampadius.

units.la: Zwinglius rogatu Italorum & Gallorum, ut ipsus fatetur, summam doctrinæ næ Christianæ libello eo complectitur, quem de vera & falsa religione inscripsit: in quo suâ quoque de Eucharistia sententiam explicat: nempe esse eam gratiarum actionem, & communionis gratulationem eorum, qui mortem Christi annunciant. Deinde multis probat, Christum capite sexto Johannis non loqui de manducatione sacramentali: Tum ex scriptura locos adducit, in quibus negari non potest, vocem est, pro significat, esse positam: Postremò evidenter demonstrat, etiam in verbis cœnæ est pro significat necessario accipi: & coronidis loco ex Patrum testimoniis manducationem oralem destruit, spiritualem adstruit. Hoc Commentario Zwinglii non pauci sic moti sunt, ut, cùm ante nihil de hac sententia audire vellent, postea mitigati, eam diligenter perpenderint.
units.tr: Zwingli, at the request of Italians and Frenchmen, as he himself confesses, sums up the whole of Christian doctrine in the little book he entitled de vera & falsa religione, On the True and False Religion. In it he also sets out his opinion on the Eucharist: namely, that it is a thanksgiving and a joyful communion of those who proclaim the death of Christ. He then proves at length that Christ in John chapter 6 is not speaking of sacramental eating. Next he adduces passages of Scripture in which it cannot be denied that the word "is" is used for "signifies." Lastly he clearly demonstrates that even in the words of the Supper "is" must necessarily be taken to mean "signifies." And, as a crown to all this, he uses the testimonies of the Fathers to destroy oral eating and to establish spiritual eating. Many were so moved by this commentary of Zwingli that, though before they would hear nothing of this opinion, they afterwards softened and weighed it carefully.

units.la: Quia vero Zwinglio festinanti quædam in hoc Commentario exciderant, ideo mense Augusto Subsidium de Eucharistia scripsit: in quo novis argumentis tropum stabilit in verbis cœnæ, & sex objectiones adversariorum diluit. Triumphare videtur hîc Zwinglius hoc argumento:
units.tr: But because some things had slipped from Zwingli in this commentary, since he had written in haste, he wrote in August a Subsidy on the Eucharist. In it, with new arguments, he establishes a trope in the words of the Supper and dissolves six objections of the opponents. Here Zwingli seems to triumph with this argument:

units.la: Si propria esset locutio HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, corpus aut pro corpore Christi naturali & patibili, aut pro corpore glorioso, aut pro corpore mystico, nempe Ecclesiâ, acciperetur.
units.tr: If THIS IS MY BODY were a proper locution, "body" would have to be taken either for the natural and passible body of Christ, or for the glorified body, or for the mystical body, namely the Church.

units.la: At non pro corpore naturali & patibili.
units.tr: But not for the natural and passible body:

units.la: 1. Sic enim edi non posset nisi dentibus: à qua manducatione ipse Christus avocat Iohann. 6. Caro non prodest quicquam,
units.tr: 1. For in that case it could be eaten only with the teeth; and from that kind of eating Christ himself calls us away in John 6: "the flesh profits nothing."

units.la: 2. Et sic discipuli aliter edissent quàm nos: tum enim nondum erat in cruce Caesus.
units.tr: 2. And in that case the disciples would have eaten differently from us, since at that time he had not yet been slain on the cross.

units.la: 3. Quomodo potuisset corporaliter edi, qui in cruce corporaliter debebat extendi?
units.tr: 3. How could he have been eaten bodily, when he was to be bodily stretched out on the cross?

units.la: Nec pro corpore glorioso:
units.tr: Nor for the glorified body:

units.la: 1. quia sic discipuli aliter edissent quam nos.
units.tr: 1. because in that case the disciples would have eaten differently from us.

units.la: 2. quia à resurrectione adscendit cœlos.
units.tr: 2. because since the resurrection he has ascended into the heavens.

units.la: Nec pro corpore mystico, quod est Ecclesia:
units.tr: Nor for the mystical body, which is the Church:

units.la: Quia sequitur: quod est traditum.
units.tr: because what follows is: which is given up (quod est traditum).

units.la: Ergo.
units.tr: Therefore.

units.la: Tandem vigesimâ tertiâ Octobris Zwinglius respondet epistolæ Joannis Bugenhagii. Docet autem: sententiam suam de cœna novam non esse, sed fuisse Christi, Apostolorum, Patrum. Scriptores cùm tropis utantur, non addere Commentarium, quo tropos exponant: se vidisse quidem, tropum inesse verbis cœnæ, sed in qua voce, non vidisse, donec epistolam Batavi cuiusdam legerit: Dictum Christi, Caro non prodest quicquam, non loqui de carnali intelligentia: quia contextus aliud urgeat, & qui statuit, carnem prodesse, is duas salutis vias statuat; Deniq; κοινωνία apud Paulum non passive accipi, ideo communionem rectius verti quàm communicationem: sensum esse: Poculum cui benedicimus, esse symbolum & protestationem, quod habeamus communionem in sanguine Christi, hoc est, quod Christiani simus, sive loci Christi, coetus ille, qui est corpus Christi, & cuius Christus est caput. Verbis illis, reus erit corporis Christi, Paulum non velle aliud, quàm, Christi institutum prodi ab eo, qui non eâ mente accedit, qua oportet. In Epilogo deprecatur certamina cum Evangelicis fratribus: monet, ut & Pomeranus & alii à convitiis sibi temperent, ac causam solis scripturis & rationibus, non clamoribus tribunitiis agant: sat hostium habituros se in grege Pontificio: concludit, Non posse ex integro Antichristum profligari, nisi & errore Consubstantiationis profligato corruat.
units.tr: At last, on 23 October, Zwingli replied to the letter of Johannes Bugenhagius. He teaches that his opinion on the Supper is not new but was that of Christ, the Apostles and the Fathers. Writers who use tropes do not add a commentary explaining them. He had indeed seen that a trope lies in the words of the Supper, but he had not seen in which word, until he read the letter of a certain Batavian. As for the saying of Christ, "the flesh profits nothing," it does not speak of carnal understanding, because the context urges otherwise; and whoever holds that "the flesh profits" posits two ways of salvation. Finally, communion (κοινωνία [κοινωνία]) in Paul is not to be taken passively, and so it is better rendered "communion" than "communication." The sense is this: the cup over which we give thanks is a symbol and a declaration that we have communion in the blood of Christ, that is, that we are Christians, or that we are in the place of Christ, in that assembly which is the body of Christ and of which Christ is the head. By the words "he will be guilty of the body of Christ," Paul wishes to say nothing other than that the institution of Christ is betrayed by one who approaches it without the right frame of mind. In his epilogue he deprecates quarrels with the evangelical brethren. He advises both Pomeranus and the others to refrain from insults, and to conduct the cause by Scripture and reasons alone, not by tribunician clamours; he will have enough enemies in the Papist flock. He concludes: Antichrist cannot be wholly overthrown unless, with the error of Consubstantiation overthrown, he too falls.

units.la: Oecolampadius Basileæ cum collegis nonnullis idem docebat quod Zwinglius. Cum igitur passim audiret Carolostadianus, & ab amicis etiam rogaretur, ut publico scripto sententiam suam de Eucharistia explicaret, libellum hoc anno edidit de genuina verborum Domini, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, expositione: in quo originem manducationis oralis refert ad Petrum Lombardum Sententiarum cõsartiatorem, quem & ipsum, scribit, errorem suum Rapsodo alii, uti Damasc. vel Gratiano, affricare posse. Lombardũ enim distinctione 10.l.4. proscindere & insectari tanquam insanos hæreticos, qui asserunt, Christũ eo tropo dixisse, hoc est corpus meum, quo Paulus dixerat: Petra est Christus: nec animadvertere Lombardũ, se hæreseos hac ratione arguere præcipuos & antiquissimos Doctores, qui in hac sententia fuerint: Deinde diluit argumentum: Quæ captũ transcendunt, non sunt virib. humanis indaganda. Ergo de sacramentis nihil inquirendum. Ac probat sacramenta non esse ex genere ἀκαταλήπτων & incõprehensibilium. Nec esse in Eucharistia quòd vel miraculum sit, vel captũ hominis excedat. Diluit calumnias cõcionatorũ, qui vociferantur, negari ab iis Evangelia & Deitatem Christi, & totũ Christianismum everti, qui oralem manducationem carnis Christi negant. Docet etiã, non fuisse grave spiritui sancto, ita moderari verba, ne alicubi ansam seducendi accipere potuissent, sed αἰνιγματικῶς nonnulla esse voluisse, ut videntes nõ videant, & ἀποκάλυψις misericordiæ Dei donum cognosceretur. Tandem trãsit ad statũ causæ, probatq;, verba cœnæ Dominicæ, hoc est corpus meum, eodem tropo dici, quo illa Apostoli, Petra erat Christus. Nèq; enim insolutam, nec ignotam scripturæ hanc esse expositionem, cũm nihil alienius sit Synusiastarũ interpretatione: tropũ necessariò hic statuendum: absurda infinita sententiam rique alii: Num tu aliis vis sapientior esse ? Credendum est, quod alii credunt. Saepenumero seipsum accusabat, quid in aliorum pectoribus lateret, non cogitans, Tune solus tam abiectus es à facie Domini, ut illic repugnes, ubi fere nemo? Saepe antiquorum Doctorum lectione infirmitatem suam vincere conabatur, sed principio non occurrebat, quo iuvaretur. Crebrò erat obvium: corpus Domini & sanguis Domini: sed qualiter corpus, qualiter sanguis rarius explicabatur, & valde obscure. Pendens itaq; ab aliorum iudicio, parum recte sentiebat. Tandem semota authoritate hominum veritas ei fulgidior affulsit, ut ultra Papisticam sententiam inferre opus non esset. Suam vero hinc inde cum amicis contulit. Integrum iam annum sermo de coena Domini per ora omnium volarat, priusquam quicquam hac de re evulgaret.
units.tr: Oecolampadius at Basel, with some of his colleagues, taught the same as Zwingli. Since he heard the Carlstadtians everywhere, and was also asked by friends to set out his opinion on the Eucharist in a public writing, he published this year his little book de genuina verborum Domini, HOC EST CORPVS MEVM, expositione, On the Genuine Exposition of the Words of the Lord, THIS IS MY BODY. In it he traces the origin of oral eating to Peter Lombard, the compiler of the Sentences, whose error, he writes, another rhapsodist, such as Damascene or Gratian, could also fasten upon. For Lombard, in distinction 10 of book 4, tears apart and harries as insane heretics those who assert that Christ used in "this is my body" the same trope that Paul used in "the Rock was Christ." Nor did Lombard notice that by this reasoning he charges the chief and most ancient Doctors, who held this opinion, with heresy. Then Oecolampadius dissolves the argument: "Things that exceed our grasp are not to be investigated by human powers; therefore nothing is to be inquired into concerning the sacraments." He proves that the sacraments are not of the class of incomprehensibles (ἀκαταλήπτων [ἀκαταλήπτων]). Nor is there anything in the Eucharist that is either a miracle or exceeds human capacity. He dissolves the slanders of the preachers, who cry out that by these views the Gospels and the Deity of Christ are denied and all Christianity overturned, since they deny oral eating of the flesh of Christ. He also teaches that it was no burden to the Holy Spirit so to moderate the words that they could nowhere offer an occasion for deception; rather, he wished some things to be enigmatic (αἰνιγματικῶς [αἰνιγματικῶς]), so that those who see might not see, and the revelation (ἀποκάλυψις [ἀποκάλυψις]) might be recognised as a gift of God's mercy. Finally he passes to the state of the question, and proves that the words of the Lord's Supper, "this is my body," are spoken by the same trope by which the Apostles' words "the Rock was Christ" were spoken. He holds that this exposition of Scripture is neither unrefuted nor unknown, since nothing is more alien to it than the interpretation of the Synusiastae. The trope must necessarily be posited here; the other opinions lead to an endless train of absurdities. "Do you wish to be wiser than the others? One must believe what the others believe." He often accused himself of what might lie hidden in the hearts of others, not reflecting: "Are you alone so cast out from the face of the Lord that you resist where almost no one else does?" Often he tried to overcome his weakness by reading the ancient Doctors, but at first no principle presented itself by which he could be helped. It frequently occurred to him: "the body of the Lord and the blood of the Lord," but how it was a body and how it was blood was explained more rarely and very obscurely. Thus, hanging on the judgement of others, he thought rather wrongly. At last, with human authority set aside, the truth shone on him more brightly, so that it was no longer necessary to go beyond the Papist opinion. He compared his own view with that of his friends here and there. For a whole year talk of the Lord's Supper had flown through everyone's mouths before he published anything on the matter.

units.la: Misit Oecolampadius libellum suum Fratribus per Sueviam Christum annuntiantibus, rogavitque ne sibi succenserent ob veritatis indagationem: scriptum suum iudicarent, at non secundum faciem: charitatem primo loco commendatam sibi habeant, addito hoc epiphonemate: Error condonari potest, modò fides adsit in Christum. Discordiam, neq; si sanguinem fundamus, expiabimus.
units.tr: Oecolampadius sent his little book to the brethren who proclaim Christ throughout Swabia, and asked them not to be angry with him for seeking the truth. They should judge his writing, but not by its outward appearance; let them keep charity, commended to them above all, and he added this epiphonema: Error can be pardoned, provided faith in Christ is present. Discord, even if we shed blood, will not be expiated.

units.la: Hac occasione arrepta duodecimâ Octobris ad Oecolampadii libellum respondent doctores Suevici numero quatuordecim, Halæ congregati, edito libello, cui titulum fecerunt Syngrammatos, quod à pluribus conscriptus esset. Afferunt in isto libello argumenta 1. contra tropum, 2. pro literali sensu, 3. pro præsentia corporali. Estq; sententia Suevorum: Quemadmodū ad serpentem æneum sanationem attulerunt verba illa: Qui percussus aspexerit eum, vivet: ita verba cœnæ, Hoc est corpus meum ad ferre ad panem corpus, & ita in pane iam corpus realiter existere. Scripserunt inter alios Erhardus Snepfius VVimpinensis, & Joannes Brentius Halensis Ecclesiæ minister, qui Syngrammatos auctor fuisse creditur.
units.tr: Seizing this occasion, on 12 October fourteen Swabian doctors, gathered at Halle, answered Oecolampadius's little book. They published a book to which they gave the title Syngrammata, because it had been written by several hands. In this book they bring arguments: 1. against the trope; 2. for the literal sense; 3. for the bodily presence. The opinion of the Swabians is this: just as those words, "whoever, when bitten, looks upon it shall live," brought healing through the bronze serpent, so the words of the Supper, "this is my body," bring the body to the bread, and thus the body already really exists in the bread. Among the others who wrote were Erhard Snepf of Wimpfen and Johannes Brenz, minister of the Church at Halle, who is believed to have been the author of the Syngrammata.

units.la: His Oecolampadius statim ac eodem hoc anno Antisyngrámma opposuit, in quo oftendit ille ministris Suevicis, ipsos quæ evertere studerent, argumentis suis propriis incogitantissimè stabilire & afferere.
units.tr: Oecolampadius responded to this at once, in this same year, with his Antisyngramma. In it he showed that the Swabian ministers, while trying to overturn others, were establishing and asserting their own arguments with the greatest thoughtlessness.

units.la: Zwinglii de Suevorum syngrammate iudicium in calce epistolæ ad Theobaldum Billicanum legitur hoc: Nihil hac tempestate in lucem prodiisse video, quod commendatione esset indignius, cùm propter vim, qua in eo libro sacris literis fermè toties intentatur, quoties adducuntur, ac immodicum fastum: tum propter novum exemplum, ac immodestiam. Oecolampadium virum innocentissimum, ac omnis tum pietatis, tatis, tum eruditionis specimen, adeo impurè tractant, à quo plerique tamen hauserunt, qua in linguis sciunt, ut non obiurgatione, sed execratione dignum sit, hoc pacto ἀντιπλαςγεῖν.
units.tr: Zwingli's judgment on the Swabian syngramma is found at the end of his letter to Theobald Billican, and reads as follows: I see that nothing has come out lately that is more unworthy of commendation, both because of the violence with which that book almost always assails the Holy Scriptures whenever it quotes them, and its immoderate arrogance; and also because of its novel example and its lack of restraint. They treat Oecolampadius, a most innocent man and a model of all piety and learning, so foully, although most of them have drawn from him what they know of the languages, that it deserves not rebuke but execration, in this way to fashion in opposition [ἀντιπλαςγεῖν].

units.la: LUTHERUS ubi rescivit Carolostadium Argentinae <bl>Wharerę</bl>, prolixam ad Argentinenses scribit epistolam, qua illis lucem doctrinae Evangelicae gratulatur, eosdemq; ad constantiam & concordiam, & ad tolerandas calumnias, iniurias & infestationes hortatur: inprimis autem, à Carolostadii veneno sibi caveant, monet, renovatā memoriā colloquii Orlamundici, quo in loco Carolostadiani etiam vitae suae essent insidiati.
units.tr: When Luther learned that Carlstadt was at Strasbourg, he wrote a long letter to the Strasbourgers, in which he congratulated them on the light of the Evangelical doctrine and urged them to constancy and harmony, and to endure slanders, injuries and attacks. Above all, he warned them to beware of Carlstadt's poison, recalling the conference at Orlamünde, where the followers of Carlstadt had also plotted against his life.

units.la: Contra, Argentinenses Gregorium Caseliū, Hebraicae linguae Professorem, VVitteberggam mittunt, rogatum, ut ne Lutherus charitatem fraternam & unionem Ecclesiae propter controversiā Eucharisticā violet, Zwinglium & Oecolampadium, viros doctos & integros pro fratrib. agnoscat: de coena scribat & edoceat, quae vera esse credat. Quibus Lutherus per Caselium respondet: pace nihil esse optabilius: silere aut perpetuo, non esse integrum: respondere non posse, si damnari non liceat: & damnandi verbum pro convitio rapiatur: se à modestissimis illis, ut carnivoram, & esculenti Dei, impanatiq; cultorem traduci: consilium Argentinensium sibi non probari, quod fideles avocandi sint, à quaestione corporis & sanguinis præsentis, & solo verbo & fide sint exercendi: alterutros esse Satanæ ministros, vel ipsos, vel se, ideo hic nulli consilio aut medio locum esse: rationes, quæ pro tropo adferantur, nullas esse. Probandum, verbum est, non alicubi in scripturis, sed in isto loco pro significat accipiendum. In illo, Petra erat Christus, Paulum non de corporali, sed de spirituali loqui, siquidem addatur: bibebant de spirituali petra. Manifestum etiam lapsum esse in illo: agnus est transitus Domini. Hanc enim phrasin nusquam in scriptura haberi. Per Christum igitur se rogare fratres, ut ab hoc errore abstineant.
units.tr: On the other side, the Strasbourgers sent Gregory Caselius, professor of Hebrew, to Wittenberg, asking Luther not to violate fraternal charity and the unity of the Church over the Eucharistic controversy, but to acknowledge Zwingli and Oecolampadius, learned and upright men, as brethren, and to write and teach about the Supper whatever he believed to be true. Luther answered through Caselius: nothing is more to be wished for than peace; but to keep silent forever is not right; he cannot reply if he is not allowed to condemn; and the word "condemn" is seized upon as an insult. He said that he was being portrayed by those most moderate men as a flesh-eater and a worshipper of a god who is eaten and a "panned" god. He did not approve of the Strasbourgers' counsel, that the faithful should be drawn away from the question of the bodily and present body and blood, and exercised only in the word and faith. Both sides, he said, were ministers of Satan, either they or he, and therefore there was no place here for any counsel or middle way. The reasons advanced for a trope are worthless. The word is must be taken not as it is used elsewhere in Scripture, but in this place as meaning signifies. In that text, the Rock was Christ, Paul speaks not of a bodily but of a spiritual rock, since it is added: they drank of the spiritual rock. There is also a plain error in that phrase, it is the Lord's passover, for this expression is found nowhere in Scripture. He therefore begged them, by Christ, as brethren, to refrain from this error.

units.la: CAROLOSTADIUS sub initium huius anni vagabatur passim per superiorem Germaniam, & tandem consedit Rotemburgi ad Tubarim, tumultuans more suo, ut loquitur de eo Lutherus, imaginibus. Sedato autem tumultu rusticorum cum ministri Evangelici Rotemburgenses securi percutantur, & ingens civium numerus, erutis luminibus, ad extremam mendicitatem redigeretur, elapsus Carolostadius per sportam de muro Rotemburgensi, dimissus est.
units.tr: Carlstadt, at the beginning of this year, wandered about through upper Germany, and at last settled at Rothenburg on the Tauber, stirring up trouble, as Luther says of him, with images as was his habit. But when the peasants' rebellion was put down, the Evangelical ministers of Rothenburg were struck down with the sword, and a great number of citizens, having their eyes put out, were reduced to extreme beggary; Carlstadt escaped by being lowered in a basket from the wall of Rothenburg and was let go.

units.la: In his angustiis positus, libellum efficit, quo se diligenter ac solicitè purgat, & ab iis, qui ipsum inter seditionis authores ponant, iniuriam sibi fieri demonstrat: & scriptis literis valde orat Lutherum, ut hunc libellum edat, & suam innocentiam tueatur, ne indicta causa vitae ac bonorum discrimen sibi sit adeundum immerenti. Lutherus edita epistola, tametsi graviter à se dissentiat ille, tamen, quod in his difficultatibus ad se confugiat potius quam ad alios, qui ipsum in se concitarint, nolle se spem illius atque fiduciam fallere, dicit, praesertim cum hoc etiam proprium sit hominis Christiani. Rogat igitur Magistratum, & in universum omnes, quandoquidem & crimen intentatum à se removeat, & notionem non recusef, & legitimo iudicio parere velit, ut hoc ipsi concedatur. Hoc enim esse plenum aequitatis & officii. Post haec Carolostadius alterum mittit Luthero libellum, quo profitetur, ea quae de coena Domini scripserit, non definiendi, sed disputandi, & veritatis eruendae causa scripsisse. Lutherus excusationem accipit: monet tamen homines, quoniam ipsemet dubitare se testetur, nec certum quid definiat, ut ab eius opinione sibi caveant, aut, si forte & ipsi dubitent, eousque differant, donec, quid certo sequantur, appareat. Nam in iis, quae nobis credenda sint, minime haerendum, aut vacillandum esse: verum adeo certam cognitionem esse comparandam, ut potius quam à sententia discedamus, millies mori non recusemus. Atq; in hoc quidem sui ipsius immemor fuit Lutherus, quippe qui initio reformationis, ad Leonem Papam & Episcopum Brandeburgicum scripserat, inter propositiones suas de indulgentiis esse quaedam, de quibus dubitet, nonnulla ignoret, aliqua neget, nulla pertinaciter asserat.
units.tr: Placed in these straits, he produced a little book in which he carefully and anxiously cleared himself, and showed that wrong was being done to him by those who count him among the authors of the sedition. He also wrote and urgently begged Luther to publish this book and defend his innocence, so that he, an innocent man, should not have to face danger to his life and property without a hearing. Luther, having published the letter, said that although he dissented from Carlstadt gravely, nevertheless, since in these difficulties he was taking refuge with him rather than with others who had stirred them up against him, he was unwilling to disappoint his hope and trust, especially since this is also the proper character of a Christian man. He therefore asked the magistrate, and indeed everyone, since he removes the charge brought against him and does not refuse a hearing, and is willing to submit to a lawful judgment, that this should be granted to him. For this, he said, is full of fairness and duty. After this, Carlstadt sent Luther another little book, in which he declared that what he had written about the Lord's Supper was written not to define but to dispute, and for the sake of drawing out the truth. Luther accepted the excuse, but warned people, since Carlstadt himself testified that he was in doubt and defined nothing with certainty, to beware of his opinion, or, if perhaps they too were in doubt, to defer until it appeared what they should certainly follow. For in those things that we must believe we must not hesitate or waver, but must obtain such certain knowledge that we would not refuse to die a thousand times rather than depart from the doctrine. Yet in this Luther himself forgot himself, for at the beginning of the Reformation he had written to Pope Leo and to the Bishop of Brandenburg that among his propositions on indulgences there are some about which he is in doubt, some which he does not know, some which he denies, and none which he asserts stubbornly.

units.la: De Carolostadio sic tum fuit iudicatum: aut serio illum ad Lutherum ista scripsisse, aut simulate. Si serio, improbandâ esse adhibitâ prius ab illo in defendenda thesi, de qua dubitaret, vehementiam: sin simulate, levitatem ingenii culpandam. Quicquid sit, per Lutherum ab Electore Saxoniae tandem impetravit, ut fide publicâ in Saxoniam sibi redire liceret. Quin antequam Elector assensisset, apud Lutherum in monasterio, nemine, nisi VVolffgango, Lutheri famulo, conscio, Carolostadium latuisse, sunt qui affirmare non dubitent.
units.tr: Concerning Carlstadt, this was the judgment at the time: either he wrote these things to Luther seriously, or in pretence. If seriously, the vehemence he had shown earlier in defending a thesis about which he was doubtful was to be condemned; but if in pretence, his levity of mind was to be blamed. Whatever the case, through Luther he at last obtained from the Elector of Saxony permission to return to Saxony under public safe-conduct. Indeed, there are those who do not hesitate to affirm that before the Elector had consented, Carlstadt had lain hidden in the monastery with Luther, no one being privy to it except Wolfgang, Luther's servant.

units.la: INTEREA Argentinenses Theologi, quamvis moderatissimi, tamen haereseos nomine passim traducebantur, inprimis Norimbergae. VVolffgangus igitur Capito 18. Novembris ad Andream Osiandrum scribit: Audio quibusdam in causa esse, cur adversa de nobis suspicentur, quod imperiosis factionum capitibus non subscribamus. Ecquid, hoc, obsecro, rei? Num decet Christi professores ab humano pendere dicto? Coram Deo tibi atque Domino ne neno nostram profiteor fidem. Credimus Christum Iesum pro nobis crucifixum, per quem Dominus salutem orbi promisit ac praestitit: hoc unum praedicamus omnes & omni tempore. Rebaptizatores non recipimus, qui ad elementum aquae vim Christianismi alligant, contra verum scriptura sensum. Deinde Christum, qui est via & veritas, tenemus in materia Eucharistia. Sunt enim, qui articulum fidei faciunt, dicentes: corpus Christi corporale verè in pane & vino esse. Rursum qui necessarium aiunt, ut nudum credamus panem. Neutrum recipimus, quia utreque puritatem fidei inficit, concordiam Ecclesiarum scindit, laqueos ponit animis simplicium, ianuam novae tyrannidi aperit. Nam sunt scriptura mysteria haud rapienda protinus ad necessitatem credendi. Mihi liberum est, quod tibi, tanquam peritiori articulus esse poterit. Scio, si quid amplius fuerit necessarium, Dominum esse revelaturum. Regulam fidei certam retinebimus mordicus, & perstabimus in libertate ad quam nos Christus redemerit.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Strasbourg theologians, although most moderate, were nevertheless everywhere denounced under the name of heresy, especially at Nuremberg. Wolfgang Capito therefore, on 18 November, wrote to Andreas Osiander: I hear that some are inclined to suspect us unfavourably, because we do not subscribe to the domineering heads of the factions. What, I ask you, is the matter? Does it befit professors of Christ to depend on human saying? Before God and the Lord I profess our faith: we believe in Jesus Christ crucified for us, through whom the Lord promised and granted salvation to the world. This one thing we all preach, and at all times. We do not receive the rebaptizers, who bind the power of Christianity to the element of water, against the true sense of Scripture. Next, we hold Christ, who is the way and the truth, in the matter of the Eucharist. For there are those who make it an article of faith, saying that the body of Christ is truly corporeal in bread and wine. And again there are those who say that it is necessary to believe that the bread is bare. We receive neither, because each defiles the purity of faith, rends the concord of the churches, sets snares for the minds of the simple, and opens the door to a new tyranny. For the mysteries of Scripture are not to be seized at once as a necessity of belief. It is free for me, which may be an article for you as the more skilled. I know that if anything further is necessary, the Lord will reveal it. We shall hold fast to the sure rule of faith with our teeth, and shall persist in the liberty to which Christ has redeemed us.

units.la: HÆC Evangelicorum certamina iucundum animi pabulum erant Pontificiis, qui se Zwinglii & Oecolampadii adversariis iungebant, eos collaudabant, in precio habebant, ac tantum non ignoscebant eis, quicquid etiam iacturae hactenus ab eis fecissent.
units.tr: These contests among the Evangelicals were a pleasant food for the minds of the Papists, who joined themselves to the adversaries of Zwingli and Oecolampadius, praised them, held them in high esteem, and all but forgave them whatever loss they had hitherto inflicted on them.

units.la: In HELVETIA rem Christi plurimùm hoc
units.tr: In Helvetia the cause of Christ was greatly hindered this year by the Anabaptist sect.

units.la: anno remorata est secta Anabaptiftica. Cum enim superioribus annis Thomas Müncerus venisset in Helvetiam, corrupit Balthasarem Hubmaierum Pacimontanum, disertissimum VValshutensium Evangelistam, Felicem Manzium, Cunradum Grebelium, Tigurinos & plures alios. Balthasar circa Pentecosten huius anni edit librum de Anabaptismo, quo multos seduxit. Zwvinglius Nonis Novembrib. ei publico scripto respondet. Manzius & Grebelius inhiabant in Reformatione Ecclesiae Tigurinae Canonicatibus & professionibus linguarum. Voti sui cum per Zwinglium non statim fieri possent compotes, amore in odiū converso, Zvvinglii actiones vituperárunt, multa in illius reformatione, praesertim restitutionem Anabaptismi desiderantes. Senatus glisecenti malo occursurus, die decimâ septimâ Januarii Zwinglium & Manzium cum assectis in Curiam vocat: Manzius rationibus Poedobaptismum oppugnat, quòd pueri non sint baptismi capaces, mysterium non intelligant: fide careant: & quod Apostoli nullos infantes baptizârint. Zwinglius ordine ad singula respondet eo modo quem expressit libro de baptismo Senatui San-gallensi dedicato. Finito colloquio, Senatus edicit, ut omnes quieti sint. Anabaptistae contra, Deo magis quàm hominib. obediendū, clamant. Vicesi-
units.tr: For when in the preceding years Thomas Müntzer had come into Helvetia, he corrupted Balthasar Hubmaier of Friedberg, a most eloquent evangelist of Waldshut, Felix Mantz, Conrad Grebel, citizens of Zurich, and several others. About Pentecost of this year Balthasar published his book on Anabaptism, by which he seduced many. Zwingli answered him in a public writing on 5 November. Mantz and Grebel were eager for canonries and professorships of languages in the reformation of the Church of Zurich. When they could not immediately obtain their wish through Zwingli, their love was turned into hatred, and they found fault with Zwingli's actions, desiring many things in his reformation, especially the restoration of Anabaptism. To meet the growing evil, the Senate, on 17 January, summoned Zwingli and Mantz with their adherents to the Council. Mantz attacked infant baptism with arguments: that infants are not capable of baptism, do not understand the mystery, lack faith, and that the Apostles baptized no infants. Zwingli answered each point in order, in the manner he set out in his book on baptism, dedicated to the Senate of St Gall. When the conference was over, the Senate ordered everyone to be quiet. The Anabaptists, on the other hand, cried out that God must be obeyed rather than men. The twenty-

units.la: Vicesimâ igitur Martii de voluntate Senatus Zwinglius iterum cum illis congreditur. Anabaptistæ cum disputationibus nihil profici viderent, & non deessent, à quibus Evangelii doctrinam prorsus exterminatâ volentibus, iâ furore suo confirmarentur, ad alia conversi, veritatem dogmatis sui se sanguine suo obsignaturos, vociferabantur. Itaq; hinc inde in urbis angulis aliquos rebaptizabât, per compita etiam clamabant: Va Tiguro, va Tiguro! Age pœnitentiam, Tigurum: brevi interibis. Magistratus, ne quid Respublica detrimenti caperet, alios in carceres coniicit, alios proscribit. Novæ hinc audiri querelæ, qui puro puto Dei verbo vel stare vel cadere vellet, illos carcerib. & exilio multari. Rogatu igitur Zwinglii Senatus ad solennem disputationem, mensis Novembris die sextâ habendam, Anabaptistas vocat. Cõparent. Triduû disputatur. Tandem prosilit Anabaptista quidam, & Zwinglium per Deum vivum adiurat, ut sibi veritatem dicat, ( persuaserat enim sibi Zwinglium in conscientia convictum tacitè favere Anabaptismo) Cui Zwinglius: Ego verò faciam. Dico te rusticorû seditiosorû in ditione Tigurina esse Principem. Ad quæ verba Anabaptista obmutuit, cæteri riserût.
units.tr: On the twentieth of March, by the will of the Senate, Zwingli met with them again. The Anabaptists saw that nothing was gained by disputation, and there were not lacking those who, wishing the doctrine of the Gospel utterly exterminated, encouraged them in their fury. So they turned to other means and kept crying that they would seal the truth of their doctrine with their blood. Here and there in the corners of the city they rebaptized some, and in the cross-roads they cried: Woe to Zurich, woe to Zurich! Do penance, Zurich: you will perish soon. The magistrate, lest the commonwealth suffer any harm, threw some into prison and banished others. Hence new complaints were heard: that those who wished to stand or fall by the pure Word of God alone were punished with imprisonment and exile. At Zwingli's request, therefore, the Senate summoned the Anabaptists to a solemn disputation to be held on the sixth day of November. They appeared, and the disputation lasted three days. At last a certain Anabaptist stepped forward and adjured Zwingli by the living God to tell him the truth, for he had persuaded himself that Zwingli, convinced in conscience, secretly favoured Anabaptism. Zwingli replied: "I will indeed. I say that you are the ringleader of the seditious peasants in the Zurich territory." At these words the Anabaptist fell silent, and the others laughed.

units.la: Disputatione finitâ Senatus Felicem Mâzium, Grebelium, & cæteros Anabaptistarum patriarchas in curiam vocat, & iis Anabaptismo graviter interdicit. Qui cùm se minimè obtemperaturos præ se ferrent, in custodiâ quidem ducti, sed statim fuêre dimissi, cum comminatione pœnæ seuerioris. Edictū etiam promulgat Senatus die Andreç Apostolo sacrâ, quâ Acta disputationis paucis repetit, Anabaptistos convictos esse, confirmat: subditis igitur mandat: ut Pœdobaptismum retineant: ab Anabaptismo sibi caveant. Omnia frustra. Sancitū igitur, ut deinceps Reipublicæ pœnas præsenti morte dependerent, qui vel Anabaptismum professuri, vel huius Professores hospitio accepturi, aut quoquo modo essent adiuturi.
units.tr: When the disputation was over, the Senate summoned Felix Manz, Grebel, and the other patriarchs of the Anabaptists to the council chamber and strictly forbade them Anabaptism. When they made it plain that they would by no means obey, they were indeed taken into custody, but were at once released, with a threat of more severe punishment. The Senate also issued an edict on the feast of the Apostle Andrew, in which it briefly recounted the acts of the disputation, affirmed that the Anabaptists had been convicted, and therefore ordered its subjects to retain infant baptism and to beware of Anabaptism. All in vain. It was therefore decreed that from then on those who either professed Anabaptism, or would receive its professors into their homes, or in any way assist them, should pay the penalty of the commonwealth with present death.

units.la: BASILEÆ hoc anno Oecolampadius quoq; cum Anabaptistis cògressus est. Cûq; passim isti de victoria ab Oecolampadio reportatâ gloriarentur, edidit ille Germanicè colloquii cum Anabaptistis habiti Acta.
units.tr: At Basel this year Oecolampadius also met with the Anabaptists. Since they everywhere boasted of the victory won over Oecolampadius, he published in German the Acts of the conference held with the Anabaptists.

units.la: WALSHUTI Balthasar Hubmeier, Pacimontanus, primus illorū Evangelista, Anabaptismum strenuè. hoc anno propagabat calamo & voce: atq; ut in casses suos, quos veller, pertraheret, simulabat, se Ecclesiam istā deserturū, quippe qui ibi sementē in petra faceret. Noverat autem, se efflictim ab auditoribus suis amari. Accurrit igitur magna multitudo, denuò tingitur: cōminuuntur baptisteria. Cives nonnulli à novitate ista abhorrent: dissidiū animorū oritur, quod Austriacis oppidum sine sanguine, & Episcopo ordinario imperium Ecclesiasticum sine vi restituit, religione Pontificia postliminio illuc reducta.
units.tr: At Waldshut, Balthasar Hubmaier of Friedberg, the first of their evangelists, vigorously spread Anabaptism this year by pen and voice. In order to draw into his snares whomever he wished, he pretended that he would desert this church, since he was sowing seed on rock there. He knew, however, that he was passionately loved by his hearers. A great crowd therefore came running, and they were baptized again; the baptisteries were broken up. Some citizens shrank from this novelty, and a division of minds arose. This restored the town to the Austrians without bloodshed, and restored ecclesiastical rule to the ordinary bishop without force, the Papist religion being brought back there by right of return.

units.la: Balthasar ex oppido elapsus, Tiguri apud viduam quandam subiit. Senatus ubi id rescivit, suspicatus hominem idem monstrum alituum, quod reliqui Catabaptistae, eo quod clam in urbe irrepsisset, stringi hominem iubet, ac in pratorio libera custodia servari. Post tertium vero, quartum, aut nescio certo, quem diem, iubet subito Engelhardum, Leonem, Myconium, Sebastianum, Megandrum, alios, eorum me adesse: ubi venimus, exponunt, qui a Senatu adhoc constituti fuerant: quomodo Balthasar dum ad se literas dederit, quibus pollicetur, se Zwinglium suis scripturis superaturum de Baptismo. Quid multa? Congrediuntur. Ibi obiicit caecus homo, quod ante annos aliquot de Catechumenis docendis tradideramus in 67. Conclusionum: non enim intellexerat, nos isti in hoc esse, quod pueri etiamnum aeque atque olim fidei rudimenta docceantur: quod ipse ad Baptismum retulit, parum prudenter: quasi dixerim meum esse consilium, ut mos non tingendi infantes postliminio reducatur, cum ego de more imbuendi pueros fidei rudimenta lacutus sim. Ubi se hac parte videret erravisse, blandulus fuit.
units.tr: Balthasar, slipping out of the town, came to Zurich, to a certain widow's house. When the Senate learned of this, suspecting the man to be the same sort of monster as the other Catabaptists, because he had crept secretly into the city, it ordered him to be seized and kept in free custody in the praetorium. Then, after the third, fourth, or I know not what day, it suddenly ordered Engelhard, Leo, Myconius, Sebastian, Megander, and others, of whom I was one, to be present. When we arrived, those appointed by the Senate for this purpose set out how Balthasar, having sent them letters in which he promised that he would overcome Zwingli with his Scriptures on Baptism. To be brief, they met. There the blind man objected what we had taught some years before about instructing catechumens, in the 67th of our Conclusions. He had not understood that we were aiming at this: that children are still taught the rudiments of the faith, just as formerly. He referred this, rather imprudently, to baptism, as if I had said it was my intention to restore the custom of not baptizing infants, whereas I had spoken of the custom of teaching children the rudiments of the faith. When he saw that he had erred on this point, he became smooth-tongued.

units.la: Processimus post multam conflictationem, in qua Testamentum istud perpetuum agnoscere noluit. Ventum est ad caput secundum Actorum, ex quo probavi, Christianorum liberos inter principia censos esse ad Ecclesiam: cumq; multa respônsaret, ad claram atq; disertam responsionem eliciebam, ut diceret: anne concederet pueros istos in Ecclesiam fuisse, nec ne: at ne quicquam, omnia tentabam. Ibi ingenuè fateor, cùm & ipsum locum 1. Corinth. 10.
