Patres nostri omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt &c. admoverem, ad compellendum eum, ut agnosceret pueros contineri, etiamsi eorum nulla prorsus mentio fiat: illeq; nollet dicere, vel non, vel etiam, me vehementius invexisse in hominem: sed non aliâ re, quàm quod Catabaptismo suo miseros cives suos traxerit in dissidium, quod iam ipsos perdiderit. Hoc ad magnum temporis modum ubi duravit, sic homo redargutus ac superatus, artem novam orditur: postulat, ut Leo, Myconius, & Sebastianus sibi dentur, ut cum illis solis conferat: sperabat arrogans homo, istos ad se blandiloquentiâ suâ pertracturum. At ubi neq; sic videt procedere consilium, eosdem iterum impetrat, ac post multas versutias huc descendit, ut dicat, se recantaturum. Id autem Senatus non cogebat, nisi non voluisset ab urbe abire: nihil enim gravius statuebat in eos, qui Catabaptismi causam deserere noluissent, quàm quod relegaret. Veniunt interim legati Imperatorii, postulantes hominem ad supplicium: qui eis breviter negatus est, per legem, quâ cavetur, ut qui ob aliquam noxam civis in nervum coniiciatur, ob eam solam reus fiat. Sic peccavit in hominem istum Senatus, defendit ab impetitione Caesaris, tanquam civem. At hic succurrit, eum fuisse in nervo, antequam in liberam custodiam sit positus: utcunque res habeat, liber tum erat, cum congrederemur, diúque postmodum in Pretorio liber adservatus fuit. Scribitur ergo revocationis forma, non ex praescripto Senatûs, aut quorumcunque, sed suâ ipsius manu. Cumq; ipsam in templo, cui Abbatia nomen est, praelegisset, finito sermone, quem nos ad populum habueramus, protinus abnegat revocationem coram totâ concione: occasionémque dicendi nactum esse putans, multa adducit contra Baptismum infantium, & Catabaptismum munit.
units.tr: We proceeded after much wrangling, in which he refused to acknowledge that this Testament is perpetual. We came to the second chapter of Acts, from which I proved that Christian children were counted among the beginnings reckoned to the Church. When he replied with much talk, I pressed him for a clear and plain answer: whether he would concede that those children were in the Church or not. But he tried everything and achieved nothing. There I frankly confess that, when I also brought forward the passage 1 Cor. 10, "Our fathers were all baptized unto Moses," and so on, to compel him to acknowledge that children are included, though no mention of them is made at all, he would neither say no nor yes. I attacked the man more vehemently, but for no other reason than that by his Catabaptism he had drawn his wretched citizens into dissension, which had now ruined them. When this had gone on for a long time, the man, thus refuted and overcome, devised a new trick. He demanded that Leo, Myconius, and Sebastian be given to him, so that he might confer with them alone; the arrogant man hoped to win them over by his smooth talk. But when he saw that this plan did not succeed either, he obtained the same request again, and after many tricks came down here, saying that he would recant. The Senate did not compel him to this, except that he did not want to leave the city: for it decided nothing more severe against those who refused to abandon the cause of Catabaptism than banishment. Meanwhile imperial envoys came, demanding that the man be handed over for punishment. He was briefly refused them, under the law which provides that a citizen who becomes liable to the stocks for some offence is answerable only for that offence. Thus the Senate defended that man against Caesar's claim, as a citizen. But here someone objects that he had been in the stocks before he was placed in free custody. However the matter stands, he was free at the time when we met, and was afterwards kept free for a long time in the praetorium. A form of recantation was therefore written, not according to the prescript of the Senate or of anyone else, but in his own hand. When he had read it aloud in the church called the Abbey, after the sermon we had delivered to the people, he at once renounced the recantation before the whole assembly. Thinking he had found an occasion to speak, he brought forward many arguments against infant baptism and fortified Catabaptism.

units.la: Hîc fama constans fuit (sed ego divinationem arbitror) clam cum hoc doctum esse, quo motus aliquis fieret: spem enim habebant, me protinus, absoluto sermone, abiturum. Coniiicitur denuo in nervum, tenetur istic mensem, aut longiùs.
units.tr: Here there was a constant rumour (but I take it as a guess) that he had secretly been instructed to provoke some disturbance, for they hoped that I would leave at once when the sermon was over. He was thrown back into the stocks and held there for a month or longer.

units.la: Ibi tandem sic ait: Dicit se prorsus ignorare, quod revocationem vitiaverit: ac si aliter sit locutus quàm promiserit, se aliquid à Dæmone passum esse. Concinnat novam revocationem.
units.tr: There at last he said this: that he entirely does not know how he spoiled the recantation, and that if he spoke otherwise than he had promised, he had suffered something at the hands of a demon. He composes a new recantation.

units.la: Nos ad amicos ubique adcurrere, orare, ut misericordia hominini impertiatur, deturque Senatus: datus est. Offerentíque sese ad palinodiam decretum per misericordiam, ut disertam revocationem faciat: quâ factâ, ocyus è finibus facessat. Hic ego, ego inquam, Engelhardum, Leonem, Megandrum, coëpiscopos adeo, ac oro, ut pro homine precibus apud Senatum velint nobiscum intercedere, Nam si protinus post revocationem eiiciatur, periculum imminere homini tam ab Helvetiis nostris, quàm à Casare. Audivit Senatus precs nostras, ac post revocationem quàm ex animo facere simulabat, cum nihil minus esset, spatium latendi immerenti dedit, donec occasione inventâ tutus abire posset. Quâ datâ, per Senatorem quendam, virum in Evangelio Christi fidelissimum, allegatus est clam, ut eius abitionem ne civies quidem senserint. Vide, mi Petre, quo candore simus hominem persequuti, quàq; perfidiâ nobis responderit. Nam ut primùm Constantiam venit apud ministros verbi: sic nos calùniatus est, victoriâq; suum de Catabaptismo iactavit, ut nesciam, an nullos in odium nostri traxerit. Tam incauti sunt quidam ad hypocrisis deprehensianem. Nos omnia dissimulavimus. Abiens bonos istos viros sic movit, ut 10. aureis eum donaverint: quum ipse plus auri secum aut cum uxorcula habeat, quàm omnes isti argenti. Sic abutuntur nostrâ simplicitate, qui pietatis simulatione quaestum faciunt. Nos dexteritatem spectamus in homine, ac mediocritatis studium: In eo autem homine (falli cupio) nihil quàm immoderatam rei gloriaque sitim deprehendisse visus sum ipse mihi. Caeterum Balthasar ille dimissus in Moraviam venit, Anabaptistis se associavit, ubi cum novos motus suscitasset, captus & cum uxore Viennam ductus, ipse quidem igne exustus, uxor verò eius aquis submersa periit.
units.tr: We ran everywhere to friends, begging that mercy be shown to the man and that the Senate be petitioned, and it was granted. When he offered himself to a palinode, a decree was passed out of mercy that he should make a clear recantation, and once this was done, he should quickly leave the territory. Here I, I say, urge and beg Engelhard, Leo, Megander, and my fellow bishops, that they will join us in interceding with the Senate on the man's behalf with prayers. For if he were thrown out immediately after the recantation, danger would threaten him both from our Helvetians and from Caesar. The Senate heard our prayers, and after the recantation, which he pretended to make in good faith when he was anything but sincere, gave the undeserving man a space in which to hide, until he could find an opportunity to leave safely. When this was granted, through a certain senator, a man most faithful in the Gospel of Christ, he was secretly sent away, so that not even the citizens noticed his departure. See, my Peter, with what candour we have pursued this man, and with what treachery he has answered us. For as soon as he came to Constance, to the ministers of the Word, he slandered us in the same way and boasted of his victory over Catabaptism, so that I do not know whether he has not stirred up hatred against us in many. Some are too incautious to detect hypocrisy. We have dissembled everything. On leaving, he so moved those good men that they gave him ten gold coins, though he himself carries more gold, with his little wife, than all those men have silver. Thus they abuse our simplicity, those who make a profit from a pretence of piety. We admire the man's dexterity and his zeal for moderation. Yet in this man (I wish I were wrong) I seemed to myself to detect nothing but an immoderate thirst for wealth and glory. Moreover, that Balthasar, once dismissed, came to Moravia, associated himself with the Anabaptists, and, having stirred up new disturbances there, was captured and taken to Vienna with his wife. He himself was burned with fire, and his wife was drowned in water and perished.

units.la: SANGALLENSIS Ecclesia per Anaba- ptistas
units.tr: The Church of St. Gall under the Anabaptists

units.la: ptiftas variè fuit exercita. Anno 1524, venit eò Laurentius quidam, discipulus. Cunradi Grebelii, & Joannis Kesleri auditorium ingressus, prælegentem VI. caput D. Pauli ad Romanos, publicè interpellavit, errorisque arguit de Pœdobaptismo, hoc argumento: quod perinde esset, infantem, ac felem baptizare, cum insciitia rerum divinarum in utroque sit eadem. Cui responsum à Keslero: magnum esse discrimen inter bruta animantia & infantes. Hos enim ad vitam æternam creatos, bruta animantia non item. Horum esse fœdus gratiæ, illorum non item. Laurentius alterum Lectorem San gallensium VVolfgangum Ulmian privatim aggressus, veneno suo infecit. Hic Ulmian hoc anno 1525. Scaphusii incidit in Cunradum Grebelium ipsum, à quo in Anabaptismo ita confirmatus fuit: ut non nisi in Rheno nudus submergi, atq; ita more Apostolico baptizari vellet. Domum reversus iactat revelationes divinas in itinere sibi factas; rogatus à civibus, ut in templo illas exponeret, renuit, forum, aut quecunq; alium locū delegit: in templo (nondum remota erant omnia idola) veritatem nec dictā, nec dici posse, ait. Obiectū, ab uno, magnis precib. à Senatu locum illum obtentū: levitatis fore, eū deserere. Ab alio, Apostolos, non coegisse homines in certo loco covenire, sed gavisos fuisse, si audiri possent, sive in synagoga, sive in templo, coram Diabolo & inferno: eosdem per verbum praedicatum Diabolos & idola eiecisse, non per Diabolos & idola eiectos fuisse. Haec omnia nihil ille moratus, cum suis in civium aedibus, in pratis, in montibus conventicula celebrat, reliquos pro Ethnicis habet. Quae prima fuit Evangelicorum in oppido Sangallensi scissio.
units.tr: The church at St. Gall was variously troubled by the Anabaptists. In 1524 a certain Laurentius, a disciple of Conrad Grebel and Johannes Kessler, came there. He entered the lecture room, and while the lecturer was expounding chapter 6 of St. Paul's Letter to the Romans, he publicly interrupted him and attacked the error of infant baptism with this argument: that baptizing an infant was no different from baptizing a cat, since both are equally ignorant of divine things. Kessler replied that there is a great difference between brute animals and infants: the infants were created for eternal life, the brute animals were not. The covenant of grace belongs to the former, not to the latter. Laurentius then approached privately the other reader at St. Gall, Wolfgang Ulmian, and infected him with his poison. In 1525 Ulmian met Conrad Grebel himself at Schaffhausen, and was so confirmed by him in Anabaptism that he wished to be submerged naked in the Rhine and so be baptized in the apostolic manner. Returning home, he boasted of divine revelations made to him on his journey. Asked by the citizens to expound them in the church, he refused and chose the marketplace or some other place instead; in the church (for the idols had not yet all been removed), he said, the truth could neither be spoken nor be told. Some objected that the Senate had obtained that church with great prayers, so it would be levity to abandon it. Others objected that the apostles did not compel people to meet in a fixed place, but rejoiced if they could be heard, whether in a synagogue or a temple, even before the Devil and hell; and that the apostles drove out devils and idols by the preaching of the word, and were not themselves driven out by devils and idols. Ignoring all this, he held his conventicles with his followers in citizens' houses, in meadows and on the mountains, and regarded everyone else as heathens. This was the first division among the Evangelicals in the town of St. Gall.

units.la: Ulmian, propter seditiosas conciones captus, oppido eicitur: anno autem 1527 cum quinque aliis Walsex cum quinq; aliis in constanti fidei Anabaptisticę professione à Pontificiis est occisus.
units.tr: Ulmian was arrested for his seditious sermons and expelled from the town; then in 1527, at Walsee, he was put to death by the Papists together with five others, for steadfastly professing Anabaptist doctrine.

units.la: Venit mox in oppidum San-gallense Grebelius ipse, concionatur ibi Dominicâ Palmarum: venit ea & Hippolytus quidam rusticus facundus, multa propter Evangelium passus: is per festos paschatos dies de insigni Anabaptismi fructu disserit: multos lectae adjungit: exacto octiduo domum reversus à Suitensibus captus, & vivus, gestibus moriendi alacritatem testantibus, est crematus.
units.tr: Soon Grebel himself came to the town of St. Gall and preached there on Palm Sunday. There also came a certain eloquent rustic, Hippolytus, who had suffered much for the Gospel. During the Easter festival he discoursed on the notable fruit of Anabaptism and added many to his followers. After eight days he returned home, was seized by the men of Schwyz, and was burned alive, showing by his gestures his eagerness to die.

units.la: Videbantur sibi Anabaptistae parvâ Hierosolymam invenisse in oppido San-gallensi. Apostolos igitur imitaturi in omnem terram egressos, quotidie manè & ipsi in vicina loca egrediebātur, pastores Evāgelicos auditorib, suspectos reddebant, loco movebant: &, ne propter imperitiam literarum autoritas sua vilescerent, exordiebantur conciones suas à dicto Christi: Gratias ago tibi, pater, Domine cæli & terræ, quòd hæc occultaveris sapientibus & intelligentibus, & ea detexeris infantibus. Deinde protestabantur, nihil se loquuturos, nisi quod divinitus sibi esset revelatum. Tum vitæ integritatem præ se ferebant; frugales in victu: viles in vestitu: in sermone parci: in disputatione autem supra modum erant vehementes: parati mori potius quàm cedere. Justitiâ operum urgebant majore zelo quàm Papistæ: qua re conscientiæ Evangelicorum plurimùm perturbabantur: ut qui non ita pridem didicerant, in fidei justitia vitam quærendam.
units.tr: The Anabaptists seemed to themselves to have found a little Jerusalem in the town of St. Gall. Intending to imitate the apostles, who went out into all the earth, they went out every morning into the neighbouring places, made the Evangelical ministers suspect to their hearers and removed them from their posts. And so that their authority should not be cheapened by their lack of learning, they began their sermons with the saying of Christ: "I thank thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hidden these things from the wise and the understanding, and hast revealed them to babes." Then they declared that they would say nothing except what had been revealed to them by God. They displayed integrity of life: frugal in food, plain in dress, sparing in speech, but in disputation excessively vehement, ready to die rather than yield. They pressed the justice of works with greater zeal than the Papists did, and so the consciences of the Evangelicals were greatly disturbed, since they had not long before been taught to seek life in the justice of faith.

units.la: Laboranti Ecclesiæ Sangallensi succurrit Zwinglius libello de Baptismo edito. Opposuit se quoq; Anabaptistis Joachimus Vadianus, Reipublicæ Medicus. At illi à defensione theseos de Anabaptismo progressi subinde longius in alios atq; alios errores in fide & vita delapsi sunt.
units.tr: Zwingli came to the aid of the troubled church of St. Gall with a booklet on baptism. Joachim Vadian, the town physician, also opposed the Anabaptists. But they, moving from the defence of their thesis on Anabaptism, gradually slid further and further into other errors in faith and life.

units.la: Venit ad Sangallenses Joannes Denckius Bavarus, Norimbergensis dictus, quod aliquando ludum literarium Norimbergæ gubernasset. Is in ea erat haeresi: neminem hominum, neminem etiam Diabolorum in æternum perditum iri: siquidem Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri: & Christus dicat: unum pastorem & unum ovile futurum. Vir fuit doctus, demissi animi, Hebraicæ linguæ peritus: qui Prophetas cum Ludovico Hetzero in Germanicam linguam transtulit. Resipuit tandem, conversus ab Oecolampadio, quo præsente peste quidem, sed pie obijt Basileæ 1528. Rediit etiam eò Antonius Kurfner, qui docebat, Christiani veri nomen tueri neminem posse, nisi qui publicè peccata sua confiteretur, abusus dicto Apostoli Jacobi: Alii alios peccata sua confiteantur. Coeperunt igitur plurimi enormia sua delicta profiteri, alius furta, alius adulteria, alia alius, non sine admiratione audientium, non sine stomacho conjugum, maritis talibus nihil non imprecantium.
units.tr: Johannes Denck, a Bavarian called "of Nuremberg" because he had once run a school there, came to the people of St. Gall. He held this heresy: that no human being, not even any devil, would be lost for ever, since "God wills all men to be saved," and Christ says there will be "one shepherd and one fold." He was a learned man of humble spirit, skilled in Hebrew, who with Ludwig Hetzer translated the Prophets into German. He finally recovered his senses, converted by Oecolampadius, and died piously at Basel in 1528, though during a plague. Anton Kurfner also returned there; he taught that no one could maintain the name of a true Christian unless he publicly confessed his sins, abusing the saying of the apostle James: "Confess your sins to one another." Accordingly many began to confess their outrageous offences, one theft, another adultery, and another something else, to the astonishment of the hearers and the indignation of their wives, who called down every curse on such husbands.

units.la: Hunc proximè excepit Anabaptista alius, Aurifaber dictus, qui fretus enunciato Servatoris, sed Nicodemicè accepto: Nisi fiatis ut parvuli, nequaquam ingredieminì regnum cœlorum, monebat homines passim in pagis, præsertim in ditione Abbatis-Cellæ: ut pueris se moribus, gestibus, sermone conformarent. Vidisses ridiculas puerorum & puellarum imitationes: fœminas præsertim, exilientes manibus plaudentes, nudas in terra sedentes, lusitantes.
units.tr: Next after him came another Anabaptist, called Aurifaber, who, relying on the saying of the Saviour, though taken in a Nicodemite sense, "Unless you become as little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven," urged people everywhere in the villages, especially in the territory of the Abbot of Cella, to conform themselves to children in manner, gesture and speech. You would have seen ridiculous imitations of boys and girls: women above all, leaping, clapping their hands, sitting naked on the ground, and playing.

units.la: In ipso oppido ad S. Gallum Magdalena Mollerina, virgo erat castis moribus. Illa rebaptizata venditabat se modò pro Christo ipso, secundum illud: Eritis sicut Dij: modò pro meretrice illa magna, Antichristum paritura, tura, de quo Apoc. xii. scriptum esset. Sedit nuda in conspectu suorum, & surgens. Qui ingrediYvult in regnum Dei, me, ait, sequatur. Anabaptistæ illam sequuntur: foris non inveniūt: paulò post comparet madida ad umbricum usq;: in lecto collocata post bihorium horrenda eloqui incipit: proculdubio Spiritu Pythonis à Marone sexto Æneidos celebrato agitata.
units.tr: In the town of St. Gall itself there was Magdalena Müllerin, a virgin of chaste life. Rebaptized, she began to pass herself off now as Christ himself, following the words "You shall be as gods," and now as that great harlot who was to give birth to Antichrist, of whom it is written in Revelation 12. She sat naked in the sight of her followers, and rising said: "Whoever wishes to enter the kingdom of God, let him follow me." The Anabaptists followed her, but outside they found nothing. Shortly afterwards she appeared, soaked right up to the navel, and placed on a bed, after two hours began to utter dreadful things, plainly driven by the spirit of Python, which Virgil celebrated in the sixth book of the Aeneid.

units.la: Non multò post Anabaptistæ omnem vitę prioris rationem immutârunt. Quos antea quælibet vestis paulo cultior, quælibet cœna lautior, quilibet sermo hilarior tantopere offenderat: ij nunc utuntur vestibus Phrygiis, acu pictis, scutulatis, holosericis & bombycinis; in vino quærunt commessationes & scorta: &, quod plane Diabolicum, turpissimis factis nomen, voluntatem, iussa Dei prætendunt. Erat qui honestissimi civis filiæ pudicitiam eripuerat: voluntatem Dei prætexebat. Thomas quidam fratrem Leonhartum in præsentia parentum decollabat: Abrahæ, Isaacum immolaturi exemplo se defendebat. Ad hæc atrocia facinora, cum connivere Magistratus amplius non posset, edictis & pœnis hominum istorum petulantiam compressit.
units.tr: Not long after, the Anabaptists changed their whole way of life. Those who had previously been offended so greatly by any somewhat finer garment, any more lavish meal or any more cheerful conversation, now wear Phrygian clothes, embroidered, chequered, of silk and of cotton; they seek drunken revelry and whores in wine; and, what is plainly diabolical, they put forward the name, will and commands of God as a cover for the most shameful deeds. One man had ravished the chastity of an honest citizen's daughter, and he pretended the will of God. One Thomas beheaded his brother Leonhard in the presence of their parents, and defended himself by the example of Abraham, who was about to sacrifice Isaac. When the magistrates could no longer tolerate these atrocious crimes, they checked the wantonness of these men by edicts and punishments.

units.la: Atq; hæc de Anabaptistis Helveticis.
units.tr: So much for the Swiss Anabaptists.

units.la: In reliqua Germania cum nullibi tuti essent, Moravia venali illos hospitio excepit. ccpit. Illuc catervatim confluxit quicquid è plebe & infima multitudine fraudibus, dolis, & impostouris suis irretitum tenebant Anabaptistae. E Bavaria eò profecti Jacobus Hutterus, & Gabriel Scherdingus, primi Ecclesiae Anabaptisticae in Moravia conditores celebrabantur. Hi consiliorum suorum ministros habebant, quibus in provincias vicinas, Silesiam, Poloniam, Austriam, Boëmiam, missis, colligebant maximam hominum multitudinem, qui bonis suis divenditis, & in manus Gabrielis, Hutteriq; traditis, durissimā in Moravia servitutem servierūt. De Huttero quid factum, ignoro. Gabriel Moraviā eiectus, in Poloniae finibus obiit: quatuor è primariis doctoribus emissariis, Glogoviae capite multati sunt: Hutterianorum reliquiae hodiéque in Moravia durant, sed quae Gabrielistas damnant.
units.tr: Since they were safe nowhere else in Germany, Moravia took them in as a hospitable refuge for a price. There flocked in crowds whatever from the common people and the lowest rabble the Anabaptists had caught and held entangled by their frauds, tricks and deceptions. Jacob Hutter and Gabriel Scherding, who had come there from Bavaria, were celebrated as the first founders of the Anabaptist church in Moravia. They had agents of their plans, whom they sent into the neighbouring provinces, Silesia, Poland, Austria and Bohemia, and gathered a very great multitude of people, who, having sold their goods and handed the proceeds into the hands of Gabriel and Hutter, served a most harsh servitude in Moravia. What became of Hutter I do not know. Gabriel, driven out of Moravia, died on the borders of Poland. Four of the leading teachers sent out as emissaries were beheaded at Glogau. Remnants of the Hutterites still survive today in Moravia, but they condemn the followers of Gabriel.

units.la: SILESIACAS Ecclesias ex alto superstitionum Papisticarum somnio vix expergefactas illico turbabat Caspar Schwenckfeldius, nobilissimo genere in Ducatu Silesiae Lignicensi natus, ad restinguendas incendii Sacramentarii flammas non aquā sed oleo allato. Negabat ille, corpus & sanguinem in pane & vino esse: sed verba institutionis ita interpretabatur: Corpus meum est hoc, id est, cibus animae, panis coelestis, qui est ipsemet Christus: cum tamen Christus, ut panis coelestis, non sit κοινωνία Christi, quod dicitur manifestè de pane fracto: & non benedicamus Christo, quod manifestè dicitur de calice. Negabat idem: naturam Christi humanam esse creaturam; tum quod originem à Deo traheret, tum quod deificata esset caro Christi: qui contra sentiunt, Creaturistae illi vocabantur. Scripturam, sive verbum Dei, ajebat literam mortuam esse, in qua neque vita est, neque salus. Qui secus docebant, eos Vocalistas & Literalistas nominabat. De justificatione idem sentiebat, quod postea Andreas Osiander: horum enim sententiae sunt eaedem, modi tantùm loquendi diversi. Fides ipsis est ipse Deus inhabitans. Praeterea multus erat in commendatione novae vitae, in detestatione malae: ardentes ad Deum preces creberrimè fundebat, vitâ agebat sobriam & castam, adeo ut magni nominis Chronologus Abraham Buchholcerus saepe dixerit: Schwenckfeldio non defuisse cor bonum, sed caput regulatum. Dementabat multos magnificis istis verbis, quae semper illi in ore: erleuchtung / offenbarung / vergöttung / innerlicher geistlicher mensch. Hoc est: illuminationis, revelationis, deificationis hominis interioris & spiritualis. Sic fascinavit Valentinum Crautwaldium & Joannem Sigismundum Wernerum, Pastores & Professores Lignicenses. A Friderico Duce Silesiae in exilium abire jussus anno 1527. oberravit passim in superiori Germania, Argentinæ (ubi Capitoni imposuit,qui libellum eius quendam præfatione ornavit) Ulmæ, (ubi cum Martino Frechto coram Senatu de doctrina sua confliatus est,) Augustæ (ubi clam conventus egit & concionatus est,)Norimbergæ,& hinc inde in Nobilium, Baronum, Comitum aulis.Scripsit multos Tractatus, plurimas epistolas Germanico idiomate : Refutatus à Theologis in Helvetia, Suevia, Hassia, Saxonia, Silesia,à Luthero autem anno 1545. plane rejectus. Summam omnium dogmatum Schwenckfeldii, eorundemque consutationem Lector reperiet in Joannis VVigandi Schwenckfeldianismo, cuius vitulâ Schlüsselburgius in Catalogo suo Hæreticorum aravit.Obiit Caspar in Suevia anno millesimo quingentesimo sexagesimo primo, ætatis septuagesimo primo, errorum suorum fautoribus hinc inde in claris familiis Nobilium & Patriciorum relictis.De discipulis eius in Silesia hoc invenio in chartis meis Abrahami Bucholceri,qui sæpe cum illis congressus est,judicium Schwenckfeldiani ter sunt miseri: nec se nec alios intelligunt. Non se: quia non intelligunt se dicere pugnantia, & quod non sit firma consequentia in eorum ratiocinationibus. Non alios,idq; non tam naturali sua tarditate ingeniorum, quàm eò, quòd tenentur irretiti suis quibusdâ Enthusiasticis laqueis,unde se extricari summam putat impietatem. Boe-
units.tr: The Silesian churches, scarcely roused from the deep dream of Papist superstitions, were immediately thrown into confusion by Caspar Schwenckfeld, born of a most noble family in the Duchy of Liegnitz in Silesia, who brought oil rather than water to quench the flames of the sacramentarian fire. He denied that the body and blood are in the bread and wine, but interpreted the words of institution thus: "This is my body", that is, the food of the soul, the heavenly bread, which is Christ himself; although Christ, as the heavenly bread, is not the "communion of Christ", which is plainly said of the broken bread, and we do not "bless Christ", which is plainly said of the cup. He also denied that "the human nature of Christ is a creature", both because it derives its origin from God and because the flesh of Christ was deified; those who thought otherwise were called "Creaturists". "Scripture, or the word of God," he said, "is a dead letter, in which there is neither life nor salvation." Those who taught otherwise he called "Vocalists" and "Literalists". On justification he held the same view that Andreas Osiander later held, for their opinions are the same, only the manner of speaking differs. For them faith is God himself dwelling within. Besides, he was lavish in commending the new life and in condemning the old, pouring out most frequently ardent prayers to God, and living a sober and chaste life; so much so that the famous chronologer Abraham Buchholzer often said: "Schwenckfeld did not lack a good heart, but a well-ordered head." He bewitched many with those grand words which were always on his lips: "illumination / revelation / deification / the inner spiritual man". That is: "of the illumination, revelation and deification of the inner and spiritual man." In this way he bewitched Valentin Krautwald and Johannes Sigismund Werner, ministers and professors at Liegnitz. Ordered into exile by Duke Frederick of Silesia in 1527, he wandered about in upper Germany: at Strasbourg, where he imposed upon Capito, who adorned one of his booklets with a preface; at Ulm, where he contended with Martin Frecht before the Senate about his teaching; at Augsburg, where he secretly held meetings and preached; at Nuremberg; and here and there in the courts of nobles, barons and counts. He wrote many treatises and very many letters in German. He was refuted by theologians in Switzerland, Swabia, Hesse, Saxony and Silesia, and was utterly rejected by Luther in 1545. The reader will find a summary of all Schwenckfeld's doctrines and their refutation in Johannes Wigand's "Schwenckfeldianism", with whose calf Schlüsselburg ploughed in his Catalogue of Heretics. Caspar died in Swabia in 1561, in his seventy-first year, leaving behind patrons of his errors here and there in illustrious families of nobles and patricians. Concerning his disciples in Silesia I find this judgement in the papers of Abraham Buchholzer, who often conversed with them: "The Schwenckfeldians are thrice wretched: they understand neither themselves nor others. Not themselves, because they do not perceive that they say contradictory things, and that their reasoning lacks a sound consequence. Not others, and this not so much from the natural dullness of their minds as because they are held entangled in certain Enthusiastic snares, from which they think it the greatest impiety to extricate themselves."

units.la: BOEMICI Regni gubernator Carolus Dux Mönsterbergensis Lutheri doctrinae faverat hactenus. At in conventu Pragae acto circa finem Januarii huius anni, Romanam fidem profitetur, Lutherum damnat. Idem fecerat paulo ante Gallus Caherus Administrator, ex summo Lutheri amico summus eius hostis factus. Horum usi auctoritate Pontificii, vicesimâ quintâ Januarii hos articulos condunt:
units.tr: The governor of the Bohemian kingdom, Duke Charles of Münsterberg, had hitherto favoured Luther's teaching. But at the diet held at Prague around the end of January of this year, he professed the Roman faith and condemned Luther. Shortly before, Gallus Caher, the administrator, who had been a close friend of Luther, had become his bitterest enemy and had done the same. Using their authority, the Papists drew up these articles on 25 January:

units.la: 1. Compactata (sic vocârunt capita quaedam, secundum quae inter Calixtinos & Pôtificios res componeretur, quę Synodus Basiliensis approbavit & confirmavit) ab omnibus approbata & recepta, à nemine violentur, aut alio sensu depraventur, sine contentione observentur.
units.tr: 1. The Compactata (the name they gave to certain heads of agreement, according to which affairs between the Calixtines and the Papists would be settled, which the Council of Basel approved and confirmed) are approved and received by all, and let no one violate them or distort them in another sense; let them be observed without dispute.

units.la: 2. Si quidem Compactata ob unitatem, pacem ac fraternum amorem colendum recepta approbataque sunt, velut & pactum pristinum tabularum regni confirmatum habet & nos repudiatâ omni haeresi observantes ritus & ceremonias antiquitus receptas in celebratione S. Missae pro filiis S. Ecclesiae sine amulatione, ob concordiam declarati sumus, nullus haereticorum factiones promoveat.
units.tr: 2. Since the Compactata were received and approved for the sake of cultivating unity, peace and brotherly love, and since the former pact confirmed in the tablets of the kingdom also holds, we, rejecting every heresy, have been declared, for the sake of concord, to observe the rites and ceremonies received from antiquity in the celebration of the holy Mass, as sons of the holy Church, without rivalry. Let no faction of heretics promote anything.

units.la: 3. Statuimus, ne posthac quis quenquam haeretico aut schismatico nomine, aut quâvis ignominiâ & injuriâ ladat, aut quoquo modo offinoffendat: imò apud Regem instabimus, ut is autoritate suâ summo Pontifici nos commendet, quatenus possimus inter alias nationes pro veris Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Matris filiis recipi & publicari.
units.tr: 3. We decree that henceforth no one shall harm anyone with the name of heretic or schismatic, or with any ignominy or injury, or offend him in any way. Rather, we shall press the King to commend us by his authority to the supreme Pontiff, so that we may be received and proclaimed among the other nations as true sons of the Catholic Church, our Mother.

units.la: 4. Quod Parochias & Ecclesias attinet, hac secundum priorem contractum, ut tabulæ Regni habent, maneant.
units.tr: 4. As for parishes and churches, let them remain as they are according to the earlier contract, as the tablets of the kingdom have it.

units.la: 5. In hoc quoque convenimus, ut verbum Dei à solis sacerdotibus & Diaconis, ritè ab Episcopis ordinatis, prædicetur, cum permissione sui Prælati: hoc tamen & laicis non prohibetur, ut in ædibus privatis Biblia legant familiæ, sine omni additione seu expositione.
units.tr: 5. In this also we agree: the Word of God is to be preached only by priests and deacons duly ordained by bishops, with the permission of their prelate. Yet this is not forbidden to laymen, so that families may read the Bibles in their private houses without any addition or exposition.

units.la: 6. Quantum ad ordinationem Diaconorum & sacerdotum, quorum penuriam sentimus, Regem rogabimus, ut apud sedem Apostolicam nobis obtinere dignetur: ut studiosi ab Archiepiscopo & Episcopis, tam sub una quam sub utraque specie, sine dilatione ordinentur.
units.tr: 6. As for the ordination of deacons and priests, of whom we feel the lack, we shall ask the King to deign to obtain for us from the Apostolic See that students be ordained without delay by the Archbishop and the bishops, under one kind as well as under both kinds.

units.la: 7. Volunt, ut Apostolica sedes & Rex hæc omnia ratificent & confirment, ne quis posthac quicquam labefactare præsumat. Pikhardorum dogmata & conventicula omnino abjiciunt, damnant, & execrantur.
units.tr: 7. They wish that the Apostolic See and the King ratify and confirm all these things, so that no one henceforth presumes to weaken any of them. The doctrines and conventicles of the Picards they utterly reject, condemn and execrate.

units.la: a Prætendebatur autem decreti severitati, quod fratrum religio sola obstaret reconciliationi Boëmorum cum Romana Ecclesia, & paciac tranquillitati, quæ exinde Regno contingeret,cum Papa, quò minus pacta Basiliensia confirmarentur, hoc unum obiiceret:esse plures diversasque sectas in Boëmia. Hæc quasi procella adversæ fortunæ Fratres afflixit non multò diutius anno uno. Nam post calamitosam & deplorandam morrem Ludovici Regis, qui anno sequente commissso prælio infelice cum Solimanno Turcarum Imperatore & cum copiosissimo atq; instructissimo exercitu, omnibus rebus impar congressus,fusis profligatisq; suis,in fuga interiit: Post huius igitur obitum rebus omnibus in Boëmia mirificè conturbatis,cum aliæ curæ hanc de exagitandis. Fratribus reprimerent: neq; cogitationes de Regno solicitos iam Proceres de religione esse sinerent, rursum ante occlusa templa Fratrum conventibus erepta, aperire & occupare licuit, quibus liberè usi sunt, nemine quidem penitus prohibente,sed multis tamen difficultatibus & adversis sese offerentibus usq; ad annum fere Christi M. D. XLVIII.
units.tr: The severity of the decree was justified on the ground that the religion of the Brethren alone stood in the way of the reconciliation of the Bohemians with the Roman Church, and of the peace and tranquillity that would thereby come to the kingdom, since the Pope, to prevent the Basel pacts from being confirmed, would object to this one thing: that there were several different sects in Bohemia. This storm of adverse fortune troubled the Brethren for not much longer than a year. For after the calamitous and lamentable death of King Louis, who in the following year, having fought an unhappy battle with Suleiman, the Emperor of the Turks, and a very large and well-equipped army, being unequal to them in everything, had his forces routed and scattered, and perished in flight, all affairs in Bohemia were wonderfully thrown into confusion. Since other cares restrained the harassing of the Brethren, and the nobles, anxious about the kingdom, no longer allowed their thoughts to be taken up with religion, it became possible again to open and occupy the churches of the Brethren, which had previously been closed to them and taken away. They used these freely, no one at all forbidding it, though many difficulties and adversities presented themselves, almost until the year of Christ 1548.

units.la: INTER impedimenta, quæ propagationi doctrinæ Evangelicæ hoc anno obiecta sunt, nuptias quoq; Lutheri retulimus. Scripserat is superiori anno ad Spalatinum, cum rumor de coniugio eius sparsus esset: Se quidem in manu Dei esse, sicut creaturam, cuius cor
units.tr: AMONG the hindrances that were set against the spread of the Evangelical doctrine this year, we have also reported Luther's marriage. In the previous year, when a rumour of his marriage had spread, he had written to Spalatin: "I am indeed in the hand of God, like a creature whose heart

units.la: S mutare ac remutare, occidere & vivificare possit singulus momentis & horis : hoc tamen corde quo hactenus fuerit, & modo sit, non fore uxorem ut ducat : non quod carnem suam aut sexum non sentiat, cum neque lignum neque lapis sit, sed quod animus alienus sit a conjugio, cum expectet quotidie mortem & meritum haretico supplicium.
units.tr: can be changed and changed back, and who can be killed and made alive by him at every moment and hour. Yet with the heart such as it has hitherto been, and as it is now, I shall not take a wife. Not that I do not feel my flesh or my sex, since I am neither wood nor stone, but because my mind is averse to marriage, since I expect death every day and the punishment due to a heretic."

units.la: Ecce autem dum Lutherus de Catharina à Bora, virgine Vestali Doctori Glacio, Pastori Orlamundico, collocanda deliberat, venit Catharina ad Nicolaum Amsdorffium, conqueriturq;, se de consilio Lutheri D. Glacio contra voluntatem suam nuptiis locandâ: scire se Lutherum familiarissimè uti Amsdorfio: itaq; rogare, ad quævis alia consilia Lutherum vocet. Vellet Luthetus, vellet Amsdorfius, se paratam cum alterutro honestum inire matrimonium: cum D. Glacio nullo modo. Hoc ubi Lutherus intellexit, audisset q; ex D. Hieronymi Schurfii ore: Si Monachus iste uxorem duceret, risuros mundum universum & Diabolum ipsum, facturumq; ipsum irritas actiones suas universas: ut aegre faceret mundo & Diabolo, ut parenti etiam hoc suadenti gratificaretur. Catharinam sibi uxorem ducendam censuit: Mensis igitur Junii die xiii. inopinato duxit Lutherus Boream, cum nullo amicorum eâ re priùs communicatâ, sed vespere ad coenam invitato Pomerano & pictore Luca, & Jurisconsulto Apello solis, peregit consueta sponsalia.
units.tr: Now while Luther was deliberating about giving Catharina von Bora, a Vestal virgin, in marriage to Dr. Glatz, minister at Orlamünde, Catharina went to Nicholas Amsdorf and complained that, by Luther's counsel, she was being given in marriage to Dr. Glatz against her will. She knew that Luther made very intimate use of Amsdorf, so she asked him to summon Luther to any other plan whatever. She would be willing to enter an honourable marriage with either Luther or Amsdorf, but with Dr. Glatz in no way. When Luther learned this, and had also heard from the lips of Dr. Hieronymus Schurf: "If that monk should take a wife, the whole world and the Devil himself would laugh, and he would make all his actions void," he resolved to take Catharina as his wife, so that he might spite the world and the Devil and also humour his father, who urged this. So on 13 June Luther unexpectedly married Bora. He had told none of his friends about it beforehand, but in the evening he invited only Pomeranus, the painter Lucas and the jurist Apel to supper, and there performed the customary betrothal.

units.la: Factum hoc amici pariter & hostes Lutheri improbabant. AMici,non quòd nuptias ipsas damnarent,sed quod hoc tempore celebratas nollent: madente adhuc universâ Germaniâ Rusticorum sanguine: lugente adhuc Friderici Electoris obitum tota Saxoniâ. Inter hos erat & magnus ille Joachimus Camerarius : cui curæ erat ut omni probro careret Lutherus.Huius in solatium judicii super nuptiis Lutheri suum exponit Melanchthon epistolâ Græcâ: quæ in Romanum sermonem conversa ita habet: Posset fortasse aliquis mirari, illum hoc infelici tempore, bonus & honestis viris ubiq; graviter laborantibus, non modo non affici simul dolore, sed videri propemodum nihil penitus curare ea mala, quæ ante oculos versantur: cum interea etiam existimatio ipsius deminuatur, dum maximè opus est Germaniæ excelsitate animi & dignitate ipsius. Atq; ego rem hanc fieri gestam esse arbitror. Est vir iste nequaquam exijs, qui homines oderunt & congressus fugiunt. Quotidianæ autem vitæ illius usum non ignoras. Unde cogitare te cætera, quàm me scribere, melius, ut opinor, fuerit. Itaque mollitum fuisse quodammodo generosum & magnum animum ipsius, non est mirandum: præsertim cum nequaquam culpandum aut reprehendendum sit. Nam si quid vulgo fertur aliud indecentius, id mendacium, & hanc calumniam esse, perspicuum est. Ego etiam naturam arbitror ipsum coegisse, ut fieret maritus. Estq; vita judicio, ne inutilis quidem casus iste ad demissionem quandam pertinens, cum alte suffolli & efferri semper sit periculosum, non solum sacerdotio fungentib. sed cunctis mortalibus. Nam actionum felicitas occasionem dat pravitatis elati animi, non modo, quemadmodum orator inquit, dementibus, sed interdum etiam sapientibus. Ad omnia, alia vita aliam quoque victus quotidiani rationem constituet, secundum proverbium. Ista ad te expósui verbosius, ne eventus inopinatus nimis te perturbaret, & tristitia afficeret. Scio enim, tibi boni nominis Lutheri celebritatem cura esse.
units.tr: Friends and enemies of Luther alike disapproved of this deed. Friends did so not because they condemned the marriage itself, but because they would not have it celebrated at this time, while all Germany was still drenched in the blood of the peasants and all Saxony was still mourning the death of Elector Frederick. Among these was the great Joachim Camerarius, who took care that Luther should be free of every reproach. To console him in his judgment about Luther's marriage, Melanchthon set out his own view in a letter written in Greek, which, turned into Latin, reads thus: "Someone might perhaps wonder that he, at this unhappy time, when good and honest men everywhere are suffering grievously, is not only not moved by grief at the same time, but seems to care almost nothing for the evils that are before our eyes, while meanwhile his own reputation is diminished, when above all Germany needs the loftiness of his spirit and his standing. I, for my part, think that this matter has been done. That man is by no means one of those who hate people and shun company. You know well the custom of his daily life. So you may think about the rest better, I suppose, than I write. Therefore it is no wonder that his generous and great spirit has been somewhat softened, especially since it is by no means to be blamed or reproached. For if anything else is said commonly that is more indecent, it is plainly a lie and a calumny. I also think that nature itself compelled him to become a husband. This event is not, in the judgment of life, even a trivial occurrence tending to some humbling, since to be lifted up and raised high is always dangerous, not only for those who hold the priesthood but for all mortals. For the good fortune of his actions gives occasion for the wickedness of an elated mind, not only, as the orator says, to madmen, but sometimes even to the wise. In all things, a different life will also establish a different manner of daily sustenance, according to the proverb. I have set this out to you rather at length, so that the unexpected event might not disturb you too much and afflict you with sadness. For I know that the celebrity of Luther's good name is a care to you."

units.la: HOSTES non solum tempus decantati Hymenæi notabant, sed nuptias etiam ipsas incestas esse confirmabant, quibus Monachus cum Vestali copularetur. Itaq; Henricus VIII. Anglorum Rex responso ad epistolam, quâ Lutherus, suasu Christierni Daniæ Regis, illum oratione demissâ placere studuerat, inter alia ei exprobrat incestum matrimonium, quo vix ullum designari possit turpius flagitium. Et Doctor Conradus Collinus Prior Coloniensis peculiarem tractatum contra hoc Lutheri matrimonium edidit, cuius titulus fuit: Eversio Lutherani Epithalamij. Hieronymus Emserus, Theologorum Pontificiorum illâ ætate facilè primus, & Duci Saxoniæ Georgio à sacris, virulentum mordaxq; epithalamion in Lutheri nuptias lusit: quod apud Cochlæum in vita Lutheri legere est.
units.tr: The enemies not only noted the time of the sung wedding-song, but also asserted that the marriage itself was incestuous, since a monk was joined with a Vestal. So Henry VIII, King of the English, in his reply to the letter by which Luther, at the urging of Christian, King of Denmark, had sought by a humble speech to please him, reproached him among other things with an incestuous marriage, than which hardly any more shameful crime could be named. And Dr. Conrad Collinus, prior at Cologne, published a special treatise against this marriage of Luther, whose title was "The Overthrow of the Lutheran Epithalamium." Jerome Emser, easily the first of the Papist theologians of that age, and chaplain to Duke George of Saxony, composed a virulent and biting epithalamium on Luther's wedding, which can be read in Cochlaeus's Life of Luther.

units.la: Quin nec ab impudentibus mendaciis si‐bi temperarunt,& Lutherum eius criminis re‐ rum peregerunt, à quo ipsum chronologia nativitatis liberorum absolvit. Erasmus ipse, quod mireris ad Danielem Manchium, Ul‐ manum,Romæ in familia Cardinalis Cam‐ pegi agentem, sextâ Octobris huius anni Ba‐ sileâ ausus fuit hæc scribere: Lutherus, quod felix faustumq;, depositio Philosophi pallio, duxit uxorem, ex clara familia Borna, puellam eleganti forma, natam annos viginti sex, sed indotatam, & quæ pridem desierat esse Vestalis. Atq; ut scias auspicatas fuisse nuptias, pauculis diebus post decatatum Hymenæum nova nupta peperit. Iocatur ille in Crisim sanguinis: verum ea crisis Orco dedit agricolarum plus minus centum millia,&c.
units.tr: Nor did they refrain from shameless lies, but charged Luther with crimes of which the chronology of his children's birth clears him. Erasmus himself, to your surprise, dared to write this to Daniel Mauchius of Ulm, who was then at Rome in the household of Cardinal Campeggio, on 6 October of this year at Basel: Luther, to say something happy and auspicious, after the philosopher laid aside his cloak, has taken a wife, a girl of the distinguished Bora family, elegant in form, twenty-six years old, but without a dowry, and who had long ceased to be a Vestal. And so that you may know the marriage was auspicious, a few days after the hymeneal song the new bride gave birth. He jokes about a crisis of blood; but that crisis has sent to Orcus some hundred thousand farmers, more or less, etc.

units.la: Lutherus etsi ob inopinatam vitæ mutatio‐ nem & varia ista hominum de se judicia, non‐ nihil perturbaretur: tamen ubi se collegit, ad Michaëlem Stifelium scribens, Tu, inquit, pro me ora, ut genus vitæ novum benedicat mihi Deus & sanctificet. Nam vehementer irritantur sapientes inter nostros. Rem coguntur Dei fateri, sed persona larva tam mea quàm puella, illos dementat, & impia cogitare & dicere facit. Sed Dominus vivit, qui major est in nobis, quàm ille, qui in mundo est, & plures nobiscum sunt, quàm cum illis.Et ad Georgium Spalatinum feriâ sextâ post Tri‐ nitatis: Os obstruxi infamantibus me cum Catharina Borana, mi Spalatine, si processerit ut epulum pareparesur pro testimonio conjugÿ mei istius, te non modò adesse oportebit, verùm etiam cooperari, si quid ferina necessarium fuerit. Tu interim nobis benedicito & bene precare. Sic me vilem & cõtemptũ his nuptiis feci: ut Angelos videre, & omnes Damønes flere sperem.Nec dum mundus & sapientes agnoscunt opus Dei pium & sacrum, & in me uno faciunt id impium & Diabolicum, quo nomine magis placet, meo conjugio illorum judicium damnari & offendi, quotquot ignorantiam Dei habere pergunt.Vale & ora pro me. Et iterum ad
units.tr: Luther, though he was somewhat disturbed by the unexpected change in his life and by the varied judgments people passed on him, nevertheless, when he had collected himself, wrote to Michael Stiefel: You, he says, pray for me, that God may bless and sanctify this new way of life for me. For the wise among our own people are greatly provoked. They are compelled to acknowledge that the thing is of God, but my person, as well as the girl's, is a mask that drives them mad, and makes them think and say impious things. But the Lord lives, who is greater in us than he who is in the world, and there are more with us than with them. And to Georg Spalatin on the Friday after Trinity: I have stopped the mouths of those who slander me with Katharina Bora, my dear Spalatin. If it comes to the point that a feast is prepared as a testimony to my wife, you will have to be not only present but also to help, if anything of wild game is needed. Meanwhile, bless us and pray well for us. Thus have I made myself vile and contemptible by this marriage, so that I hope to see angels and all demons weep. Nor do the world and the wise yet recognize the pious and sacred work of God, and in my case alone they do the impious and diabolical thing, by which name it pleases me more to say that their judgment on my marriage is condemned and offended, as many as persist in their ignorance of God. Farewell, and pray for me. And again,

units.la: Stifeliũ die Michaëlis: Mi Michaël, fortis esto in Domino frater charissime, & roborare in potentia virtutis ejus.Si meum conjugiũ est opus Dei, quid mirũ, si in illo caro offendatur, offertur etiam in carne ipsius divinitatis & creatoris, quam ipse pro salute mundi in precium & cibum dedit: si non offenderetur mundus in nobis, ego offenderer in mundo, metuens ne non esset divinum quod gerimus. Nunc illo offenso & impatiente in me, ego edificor & consolor in ipso, ita fac & tu.
units.tr: to Stiefel on Michaelmas: My Michael, be strong in the Lord, most beloved brother, and be strengthened in the power of his might. If my marriage is a work of God, what wonder if the flesh is offended by it, since the flesh of the very divinity and Creator is also offended, which he himself gave for the salvation of the world as price and food. If the world were not offended by us, I would be offended by the world, fearing that what we do is not divine. Now that it is offended and impatient with me, I am built up and comforted in him; so do you also.

units.la: Sic igitur impeditus est cursus Evãgelii hoc anno per bellum rusticanũ & sacramentariũ: per Anabaptistas, per Schwenckfeldium: per Apostasiam Ducis Mõnsterbergensis & Administratoris Pragensis: per nuptias denique Lutheri. Ejusdē Evangelii publicos hostes se declararunt, Aloisia Francisci captivi Regis mater: Clemēs Papa: Henricus Rex Angliæ: Andreas Critius Episcopus Ploecensis, deinde Gnesnensis Archiepiscopus.
units.tr: Thus the course of the Gospel was hindered this year by the Peasants' War and the sacramentarians, by the Anabaptists, by Schwenckfeld, by the apostasy of the Duke of Münsterberg and the Administrator of Prague, and finally by Luther's marriage. The public enemies of this same Gospel declared themselves: Louise, mother of the captive King Francis; Pope Clement; Henry, King of England; Andreas Critius, Bishop of Płock, and afterwards Archbishop of Gniezno.

units.la: ALOISIA summam rerum administrabat in Gallia, dum filius Rex Franciscus in Hispania captivus detineretur. Illa retinendæ Pontificis causâ sæviebat in Lutheranos, deq; hoc suo in Ecclesiam animo Pontifici literis & internuntiis significabat.
units.tr: Louise administered the chief affairs in France while her son King Francis was held captive in Spain. For the sake of keeping the Pope's cause, she raged against the Lutherans, and she made known to the Pope by letters and go-betweens this her attitude toward the Church.

units.la: CLEMENS VII. datis literis ad Senatum Parisiensem (vulgo Parlamentum vocant) ex illa se cognovisse dicit, quemadmodum & per Galliam serpere jam incipiant impiarum haeresium mala, & ipsi prudenter atq; provide quosdam delegerint, qui dent operam, ut in eos, qui fidem atq; veterem religionem oppugnare conantur, animadversio fiat. Hos ipsos ad eam rem delectos auctoritate suâ se comprobare etiam. In hoc nimirum tanto tamque gravi tumultu, quem Satana malitia & satellitum illius furor atque malitia excitarit omnibus elaborandum esse, ut salus omnium communis conservetur, quandoquidem haec rabies non religionem modò, sed omnem principatum, nobilitatem, leges, ordinesq; confundere atq; permiscere cogitet. Se quidem nulli parcere nec labori neq; cura, ut medicinâ huic malo faciat. Ipsos etiâ, quorum virtus atq; prudentia sit ubiq; memorabilis, debere in hoc esse totos, ut nō solùm veritas & recta fides, verùm etiâ istius regni salus, & ipsorum ordinis dignitas à domesticis periculis & calamitatib. custodiatur, quas haec perniciosa & pestifera haeresis ubiq; disseminet. Ipsos qdē hortatione nō indi gere, qui suæ sapientiæ documenta iam ostende-rint: sed tamen pro suo, quod obtineat, munere, proq; ea quâ complectatur ipsos, benevolentia, voluisse hoc etiam addere. Nam & placere sibi vehementer, quæ adhuc egerint, & hortari, ut imposterum simili animo & virtute pro gloria Dei, & pro totius regni salute contra impiam hanc haereticorum pestem, diligenter excubent. Hoc & Deo fore longè gratissimum, & apud homines etiam maximis laudibus celebratum iri: se quoq; suam ipsis operam omnem in eo communicaturum esse. Hæ literæ xx. die Maii Romæ scriptæ Senatui redditæ sunt Lutetiæ xvi die Junii.
units.tr: Pope Clement VII, by letters sent to the Parisian Senate (commonly called the Parlement), says that he learned from them how the evils of impious heresies were beginning to creep through France too, and how they had wisely and providently chosen certain men to take care that punishment be inflicted on those who attempt to attack the faith and the old religion. He himself also approves those very men chosen for this business by his own authority. In this great and grave tumult, which the malice of Satan and the fury and wickedness of his henchmen have stirred up, everyone must labour so that the common welfare of all may be preserved, since this madness plans to confound and mix up not only religion but every government, nobility, laws and orders. He, for his part, spares no one, nor labour, nor care, so that he may apply a remedy to this evil. Those men too, whose virtue and prudence are remembered everywhere, ought to be wholly devoted to this, so that not only truth and right faith, but also the safety of this kingdom and the dignity of their own order, may be guarded from the domestic dangers and calamities which this pernicious and deadly heresy spreads everywhere. They do not indeed need exhortation, since they have already shown proofs of their wisdom; yet he wished to add this too, by reason of his office and of the goodwill with which he embraces them. For he is greatly pleased with what they have done so far, and urges them that from now on, with the same spirit and virtue, they diligently keep watch for the glory of God and the salvation of the whole kingdom against this impious plague of heretics. This will be most pleasing to God, and will also be celebrated with the greatest praises among men; and he himself too will share all his effort with them in this. These letters, written at Rome on 20 May, were delivered to the Senate at Paris on 16 June.

units.la: REX ANGLIÆ cum Aloisia Gallia sub Augusti exitum fœdus pangit: cuius hoc pri- mum caput erat: ut & Turcarum impetus, & pestifera Secta Lutherana profligaretur, à qua non minus periculi sit, quàm à Turcis.
units.tr: THE KING OF ENGLAND concludes a treaty with Louise of France toward the end of August. Its first article was that both the attacks of the Turks and the pestilent Lutheran sect should be crushed, since the sect posed no less danger than the Turks.

units.la: Idem Rex, quo esset in Religionem reformatam animo, abundè expressit Responso ad Lutheri epistolam, cuius, ut & ipsius Responsi regii summa vel propter anni huius historiam necessariò hoc loco recitanda est: Fuerat Lutherus nonnihil suboloratus de proposito Regis in uxore Catharina repudianda & alia ducenda, idq; per Christiernum profugum Danorum Regem, qui illum coram & per literas non desiit rogare, ut amanter ad eum scriberet, & illius prædicatâ humanitate spem fecerat, fore, ut leniter tractatus puriorem doctrinam reciperet. Et ille quidem animo prævidens, quod huius divortii ratione mox sequutum est, haud difficulter acquievit. Scripsit itaq; ad eum, idq; demissè admodum, & in hanc sententiam. Non se dubitare, quin graviter illum offenderit edito libello, sed id factū esse non tam suâ sponte quàm aliorum impulsu. Quod verò nunc ausit his literis interpellare, summâ ipsius humanitate fieri, quæ valde prædicetur à multis; deinde quod libelli contra se scripti non ipsum esse autorem, & à sophistis hoc insidiosè fuisse captatum intelligat. Hîc autem per occasionem de Eboracensi Cardinali loquutus, Angliæ pestè nominat. Audire etiam se magna sanè cum voluptate, ipsum & fastidire genus illud perditorū hominum, & ad veri cognitionem animum adiicere. Quapropter orat, ut sibi factum illud condonet, utq; meminisse velit, cum sit mortalis, non oportere inimicitias esse immortales. Quod si iubeat, velle se peccatum hoc suum profiteri palàm, & ipsius virtutem alio celebrare scripto. Pòst hortatur, ut calumniatorum voces defugiat, qui se vocent hæreticum: nam doctrinæ suæ caput hoc esse, quemadmodum fide per CHRISTUM nos oporteat fieri salvos, qui nostrorum scelerum pœnam collo, cervice & corpore toto sustinuit, qui pro nobis mortuus ac resuscitatus, cum patre in sempiternū regnat. Hāc esse Prophetarum & Apostolorum doctrinā, eo posito fundamento, docere se, quæ sint charitatis officia, quid invicem nos oporteat alterū alteri præstare, quomodo sit obediendum Magistratui, & Evangelii professioni omnis accommodanda vita. Si quid in ea doctrina sit impietatis & erroris, cur eum non demonstrent adversarii? cur se nec auditum neq; convictum damnent atq; proscribant? Quod si Pontificatū, & ipsius omnem clientelam reprehendat, eò facere, quòd illi diversum à Christo & ab Apostolis docent, quæstûs & emolumenti causâ, quò videlicet reliquis omnibus imperent, & in summis deliciis helluentur: hunc enim in scopum cogitationes illorum omnes atq; facta dirigi: hoc ętiam vulgo notum esse atq; testatum, ut nec ipsi quidem negare possint. Quod si mores emendarent nec alieno cum dispendio & iniuria vitam hanc ignavam ducerent atq; turpem, facilè posse dissidiū sedari. Germaniæ Principibus ac civitatib. non paucis dogmata sua probari, qui beneficium hoc Dei reverenter agnoscat: cupere se plurimū, ut & ipse in eo numero cēseatur. Quod verò Cæ-sar & quidam alii cōrra se moliantur, non esse novū: Davidem multis ante seculis prænun-ciasse ciasse futurum, ut Reges atque populi contra Dominum atque Christum varia meditentur, & imperium eius proiiciant. Sibi quidem ad eiusmodi scripturæ loca respicienti, mirum etiam videri, ullum esse Principem, qui faveat Evangelii doctrinæ. Postremo loco responderi sibi benignè petit. Acceptâ hac Lutheri epistolâ acerbè Rex respondet, inconstantiam & levitatem illi obiiciens. Libellum quoque suum defendit, & multis viris bonis atque doctis pergratum esse dicit. Quod Cardinali Eboracensi (reverendo Patri) convitium fecerit, non in eo se mirari, qui nec à Divorum, nec ab hominum abstineat contumelia. Sibi toticque regno perquam utilem esse ac salutarem Cardinalis operam, & cum antehac illum valde semper dilexerit, nunc demum esse maiori benevolentiâ complexurum, postquam eum ipse criminetur. Nam illum inter alia hoc etiam utiliter & magna cum fide atque diligentia præstare, ne quid ipsius lepræ contagionis & hæresis in suo regno disseminetur & adhæresçat. Post exprobrat, quòd incestum matrimonium cum sanctimoniali virgine contraxerit, quo vix ullum possit designari turpius flagitium. Hanc suam responsionem Rex publicè typis evulgandam curavit, magnopere dolente Luthero, & amicos incusante, qui eius rei autores sibi exstitissent: iis gratificatum adeo demisse scripsisse sa, dicens, nunc autem intelligere, quantum erraverit. Idem sibi accidisse in Cardinale Caietano, Georgio Saxoniae Duce, & Erasmo Roterodamo, quibus omnibus aliorum hortatu amanter scripserit, nec aliud sit consequutus, quam quod eos ferociores reddiderit. Stulte factum a se, qui pietatem in aulis Principum invenire se posse putet, qui Christum quaerat, ubi principatum Satanas obtineat, qui Joannem Baptistam inter purpuratos investiget. Cum igitur placido & amico scribendi genere nihil proficiat, aliam rationem initurum esse deinceps.
units.tr: The same King, to show how inclined he was toward the reformed religion, gave a full answer to Luther's letter. Because of the history of this year, the substance of the royal reply must be recited here. Luther had somewhat suspected the King's plan to repudiate his wife Catherine and take another. Christian, the exiled King of Denmark, had pressed Luther both in person and by letter to write kindly to the King, and had held out hope that, if handled gently, the King would accept purer doctrine. Luther, foreseeing in his mind what would follow from this divorce, readily complied. He therefore wrote to the King, very humbly, to this effect: he did not doubt that he had gravely offended him by publishing his book, but that this had been done not so much of his own accord as at the urging of others. As for now venturing to interrupt him with this letter, that was owing to the King's great humanity, which many praised highly; and also because he understood that he himself was not the author of the book written against him, and that the sophists had craftily seized upon this. Here, speaking in passing of the Cardinal of York, he calls him the plague of England. He also said that he heard, with considerable pleasure, that the King himself scorned that kind of wicked men and was turning his mind to the knowledge of the truth. He therefore begged that the King would pardon him for that deed, and would remember that, since he was mortal, enmities ought not to be immortal. If the King commanded it, he would gladly confess his fault openly and celebrate the King's virtue in another writing. Afterwards he urged him to avoid the voices of slanderers who call him a heretic, for the chief point of his teaching is this: as we must be made safe by faith in Christ, who bore the punishment of our sins on his neck, shoulders and whole body, who, having died and risen for us, reigns with the Father for ever. This, he said, is the doctrine of the prophets and apostles; laying this foundation, he teaches what the duties of love are, what we owe to one another, how the magistrate is to be obeyed, and how the whole of life ought to be shaped to the profession of the Gospel. If there is any impiety or error in that teaching, why do his adversaries not demonstrate it? Why do they condemn and proscribe him without being heard or convicted? But if the King rebukes the Papacy and all its clientele, he does so because they teach things contrary to Christ and the apostles, for the sake of gain and profit, namely that they may rule over all others and gorge themselves in the greatest luxury. For all their thoughts and deeds are directed to this end; this too is commonly known and attested, so that they cannot even deny it themselves. But if they amended their manners and did not lead this idle and shameful life at others' expense and injury, the dispute could easily be settled. He said that his doctrines were approved by not a few princes and cities of Germany, who reverently acknowledge this gift of God; and he very much desired that he himself might be counted among their number. As for the fact that Caesar and certain others are plotting against him, this is nothing new: David many centuries before had foretold that kings and peoples would devise various schemes against the Lord and Christ and cast off his rule. Looking at such passages of Scripture, he himself thought it remarkable that there should be any prince who favours the doctrine of the Gospel. Finally, he kindly asked that a reply be given to him. Having received this letter of Luther, the King answered harshly, charging him with inconstancy and fickleness. He also defended his own book and said that it was very pleasing to many good and learned men. As for the fact that he had reviled the Cardinal of York, the reverend father, he did not wonder at this in one who spares neither divine nor human reproach. The Cardinal's work was most useful and salutary to himself and to the whole kingdom; and although he had always loved him greatly before, he would now embrace him with still greater goodwill, now that Luther had accused him. For among other things he performs this service usefully and with great faithfulness and diligence, so that nothing of his leprous contagion and heresy spreads and clings in the kingdom. Afterwards he reproached Luther for having contracted an incestuous marriage with a consecrated virgin, a crime which scarcely any other could be called more shameful. The King took care that this reply be published in print, to Luther's great distress; Luther blamed his friends who had been the authors of this affair for him, saying that he had written so humbly in order to gratify them, but that he now understood how greatly he had been mistaken. The same thing, he said, had happened to him with Cardinal Cajetan, George, Duke of Saxony, and Erasmus of Rotterdam, to all of whom he had written kindly at the urging of others, and had gained nothing except to make them fiercer. He had acted foolishly, since he thought he could find piety in the courts of princes, that he could seek Christ where Satan holds the principality, and look for John the Baptist among the purple-clad. Since nothing was achieved by a gentle and friendly manner of writing, he would therefore adopt another method from now on.

units.la: Et sane mire exagitata fuit Lutheri ad Anglum epistola ab eius adversariis, praesertim vero a Cochlaeo & Eccio. Hic enim utramque epistolam, Lutheri puta & Regis, Ingolstadii edidit, cum virulentis epithalamiis in nuptias Lutheri, Joannis Hessi Uratislaviensis, & Urbani Regii Augustani, Theologorum.
units.tr: And indeed Luther's letter to the Englishman was roundly attacked by his opponents, especially by Cochlaeus and Eck. For Cochlaeus published both letters, those of Luther and of the King, at Ingolstadt, together with virulent wedding songs for the marriage of Luther, of Johann Hess of Breslau, and of Urban Regius of Augsburg, theologians.

units.la: ANDREAS CRITIUS Episcopus Plo- censis ad Sigismundum I. Poloniae Regem
units.tr: Andreas Critius, Bishop of Płock, to Sigismund I, King of Poland

units.la: orationem hoc anno habuit, qua ipsum vehementer hortatus est, ut haeresi, quam sic vocat, Lutheranae, omnes vias in suo Regno praecludat. Misit illam typis descriptam non sine auctario carminum ad denigrandum dum Lutherum compositorum ad Erasmum Roterodamum: qui collaudatâ Episcopi poësi & eloquentiâ, quid sibi de oratione ipsa videretur, non aperuit.
units.tr: This year he delivered an oration, in which he earnestly urged the king to block every route into his kingdom for the heresy, as he calls it, of Luther. He sent it in print, together with an appendix of poems composed to disparage Luther, to Erasmus of Rotterdam. Erasmus praised the bishop's poetry and eloquence but did not reveal what he himself thought of the oration.

units.la: NON officientibus tot impedimentis, non obstantibus tot hostibus, religio purior non solum plura loca occupavit, sed etiam in iis, quæ superioribus annis occupaverat, incrementa minimè contemnenda sumpsit.
units.tr: Although so many obstacles stood in its way and so many enemies opposed it, the purer religion not only occupied more places but also gained considerable growth in those places it had already occupied in earlier years.

units.la: Occupavit, Regnum Sueciæ, Landgraviatum Hasliæ, Marchionatū Lusatiæ, magnam partem Rhetiç: Comitatus, Hanovicum, Altenburgicum, Tecklenburgicū: Dominium Esense: urbes præterea, Northusam in Thuringia, & Haganoam in Alsatia.
units.tr: It occupied the kingdom of Sweden, the landgraviate of Hesse, the margraviate of Lusatia, a large part of Rhaetia; the counties of Hanover, Altenburg and Tecklenburg; the lordship of Esens; and, besides these, the cities of Nordhausen in Thuringia and Hagenau in Alsace.

units.la: SUECIÆ Rex Gustavus ab Erxen religionem Pontificiam in Evangelicam vertit, suafore M. Olao Petri Sueco, Academico VVittembergensi. Suasor Holmiæ in primaria æde sepultus est, cuius Ecclesiaften Rex designârat, ante suggestum. Rex sine ullo rerum motu tantam rem incepit & perfecit, temporis momento penè. Nam Antistites in Regiam accitos qui opibus validi erant, comprehendit, & statim per conquisitores horū cohortem ac clientes in verba sua adegit sacramento. Ipsos post è custodia & Regno emisit. Quibus patria erat charior quàm religio Pontificia, tulit hos, sed non in veteri, at moderatiori fortuna.
units.tr: In Sweden, King Gustavus Eriksson turned the Papist religion into the Evangelical one, at the urging of Master Olaus Petri of Sweden, an academic of Wittenberg. The promoter of this change was buried in Stockholm in the principal church, in front of the pulpit, for which the king had designated him as minister. The king began and completed this great undertaking without any disturbance, in almost the blink of an instant. For he seized the bishops, who were powerful in wealth, after summoning them to the royal court, and at once, through his agents, forced their household and dependants to swear allegiance to him. He later released the bishops themselves from custody and from the kingdom. To those for whom their fatherland was dearer than the Papist religion, he granted a fate that was not as harsh as before, but milder.

units.la: PHI-
units.tr: PHI-

units.la: ANNUS M DXXV.
units.tr: YEAR 1525.

units.la: PHILIPPUS Hassiæ Princeps Gulielmi Medii & Annæ Megapolitanæ filius, Ludovici nepos, superiori anno ad ludos indictos Heidelbergæ profecturus, non longè Francofurto obviam factus erat Melanchthoni, è patria VVittembergam redituro, & ad quæstiones quasdam sibi responderi scripto postulârat. Hoc autem anno, die Lunæ pòst Oculi cum Joanne Saxoniæ Electore & Joanne Friderico, Electoris filio, Creutzbergæ de religione colloquutus, amore religionis purioris ita incensus est, ut, referente Duce Joanne Friderico, palàm dixerit: malle se fortunas & vitâ hanc perdere, quàm agnitam Evangelii veritatem deserere. Nicolaus Herborn Guardianus Marpurgensis Landgravium per epistolam hortabatur: à fide Romana ne recederet: causas proponebat has: Fidem negz salvum neq; pium facere. Mariam revera intercedere pro nobis ad Deum. Laicis, inprimis rusticis, Evangelii mysteria non esse revelanda.
units.tr: Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, son of William the Middle and Anna of Mecklenburg, and grandson of Ludwig, had set out the previous year for the games announced at Heidelberg. Not far from Frankfurt he met Melanchthon, who was returning from his homeland to Wittenberg, and asked him to answer certain questions in writing. This year, on the Monday after Oculi, he conferred about religion at Creuzburg with John, Elector of Saxony, and John Frederick, the Elector's son. He was so fired with love of the purer religion that, as Duke John Frederick reported, he openly said he would sooner lose his property and his life than abandon the recognized truth of the Gospel. Nicolaus Herborn, guardian of Marburg, urged the Landgrave by letter not to depart from the Roman faith, and put forward these reasons: Faith does not make a man either safe or pious. Mary truly intercedes for us with God. The mysteries of the Gospel are not to be revealed to laymen, especially peasants.

units.la: Huic publico scripto Landgravius respondebat: assertioni primæ Guardiani reclamare scripturæ dicta & exempla, contestátia: iustos fide vivere & vixisse. Assertioni secundæ refragari effatum Apostolicum: unus Deus & unus mediator Dei & hominum Iesus Christus. Assertioni tertiæ repugnare sententiam Evangelicam, quæ omni creatura vult Evangelium annunciari, & nullum personarum respectum apud Deum esse, evincit.
units.tr: The Landgrave replied to this public writing. The sayings and examples of Scripture, which bear witness, cry out against the guardian's first assertion: the just live by faith and have lived by it. The apostolic saying, one God and one mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, opposes his second assertion. The evangelical sentence, which wills that the Gospel be proclaimed to every creature and shows that God has no respect of persons, refutes his third.

units.la: In MARCHIONATU LUSATIÆ mutationem religionis urbs elegans GORLITIUM, & huic vicina LAUBA admiserunt. Vigesimâ septimâ Aprilis pagorum Gorlicensis territorii Pastores conventum in urbe egêre, in quo plerique omnes unanimi cōsensu se Præsulis Misnensis obedientiæ subtraxerunt, ita ut in posterum nec tributum ei penderent, nec iurisdictionem seu autoritatem eius agnoscerent. Pertinuit enim utraque Lusatia ad Misnensis Episcopi administrationem seu dicecesin. Unde etiamnum Budissinensis Decanus se Episcopatûs Misnensis per superiorem & inferiorem Lusatiam administratorem vocat. Gorlicensibus in repurganda ipsorum Ecclesia, & impiis ac superstitiosis ritibus abrogandis primus operam navavit suam M. Franciscus Ænobarbus (Rotbart sive Rupert) Gorlicius, coriario patre natus, Sprottaviensium antea Diaconus, Georgio Roslero Consule. Is cum superioribus annis fuisset remotus, revocatur hoc anno intercedentibus nonnullis opificum collegiis, & venit Gorlicium permittente Senatu quintâ Aprilis. Mox abrogantur multi superstitiosi ritus Ecclesiastici
units.tr: In the March of Lusatia, the elegant city of Görlitz and its neighbour Lauban admitted a change of religion. On 27 April the pastors of the villages of the Görlitz territory held a meeting in the city, at which almost all of them, by unanimous consent, withdrew from obedience to the Bishop of Meissen, so that from then on they would neither pay him tribute nor acknowledge his jurisdiction or authority. For both Lusatias had belonged to the administration or diocese of the Bishop of Meissen; hence even now the Dean of Bautzen calls himself administrator of the Bishopric of Meissen for Upper and Lower Lusatia. The first to labour in reforming the church of the Görlitz people and abolishing impious and superstitious rites was Master Franciscus Ænobarbus (Rotbart or Rupert) of Görlitz, son of a tanner, formerly deacon at Sprottau under the consul George Rosler. He had been removed some years before, but was recalled this year through the intercession of several guilds of craftsmen, and came to Görlitz with the Senate's permission on 5 April. Soon many superstitious ecclesiastical rites were abolished

units.la: Annales Gorlicenses. stici nolente volente Senatu. Viridibus non abluuntur altaria, ut priùs moris erat. Dies palmarum non producitur asinus cum suo idolo. Soteriis non circumgestatur in templo Salvator, panis tamen consecratus in sepulcrum Christi reponitur. In Vigilia Paschatis non consecratur ignis, nec in sequente nocte imago resurgentis & triumphantis Christi circumgestatur per domum publicam novi fori, in qua sal venditur. Die Dominicâ Paschatis instituitur confessio Evangelica in sacello, quod vocant D. Georgii, & confitentur homines circiter ducenti: apud summum altare circiter triginta.
units.tr: (the Görlitz Annals) whether the Senate willed it or not. The altars are no longer washed with green boughs, as had been the custom. On Palm Sunday the donkey is no longer led about with its idol. On the feast of the Saviour the image of the Saviour is no longer carried about the church, though consecrated bread is still placed in the sepulchre of Christ. On Easter Eve the fire is not blessed, nor on the following night is the image of the risen and triumphant Christ carried around the public house of the new market, where salt is sold. On Easter Sunday an evangelical confession was instituted in the chapel called St George's, and about two hundred people confessed there; at the high altar about thirty.

units.la: Proximâ Dominicâ post Pascha, qui fuit dies vicesimus tertius Aprilis de suggestu Pastor significat, ut si qui posthac sub utraque, quod vocant, specie communicare velint, vel populari idiomate baptizari suos cupiant, id liberum ipsis futurum. Ac utrumq; tum factum fuit. Sunt praterea abrogatæ hoc anno processiones quotannis servari solitæ: abrogatæ item fuêre Missæ & Vesperæ pro defunctis. Sacerdotes rasuram amplius non admiserunt: nec die ascensionis Domini Christi imago per tholû funib. attracta fuit, sed pro istis nugis habita est à meridie concio: deniq; pauci observârunt veteres ritus.
units.tr: On the next Sunday after Easter, which was 23 April, the minister announced from the pulpit that if anyone wished henceforth to communicate under both kinds, as they call it, or wished to have their children baptized in the vernacular, this would be permitted to them. Both were done at that time. Moreover, the processions customarily held every year were abolished this year, and likewise the Masses and Vespers for the dead. The priests no longer admitted the tonsure. On Ascension Day the image of Christ was not drawn up through the dome on ropes; instead a sermon was preached at noon, as these trifles were regarded. In the end, only a few observed the old rites.
