units.tr: In Switzerland the men of Schwyz burned a certain priest, because he had attacked the papacy from the Scriptures, and also a sailor, Eberlin Bolt, because he had spoken somewhat differently about baptism and the Lord's Supper from the way monks speak under the papacy. Both were charged with the heresy of Anabaptism.

units.la: IOANNES PISTORIUS (Germanis Beck) Wordensis Hollandis sacris initiatus, quod uxorem duxisset, indulgentias VVordeç tum gratis propositas, contempsisset, Missae officium neglexit, captus, & Hagam Comitis ductus, diuq; & multùm ab inquisitoribus vexatus, tandem mense Junio constanti fide & patientiâ martyrii coronam in mediis flammis meruit. Historiam conscripsit Guilielmus Gnapheus Hagensis Germanicè reperitur apud Ludovicum Rabum.
units.tr: John Pistorius (in German, Beck) of Worden, ordained in Holland, was dismissed from his office because he had taken a wife. He scorned the indulgences then offered free at Worden and neglected the office of the Mass. He was seized and led to The Hague, to the Count's court, and for a long time he was much harassed by the inquisitors. At last, in June, with steadfast faith and patience, he won the crown of martyrdom in the midst of the flames. An account of his history was written by William Gnapheus of The Hague; a German version is found in Ludwig Rabus.

units.la: MECHLINIAE Bernhardus quidam Carmelita propter Evangelii liberam professionem combustus est.
units.tr: At Mechelen a certain Bernhard, a Carmelite, was burned for freely professing the Gospel.

units.la: MATTHIAS VVEIBELIUS Martiscellae in Algovia natus & Campoduni in schola ab Abbate illius loci erectâ educatus, sexennium sacerdotis officio functus erat in templo Montis propè Campodunum: atqp illustratus Evangelii luce, doctrinam de gratuita iustificatione hominis coram Deo, & consequente ex ea sanctificatione, idolomaniam item Papatus auditorio suo patefecerat: hoc autem anno à Pontificiis captus, vulneratus, & septimâ Septembris de arbore suspensus, vitam laetus finiit.
units.tr: Matthias Weibelius, born at Martiscella in Allgäu and educated at Kempten in the school set up by the abbot of that place, had for six years discharged the office of priest in the church on the mountain near Kempten. Enlightened by the light of the Gospel, he had set before his hearers the doctrine of the free justification of man before God and the sanctification that follows from it, and he had also exposed the idolatry of the papacy. This year, however, he was seized by the Papists and wounded, and on 7 September he was hanged from a tree, and he ended his life joyfully.

units.la: FELIX ULSENIUS, iuvenis pius ac integer, Evangelii assertor capitur à Gubernatoritoribus provinciæ Ensheimensis in Alsatia, captus miserè torquetur. Capito Petrum VVickram Pastorem in Ensheim rogat, fratris laborantis patrocinium suscipiat.
units.tr: Felix Ulsenius, a pious and upright young man and a defender of the Gospel, was seized by the governors of the province of Ensisheim in Alsace. Taken prisoner, he is miserably tortured. Capito asks Peter Wickram, minister at Ensisheim, to take up the protection of his suffering brother.

units.la: LUTHERUS hoc anno scripsit librum de abominatione Canonis Missæ, de quo id semel monendus est Lector, Lutheri libris de abroganda Missa contradixisse (ut autor est Cochlæus) plurimos ex Catholicis Theologis: in Anglia, Joannem Episcopum Röffensem: in Germania, Joannem Episcopum Viennensem: in Gallia, Clichtonæum: in Hispaniis, Quintanam: in Bavaria, Eccium: in Marchia, Mensingum: sermone Germanico, Dietebergium Emserum, Cochlæum, plurimosq; alios.
units.tr: Luther wrote this year a book on the abomination of the Canon of the Mass. On this matter the reader should be reminded once: as Cochlaeus is the authority for it, many Catholic theologians opposed Luther's books on the abolition of the Mass. In England, John, Bishop of Rochester; in Germany, John, Bishop of Vienna; in France, Clichtoveus; in Spain, Quintana; in Bavaria, Eck; in the March, Mensing; and in German, Dietenberger, Emser, Cochlaeus, and many others.

units.la: Idem Lutherus hoc anno epistolam scripsit ad Christianos Antuerpiæ congregatos, quam multis nominibus Lectori commendamus. Nam & historiam habet de novis Prophetis Antuerpiæ tum exorcis: & consessionem manifestam distinctionis voluntatis Dei occultæ à revelata, & præterea refutationem calumniæ, quod is Deum autorem peccati faciat, qui Deo volente peccata fieri agnoscit. Epistolæ ipsissima verba hæc sunt:
units.tr: Luther himself wrote a letter this year to the Christians gathered at Antwerp, which we commend to the reader on many grounds. For it contains an account of the new prophets then dealt with at Antwerp, a clear statement of the distinction between God's hidden will and his revealed will, and also a refutation of the calumny that he makes God the author of sin, because he acknowledges that sins come about by the will of God. The very words of the letter are these:

units.la: OMNIBUS CHRISTIA- nis Antuerpia Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: To all Christians at Antwerp, Martin Luther.

units.la: Gratiam & pacem à Deo Patre nostro & Domino Iesu Christo, Christianæ charitatis solicitudine compulsus, amici in Christo charissimi, has ad vos literas non potui non scribere. Relatum est enim mihi, isthic etiam apud vos spiritus erroneos suboriri, qui suâ vesaniâ doctrinam Christianam impedire & commaculare moliuntur, id quod & alibi ab eius farinâ hominibus cæptum est. Itaut, quantum in me est, officii mei esse putem, vos monere fideliter, ne meâ taciturnitate aut silentio ullius sanguinis seduƈti iactura mihi imputetur, cui consiliis aut monitis auxilio esse potuissem in tempore.
units.tr: Grace and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. Moved by the concern of Christian love, dearest friends in Christ, I could not help writing this letter to you. For it has been reported to me that false spirits are also rising up among you there, who by their madness are trying to hinder and defile Christian teaching, as has already begun elsewhere with men of that sort. So, as far as I am concerned, I think it is my duty to warn you faithfully, so that I am not charged with the loss of any soul, through my silence or quiet, whom I might have helped in time with counsel or warning.

units.la: Quamobrem vos obsecro, amici charissimi, qui hactenus praeter sedulitatem & fidi pectoris officia, quibus magno meo cum periculo Christiana Reipublica commodare & prodesse semper studui, in me aliud observastis nihil, velitis & hanc amoris erga vos mei amicam admonitionem, candidè susceptam, boni consulere.
units.tr: Therefore I beg you, dearest friends, who until now have noticed nothing else in me, apart from the diligence and faithful service of a sincere heart by which I have always striven, at great risk to myself, to serve and benefit the Christian commonwealth, to be willing also to receive kindly this admonition, which comes from my love for you as a friend.

units.la: Neque enim meum in hoc sed vestrum quaero cum compendium tum salutem. Cum mea utilitatis rationem habiturus, compressis digito labellis, tacere potuissem, & quietus esse, aut aliam venanda utilitatis inire viam.
units.tr: For I seek not my own advantage in this, but yours, both your profit and your salvation. If I had considered my own interest, I could have kept silent with my finger on my lips and remained at rest, or taken another path to advantage.

units.la: Multo tempore hactenus sub Papistica tyrannide varias & graves imposturarum seductiones perpessi sumus, à spiritibus tumultuantibus & nocturnis adornatas: quos quos tredimus & putavimus pro defunctorum animabus in igne purgatorio constitutis cruciatos, & ope implorates obambulare. Cuius erroris techna Diabolica exorto Evangelij lumine iam detecta est, & falsa reperta, adeo ut neminem posthac esse opinor dubitantem non hominum animas, sed Spiritum malignorum esse spectra, que fictitiis responsis hominum simplici credulitati imposuerunt, multis idololatriis per totum mundum hac fraude erectis. Vbi vero sui tumultus, nullam posthac apud homines esse rationem, κοὶ ἀδένα λέγον animadvertit Diabolus, patefactâ nequitiâ, novae impostura novo excogitato dolo aliud aggreditur, capitá in membris suis, hoc est, hominibus impiis tumultuari & insanire, variamq; & multiplicem, cùm doctrinam tum fidem comminisci.
units.tr: For a long time under Papal tyranny we have suffered various and grave seductions of deceit, contrived by tumultuous spirits that come by night: spirits whom we thought and believed to be the souls of the dead, tormented in the fire of purgatory, and wandering about seeking help. With the light of the Gospel now risen, the diabolical craft of this error has been uncovered and found to be false, so that I think no one now doubts that these are not the souls of men but evil spirits, phantoms, who deceived the simple credulity of men with fictitious answers, and by this fraud many idolatries were set up throughout the world. But when the devil noticed that, with his wickedness exposed, he no longer had any standing among men [κοὶ ἀδένα λέγον], he turns to a new imposture, with a newly devised trick, namely to rage and rave in his members, that is, in impious men, and to invent varied and manifold doctrines as well as faiths.

units.la: Hic super vacaneam Christianis baptismum esse affirmat: ille ᾽Ευχαρίστιας Sacramentum pernegat. Est qui alium mundum inter hunc & supremi diei adventum confinxit & excogitavit. Nonnulli docent, Christum non fuisse Deum. Nec desunt qui fidei iustificationem adimunt, operibus nostris adscribentes. Partim hoc dicunt, partim vero aliud.
units.tr: One man declares that baptism is an empty thing for Christians; another denies the sacrament of the Eucharist [Εὐχαριστίας]. One has framed and devised another world between this one and the coming of the last day. Some teach that Christ was not God. Nor are there lacking those who take away justification by faith, ascribing it to our works. Some say this, others something else.

units.la: Nec ullus est Morychus adeo stupidus, ἢ ὥτως τι ἢ ἀκαύσειτ[?], qui non quicquid probè adpotus somniavit, protinus à Spiritu S. sibi suggestum esse contendit, & mox Propheta esse laborat. Exempli gratiâ unus hic mihi producendus est. Hi enim Spiritus multum mihi facessunt negotii. Nullus est, qui non velit Luthero esse doctior. Et nemo est, qui non de me prostrato victoria palmam auferre cupiat. Et ô utinam essent, quod esse contendunt, & ego nihil essem. Inter catera sic dicebat ad me quidam: se missum à Deo cæli & terræ conditore ad me, magnificis & sesquipedalibus verbis utens, quanquam satis quóque rusticis. Breviter, hoc se à Deo accepisse in mandatis, ut illi libros Mosaicos legerem. Dum ego ex eo quærebam eius mandati signum, respondet, hoc scriptum esse in Evangelio Ioannis. Hic ego primo statim gustu perspectam hominis stultitiam fastidiebam, iubens eum alio redire tempore, hoc enim temporis punctum non ferre, ut libri Mosaici legantur. Ita mi Domine, inquit, cælestis pater, qui suum pro nobis effudit sanguinem, dirigat nos per viam rectam ad filium suum Iesum. Ecce Prophetarum circumforaneorum vesaniam. Nam, nisi me fallit animus, hic clarè perspicis, quales ii sunt Spiritus, ita superbè se venditantes, & iactantes, neque tamen Christum nec Deum satis intelligentes, sed furiosorum in morem loquentes. Eius ordinis homines miseros & vecordes per annū non paucos audire cogor, alia enim ratione Diabolus me divexare nescit. Hoc itaq; dico. Hucusque orbem terrarum Spirituum tumultuantium ἀσωματικῶν pro animabus hominum se venditatium fuisse refertissimum: hoc vero aetatis mundum esse Spirituum σωματικῶν tumultuantium, & pro meris Angelis cælestibus sese venditantium. tium, plenissimum. Quamobrem Christianum confidentem esse oportet, nec consternari animo, emergentibus indies sic diversis sectis & haeresibus, nec aliter animatum cogitare, quam quod in diversis locis, ut hactenus, spirituum tumultuantium excitarentur turba. Non potest non tumultuari Diabolus, quo certum habeant homines, eum adhuc esse in vivis ac regnare. Mundus vero suis tumultus scena est. Tumultuantis tragoedia histriones sunt Prophetae furiosi. Si parum successerit tumultus in Angelis extra corpus a se excitatus, succedat ille in vesanis & distortis insanientium Prophetarum capitibus & cerebris expergefactus. Vult esse tumultus S. Paulus: ait enim, oportet haereses esse, ut probati manifesti fiant.
units.tr: Nor is there any Morychus so stupid that he does not at once insist that whatever he has dreamed up in a state of slight drunkenness has been suggested to him by the Holy Spirit, and soon labours to be a prophet. For example, let one be produced here for me, for these spirits give me a great deal of trouble. There is no one who does not want to be more learned than Luther, and no one who does not desire to snatch the palm of victory from me, laid low. Oh, would that they were what they claim to be, and I were nothing! Among other things, a certain man said to me that he had been sent to me by God, the creator of heaven and earth, using magnificent and high-flown words, though quite rustic ones too. In short, he said he had received this command from God, that I should read the books of Moses to him. When I asked him for a sign of this command, he replied that it was written in the Gospel of John. At once, from the first taste, I perceived the man's folly and was disgusted, bidding him return another time, since this moment could not bear the reading of the books of Moses. "So, my Lord," he said, "heavenly Father, who poured out his blood for us, direct us by the right way to his Son Jesus." Behold the madness of these roving prophets! For, unless my mind deceives me, you plainly see what sort of spirits these are, so arrogantly showing off and boasting, yet understanding neither Christ nor God well, and speaking like madmen. I am forced to listen to men of this order, wretched and mad, and not a few of them over the course of a year, for the devil knows no other way to vex me. So I say this: until now the world has been very full of raging spirits, incorporeal [ἀσωματικῶν], who sold themselves as the souls of men; but in this age the world is full, most full, of raging corporeal [σωματικῶν] spirits, who sell themselves as mere heavenly angels. Therefore a Christian ought to be confident and not dismayed in spirit when such diverse sects and heresies rise up daily, nor should he think otherwise than that, as hitherto, a crowd of raging spirits is stirred up in various places. The devil cannot but rage, so that men may be certain that he is still alive and reigning. The world is indeed the stage for his tumults, and the mad prophets are the actors in the tragedy of the raging one. If the tumult he has stirred up in angels outside the body has had little success, let him bring it about instead in the crazed and twisted heads and brains of raving prophets. St Paul wants there to be tumults; for he says, "There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest."

units.la: Sub regno Papistico omnia erant tranquilla ab huiusmodi sectis & haeresibus, siquidem fortis & armatus compositâ pace custodiebat atrium suum. Porro ubi iam fortior venit, & superatum imbecilliorem exegit atrio, iuxta doctrinam Evangelicam, furere coepit, & tumultuari invitus emigrans. Ita quoque amici charissimi, subortus etiam inter vos Spiritus corporeus & tumultuans, qui vos perturbare, atque à vera cognitione in suam tenebricosam & fallibilem opinionem perducere statuit. Proinde moniti vobis prospicite. Porrò quo melius eius observare, & cavere queatis offutias & perfidiam, nonnullos articulos ab ipso perperam assertos, subjiciam:
units.tr: Under the Papal kingdom all was calm from sects and heresies of this kind, since the strong man, armed, kept his court in peace. But when one stronger came, and drove out the weaker from his court, according to the Gospel teaching, he began to rage and rave, departing unwillingly. So too, dearest friends, a bodily and raging spirit has arisen among you, which has resolved to disturb you and to lead you from true knowledge into its own dark and deceptive opinion. Therefore, being warned, look to yourselves. Moreover, that you may better observe and guard against its deceits and treachery, I shall set out some articles which it has wrongly asserted:

units.la: 1. Omnem hominem habere Spiritum S.
units.tr: 1. That every man has the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 2. Spiritum S. nihil aliud esse, quàm nostram rationem & intelligentiam.
units.tr: 2. That the Holy Spirit is nothing other than our reason and understanding.

units.la: 3. Omnem hominem credere.
units.tr: 3. That every man believes.

units.la: 4. Non esse inferos aut condemnationem, sed solum corpus damnari.
units.tr: 4. That there is no hell or condemnation, but only the body is damned.

units.la: 5. Omnem animam vitam aeternam possessuram.
units.tr: 5. That every soul will possess eternal life.

units.la: 6. Ductu naturae doceri nos illud proximo facere, quod ab illo nobis fieri velimus. Et hanc voluntatem esse fidem.
units.tr: 6. That by the guidance of nature we are taught to do to our neighbour what we would wish done to us; and that this will is faith.

units.la: 7. Adversus legem non peccari concupiscentiis, quatenus concupiscentiis voluntate non consenserimus.
units.tr: 7. That sin is not committed against the law by concupiscences, so long as we have not consented to them in will.

units.la: 8. Spiritum S. non habentem nec peccatum habere, eo quod ratione careat, quam Spiritum S. vocat.
units.tr: 8. That one who does not have the Holy Spirit does not have sin either, because he lacks reason, which he calls the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Omnes ii articuli, excepto septimo, magnâ temeritate sunt asserti, nec digni confutatione aut responsione. Et non male feceritis, si hunc Spiritum iuxta doctrinam suam contempseritis. Neque enim dissimilis est etiam aliis nonnullis sursum ac deorsum incertâ sede vagantibus, nihil pensi habentibus, quid doceant aut asserant, sed gaudent famigerabiles per ora virûm volitare, & esse mundo fabula, ut laudentur & celebrentur passim ab omnibus. Sed & Diabolus ipse harum sectarum autor nihil aliud quaerit perinde, quàm quòd excitatis hominibus seditiosis vos impeditos à vera doctrina abducat, cat, aut non permittat horum furiis obstantibus eandem vos exercere: veluti aliis spectris homines frequenter deceptos totâ viâ aberrare fecit: non secus quoque hic Spiritus suis vobiscum agit articulis. Quamobrem cautè agentes date operam, ut omnia nova & insolita, animarum saluti parum conducentia, missa faciatis. His enim spectris homines otio deditos illaqueare statuit. Quanquam vester Spiritus dum apud me erat, omnes hos pernegabat articulos, tametsi de aliis convincebatur testimonio. Sed & inter loquendum suomet iudicio se prodebat sorex, & aliquot confitebatur, sic ut pro vero testari possim, me Spiritum inconstantiorem, mendaciorem, impudentiorem, & petulantiorem vidisse & audivisse nunquam: ut qui eodem tempore & uno ore idem dicat & perneget, & aliud stans, aliud sedens comminiscatur: praeterea ita ambitiosum, & nominis avidum, ut haud sciam an uspiam miserius gloria mancipium inveniri possit, prater gloriam & nominis celebritatem nihil ambiens, quòdque dignus sit habitus nostro colloquio, cuique voluptati sit suum quoque fimum fœtere, qui mos multorum nunc est, nec dissimilium. Potissimum vero hic acriter depugnabat, Dei praeceptum esse bonum, & Deum peccata habere nolle. Qua res nunquam mihi venerat in dubium, nec satis erat, tametsi nos quoque id ipsum affirmaremus. Huc vero adducti non poterat, quod DEVS, quamquam peccatum detestaretur, & huic inhibendo praeceptum dedisset, peccatum tamen nihilominus fieri permitteret. Eam permissionem citra voluntatem Dei non posse fieri. Quis enim adigit eam, ut permittat fieri peccatum? Quin etiam qui possit permittere peccatum, si nolit permittere aut consentire? Hic vertice caelum perrumpere tentabat furiosus Propheta, volens indagare, unde nam DEVS peccatum non volens, fieri tamen consentiret aut permitteret: putabatque Majestatis divina abyssum se haud dubie exhaurire posse, qua nam ratione hae duae diametro repugnantes in DEO voluntates constare possent. Hic neminem audire volens, pertinaciter contendebat, alteram tantum voluntatem in DEO esse. Quid vero sua pertinacia monstri aluerit, satis indicio sunt articuli superius positi. Nec dubium est, quin me falso apud vos delaturus sit, ac dixissem, DEVM velle habere peccata. Cuius criminationi sic responsum volo, mihi iniuriam fieri, atque eundem, ut alias portentum, ex mendaciis & sycophantia consutum, & hic impudenter mentiri. Ita dico, DEVM datis in hoc praeceptis peccata inhibuisse, & hanc voluntatem satis liquere, & nobis cognitu necessariam esse. Quid vero fiat, ut homines peccare permittat, ut peccatis perpetrandis consentiant, nos scire non voluit: alioqui palam secisfecisset , si adeo eius consilii nos voluisset esse conscios. Atqui & ipse Paulus hac scire noluit scribens Rom. 9. o homo , tu quis es , qui ex adverso respondebis DEO ? Quamobrem oratos vos volo , fratres, ut aversemini Spiritum hac sublimi quaestione de occulta DEI voluntate vos molestantem , & impugnantem dicentes : putasne parum esse , quod DEVS manifesta voluntatis suae in praeceptis expresse nos voluerit esse conscios ? Quid itaque tu nos infatuas eo nos inducendo , quod scire nefas , adeoque interdictum est , nec possibile cognitu , & in quo tu vesane nobiscum ex aequo caecutis & hallucinaris ? Qui haec fiant , DEO committenda putamus, sufficit nobis , DEVM peccata detestari: qui vero peccatis consentiat, missum faciendum est. Servus heri sui arcana explorare , multo minus nosse debet, sed quid praecipiat herus , effectum reddere. Multo minus fas est miseram creaturam sui creatoris, divinae nimirum Maiestatis pervestigare mysteria. Videtis nunc optimi amici , qui Diaboli sint conatus , qua consilia, qua rerum novandarum studia , quibus unum hoc molitur, ut non necessariis & utilibus , cognitu impossibilibus articulis hominum levium animos occupet atq; detineat , a vera via alienos. Proinde, videte, ut id, quod scitu est utile, & vobis necessarium, atq; a Deo praeceptum, amplectamini, posthabitis , nugis futilibus non adificantibus, & nihil, perinde[?] atque contentiones producentibus, iuxta sapientis viri consilium: quod supra ingenij tui captum est, ne perquiras, sed mane in iis, quae à Deo tibi praecepta sunt. Tota vita opus est Christo rectè perdiscendo, & eius praeceptis cognoscendis, etiam nullis aliis rebus intentis. Quibus probè iam cognitis ad scrutanda mysteria animu deinceps applicabimus, quae Diabolicus hic spiritus ne quicquam movet aucupanda gloriola gratia. Regressi igitur in viam discite, quid Paulus Romanos docuit, cuius prologum eius epistolae à me praefixum inspicientibus perspicuum fiet, qui sit orda sacras literas perdiscendi, & quem locum scrutanda mysteria obtineant. Vos ineptè garrulos & futiliter loquaces devitate. Gratia Christi sit vobiscum. Orate vos quoque pro me, fratres, Amen.
units.tr: All these articles, except the seventh, have been asserted with great rashness, and they are not worth refutation or reply. You would do well to despise this Spirit for his teaching. He is not unlike certain others who wander up and down without a fixed seat, caring nothing what they teach or assert, but rejoicing to fly by word of mouth among men and to be a talk for the world, so that they are praised and celebrated everywhere by all. The Devil himself, the author of these sects, seeks nothing else than this: that, by stirring up seditious men, he may draw you away from true doctrine when you are hindered, or may not allow you to practise that doctrine while these madmen stand in your way. Just as he has often caused men deceived by other phantoms to wander off the whole way, so this Spirit works in the same manner with his articles against you. Therefore, acting cautiously, take care to set aside all new and unusual things that do little to help the salvation of souls. For he has determined to ensnare with these phantoms men who are given to idleness. Yet while your Spirit was with me, he denied all these articles, although he was convicted of others by testimony. Moreover, in conversation he betrayed himself by his own judgement as a shrew, and confessed several things, so that I can truthfully testify that I have never seen or heard a Spirit more inconstant, more lying, more shameless and more petulant: one who at the same time, with the same mouth, says and denies the same thing, and who invents one thing standing and another sitting. Besides, he is so ambitious and so greedy for a name that I do not know whether a more wretched slave of glory could be found anywhere. He seeks nothing but glory and fame for his name, and he is pleased that he was thought worthy of our conversation, and that his own dung should stink to himself as well, a habit now common among many, and not unlike theirs. But above all, he fought fiercely here that God's command is good, and that God does not wish to have sins. This matter had never come into doubt for me, nor was it necessary, even though we ourselves affirm the very same thing. But he could not be brought to this: that God, although he detests sin and has given a command to restrain it, nevertheless allows sin to be committed. He says that this permission cannot happen without the will of God. For who compels him to permit sin to happen? Indeed, how could he permit sin if he were unwilling to permit it or to consent to it? Here the raving prophet tried to break through the heavens with his head, wanting to investigate how God, though not willing sin, nevertheless consents to or permits it. He thought he could undoubtedly drain the abyss of the divine Majesty, by what means these two wills, diametrically opposed, could exist in God. Unwilling to hear anyone here, he obstinately contended that there is only one will in God. What monstrous things his obstinacy has nourished is sufficiently shown by the articles set out above. There is no doubt that he will falsely report me to you as having said that God wishes to have sins. To this accusation I wish this reply to be made: I am being wronged, and this same man, like a monster on other occasions, stitched together from lies and sycophancy, is shamelessly lying here too. I say that God, by his commands given in this matter, has forbidden sins, and that this will is clear enough and necessary for us to know. But how it comes about that he permits men to sin, and that he consents to the committing of sins, he did not wish us to know; otherwise he would have made it plain, had he wished us to be privy to this counsel. And yet Paul himself did not wish to know these things, writing in Romans 9: "O man, who are you who answers back against God?" Therefore I beg you, brothers, to turn away from the Spirit who troubles and assails you with this lofty question about the hidden will of God, saying: do you think it a small thing that God has expressly willed us to be aware of his manifest will in the commands? Why then do you make us foolish by leading us into what it is wrong to know, and what is forbidden and not possible to know, and in which you, madman, grope and wander in the dark along with us? As for how these things happen, we think they should be committed to God. It is enough for us that God detests sins; as for the one who consents to sins, he must be set aside. A servant ought to search out the secrets of his master much less, and to know them much less; rather, he should carry out what the master commands. Still less is it right for a wretched creature to investigate the mysteries of his Creator, that is, of the divine Majesty. You see now, best of friends, what the efforts of the Devil are, what his plans and what his zeal for upheaval are, by which he strives for this one thing: to occupy and hold the minds of light men with articles that are neither necessary nor useful, that cannot be known, and that turn them away from the true way. Therefore, see to it that you embrace what is useful to know, what is necessary for you, and what God has commanded, setting aside futile trifles that do not build up but produce only quarrels, in accordance with the counsel of the wise man: "Do not search out what is beyond the grasp of your intellect, but abide in those things which God has commanded you." The whole of life is needed to learn Christ rightly and to come to know his commands, even if one is intent on nothing else. Once these are well known, we shall then apply our minds to searching out mysteries, which this diabolical spirit does not stir us to hunt after, for the sake of a little empty glory. Return, then, to the way and learn what Paul taught the Romans. Those who look at the preface to his epistle, which I have prefixed to it, will see clearly how one should begin to learn the sacred letters, and what place the searching out of mysteries should hold. Avoid them, as foolishly chattering and frivolously talkative people. The grace of Christ be with you. Pray for me also, brothers. Amen.

units.la: Occiderunt hoc anno duo renovatae Ecclesiae sidera, FRIDERICUS Saxoniae Elector & ELISABETHA Caroli V. Imperatoris soror, Regina Daniae.
units.tr: This year two stars of the renewed Church went down: Frederick, Elector of Saxony, and Elizabeth, sister of the Emperor Charles V, Queen of Denmark.

units.la: FRIDERICUM tria admirabilem secerunt: pietas, quâ motus Academiam VVitembergensem condidit: magnitudo animi, quâ oblatam Imperii coronam Francofurti, respuit: prudentia, quâ usus est initio motuum Ecclesiasticorum, quando doctrinam Lutheri neque defendit, neque aboleri passus est, nisi errorum convinceretur. Obiit autem quintâ Maij, sexagesimo simo tertio ætatis anno, in ipso tumultu rusticano. Melanchthon, qui sæpè dicere solitus fuit, Fridericum Electorem selegisse florem ex omnibus virtutibus, memoriam eius gratæ posteritati erudito epigrammate commendavit: Ante petet cursu Boiemica rura supino, Unde in Saxonicos defluit Albis agros: Inclyta quàm possit meritorum fama tuorum Occidere in populis, Dux Friderice, tuis: Aurea viderunt hæ gentes secula, regni Dum tibi Saxonici sceptra tenere datum est, Dace frui placidâ campiq; urbesq; solebant, Horrenda extimuit Classica nulla nurus. Bella alij ferro, sed tu ratione gerebas, Et sine vi victi sæpe dedêre manus, Ingenio claros meruisti sæpe triumphos Militeq; haud ullo fixa tropaa tibi, Et pacis studijs, florere, ac artibus urbes Contigit auspicio, Dux Friderice, tuo. Fovisti spretas hac tempestate Camœnas, Unicus & studijs pramia digna dabas. Namq; tuo sumptu flavum schola condita ad Albim est, Ut vita verum traderet illa modum. Hic Evangelij primùm doctrina renata, Deterso cæpit pura nitere situ. Induit hîc veros vultus, iterumq; colorem Accepit tandem Religio ipsa suum:
units.tr: Three things made Frederick admirable: piety, which moved him to found the University of Wittenberg; greatness of spirit, by which he rejected the crown of the Empire offered to him at Frankfurt; prudence, which he showed at the beginning of the ecclesiastical disturbances, when he neither defended the doctrine of Luther nor allowed it to be abolished unless it were proved to contain errors. He died on the fifth of May, in the sixty-third year of his age, in the very uproar of the peasants. Melanchthon, who often used to say that Elector Frederick had chosen the flower of all the virtues, commended his memory to grateful posterity in a learned epigram: Sooner would he race on his back through the Bohemian fields, whence the Elbe flows down into the Saxon lands, than the famed renown of your merits, Duke Frederick, could perish among your people. These peoples saw golden ages while it was given to you to hold the sceptre of the Saxon realm; they used to enjoy peace and fields and cities, and no daughter-in-law feared any dreadful trumpet-call. Others waged war with the sword, but you with reason, and often conquered men surrendered their hands without force. By your talent you often earned famous triumphs, and no trophies were set up for you in any soldiery. It was by your auspices, Duke Frederick, that cities flourished in the pursuits of peace and the arts. You cherished the Muses, despised in this age, and you alone gave rewards worthy of learning. For at your expense a school was founded beside the yellow Elbe, so that it might hand down to life the true measure. Here first the doctrine of the Gospel was reborn, and, cleansed of its dirt, began to shine pure. Here at last religion itself put on its true face and received again its own colour.

units.la: Et cum Germani sumpsissent arma tyranni,Contra Evangelium, sanctaq; jussa Dei.
units.tr: And when the German tyrant had taken up arms against the Gospel and the holy commands of God,

units.la: Doctores tibi cura pios defendere soli, Et late Christi spargere dogma fuit. His tibi pro meritis grata praconia voce Posteritas omnis, virq; puerq; canent. Nulla tuas unquam virtutes nescient atas, Non jus in laudes, mors habet atra tuis.
units.tr: You alone took it upon yourself to defend the pious teachers, and it was your task to spread the doctrine of Christ far and wide. For this, every age of posterity, man and boy alike, will sing your praises with grateful voice in return for your deserts. No age will ever be ignorant of your virtues, and black death does not have power over your praises.

units.la: Vivente adhuc in his terris Friderico, à Pontificiis Ecclesiasticis æquè ac Politicis crebris hoc sermonibus fuit usurpatum: Moriente Friderico, moritaram quoque doctrinam Lutheri. Sed istos falsos fuisse, duorum & nonaginta annorum experientia nosdocet.
units.tr: While Frederick was still alive on these lands, the Papists, both ecclesiastical and civil, often used this saying: "When Frederick dies, the doctrine of Luther dies too." But the experience of ninety-two years teaches us that these men were false prophets.

units.la: ELISABETHA, cuius heroica virtus & fides in rebus mariti Christierni II. Daniæ Regis adversis, eximia & illustris fuit (Nam illi fida exilii comes esse, quàm in Dania sola regnare maluit) Gandavi decessit decimâ nonâ Januarii. De qua Lutherus ad Joannem Agricolam ista: Regia illa mulier, & verè Regina, Elisabeth Danorum Regis uxor excessit è vivis, ut ipse mihi scripsit Christiernus Rex, sed magnâ fide excessit, acceptâ cænâ Domini legitimo ritu Christi, nec persuaderi potuit licet fortiter tentata per Proceres, ut in Papæ fidem rediret. Scilicet Christus etiam aliquando Reginâ voluit in cælũ vehere.Cornelius Scepperus hoc illi epitaphium scripsit.
units.tr: ELIZABETH, whose heroic virtue and faith were outstanding and illustrious in the adversities of her husband Christian II, King of Denmark (for she preferred to be the faithful companion of his exile rather than to reign alone in Denmark), died at Ghent on the nineteenth of January. Luther wrote of her to John Agricola as follows: "That royal woman, truly a queen, Elizabeth, wife of the King of Denmark, has departed this life, as King Christian himself wrote to me; but she departed with great faith, having received the Lord's Supper in the lawful manner of Christ, nor could she be persuaded, though the nobles tried hard, to return to the faith of the Pope. Clearly Christ also wished at some time to carry the queen up into heaven." Cornelius Scepperus wrote this epitaph for her:

units.la: Dania me coluit, pulsam Germania vidit,
units.tr: Denmark cherished me; Germany saw me driven out,

units.la: Primum ortum dederat terra Brabantia prius.
units.tr: The land of Brabant had earlier given me my first birth.

units.la: Nulla harum potuit morientem cernere, sed quae
units.tr: None of these could see me dying, but the place

units.la: Gandavi habuit mente, nunc quoq; corpus habet.
units.tr: That held me in mind at Ghent now also holds my body.

units.la: In ANGLIA quadraginta minoris notae monasteria, Cardinale Volsaeo petente, & Papa Clemente annuente, hoc anno diruta, & reditus illorum duobus Collegiis à Cardinale nuper exstructis addicti sunt. Negotium hoc (ut nonnulli animadverterunt) tanquam aurum Tholosanum, omnibus qui illud attigissent, aut perniciem, aut saltem maximas calamitates attulisse creditur. Papa post biennium captus, & ludibrium orbis factus est. Volsaeus in turrim Londinensem jam jam condendus, non tam obiit quàm interiit, cum semetipsum detestatus esset, quod Regi potius quàm Deo studuisset placere. Ex ministris autem quinque, quorum opera hic usus est in tot piorum hominum donariis intervertendis, evenit postea, ut duobus duello decertantibus alter alterum occideret, & homicida suspendio plecteretur, tertius in puteum se dederit praecipitem, ac spontaneâ morte submersus periit: quartus homo opulentus ad eam egestatem devenerit, ut victum ostiatim emendicare ante obitum cogeretur, alius denique Doctor quidam Alanus, qui autoritate inter caeteros principe pollebat; quo tempore
units.tr: In England, forty monasteries of lesser note were this year demolished at the request of Cardinal Wolsey and with the assent of Pope Clement, and their revenues were assigned to two colleges recently founded by the Cardinal. This business (as some have observed) is believed, like the Toulouse gold, to have brought ruin, or at least very great calamities, upon all who had touched it. The Pope was taken captive two years later and made the mockery of the world. Wolsey, about to be shut up in the Tower of London, did not so much die as perish, since he had cursed himself for having sought to please the King rather than God. Of the five ministers whose work was used in dispersing the gifts of so many pious people, it later came about that two fought a duel and one killed the other, and the killer was hanged; a third threw himself headlong into a well and perished, drowned by a death he chose himself; a fourth, a wealthy man, was reduced to such poverty that before his death he was forced to beg his food from door to door; and finally another teacher, one Alan, who held the greatest authority among the rest, [...] at the time when

units.la: Archiepiscopus Dublinensis in Hibernia agebat, ab inimicis crudeliter confossus periit. Utinam his & similibus exemplis edocti, discant homines res semel Deo consecratas timide attrectare: Si istos iustitia divina tam severe puniit, qui bona Ecclesiæ dicata, sed parum sancte administrata, ad usus haud dubie meliores converterunt, hoc tamen non spectates, sed pravis ducti cupiditatibus; quid illis putabimus imminere, qui res Ecclesiasticas, quâcunq; data occasione sine delectu diripiunt & expilant, semet tantùm locupletandi gratiâ?
units.tr: the Archbishop of Dublin was ruling in Ireland, was cruelly stabbed to death by his enemies. Would that, taught by these and similar examples, men might learn to handle timidly things once consecrated to God. If divine justice punished so severely those who, not looking to this but led by wicked desires, turned the goods of the Church, dedicated but poorly administered, to uses that were doubtless better; what, then, shall we think awaits those who, whenever an occasion is given, tear apart and plunder the ecclesiastical property without discrimination, for the sole purpose of enriching themselves?

units.la: Finio heic primam Annalium Evangelii renovati Decadem, beati Melanchthonis votum tetrasticho inclusum repetens: Te maneat semper servante Ecclesia Christe, Insertosq; ipsi nos tua dextra tegat. Tres velut in flamma testes Babylonide servas, Rex ubi præsentem Te videt esse Deum.
units.tr: Here I end the first decade of the Annals of the renewed Gospel, repeating the wish of the blessed Melanchthon, enclosed in a tetrastich: "May the Church, Christ, always keep you safe, and may your right hand cover us who are grafted into you. As in the flame of Babylon you preserved three witnesses, where the King sees you present as God."

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END.
